Part 0 — How to Understand Any Technology

  • 1 h 20 min read
  • 7 sections
  • 8 diagrams
  • 15 code examples

What you will learn

  1. 0.1Why a method beats memorising tools
  2. 0.2The ten questions to ask of any technology
  3. 0.3The method applied three times
  4. 0.4Reading: docs, specs, codebases, errors, and asking for help
  5. 0.5The layers under every technology
  6. 0.6Switching languages
  7. 0.7A learning loop that lasts a career

This is the first page of the book, and it is not about any one tool. It is about how to learn tools. Everything after this Part teaches a specific technology (JavaScript, HTTP, Git, NestJS, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, Kubernetes) using the same small set of questions: why does it exist, what is the mental model, how does it work inside, how does it fail, what does it trade away. This Part names that method, gives it to you as a checklist you can carry to any technology the book does not cover, and then digs one layer down, to the computer and the language underneath every tool you will ever use.

If you are a complete beginner, read this Part first and do not worry if some examples mention tools you have not met yet. They are here to show the method moving from tool to tool, and every one of them is taught properly later. If you are already senior, read 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 closely: the checklist, the reading habits and the language-switching map are the parts experienced engineers most often do implicitly and badly.

0.1 Why a method beats memorising tools

Concept

A technology in this book means any piece of software you build on: a language, a framework, a database, a message broker, a cloud service, a library. A method is a fixed set of questions you ask of every new technology, in the same order, until you can explain it, predict how it behaves under load and failure, and decide whether to use it.

Tools change every few years. The problems they solve barely change at all. A caching layer in 2005 (memcached), 2015 (Redis) and 2025 (Redis, Valkey, a CDN, an in-process LRU) solves the same problem: reading slow data quickly by keeping a copy closer to the reader, and paying for it with staleness. If you understand caching, each new cache is a weekend. If you memorised memcached commands, each new cache is a fresh start.

Why does it exist?

Because the tool list is endless and your time is not. A backend engineer meets a new library every week and a new "everyone is moving to X" every quarter. Engineers who chase them all know many tools shallowly: they can follow the getting-started guide but cannot predict what happens when the tool is full, slow, partitioned or upgraded, which is exactly when it matters.

The ideas underneath repeat. Here are the ones you will meet again and again in this book, in tool after tool:

Idea What it means in one line Where you meet it
Caching Keep a copy closer to the reader; accept that it can be stale CPU caches, browser cache, CDN, Redis, PostgreSQL shared buffers, React Query
Queues Put work in a line so producer and consumer can run at different speeds Event loop task queue, RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka, BullMQ, OS run queue
Indexes A second, sorted structure that makes finding things fast and writing things slower PostgreSQL B-tree, Elasticsearch inverted index, a Map in your code
Retries Try again after a failure, which can duplicate the work HTTP clients, Kafka producers, job queues, TCP itself
Consistency Who sees which version of the data, and when Database transactions, replicas, caches, distributed systems
Logs An append-only record you can replay PostgreSQL WAL, Kafka topics, Git history, event sourcing
Backpressure A slow consumer pushes back on a fast producer instead of drowning Node streams, TCP windows, Kafka consumer lag, connection pools

Learn the column on the left once and the column on the right becomes a set of variations.

Mental model

Imagine learning to drive. You learn one car properly: steering, braking distance, mirrors, what a skid feels like. Then you rent a different car abroad. The wipers are on the wrong stalk and the handbrake is a button, and for ten minutes you fumble. But you never have to relearn braking distance, because physics did not change. Tools are the stalks and buttons. Ideas are the physics. A method is the habit of asking "where are the wipers, where is the handbrake, how does it brake" in the first five minutes of every rental.

How it works

The method has three steps, and the rest of this Part fills them in.

  1. Ask the ten questions (0.2).
  2. Read the primary sources the right way (0.4): docs, specs, the code, the error messages.
  3. Build a small thing and break it on purpose (question 10, and 0.7). Reading tells you what the authors claim; an experiment tells you what is true.

Underneath all three sits the layer every technology shares (0.5). When a tool surprises you, the explanation is usually down there.

Practical example

Your team lead says: "We are adding a search box to the product catalogue. Look at Meilisearch." You have never heard of it. Without a method, you open the quickstart, copy the Docker command, index ten products and report back "it works and it is fast". With the method, you spend the same afternoon and come back with:

  • It solves full-text search with typo tolerance; before it, you would use PostgreSQL full-text search or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (see Part 37 — Search: PostgreSQL Full-Text to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch).
  • Its core abstraction is an index of JSON documents, separate from your database, so you now have two copies of every product and a sync problem.
  • Indexing is asynchronous: you submit a task and it completes later, so a product saved at 10:00:00 might not be searchable until a moment after. You must decide whether that is acceptable.
  • You checked how it stores data on disk, what happens if the container is killed mid-index, and what the upgrade path looks like between major versions.
  • The alternative for your 40,000 products is probably PostgreSQL full-text search with a GIN index, which needs no new server.

Same afternoon. Completely different quality of answer. That is the whole argument for a method.

Production scenario

A 30-engineer company running PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ and a NestJS monolith requires every new-technology proposal to answer the ten questions on one page (Part 88 — Writing as an Architect: RFCs, Design Docs and Decision Records covers the document). Of six proposals in two years, four die at question 9 ("PostgreSQL already does this well enough at our size"). The two adopted arrive with a runbook, because questions 6 and 8 forced someone to write down failure and operations before the first incident.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior is not someone who knows more tools. A senior is someone who, given a tool they have never seen, can within a day say what it is for, what it will cost to run, how it will break and whether it is worth it. They also hold a strong default: every new technology is a liability until proven otherwise. It is one more thing to monitor, upgrade, secure, back up, hire for and debug at 03:00. The question is never "is this tool good?" It is "is this tool better enough than what we already run to pay that cost for years?"

When a product manager asks why the team does not adopt the shiny thing, the senior's answer is plain: "It solves a problem we do not have yet, and it brings three problems we would have on day one."

Common mistakes

  • Learning the API before the problem. You can call the functions but you cannot say when you would not call them.
  • Trusting the benchmark on the homepage. It measures the vendor's best case, not your workload.
  • Equating "I ran the quickstart" with "I understand it". The quickstart is designed never to fail. Production is not.
  • Ignoring the boring alternative. The database you already run, used well, beats the new database used badly.

Interview questions

  1. You are asked to evaluate a technology you have never used. Walk me through your first day.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: name the problem and what came before; find the core abstraction and data model; trace one operation end to end; find where state lives and how it survives a crash; check scaling limits, failure modes, operational cost; list the simpler alternative; run a small experiment that tries to break it. Why it matters: it shows whether the candidate evaluates or just follows tutorials. Follow-up: what would make you say no?
  2. Name three ideas that appear in many different tools.
    Show answerHide answer
    Caching, queues, indexes, retries, logs, consistency. A strong answer gives two concrete tools for each and the shared tradeoff (a cache trades freshness for speed everywhere).
  3. Why might a team reject a tool that is genuinely excellent?
    Show answerHide answer
    Because operating cost, team skills, and overlap with existing systems can outweigh the benefit. Follow-up: how would you write that up so the proposer does not feel dismissed?

Practical exercise

Pick a technology you use every day but have never questioned: your HTTP client library, your logging library, or npm itself. Write one paragraph for each of these three questions: what problem does it solve and what did people do before; where does its state live; what happens when it fails. Acceptance criteria: each paragraph names at least one concrete fact you had to look up rather than already knew, and the third paragraph describes a failure you could reproduce on your laptop.

0.2 The ten questions to ask of any technology

0.2.1 The checklist

Here is the method itself. Print it, pin it, paste it into the template your team uses for design documents. The questions are ordered so that each one builds on the last: you cannot reason about scaling (5) until you know where state lives (4), and you cannot say when not to use something (9) until you know what it trades away (7).

# Question What you are really looking for A weak answer sounds like A strong answer sounds like
1 What problem does it solve, and what came before it? The pain that made someone build it, and the older tool it replaced "It is fast and modern" "Before it, teams polled the database every second for new orders; this pushes changes instead"
2 What is its core abstraction or data model? The one or two nouns everything else is built from A list of features "Everything is an append-only, partitioned log of records with offsets"
3 How does one request or operation flow through it? The step-by-step path of a single read or write "You call the API and it returns" "Client, connection, parse, plan, execute, buffer cache, WAL, fsync, reply"
4 Where does state live, and how does it survive a crash? Memory vs disk, replication, what is lost on kill -9 "It is persistent" "Written to the WAL and fsynced before commit returns; a crash replays the WAL"
5 How does it scale, and what is the bottleneck? The resource that runs out first and the unit of parallelism "It scales horizontally" "Throughput scales with partitions; one partition is read by one consumer in a group"
6 How does it fail, and what does failure look like from outside? Error messages, timeouts, silent data loss, duplicate delivery "It is highly available" "On leader failover, producers see errors for a few seconds and retry, which can duplicate"
7 What does it trade away? The cost of its main benefit "Nothing, it is just better" "It gives up per-message acknowledgement and arbitrary routing to get throughput and replay"
8 How is it operated? Config, monitoring, backups, upgrades, the knobs that matter "We will use the defaults" "Watch consumer lag and disk; major upgrades need a rolling restart in a set order"
9 When should I NOT use it, and what are the alternatives? The boundary of its usefulness and the cheaper option "It works for everything" "Under 1,000 messages a second with no replay need, a PostgreSQL table or SQS is simpler"
10 How can I prove it to myself in 30 minutes? A small experiment that confirms one claim and one failure "I read the docs" "I killed the consumer mid-batch and watched the same messages arrive again"

Three notes. The weak answers are marketing: "fast", "scalable", "highly available" and "persistent" carry no information until you attach a number, a mechanism or a condition. Questions 4, 6 and 7 are the ones beginners skip and seniors start with: state, failure and trade-offs decide whether a tool hurts you in production; features decide whether a demo looks good. Short answers are fine: for a small library, question 4 may be "no state". The point is to have asked.

0.2.2 Where to find the answers

Each question has a usual hiding place. Questions 1 and 2 live in the project's "why" page, its announcement post and its "concepts" or "architecture" page, which is rarely the first page of the docs. Question 3 lives in the architecture page and in talks by the authors; draw it as boxes and arrows, because every later question is answered by pointing at a box. Questions 4 to 8 live in the "limits", "production checklist", "operations" and "known issues" pages, and in other teams' postmortems. Question 9 lives in comparisons written by people who chose something else (Part 68 — Architecture Decision Framework has worked decision tables). Question 10 lives only on your own laptop. Throughout, apply the senior mantra: Can it time out? Can it fail? Can it become slow? Can it duplicate? Can it return a wrong response? Can it partially succeed?

0.2.3 An incident: the cart store nobody questioned

At 19:40 on the first evening of a sale, the support channel of a mid-sized online shop started filling with the same complaint: "My cart is empty." Customers had added items, browsed for a few minutes, come back, and found nothing. Conversion dropped by a third in an hour.

Six months earlier, a developer had moved shopping carts out of PostgreSQL and into Redis. The reasoning was sound as far as it went: carts are read on every page view, Redis answers in well under a millisecond, and the cart table had become a noticeable share of database load. The change was reviewed for correctness (keys, expiry of 30 days, JSON serialisation) and shipped. Nobody asked the ten questions.

The investigation took twenty minutes once someone looked at Redis itself. The INFO memory output showed the instance at its memory limit, and the evicted_keys counter was climbing by thousands per minute. The Redis cluster had been created by copying the configuration of the team's existing caching cluster, which used maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru: when memory is full, evict the least recently used key, any key. For a cache, that is exactly right; a missing cache entry is just a slower read. For carts, it meant that during the sale, as product-page caches flooded in, Redis quietly deleted the carts of anyone who had not touched theirs in the last few minutes. No error. No log line in the application. The cart simply was not there.

Here is how the ten questions would have caught it before the sale:

Question The answer nobody wrote down
4. Where does state live, and how does it survive a crash? In memory. Persistence depends on RDB snapshots or the AOF being enabled; the copied config had snapshots every 15 minutes, so a crash would also lose up to 15 minutes of carts
5. What is the bottleneck? Memory. Carts shared one instance with caches whose volume spikes during a sale
6. What does failure look like from outside? Under allkeys-lru, a full instance silently deletes keys. The application sees "cart not found", which looks like a new visitor
7. What does it trade away? Durability and capacity for speed. Acceptable for a cache; not automatically acceptable for user data
8. How is it operated? maxmemory-policy, evicted_keys, used_memory, and persistence settings are the knobs that matter, and none were on a dashboard

The fix had three parts. Carts moved to a separate Redis instance with maxmemory-policy noeviction, so a full instance returns an error on write (loud) instead of deleting data (silent), and with AOF persistence enabled. An alert on evicted_keys > 0 was added for that instance. And the team added a rule to their design-review template: any proposal that stores user data in a new system answers questions 4, 6 and 7 in writing. The deeper lesson in the postmortem was one line: the tool did exactly what it was configured to do; we never asked what that was. Part 30 — Caching and Redis covers eviction policies and persistence in depth.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The questions get answered once and never again. A tool's defaults and failure behaviour change between major versions. Re-ask questions 4, 6 and 8 at every major upgrade.
  • Copied configuration carries the original system's trade-offs with it, as in the cart incident.
  • "Managed" read as "no failure modes". A managed service still fails, throttles and has limits; you just cannot fix it yourself.
  • The proof skipped because "the docs are clear". Docs describe intent; question 10 catches the gap between intent and behaviour.

Interview questions

  1. Apply the ten questions to Redis in two minutes.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: an in-memory server of keys to typed values; one thread executes commands in order; state in memory, optionally persisted by RDB or AOF; bottlenecks are memory and that thread; fails by evicting, losing recent writes on crash, or stalling on slow commands like KEYS *; trades durability for speed; never the only copy of important data unless persistence is understood. Follow-up: which eviction policy would you choose for a session store, and why?
  2. Which of the ten questions do you think teams skip most often, and what does it cost?
    Show answerHide answer
    Strong answers pick 4, 6 or 8 and give a story.
  3. What is a "silent failure", and why is it worse than a crash?
    Show answerHide answer
    A failure that produces no error and no alert, such as an evicted key or a dropped message. Crashes get fixed in minutes; silent failures are discovered by customers weeks later.

Practical exercise

Run Redis in Docker with --maxmemory 5mb --maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru. Write a short TypeScript script that stores 1,000 "cart" keys, then writes 50,000 "cache" keys of 1 KB each, then counts how many carts survive. Repeat with noeviction and observe what your script sees instead. Acceptance criteria: you report the number of surviving carts under allkeys-lru, the exact error message your Redis client throws under noeviction, and one sentence on which behaviour you would want for user data and why.

0.3 The method applied three times

A method is only worth something if it transfers. Here are the ten questions applied to three very different technologies: a database (PostgreSQL), a distributed log (Kafka) and a user-interface library (React). Each answer is a page you could write after one focused day, and each points to the Part that goes deep.

0.3.1 PostgreSQL

# Question Short answer
1 Problem and history Many users must change shared data at once without corruption, and survive crashes. Before: hand-rolled file formats and hierarchical databases navigated record by record. Codd's relational model (1970) separated what you want from how to fetch it.
2 Core abstraction Tables of rows with typed columns, queried with SQL, changed inside transactions that are atomic, consistent, isolated and durable (ACID).
3 One operation SQL arrives on a connection served by its own backend process; it is parsed, planned (the planner picks indexes and join order by estimated cost) and executed against pages in shared buffers. On COMMIT, the change is written to the write-ahead log (WAL) and flushed to disk before success returns.
4 State and crashes Table and index files on disk, cached in shared buffers. After a crash, PostgreSQL replays the WAL: committed transactions survive, uncommitted ones vanish.
5 Scaling and bottleneck Scales up on one machine; reads scale out with replicas; writes go to one primary. A common first bottleneck is connections: each is a process using several megabytes, hence poolers like PgBouncer.
6 Failure from outside FATAL: sorry, too many clients already when connections run out; queries that hang waiting for a lock; slow queries after a plan changes; ERROR: could not extend file when the disk fills; stale reads from a lagging replica.
7 Trade-off Strong consistency and rich queries, in exchange for limited horizontal write scaling. MVCC (old row versions for concurrent readers) trades disk and VACUUM work for readers never blocking writers.
8 Operations Tested restores, autovacuum, pg_stat_activity, pg_stat_statements, replication lag, connections, disk growth, major upgrades via pg_upgrade or logical replication.
9 When not Analytical scans over billions of rows (use a columnar warehouse); writes beyond one machine; extreme-rate key lookups (put an in-memory store in front); relevance-ranked fuzzy search at scale (a search engine). For most product backends, it is the right default.
10 30-minute proof Below.

The experiment checks one claim (an index turns a scan into a lookup) and one failure (a forgotten transaction holds a lock and blocks everyone).

Shell
docker run --name pg-lab -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=lab -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:16
docker exec -it pg-lab psql -U postgres
SQL
-- One million fake users, generated inside the database.
CREATE TABLE users (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO users (email) SELECT 'user' || g || '@example.com' FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) g;
ANALYZE users;

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user777777@example.com';
-- Expect: Seq Scan on users ... Execution Time: roughly 40-100 ms

CREATE INDEX users_email_idx ON users (email);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'user777777@example.com';
-- Expect: Index Scan using users_email_idx ... Execution Time: well under 1 ms

-- Failure: in this session, start a transaction and do not finish it.
BEGIN;
UPDATE users SET email = 'locked@example.com' WHERE id = 1;
-- Now open a second psql session and run:
--   UPDATE users SET email = 'other@example.com' WHERE id = 1;
-- It hangs. Back here, run COMMIT and watch the other session finish.

The second half is the important half. You have just reproduced, in one minute, the "idle in transaction" problem that takes down real APIs when application code opens a transaction and then awaits a slow HTTP call inside it. Deep dives: Part 20 — Databases and the Relational Model, Part 22 — PostgreSQL Internals, Part 23 — Database Indexing, Part 24 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control.

0.3.2 Kafka

# Question Short answer
1 Problem and history Many systems need the same high-volume stream of events, and some must re-read history. Before: point-to-point pipelines between every pair of systems, or queues that delete a message once consumed. Built at LinkedIn around 2010.
2 Core abstraction A topic is a named, append-only log, split into partitions. Each record in a partition has an increasing offset. Consumers in a consumer group share the partitions and remember how far they have read by committing offsets.
3 One operation The producer hashes the record key to pick a partition (same key, same partition) and sends to that partition's leader broker, which appends and replicates to followers; with acks=all, success means the in-sync replicas have it. A consumer polls from its last offset, processes, then commits the new offset.
4 State and crashes Segment files on broker disks, replicated, kept for a retention period (say seven days) whether read or not. Consumer offsets live in an internal topic; a crashed consumer resumes from its last commit.
5 Scaling and bottleneck The partition is the unit of parallelism: in one group, each partition has at most one consumer, so ten partitions allow at most ten parallel consumers. Brokers are fast; the usual bottleneck is consumer processing, visible as consumer lag.
6 Failure from outside Ever-growing lag; rebalances (partitions reassigned when a consumer joins, leaves or polls too slowly) that pause consumption; duplicates after a crash between processing and committing; one bad record retried forever, stalling its partition.
7 Trade-off High throughput, durable replayable history and many independent readers, in exchange for ordering only within a partition, no built-in per-message dead-letter queue, no arbitrary routing, and real operational complexity.
8 Operations Partitions and replication factor per topic, retention, disk, under-replicated partitions, lag per group, rolling upgrades. Recent versions run in KRaft mode without ZooKeeper. Managed offerings remove much of this.
9 When not A few hundred jobs a minute with no replay need: BullMQ, SQS, RabbitMQ or a PostgreSQL table with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Request/response: HTTP or gRPC. Per-message delayed retries and priorities: RabbitMQ or SQS.
10 30-minute proof Below.
Shell
docker run -d --name kafka-lab -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:3.8.0
docker exec -it kafka-lab /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --create --topic orders --partitions 3
# Terminal 1: a consumer in group "billing"
docker exec -it kafka-lab /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders --group billing
# Terminal 2: produce keyed records, typed as key:value
docker exec -it kafka-lab /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders --property parse.key=true --property key.separator=:
# Terminal 3: inspect the group's partitions, offsets and lag
docker exec -it kafka-lab /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --describe --group billing

Try: a second consumer in the same group (partitions split between them); a fourth consumer with three partitions (one sits idle); stop all consumers, produce 20 records and read the lag; a consumer in a new group with --from-beginning reads history the first group already consumed, which a classic queue cannot do. Deep dive: Part 31 — Messaging: Queues, Topics, Kafka, RabbitMQ and SQS, especially 31.3 and 31.3.8 "When Kafka is overkill".

0.3.3 React

# Question Short answer
1 Problem and history Hand-written DOM updates (find this element, change its text) drifted out of sync with data as pages became applications. Before React (2013): jQuery patching the DOM, or two-way binding that was hard to trace.
2 Core abstraction A component: a function of its inputs (props) and its own state that returns a description of the UI. "UI is a function of state": you change state; React works out the DOM edits.
3 One operation Click, handler calls a state setter, React re-runs the component functions, reconciles the new description against the old, commits only the differences to the DOM, the browser paints.
4 State and crashes In the memory of one browser tab. A refresh wipes it unless you saved it to the URL, localStorage or the server. An uncaught error during rendering unmounts the whole component tree (a blank page) unless an error boundary catches it.
5 Scaling and bottleneck Re-rendering: a state change high in a large tree re-renders everything below. Long lists and expensive renders per keystroke are classic; fixes are moving state down, memoisation, virtualisation. Bundle size limits first load on phones.
6 Failure from outside A white screen; a page that freezes while typing; an effect that fetches in a loop and hammers your API with requests; stale data shown after an update; a double-submitted form that creates two orders.
7 Trade-off A predictable model and a vast ecosystem, in exchange for shipping a runtime library to every browser, an abstraction between you and the DOM, and a build toolchain.
8 Operations Build and bundle, static files on a CDN, browser error monitoring, bundle-size budgets, ecosystem upgrades.
9 When not Mostly static content is better as server-rendered HTML; one small widget may not justify a framework; many apps should adopt a React-based server-rendering framework such as Next.js instead.
10 30-minute proof npm create vite@latest order-lab -- --template react-ts; log in three nested components, click a counter in the parent and watch which children re-render. Then add an effect with no dependency array that fetches and sets state, and watch the Network tab fill.

React row 6, "an effect that fetches in a loop", is a backend problem too: it arrives at your API as thousands of identical requests per minute from one user. Part 7 — Your First Frontend introduces the browser side from scratch; Part 77 — React Fundamentals for Backend Engineers goes deep, including 77.4 "Effects: useEffect done right" and 77.8 "Double-submit protection and idempotency from the form".

0.3.4 What transferred

The three tools share nothing at the surface, yet the same questions found the same kinds of truth. Question 3 exposed each internal pipeline, and the word "commit" appeared in all three, meaning "the point after which this change is real". Question 4 found what decides durability (the WAL, the replicated log, the tab's memory). Question 6 found the incident you will one day be paged for (a held lock, growing lag, a fetch loop). Question 9 found the simpler alternative every time.

How deep you go depends on how much the technology can hurt you. A decision table for that:

You are evaluating... Holds important state? Questions you must answer in writing Depth of experiment
A small utility library (date formatting, a CSV parser) No 1, 2, 7, 9 Run its examples against your real edge cases (time zones, a malformed row)
A framework you will build on (NestJS, React, Spring) No, but hard to remove later 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9 Build one realistic feature end to end
A datastore, broker or cache Yes All ten Load it, kill it mid-write, restore it from backup
A managed cloud service Yes, and you cannot see inside All ten, with extra care on 6 and 8 (limits, quotas, throttling, regional outages) Hit its documented limits on purpose in a test account
A tool for your laptop only (an editor plugin, a CLI) No 1, 9 Use it for a week

0.4 Reading: docs, specs, codebases, errors, and asking for help

Most of an engineer's learning is reading, and technical reading is a skill: out of order, with a question in mind, stopping once it is answered.

0.4.1 How to read documentation

Concept

Good documentation usually comes in four kinds, and knowing which kind you are reading saves hours. A widely used way to name them (the Diátaxis framework) is: tutorials (a guided lesson for a beginner), how-to guides (steps for one specific task), reference (every option, parameter and return value, dry and complete) and explanation (concepts, architecture, design reasons).

How it works

  1. Start with explanation, not the tutorial. Look for pages titled "Concepts", "Architecture", "How it works", "Design" or "Internals". They answer questions 1 to 4. The tutorial only shows the happy path.
  2. Do the tutorial once, fast, then use reference with a question in hand. Never read reference front to back. Look up the default timeout, the meaning of a status, the exact return type.
  3. Read the limits and FAQ pages. "Limits", "Quotas", "Known issues", "Caveats", "Production checklist" and "Operations" pages are where the authors admit the trade-offs. They answer questions 6 to 9 better than anything else.
  4. Read the changelog for the last two major versions. It tells you what used to be broken, which default changed, and which blog posts you find online are now wrong.
  5. Check the version. Docs sites default to the latest version; your production may run an older one.

0.4.2 How to read a specification or an RFC

A specification defines exactly how something must behave so that independent implementations agree: the ECMAScript spec for JavaScript, the SQL standard, the OpenAPI specification. An RFC ("Request for Comments") from the IETF is the form internet protocols are published in: HTTP semantics is RFC 9110, TCP is RFC 9293, JSON is RFC 8259, UTF-8 is RFC 3629.

You read specs when two systems disagree and you need to know who is right: "May a DELETE have a body?", "Is a PUT retry safe?". A method that works:

  1. Find the terminology section first. RFCs define their words precisely, and RFC 2119 fixes the meaning of MUST, SHOULD and MAY in capitals. "MUST" is a requirement; "SHOULD" means "do this unless you have a good reason"; "MAY" is optional. Many real interoperability bugs come from an implementation treating a SHOULD as a MUST or the other way round.
  2. Jump to your question with the table of contents, and read the examples there.
  3. Check whether it is obsoleted. Every RFC header says "Obsoletes" and the IETF data tracker says "Obsoleted by". HTTP/1.1 was RFC 2616, then RFCs 7230 to 7235, and now RFC 9110 to 9112. A blog post quoting RFC 2616 is quoting a dead document.

For example, RFC 8259 says object member names "SHOULD be unique", not "MUST". That single word explains why different JSON parsers handle {"amount": 100, "amount": 1} differently (most keep the last value, but you cannot rely on it), and why a payment API that forwards raw JSON between two services written in different languages can be tricked by duplicate keys: one service validates the first value, the other acts on the last. Parsing differences between systems are a classic source of security bugs; Part 44 — Security (44.27 and 44.29) covers the wider family.

0.4.3 How to read an unfamiliar codebase

Joining a team means inheriting tens of thousands of lines you did not write. Nobody reads them top to bottom. Here is a reliable order:

  1. Read the README, the package.json (or pom.xml, go.mod, pyproject.toml) and the CI file. Together they tell you the language version, the dependencies, how to build, how to test and how it deploys. The dependency list alone tells you the architecture: a codebase with @nestjs/typeorm, ioredis and kafkajs has already told you its shape.
  2. Find the entry points. For a NestJS app: main.ts, then app.module.ts, then the modules it imports. For a worker: the file that starts consuming. Entry points are the roots of the tree.
  3. Trace one real request end to end. Pick an important endpoint (POST /orders) and follow it: controller, service, repository, database, any events published. This is question 3 of the method, applied to code. Write the path down.
  4. Run it and break it. Start the app locally, call the endpoint, put a breakpoint or a log in the service, change one line and watch a test fail. Running code teaches more in ten minutes than reading does in an hour.
  5. Read the tests: executable documentation of what the authors thought mattered.
  6. Use history and ask why. git log --follow and git blame (Part 5 — Git Basics and the Development Workflow, 5.8) usually lead to the commit that explains a strange line, which is often a fix for an incident you have not heard of.
Text
README / package.json / CI file
        ↓
main.ts → app.module.ts → orders.module.ts
        ↓
POST /orders: controller → service → repository → PostgreSQL
                                   ↘ publishes "order.created"
        ↓
tests for that path → git log / blame for the odd parts

0.4.4 How to read an error message and a stack trace

Concept

An error message is the system telling you, in one line, what went wrong. A stack trace is the list of function calls that were in progress when it went wrong, innermost first (in Node.js, Java and most languages) and outermost at the bottom. Python prints them the other way round, most recent call last. Beginners panic at a 40-line trace. Seniors read two lines of it.

How it works

Here is a real-shaped Node.js trace from a NestJS app:

Text
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
    at OrdersService.totalFor (/app/dist/orders/orders.service.js:41:32)
    at OrdersController.getTotal (/app/dist/orders/orders.controller.js:22:39)
    at /app/node_modules/@nestjs/core/router/router-execution-context.js:38:29
    at process.processTicksAndRejections (node:internal/process/task_queues:95:5)

Read it in this order:

  1. The first line: the type and the message. TypeError means a value was not the type the code assumed. "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')" means something was undefined and the code called .map on it. You now know the bug class before looking at any code.
  2. The first frame that is your code. OrdersService.totalFor, file orders.service.js, line 41, column 32. Frames inside node_modules and node:internal are almost never where the bug is; they are the framework calling you.
  3. Map back to source. The path says dist/...js, compiled output. With source maps enabled ("sourceMap": true in tsconfig.json and Node started with --enable-source-maps), the trace points to the .ts file instead.
  4. Ask what was undefined and why. Line 41 is probably order.items.map(...). So order.items was undefined. Was the relation not loaded? Did the API return a different shape? That is the real question, and the trace has walked you straight to it.

Database and network errors have their own reliable shapes. Learn to read the parts:

Text
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_idempotency_key_key"
DETAIL:  Key (idempotency_key)=(a1b2c3) already exists.

PostgreSQL names the constraint, column and value, and every error carries a five-character SQLSTATE code (23505 for unique violation) to switch on instead of message text. connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432 means nothing is listening there (wrong host or port, or the database is down); ETIMEDOUT means no answer came in time (firewall, network, overload). They send you to completely different places.

Common mistakes

  • Reading the last line of the trace (the framework's internals) instead of the first frame of your own code.
  • Fixing the symptom (order.items?.map(...)) without asking why the value was missing, which turns a loud bug into a silent one.
  • Throwing away the original error when re-throwing. In TypeScript, pass it as the cause: throw new Error('Failed to total order', { cause: err }).

0.4.5 How to ask a good question: the minimal reproduction

When you are stuck and ask a colleague, a forum or an AI assistant, the answer is capped by the question. The most powerful tool is the minimal reproduction: the smallest code and setup that still shows the problem. Building one is itself debugging: remove parts one at a time, checking the problem is still there. Often the removal that makes it disappear names the cause, and you never need to ask.

A good question contains:

  1. What you are trying to do, in one sentence, including the goal behind it (people often know a better way to reach the goal).
  2. What you expected and what happened instead, with the exact error message and stack trace pasted as text, not a screenshot.
  3. The minimal reproduction: code that someone can paste and run.
  4. Versions: language runtime, framework, database, operating system.
  5. What you already tried, so nobody suggests it again.
TypeScript
// A minimal reproduction for "my timeout never fires".
// Node 20, no framework, no database: only the parts that show the bug.
async function slowProvider(): Promise<string> {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 5_000)); // pretends to be a slow API
  return 'charged';
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const timeout = new Promise<never>((_, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timed out after 1000 ms')), 1_000),
  );
  try {
    console.log(await Promise.race([slowProvider(), timeout]));
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('caught:', (err as Error).message); // prints after 1 s, as expected
  }
  // Observed: the process stays alive about 4 s more after the error is printed, until the 5 s mark.
  // Question: why does Node not exit, and does the slow call keep running?
}

void main();

That reproduction is 20 lines, runs anywhere, and already contains its own answer for anyone who knows the event loop: Promise.race does not cancel the losing promise, so the five-second timer keeps the process alive and the "slow call" keeps running. Part 2 — Asynchronous JavaScript (2.5) covers why, and how AbortSignal fixes it.

Interview questions

  1. You join a team with a 200,000-line codebase. What do you do in your first week?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: run it locally, read the dependency file, CI and entry points, trace one or two critical requests end to end, read their tests, use git log and blame on confusing parts, ask people why before judging. Follow-up: how do you know when you understand enough to make your first change?
  2. What is the difference between ECONNREFUSED and ETIMEDOUT, and why does it matter during an incident?
    Show answerHide answer
    Refused means the remote host actively rejected the connection because nothing listens there; timed out means no answer came. One points to a stopped process or wrong address; the other to network, firewall or overload.
  3. Why switch on a PostgreSQL SQLSTATE code instead of the error message?
    Show answerHide answer
    Codes are stable and documented; message text can change between versions and locales.

Practical exercise

Take a real error you hit in the last month (or create one: call a NestJS endpoint that reads a relation you did not load). Write it up as a question following 0.4.5: goal, expected versus actual, the exact trace, a minimal reproduction under 30 lines, versions, and what you tried. Acceptance criteria: a colleague can paste your reproduction into an empty folder, run it with one command, and see the same error.

0.5 The layers under every technology

Every tool in this book runs on the same few layers: a CPU, a hierarchy of memories, bits that encode numbers and text, an operating system that hands out processes, files and sockets, and a network. When a technology surprises you (a query 100 times slower than expected, a total off by a cent, a username that breaks the database, a service out of "files"), the explanation is almost always down here. Each layer below comes at beginner depth, with real numbers and a pointer to the Part that goes deeper.

0.5.1 The CPU and the memory hierarchy

Concept

The CPU (central processing unit) is the chip that executes your program's instructions, one simple step at a time: load a number, add two numbers, compare, jump. A modern server CPU core runs at around 3 billion cycles per second (3 GHz), so one cycle is about a third of a nanosecond. A typical server has between a handful and a hundred or more cores, each able to run one instruction stream at a time.

The CPU is fast. Fetching data for it is slow. So computers keep data in a memory hierarchy: small, fast, expensive storage close to the CPU, and large, slow, cheap storage further away. Each level is a cache for the level below.

Why does it exist?

Because no memory can be huge, fast and cheap at once. The hierarchy is the compromise, and it works because programs reuse the same data soon (temporal locality) and use data stored next to what they just used (spatial locality).

Mental model

Imagine cooking. The knife in your hand is a register, the spices on the counter are L1, the fridge is RAM, the supermarket is the SSD, and a farm abroad reached by mail order is a server across the network. A good cook does not drive to the supermarket for each pinch of salt.

How it works

Here are the numbers. They are approximate and vary by hardware, but the ratios between them have stayed roughly stable for decades, and the ratios are what you should remember. The right-hand column rescales everything so that one L1 access takes one second.

Where the data is Typical size Approximate time to read If L1 took 1 second
CPU register Bytes Under 1 ns Instant
L1 cache (per core) 32 to 64 KB About 1 ns 1 second
L2 cache (per core) 0.5 to 2 MB About 3 to 5 ns 4 seconds
L3 cache (shared) Tens of MB About 10 to 20 ns 15 seconds
Main memory (RAM) Tens to hundreds of GB About 80 to 100 ns 1.5 minutes
Local NVMe SSD, random read Terabytes About 20 to 100 µs 6 hours to a day
Cloud network disk (block storage) Terabytes About 0.5 to 1 ms 6 to 12 days
Spinning hard disk, random seek Terabytes About 5 to 10 ms 2 to 4 months
Round trip inside one data centre About 0.2 to 0.5 ms 2 to 6 days
Round trip across a continent or ocean About 80 to 150 ms 2.5 to 5 years

Read the last column slowly. If reading from the CPU's cache takes a second, reading from RAM takes a minute and a half, reading from an SSD takes most of a day, and asking a server on another continent takes years. That one table explains most of performance engineering:

  • Why caches win. A Redis lookup in the same data centre (about 0.2 to 1 ms, mostly network) beats a PostgreSQL query that reads pages from disk (several ms); a value in your process's memory (about 100 ns) beats both by thousands of times. PostgreSQL keeps hot pages in RAM (shared buffers) for the same reason.
  • Why round trips dominate. 20 sequential queries at 1 ms each cost 20 ms of waiting even if each does no work. The N+1 query problem is a memory-hierarchy problem before it is an ORM problem.
  • Why data layout matters. An array's elements sit side by side, so one 64-byte cache line brings the next few along; a linked structure scattered across memory pays a RAM trip per element. Part 10 — Computer Science Fundamentals: Data Structures returns to this.

Production scenario

A product listing endpoint takes 180 ms at the 95th percentile. Tracing shows 3 ms in application code and the rest in 60 sequential queries to PostgreSQL, each around 2.5 ms including the network round trip, one per product to load its price. Rewriting it as one query with a join or WHERE id = ANY($1) drops it to 12 ms. No code got "faster"; the endpoint simply stopped paying for 59 round trips. Part 60 — Capacity Estimation and Back-of-the-Envelope Math (60.1) has the full table of numbers to carry in your head, and Part 46 — Performance Engineering shows how to find these costs.

Interview questions

  1. Roughly how long does a RAM access take compared with an SSD read and a cross-region network call?
    Show answerHide answer
    About 100 ns, about 20 to 100 µs, and about 80 to 150 ms: each step is roughly a thousand times slower. Why it matters: it tells you where to look first when something is slow.
  2. Why does iterating over an array beat iterating over a linked list of the same size, even though both are O(n)?
    Show answerHide answer
    Spatial locality: contiguous memory fills cache lines usefully and lets the CPU prefetch. Follow-up: where does the same idea appear in databases? Sequential scans versus random index lookups, and why clustered data reads faster.

0.5.2 Binary, integers and two's complement

Concept

Computers store everything as bits, each 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte, which can represent 2^8 = 256 different values. Numbers, text, images and your code are all patterns of bytes; what the bytes mean depends entirely on how the program interprets them. Programmers often write bytes in hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0 to 9 and A to F) because two hex digits are exactly one byte: 0xFF is 255, 0x2A is 42.

How it works

An unsigned integer uses all its bits for magnitude. An 8-bit unsigned integer runs from 0 (00000000) to 255 (11111111).

To store negative numbers, almost every computer uses two's complement. The top bit carries a negative weight: in 8 bits, the place values are -128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. So 11111111 is -128 + 127 = -1, and 10000000 is -128. To negate a number, flip every bit and add one: 5 is 00000101, flipped is 11111010, plus one is 11111011, which is -5. The beauty of the scheme is that the CPU's ordinary addition circuit works for negative numbers unchanged.

Width Signed range (two's complement) Where you meet it
16-bit -32,768 to 32,767 PostgreSQL smallint
32-bit -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647 (about 2.1 billion) PostgreSQL integer/serial, Java int, Go int32
64-bit About -9.2 to 9.2 quintillion PostgreSQL bigint, Java long, Go int64

When a calculation goes past the top of the range, it overflows. What happens next depends on the system, and this is exactly the kind of fact the ten questions should dig out:

  • Java and Go integers wrap around silently. Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 in Java is -2,147,483,648. A counter or a money total can turn negative with no error.
  • PostgreSQL refuses. Inserting past the range of an integer column raises ERROR: integer out of range. Right for data, but a table with an integer primary key stops accepting rows at about 2.1 billion; teams with a serial key on a busy events table have hit this as a full outage, fixed by a slow migration to bigint (see Part 20 — Databases and the Relational Model, 20.4.1).
  • JavaScript is different again. Every number is a 64-bit floating-point value (next section), which represents integers exactly only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER = 2^53 - 1 = 9,007,199,254,740,991. Past that, integers silently lose precision. And JavaScript's bitwise operators convert to 32-bit signed integers first, so (2 ** 31) | 0 is -2147483648.
TypeScript
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER);            // 9007199254740991
const big: number = 2 ** 53;                      // 9007199254740992
console.log(big + 1 === big);                     // true: 2^53 + 1 rounds back to 2^53
console.log(2n ** 63n - 1n);                     // 9223372036854775807n, a bigint, exact

// node-postgres returns PostgreSQL bigint (int8) columns as strings by default,
// precisely so that IDs above 2^53 are not silently corrupted.
const row = { id: '9007199254740993' };          // what the driver hands you
const id = BigInt(row.id);                        // exact; Number(row.id) would not be

Common mistakes

  • Using a 32-bit integer or serial primary key for a table that may one day hold billions of rows. Use bigint.
  • Converting a 64-bit database ID to a JavaScript number. Keep IDs as strings or bigint.
  • Assuming overflow throws an error in every language. In most it does not.

0.5.3 Floating point, and why money is stored in integer cents

Concept

A floating-point number stores a value as a sign, a fraction and an exponent, like scientific notation in binary: roughly 1.0101 x 2^5. The standard almost every language uses is IEEE 754. A 64-bit "double" (JavaScript's number, Java's double, Python's float, Go's float64) gives about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits and a huge range.

Why does it exist?

Science and graphics need very large and very small numbers (the mass of a planet, the width of an atom) with a fixed amount of relative precision, and need the arithmetic to be fast in hardware. Floating point delivers that. It was never designed for exact decimal quantities like money.

Mental model

Imagine writing one third as a decimal with eight digits: 0.33333333. Add three of them and you get 0.99999999, not 1. Decimal cannot represent one third exactly. Binary has the same problem with one tenth: 0.1 in binary is an infinitely repeating pattern, so the computer stores the nearest value it can, which is very slightly off.

How it works

TypeScript
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);          // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(1.15 * 100);         // 114.99999999999999, not 115
console.log(Math.round(1.15 * 100)); // 115: rounding hides the error, once

// Converting user input "19.99" to cents, done safely:
function toCents(amount: string): number {
  if (!/^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$/.test(amount)) throw new Error(`Invalid amount: ${amount}`);
  const [whole, fraction = ''] = amount.split('.');
  return Number(whole) * 100 + Number(fraction.padEnd(2, '0')); // pure integer arithmetic
}

console.log(toCents('19.99')); // 1999
console.log(toCents('1.15'));  // 115

The tiny errors are harmless in a physics simulation. In money they are not, because money must add up exactly and must match someone else's ledger. So backends represent money one of two ways:

  1. Integer minor units: store 1999 meaning 19.99 dollars or rupees, in an integer or bigint column. All arithmetic is exact integer arithmetic. Part 1 — Programming Fundamentals in JavaScript and TypeScript introduces this habit in 1.1.1.
  2. A decimal type: PostgreSQL numeric(12,2), Java BigDecimal, Python decimal.Decimal. These store base-10 digits exactly, at some cost in speed. Part 20 (20.4.2 "Money: numeric vs float") compares the two, and Part 67 — Backend Anti-Patterns and Why They Hurt (67.32) tells the story of getting it wrong.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Not every currency has two decimal places. Japanese yen has none and some dinars have three. Store the currency alongside the amount and know each currency's minor unit.
  • Division still needs a rounding rule. Splitting 1000 cents three ways gives 333, 333 and 334; decide who gets the extra cent, and write it down.
  • JSON has only one number type, and many parsers read it as a double. Large amounts or IDs sent as JSON numbers can be silently rounded; send them as strings (Part 80 — Frontend–Backend Contracts, 80.7).
  • NaN and Infinity are floating-point values too. 0 / 0 is NaN and 1 / 0 is Infinity in JavaScript, with no exception. Validate before you store.

Interview questions

  1. Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3?
    Show answerHide answer
    0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation; IEEE 754 stores the nearest values, and the rounding errors show in the sum. Follow-up: is this a JavaScript bug? No, every language using IEEE 754 doubles behaves the same.
  2. How would you store prices and order totals?
    Show answerHide answer
    Integer minor units or a decimal type, with the currency code; never a float. Follow-up: how do you split a total across three payments?

0.5.4 Text: bytes, characters, Unicode and UTF-8

Concept

Text looks simple and is not. A computer cannot store "a letter"; it stores bytes. An encoding is the rule that maps characters to bytes and back. Unicode is the universal catalogue that gives every character in every writing system a number called a code point, written like U+0041 (A), U+00E9 (é), U+0939 (the Devanagari letter ह) or U+1F600 (😀). UTF-8 is the encoding that turns those code points into bytes, and it is the encoding of the web, of JSON, and of almost every modern database and file.

Why does it exist?

ASCII used 7 bits for 128 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation. Other languages invented incompatible encodings, so a file from one country became garbage in another. Unicode gave everyone one catalogue; UTF-8 gave a byte format that is backwards compatible with ASCII and covers every code point.

Mental model

Imagine a library catalogue (Unicode) where every book has a unique number, and a shipping company (UTF-8) that packs each book into one, two, three or four boxes depending on its size. Short English books fit in one box. Most European and Indian-script books need two or three. Emoji need four. When someone asks "how big is this order?", you must say whether you are counting books or boxes.

How it works

UTF-8 uses 1 byte for code points up to U+007F (ASCII), 2 bytes up to U+07FF (most Latin accents, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic, Hebrew), 3 bytes up to U+FFFF (Devanagari, Chinese, Japanese, most other scripts) and 4 bytes beyond (emoji and rarer scripts).

There is one more layer that catches JavaScript developers. JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units, 16 bits each. Code points above U+FFFF, such as most emoji, need two code units (a "surrogate pair"). And .length counts code units, not characters. On top of that, what a human sees as one character (a grapheme) can be several code points: a letter plus a combining accent, or an emoji plus a skin-tone modifier.

TypeScript
const composed = 'é';          // é as one code point
const decomposed = 'é';       // e + combining acute accent: looks identical
console.log(composed.length, decomposed.length);   // 1 2
console.log(composed === decomposed);               // false
console.log(composed === decomposed.normalize('NFC')); // true: normalise before comparing

console.log('😀'.length);                    // 2: one code point, two UTF-16 code units
console.log([...'😀'].length);               // 1: spreading iterates by code point
console.log(Buffer.byteLength('é', 'utf8')); // 2 bytes
console.log(Buffer.byteLength('😀', 'utf8')); // 4 bytes

// Counting what a user sees as characters (graphemes):
const seg = new Intl.Segmenter('en', { granularity: 'grapheme' });
console.log([...seg.segment('👍🏽')].length, '👍🏽'.length); // 1 4

So 'é'.length is 1 or 2 depending on how the é was typed or pasted, and the two strings are not === equal even though they look identical. That one fact is behind duplicate usernames, failed logins and search misses.

Production scenario

Two real-shaped bugs, both from this one layer:

  • The emoji that broke sign-up. A service on MySQL used the column character set utf8, which in MySQL means at most 3 bytes per character. The first user to put an emoji in their display name got Incorrect string value and a 500 error. The fix was utf8mb4, MySQL's real 4-byte UTF-8. PostgreSQL databases created with UTF8 encoding do not have this trap, and PostgreSQL's varchar(n) counts characters, not bytes.
  • The SMS that cost double. An SMS segment holds 160 characters in the basic GSM alphabet but only 70 once any character outside it appears, because the message switches to a 16-bit encoding. One curly apostrophe pasted from a word processor into a template doubled the number of segments, and the bill, for a month of order-confirmation messages.

And a third you will meet on day one: mojibake, the garbage you see as cafÃ© instead of café. It means UTF-8 bytes were decoded as a different encoding (usually Latin-1 or Windows-1252). The bytes are fine; the label is wrong. Fix the label (a charset=utf-8 in the Content-Type header, the database connection's client encoding, the file reader's encoding argument), never the bytes.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Content-Length and most size limits (request body limits, Kafka message size, column byte limits) count bytes, not characters.
  • Validation like "name must be at most 50 characters" needs a definition of character: code units, code points or graphemes. Pick one deliberately.
  • Lookalike characters (Latin a and Cyrillic а) let attackers register usernames that look like someone else's.

0.5.5 The operating system: processes, files and sockets

The operating system (Linux, on almost every server you will deploy to) is the program that shares one machine among many programs. For a backend engineer, it provides three things you touch every day.

  • Processes. A process is one running program with its own private memory, an ID (PID), and one or more threads (independent streams of execution inside it that share its memory). Your NestJS app is one Node.js process; PostgreSQL runs one process per connection; a Go service is one process with many lightweight goroutines. The OS scheduler decides which thread runs on which core, switching between them many times per second.
  • Files and file descriptors. When a process opens a file, the OS hands it a small integer called a file descriptor. On Linux, the same mechanism is used for almost everything you read or write: files, pipes, and network connections. Each process has a limit on how many it may hold open (see ulimit -n), and hitting it produces EMFILE: too many open files, which in a busy API usually means a connection leak, not a file problem.
  • Sockets. A socket is one end of a network connection: an IP address and a port on each side. When your app "listens on port 3000", it asks the OS for a listening socket; each incoming client gets its own connected socket, and its own file descriptor. Your code never touches the network card; it reads and writes sockets through system calls (requests from a program to the OS kernel), and the kernel does the rest.
Text
Your NestJS process (PID 4182)
  ├── thread: main (the event loop runs your JavaScript)
  ├── threads: libuv pool (file I/O, DNS, crypto)
  ├── fd 0, 1, 2   stdin, stdout, stderr
  ├── fd 21        listening socket  0.0.0.0:3000
  ├── fd 22..41    client sockets    one per open HTTP connection
  └── fd 42..51    sockets to PostgreSQL (the connection pool)

That picture explains why a pool of 10 database connections means 10 sockets and why a connection leak ends as "too many open files". Part 4 — Linux and the Command Line teaches the commands to inspect all of this (4.3 and 4.10), and Part 13 — Operating Systems and the Node.js Runtime goes deep: processes and threads (13.1), memory (13.3, 13.4), file descriptors (13.5), signals and graceful shutdown (13.6) and the event loop (13.16).

0.5.6 The network in one picture

Every API call you make crosses a network, and every one pays for the same steps before your first byte of business data moves. Here is a first HTTPS request from a NestJS service to a payment provider, in one picture:

Count the round trips before the request leaves: DNS (often cached), the TCP handshake, one or two for TLS. At 100 ms per round trip, that is 200 to 300 ms of setup before the provider starts on your charge, which is why connection pooling and keep-alive matter and why the first request after a deploy is the slowest.

The layers stack like envelopes: your JSON goes inside an HTTP message, which is encrypted by TLS, carried as a reliable byte stream by TCP, split into packets addressed by IP, and sent over Ethernet or Wi-Fi. Each layer only talks to the layer directly above and below it. When something breaks, the error usually tells you the layer: ENOTFOUND is DNS, ECONNREFUSED and ETIMEDOUT are TCP, certificate has expired is TLS, and a 502 or 504 is HTTP from a proxy in the middle. Part 3 — How the Web Works builds this from scratch; Part 14 — Networking and HTTP goes deep, ending with 14.14 "What exactly happens when I call a NestJS API from a browser or Postman?".

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior uses a rough model of these layers to sanity-check claims. "This cache will make it faster": is the slow part memory, disk or network? "Another region adds a little latency": 100 ms per call, times how many calls? "We store the amount as a number": what happens at 2^31 or with 0.1? "Names can be 50 characters": bytes, code points or graphemes? No deep expertise needed, only the habit of looking one layer down.

Interview questions

  1. What does 'é'.length return in JavaScript, and why might it not be 1?
    Show answerHide answer
    It returns the count of UTF-16 code units: 1 for the composed form U+00E9, 2 for e plus a combining accent. Follow-up: how do you compare such strings safely? Normalise both to NFC first.
  2. How many bytes does an emoji take in UTF-8, and why does that matter for a backend?
    Show answerHide answer
    Usually 4. Size limits and some column types count bytes, and MySQL's legacy utf8 cannot store 4-byte characters at all.

Practical exercise

Write a TypeScript script that, for each of these strings, prints .length, the number of code points ([...s].length), the number of graphemes (Intl.Segmenter) and the UTF-8 byte length (Buffer.byteLength): "order", "café" typed both composed and decomposed, "नमस्ते", "😀", "👍🏽". Then write a truncatePreview(text, maxGraphemes) function for notification previews. Acceptance criteria: the table of counts is printed for all six strings, and truncatePreview never cuts an emoji or an accent in half (test it with a string whose limit falls inside "👍🏽").

0.6 Switching languages

0.6.1 Why one language deeply is enough to start

Concept

This book teaches backend engineering in TypeScript. Sooner or later you will need another language: a Go service your new team owns, a Java monolith, a Python pipeline. Mastering one language deeply is what lets you switch. Variables, functions, types, modules, errors, HTTP, SQL, testing and debugging are the same ideas everywhere; a new language changes the spelling and a handful of real design decisions.

Why does it exist?

Because engineers waste weeks learning a language the slow way: syntax first, idioms last, while the parts that bite in production (concurrency, who frees memory, what happens on an error, how it builds and tests) sit in chapter 12 of the tutorial. Apply the ten questions of 0.2 to a language and you get the six below.

Mental model

Imagine you drive well and move to a country that drives on the other side of the road. You do not take lessons again; you learn a short list (which side, roundabout priority, the signs) and drive carefully for a week. The checklist below is that list for languages.

0.6.2 The checklist for a new language

# Ask Why it matters in a backend TypeScript/Node.js answer, for reference
1 What is the concurrency model? Decides how one process serves many requests, and which bugs are possible One event loop runs your code on one thread; I/O is asynchronous; async/await on promises
2 How is memory managed? Decides whether you can leak, crash or corrupt memory, and how much you must think about it Garbage collected by V8
3 What is the type system? Decides which mistakes the compiler catches and which reach production Static types checked at compile time, structural, erased at runtime; JavaScript underneath coerces loosely
4 What is the error model? Decides how failures travel and how easy they are to ignore Exceptions (throw, try/catch), rejected promises
5 What are the build tool, package manager and test runner? You need all three on day one npm or pnpm, tsc, Jest or Vitest
6 What are the idioms and conventions? Code that works but ignores idioms gets rejected in review and is hard for the team to maintain ESLint and Prettier, camelCase, discriminated unions, async everywhere

The first two are the deep ones. The last four are a few days each.

0.6.3 Concurrency model

Concurrency means making progress on many tasks in overlapping time; parallelism means literally running several at the same instant on several cores. A backend's job is to serve many requests at once, so every language must answer: when request A is waiting for the database, what runs?

Model Languages How waiting is handled What you must watch for
Event loop with async/await JavaScript/TypeScript (Node.js), Python (asyncio) One thread runs your code; I/O is handed to the OS or a thread pool; await gives the thread to other work Any CPU-heavy or blocking call freezes every request on that process
Operating-system threads Java (classic Spring MVC), C#, C++, Python threads One thread per request blocks while waiting; the OS switches threads Shared memory between threads: race conditions, locks, deadlocks; each thread costs memory
Virtual threads Java 21 and later Code looks blocking, but the runtime parks a cheap virtual thread and reuses the OS thread Same shared-memory hazards; some blocking operations can still pin an OS thread
Goroutines and channels Go Code looks blocking; the Go runtime schedules millions of cheap goroutines onto a few OS threads Data races on shared variables, goroutine leaks, forgotten cancellation
Async/await on a thread pool C#, Rust (with a runtime such as Tokio) await frees the thread; continuations may resume on any pool thread, so code also runs in parallel Both async pitfalls and thread-safety rules apply

Python wrinkle: standard CPython has a Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), so only one thread runs Python code at a time; threads help with I/O waits, not CPU work, which needs multiple processes. Recent releases offer an optional GIL-free build, so check your version.

The most important consequence when moving from Node.js to Java, Go or C#: your code now really runs in parallel. In Node.js, two requests never execute JavaScript at the same instant, so this.counter++ on a shared object is safe (though async interleaving between awaits is not). In Java or Go, two threads can run counter++ at once and lose an update (++ is read, add, write), so you need a lock, an atomic, or no sharing. Part 13 — Operating Systems and the Node.js Runtime covers race conditions (13.8), deadlocks (13.9), mutexes (13.10) and atomic operations (13.12); read those before you write your first multi-threaded service. Part 35 — Concurrency in Node.js and NestJS covers the event-loop side.

0.6.4 Memory management: the one real learning curve

Every program allocates memory for its data, and that memory must eventually be given back. Languages split into two families by who gives it back.

Garbage-collected languages: JavaScript, Java, Go, Python, C#, Kotlin, Ruby. A garbage collector (GC) is part of the runtime that periodically finds objects nothing refers to any more and frees them. You allocate freely and never free anything by hand. Moving between these languages is easy because the model is the same. What you still have to know:

  • You can still leak, by keeping references you no longer need: a global Map used as a cache with no eviction, listeners never removed, closures holding large objects. Part 13 (13.13 and 13.25) covers how.
  • The GC costs CPU and can pause your program briefly, and heap limits are set differently in each runtime (--max-old-space-size for Node, -Xmx for the JVM, GOMEMLIMIT for Go).

Manual or ownership-based languages: C, C++, Rust. Here memory management is part of your job, and this is the only part of switching languages that is a genuine learning curve rather than a list of facts.

  • In C, you call malloc to allocate and free to release. Forget to free and you leak. Free twice, or use memory after freeing it, and the program can crash or, worse, keep running with corrupted data. Write past the end of a buffer and you have a classic security vulnerability.
  • C++ adds destructors and smart pointers (std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr) that free memory automatically when an owner goes out of scope (a pattern called RAII), which removes most manual frees but not the need to think about lifetimes.
  • Rust makes ownership part of the type system. Every value has one owner and is freed when the owner goes out of scope; other code may borrow a reference, and the compiler proves that no reference outlives the value and no two places mutate the same data at once. You get memory safety and no data races without a GC; the price is satisfying the "borrow checker". The first weeks feel like arguing with the compiler; that argument is the learning.

Why is this the real curve? In a GC language, "who owns this object and when does it die?" never needs an answer. In C, C++ and Rust you answer it for every value, and your data structures change to keep the answer simple. Everything else on the checklist is new spelling for ideas you already have; this is a new idea.

0.6.5 Types, errors, tooling and idioms

Type system. Two separate questions. Static or dynamic: are types checked before the program runs (TypeScript, Java, Go, C#, Rust) or only while it runs (JavaScript, Python, Ruby)? Strict or loose: does the language convert between types silently? JavaScript does ('5' * 2 is 10); Python does not ('5' + 1 raises TypeError), even though both are dynamic. Two more details trip TypeScript developers:

  • TypeScript is structural (any object with the right shape fits an interface); Java and C# are nominal (a class must declare implements OrderRepository); Go satisfies interfaces implicitly, with no implements keyword.
  • TypeScript types vanish at runtime, hence class-validator or zod for incoming JSON. Python hints are not enforced at runtime either (mypy or pyright check them). Java erases generic parameters, so List<Order> is just List at runtime.

Error model.

Model Languages What it looks like The trap
Exceptions TypeScript, Java, Python, C# throw unwinds the stack to the nearest catch Easy to forget that a call can throw; errors travel invisibly
Checked exceptions Java (some) The method signature must declare throws IOException Teams wrap everything in unchecked exceptions to escape the noise
Returned errors Go order, err := repo.Find(ctx, id), then if err != nil { return ..., err } Ignoring err with _; losing context by not wrapping with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)
Result types Rust fn find(id: &str) -> Result<Order, DbError>; the ? operator returns early on error Calling .unwrap() everywhere, which crashes on any error

Go's verbosity is deliberate: every call that can fail shows it at the call site. Go's panic is reserved for programmer errors, not for "order not found".

Build tool, package manager, test runner. On day one, find the equivalents of the commands you already use:

Language Dependencies and build Test runner Format and lint
TypeScript/Node.js npm, pnpm or yarn; tsc Jest, Vitest, node --test Prettier, ESLint
Java Maven (pom.xml) or Gradle (build.gradle) JUnit 5, with Mockito for mocks Checkstyle, Spotless
Go Go modules (go.mod), go build go test (built in) gofmt, go vet (built in)
Python pip with a virtual environment, Poetry or uv (pyproject.toml) pytest Ruff, Black
C# dotnet CLI and NuGet xUnit or NUnit dotnet format
Rust Cargo (Cargo.toml) cargo test (built in) rustfmt, Clippy

Idioms. Code review will enforce each community's conventions. Go prefers small interfaces, plain structs, short names, explicit error checks and no class hierarchies. Java leans on classes, interfaces and Spring dependency injection. Python has PEP 8, comprehensions and "easier to ask forgiveness than permission". Read the official style guide once (Effective Go, PEP 8), read one well-maintained open-source project, and let the formatter and linter correct you.

0.6.6 NestJS and Spring Boot, side by side

NestJS was openly inspired by Angular, which borrowed many ideas from Spring. So a NestJS developer who moves to Spring Boot, the dominant Java backend framework, finds a lot of familiar shapes. This table maps the concepts using only real annotations and APIs.

Concept NestJS Spring Boot
Application entry NestFactory.create(AppModule) in main.ts A class annotated @SpringBootApplication calling SpringApplication.run(...)
Module @Module({ imports, controllers, providers, exports }) No direct equivalent: components are found by package scanning; @Configuration classes with @Bean methods and @Import group wiring
Controller @Controller('orders') @RestController with @RequestMapping("/orders")
Route handlers @Get(':id'), @Post() @GetMapping("/{id}"), @PostMapping
Path, query, body @Param('id'), @Query('page'), @Body() @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody
Service (injectable class) @Injectable() @Service (or the general @Component)
Dependency injection Constructor parameters Constructor parameters (a single constructor is injected automatically; @Autowired is optional)
DTO validation class-validator decorators (@IsString(), @IsInt(), @Min(1)) with ValidationPipe Jakarta Bean Validation (@NotBlank, @NotNull, @Min(1), @Size) with @Valid on the parameter
Entity TypeORM @Entity(), @PrimaryGeneratedColumn(), @Column() JPA @Entity, @Id with @GeneratedValue, @Column
Repository @InjectRepository(Order) giving a Repository<Order> An interface extending Spring Data's JpaRepository<Order, Long>; Spring generates the implementation
Transactions dataSource.transaction(...) or a QueryRunner @Transactional on a service method
Error handling Exception filters (@Catch()), NotFoundException @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler, ResponseStatusException
Configuration @nestjs/config and ConfigService application.yml with @Value or @ConfigurationProperties
Auth Guards (CanActivate), @nestjs/passport Spring Security's filter chain
Cross-cutting logic Interceptors HandlerInterceptor, or aspects with @Aspect
Tests Jest with Test.createTestingModule JUnit 5 with @SpringBootTest or @WebMvcTest, Mockito

The biggest real difference is not in this table. A classic Spring MVC application handles each request on its own thread (0.6.3), so blocking calls are normal and shared mutable state needs care, while NestJS runs on one event loop where blocking calls are forbidden. Same shapes, different physics.

0.6.7 One task in four languages

The task: fetch an order from an internal HTTP API, total its items in integer cents, and give up after two seconds. It is small, but it touches everything on the checklist: concurrency, types, errors, money as integers, and a timeout.

TypeScript
// TypeScript (Node.js 18+): global fetch, AbortSignal.timeout
interface OrderItem { sku: string; priceCents: number; quantity: number }
interface Order { id: string; items: OrderItem[] }

export class OrderFetchError extends Error {}

export async function fetchOrderTotal(baseUrl: string, orderId: string, timeoutMs = 2_000): Promise<number> {
  const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/orders/${encodeURIComponent(orderId)}`, {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs), // one deadline for connect, headers and body
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new OrderFetchError(`GET order ${orderId} failed: HTTP ${res.status}`);
  const order = (await res.json()) as Order; // a type assertion only; validate with zod in production
  return order.items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.priceCents * item.quantity, 0);
}
Java
// Java 17+: java.net.http.HttpClient, records, Jackson for JSON
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.URLEncoder;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;

public class OrderTotals {
    record OrderItem(String sku, long priceCents, long quantity) {}
    record Order(String id, List<OrderItem> items) {}

    private static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build();
    private static final ObjectMapper JSON = new ObjectMapper();

    public static long fetchOrderTotal(String baseUrl, String orderId) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                .uri(URI.create(baseUrl + "/orders/" + URLEncoder.encode(orderId, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) // HttpTimeoutException if the response does not arrive in time
                .GET()
                .build();
        HttpResponse<String> response = CLIENT.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()); // blocks this thread
        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
            throw new IOException("GET order " + orderId + " failed: HTTP " + response.statusCode());
        }
        Order order = JSON.readValue(response.body(), Order.class);
        return order.items().stream()
                .mapToLong(item -> Math.multiplyExact(item.priceCents(), item.quantity())) // throws on overflow
                .sum();
    }
}
Go
// Go: net/http, context deadline, returned errors
package orders

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "time"
)

type OrderItem struct {
    SKU        string `json:"sku"`
    PriceCents int64  `json:"priceCents"`
    Quantity   int64  `json:"quantity"`
}

type Order struct {
    ID    string      `json:"id"`
    Items []OrderItem `json:"items"`
}

func FetchOrderTotal(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, baseURL, orderID string) (int64, error) {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second) // deadline covers the whole call, body included
