    defer cancel()

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+"/orders/"+url.PathEscape(orderID), nil)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("build request: %w", err)
    }
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("get order %s: %w", orderID, err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("get order %s: HTTP %d", orderID, resp.StatusCode)
    }

    var order Order
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&order); err != nil {
        return 0, fmt.Errorf("decode order %s: %w", orderID, err)
    }
    var total int64
    for _, item := range order.Items {
        total += item.PriceCents * item.Quantity
    }
    return total, nil
}
Python
# Python 3.11+: asyncio and the httpx library
import asyncio
from urllib.parse import quote

import httpx


async def fetch_order_total(base_url: str, order_id: str, timeout_s: float = 2.0) -> int:
    async with asyncio.timeout(timeout_s):  # one overall deadline; raises TimeoutError
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=base_url, timeout=timeout_s) as client:  # per-phase limits
            response = await client.get(f"/orders/{quote(order_id, safe='')}")
            response.raise_for_status()  # raises httpx.HTTPStatusError on 4xx and 5xx
            order = response.json()
    return sum(item["priceCents"] * item["quantity"] for item in order["items"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(asyncio.run(fetch_order_total("http://localhost:3000", "ord_123")))

What changed and what stayed the same:

Aspect TypeScript Java Go Python
Waiting for the network await: the event loop serves other requests send blocks this thread; other requests run on other threads client.Do blocks this goroutine; the runtime runs others await: the asyncio loop runs other tasks
Timeout AbortSignal.timeout: one deadline Connect timeout plus request timeout on the builder context.WithTimeout, passed down explicitly asyncio.timeout for the total; httpx's timeout limits each phase (connect, read, write, pool) separately
Error on timeout DOMException named TimeoutError is thrown HttpTimeoutException is thrown client.Do returns an error wrapping context.DeadlineExceeded TimeoutError is raised
JSON to typed data Cast only; no runtime check Jackson maps to records, and fails on unknown fields by default Struct tags map fields; unknown fields are ignored by default Plain dicts; no types unless you add a library such as Pydantic
Money arithmetic number (exact up to 2^53) long with Math.multiplyExact to catch overflow int64, wraps silently on overflow int, arbitrary precision, never overflows

And what stayed exactly the same, in all four: build the URL with the ID escaped; set a deadline; send the request; treat non-200 as an error; parse the JSON; sum integer cents. That list is the engineering; the table is the spelling. Note that "a timeout" means four slightly different things: a two-second per-phase read timeout can let a slowly dripping response run far longer than two seconds overall. Part 34 — Reliability Engineering: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Backpressure goes deep on deadlines.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior learns a language through the six checklist questions, one small real service (endpoint, database call, test, Dockerfile) and the team's existing code. They do not judge a language by syntax, the cheapest part, but by its concurrency, memory and error models and its ecosystem fit. When choosing a language for a new service, they weigh team skills heavily: a slightly better language nobody can operate at 03:00 is a worse choice.

Common mistakes

  • Writing TypeScript in Go (classes simulated with structs and interfaces everywhere, exceptions simulated with panic) or Java in Python. Learn the idioms; reviewers will notice.
  • Carrying event-loop assumptions into a threaded language and sharing mutable state without locks.
  • Ignoring Go's returned errors with _, which is the exact equivalent of an empty catch block.
  • Assuming "timeout" means the same thing in every HTTP client.

Interview questions

  1. You are moving from Node.js to Go. What do you learn first?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: the concurrency model (goroutines, channels, context cancellation, data races and the -race detector), the error model (returned errors, wrapping with %w), then tooling (go test, modules) and idioms. Why it matters: these decide correctness; syntax does not. Follow-up: what Node.js habit is dangerous in Go? Assuming code never runs in parallel.
  2. Why is memory management the steepest part of moving to Rust or C++?
    Show answerHide answer
    You must reason about ownership and lifetime of every value; in GC languages the runtime does it. Follow-up: can a garbage-collected program leak memory? Yes, by keeping unneeded references reachable.
  3. Compare exceptions with Go-style returned errors.
    Show answerHide answer
    Exceptions keep the happy path clean but hide which calls can fail; returned errors make every failure visible at the call site at the cost of verbosity. Follow-up: what is the equivalent mistake in each? An empty catch versus _ on the error.
  4. Map a NestJS module, controller, service and repository to Spring Boot.
    Show answerHide answer
    Package scanning plus @Configuration; @RestController; @Service; a Spring Data JpaRepository interface.

Practical exercise

Implement fetchOrderTotal from 0.6.7 in a language you do not know (Go is a good first choice) and point it at a tiny stub server that sleeps a configurable time before answering. Acceptance criteria: with a 500 ms delay it returns the correct total; with a 3 s delay it fails after about 2 s with an error that clearly says "timeout"; with a 404 it returns an error containing the status; and you write three sentences on what surprised you, mapped to the checklist in 0.6.2.

0.7 A learning loop that lasts a career

0.7.1 Build, space, teach

Concept

A learning loop is a repeatable cycle you run for every new technology: read just enough, build something small with it, break it, explain it back, and return to it later. It turns the ten questions from a checklist you read into knowledge you can use under pressure.

Why does it exist?

Because reading feels like learning and mostly is not: you nod through a page on Kafka rebalancing and a month later cannot explain it. Learning research consistently points to retrieval (pulling it from your own head), spacing (returning over days and weeks) and application (using it on a real problem). The loop builds in all three.

How it works

  1. Build one small, real project, the same one in every new technology: an orders service with a write endpoint, a read endpoint, a table, a test and a Dockerfile. You know the domain cold, so all attention goes to the new tool. Part 6 — Your First Backend is exactly that project in NestJS.
  2. Break it on purpose. Kill the database mid-request, send a duplicate, slow the downstream API. This is question 10 at project scale.
  3. Teach it back. Write a one-page explanation for a beginner. Where you cannot explain a step simply, you have found your gap (the Feynman technique).
  4. Space your practice. Revisit after a day, a week and a month, answering from memory first. Spaced-repetition cards suit facts; rebuilding the project suits skills.

Common mistakes

  • Collecting tutorials and courses instead of finishing one small project.
  • Only ever building the happy path, so the first failure you see is in production.
  • Never writing anything down, so every relearning starts from zero.

0.7.2 Using AI assistants as a tutor, not a replacement

AI coding assistants are a superb learning tool, and also the fastest way yet invented to feel you understand something you do not. The difference is whether the assistant thinks with you or for you.

Ways to use an assistant that build understanding:

  • Ask it to explain, then explain back. "Explain Kafka consumer group rebalancing to someone who knows HTTP but not Kafka." Then write your own explanation and ask it to find the mistakes.
  • Ask it to quiz you on the ten questions, and for the failure modes and alternatives (questions 6 and 9) that tutorials skip. Then verify each claim.
  • Write the code first, then compare. Solve the exercise yourself, then ask for a review or an alternative, and make sure you understand every difference.

Rules that keep your understanding yours:

  • Verify against primary sources. Assistants can state outdated or invented APIs and settings with complete confidence. No default, limit or guarantee is true until the docs for your version, or an experiment, confirm it.
  • Never ship code you cannot explain line by line. "The assistant wrote it" is not an answer in review. You own every line you commit.
  • Keep the hard thinking. Let the assistant draft boilerplate and test skeletons; do the design, failure analysis and trade-offs yourself, because those skills only grow with use.
  • Do not paste secrets or customer data into a tool your company has not approved for it.

Part 57 — AI-Assisted Engineering covers working with AI assistants in production engineering in depth, and Part 69 — The Knowledge Map and Learning Roadmap lays out what to learn in which order across this book.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats learning as part of the job: a running "learned this week" file, the ten questions in writing for any tool entering the system, the standard project rebuilt in each new stack, and AI assistants used hard while they stay the one who decides. Above all, they can say "I do not know how this works yet; give me a day", and they know exactly how to spend that day.

Interview questions

  1. How do you learn a new technology quickly enough to make a decision about it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: the ten questions, the explanation and limits pages of the docs, a 30-minute experiment that tries to break it, and a one-page write-up. Follow-up: how do you know when to stop learning and decide?
  2. How do you use AI assistants without losing your own understanding?
    Show answerHide answer
    Use them to explain, quiz and review; verify every factual claim against docs and experiments; never commit code you cannot explain.
  3. Tell me about a technology you learned recently. What surprised you?
    Show answerHide answer
    A strong answer names a specific failure mode or trade-off found by experiment, not a feature.

Practical exercise

Choose a technology this book teaches later that you have never used (Redis, RabbitMQ or Docker are good choices). Spend at most three hours: answer the ten questions in a one-page document, run one 30-minute experiment that breaks it, and ask an AI assistant to critique your page. Acceptance criteria: every one of the ten questions has a concrete answer; at least one answer was corrected by your experiment or by checking the docs (note which); and one week later, you can re-answer questions 3, 4 and 6 from memory.

Senior Checklist — Part 0

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can apply the ten questions to a technology I have never used, and write the answers on one page
  • I can name what a tool trades away and when I would not use it
  • I read explanation and limits pages before tutorials, and I check the docs version
  • I can read a stack trace from the first frame of my own code, and tell ECONNREFUSED from ETIMEDOUT
  • I can build a minimal reproduction before asking for help
  • I know the rough latency of RAM, SSD, a data-centre round trip and a cross-continent round trip
  • I store money as integer minor units or a decimal type, and I know where integers overflow
  • I know the difference between bytes, code points and graphemes, and why 'é'.length can be 2
  • I can learn a new language through its concurrency, memory, type and error models first
  • I can map NestJS concepts to Spring Boot
  • I use AI assistants as a tutor and verify what they say

Part 0 — Key Takeaways

  • Tools churn; ideas repeat. Caching, queues, indexes, retries, logs and consistency show up in every stack.
  • Ask the ten questions of every technology; questions 4, 6 and 7 (state, failure, trade-off) are where production pain hides.
  • Every new technology is a liability until it proves it is better enough than what you already run.
  • A 30-minute experiment that tries to break a tool beats a day of reading about it.
  • Read the explanation, limits and changelog pages first; the tutorial only shows the happy path.
  • In a stack trace, read the message and the first frame of your own code; the framework frames are rarely the bug.
  • A minimal reproduction solves half your problems before you ask anyone.
  • Each step down the memory hierarchy is roughly a thousand times slower; round trips, not computation, usually dominate latency.
  • Floats cannot hold money exactly, integers overflow at fixed widths, and text length depends on whether you count bytes, code points or graphemes.
  • Mastering one language lets you switch: learn the concurrency, memory, type and error models first, then the tools and idioms.
  • Manual or ownership-based memory management is the one genuinely new idea when moving from garbage-collected languages.
  • Use AI assistants to explain, quiz and review, never to replace your own understanding; verify every claim and own every line.

Volume 0: From Scratch

Part 1 — Programming Fundamentals in JavaScript and TypeScript

  • 2 h 5 min read
  • 8 sections
  • 5 diagrams
  • 107 code examples

What you will learn

  1. 1.1Values, variables and types
  2. 1.2TypeScript types: the second half of the language
  3. 1.3Checkpoint: what you have so far
  4. 1.4Functions
  5. 1.5Objects and arrays
  6. 1.6Control flow
  7. 1.7Modules, interfaces and generics
  8. 1.8Classes and object-oriented code

Welcome to Volume 0. This volume exists for one reader: the person who wants to become a backend engineer and is starting close to zero. Maybe you have written a little JavaScript in a browser, maybe you have followed a tutorial once, maybe you have never written a line. Either way, this volume takes you from "I can run node file.js" to "I can build a small, correct NestJS API backed by PostgreSQL". The rest of the book (Parts 10, 11, 13–42, 44–56, 59–71, 73, 74 and 88–95) assumes you already have that foundation. This volume builds it.

This Part is about the language. Not toy JavaScript, and not clever tricks. We teach the parts of JavaScript and TypeScript that you will actually use every day in a backend: values and variables, the type system, functions, objects, arrays, control flow, modules, and error handling. We deliberately build toward the backend. The examples use orders, users, products and payments from the first page, because those are the nouns you will model for the rest of your career, not foo and bar.

A note before we start. JavaScript is the language that runs in the browser and, through Node.js, on the server. TypeScript is JavaScript with a type checker bolted on top. You write TypeScript, a compiler checks it and strips the types away, and what actually runs is plain JavaScript. Every backend in this book is written in TypeScript, so we teach both together: the JavaScript mechanism first, then the TypeScript type that describes it.

1.1 Values, variables and types

1.1.1 What a value is, and the primitive types

Concept

A value is a piece of data your program works with. The number 4200, the text "pending", the fact true — each is a value. JavaScript has a small set of built-in kinds of value called primitive types. You will use these constantly.

The primitives are: number (every number, whole or decimal, like 42 or 19.99), string (text, like "alice@example.com"), boolean (true or false), null (a deliberate "no value"), undefined (a value that was never set), bigint (for integers too large for number), and symbol (rare, a unique marker). For a backend developer, the first five matter every day; bigint and symbol you can learn later.

Why does it exist?

A program is useless if it cannot hold data. An order has a total, a status, a flag for whether it is paid. Those are a number, a string and a boolean. The type system exists so the language — and later, TypeScript — knows what kind of thing it is holding, which decides what you are allowed to do with it. You can add two numbers. Adding two booleans is almost always a bug.

Mental model

Imagine a warehouse with labelled bins. Each bin holds one thing. Some bins hold weights (numbers), some hold written notes (strings), some hold a yes/no switch (boolean). The label on the bin tells the warehouse worker what kind of thing is inside without opening it. A type is that label. A value is the thing in the bin. A variable is the bin itself with its name painted on the front.

How it works

JavaScript figures out the type of a value automatically from how you write it. 42 is a number. "42" with quotes is a string. true is a boolean. There is no step where you declare "this is a number" in plain JavaScript — the quotes, or their absence, decide.

JavaScript
// Plain JavaScript. Node figures out each type from the literal.
const orderTotalCents = 4299;        // number
const currency = 'USD';              // string
const isPaid = false;                // boolean
const cancelledAt = null;            // null: we deliberately have no cancel time
let discountCode;                    // undefined: declared but not yet assigned

console.log(typeof orderTotalCents); // "number"
console.log(typeof currency);        // "string"
console.log(typeof isPaid);          // "boolean"
console.log(typeof cancelledAt);     // "object"  <-- a famous JavaScript quirk
console.log(typeof discountCode);    // "undefined"

The typeof null returning "object" is a 25-year-old bug in the language that can never be fixed without breaking the web. Memorize it as a quirk and move on.

Practical example

Here is a tiny piece of order logic written with primitives only. It decides whether an order qualifies for free shipping.

JavaScript
const orderTotalCents = 4299;        // $42.99
const freeShippingThresholdCents = 5000; // $50.00
const isPrimeMember = true;

const qualifiesForFreeShipping =
  orderTotalCents >= freeShippingThresholdCents || isPrimeMember;

console.log(qualifiesForFreeShipping); // true, because the member flag is set

Notice we store money in cents as an integer, not 42.99 as a decimal. This is the first real backend habit: floating-point numbers like 0.1 + 0.2 do not equal 0.3 exactly in any language that uses the IEEE 754 standard, and JavaScript does. Storing money as integer cents avoids rounding errors that turn into off-by-a-penny bugs and angry customers.

JavaScript
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);              // 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);      // false

Production scenario

A real payment service receives an order total, a tax amount and a shipping fee, all in cents, and sums them. Because every value is an integer number of cents, the sum is exact. If the same service had stored 42.99 and 3.50 as floating-point dollars, a few million additions per day would accumulate fractional-cent errors, and the daily reconciliation job that compares your totals against the payment provider's totals would fail by a few cents — which, to a finance team, is an all-hands incident, because a payment system that cannot add up is a payment system nobody trusts.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • NaN ("not a number") is itself of type number. It appears when a calculation makes no sense, like Number("abc"). Worse, NaN === NaN is false; use Number.isNaN(x) to test for it.
  • undefined means "never set"; null means "set to nothing on purpose". Mixing them up causes real bugs. A database column that is NULL maps to null; a function argument you forgot to pass is undefined.
  • Numbers lose precision above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (about 9 quadrillion). Database IDs that large must be handled as bigint or strings, which is why some APIs return IDs as strings.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior picks the representation that makes wrong states impossible. Money is integer cents. A status is a small fixed set of strings, never a free-form string. A timestamp is stored as a proper date type, never "March 3rd" as text. The type you choose on day one decides which bugs are possible for the life of the system, so you choose it on purpose, not by accident.

Common mistakes

  • Storing money as floating-point dollars. Use integer cents.
  • Using == instead of === (covered in 1.1.3); == does surprising type coercion.
  • Treating undefined and null as interchangeable, then crashing on cancelledAt.getTime() when cancelledAt is null.

Interview questions

  1. Why is 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 in JavaScript?
    Show answerHide answer
    Because numbers are IEEE 754 doubles and 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary, so the sum carries a tiny error. Follow-up: how do you store money? Integer cents, or a dedicated decimal type in the database.
  2. What is the difference between null and undefined?
    Show answerHide answer
    undefined is the absence of assignment; null is an intentional empty value. Why it matters: database NULLs map to null, and conflating the two causes crashes.
  3. What does typeof NaN return, and how do you test for NaN?
    Show answerHide answer
    "number"; test with Number.isNaN. Why it matters: a stray NaN from bad input silently poisons every calculation downstream.

Practical exercise

Write a function-free script (just variables and console.log) that computes the grand total of an order: subtotal 3499 cents, tax 280 cents, shipping 599 cents, minus a discount of 500 cents. Print the grand total in cents and also as a dollar string like $38.78. Acceptance criteria: the dollar string must always show exactly two decimal places, even for a total like 4000 cents ($40.00).

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
// grand-total.ts: no functions, just variables and console.log.
const subtotalCents = 3499;
const taxCents = 280;
const shippingCents = 599;
const discountCents = 500;

// All the arithmetic happens in whole cents, so it is exact.
const grandTotalCents = subtotalCents + taxCents + shippingCents - discountCents;

// Divide by 100 only at the very end, for display, and force two decimals.
const grandTotalDollars = `$${(grandTotalCents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

console.log(grandTotalCents);   // 3878
console.log(grandTotalDollars); // $38.78

// The acceptance check: a round total must still show two decimals.
const roundTotalCents = 4000;
console.log(`$${(roundTotalCents / 100).toFixed(2)}`); // $40.00
console.log(`$${roundTotalCents / 100}`);              // $40 (what you get without toFixed)

Run it with npx tsx grand-total.ts:

Text
3878
$38.78
$40.00
$40

Why it is right: every addition and subtraction works on whole numbers of cents, so there is no floating-point error to accumulate (3499 + 280 + 599 - 500 = 3878). Division by 100 happens exactly once, at the edge, only to make a string for a human. toFixed(2) always returns a string with exactly two digits after the decimal point, which is what turns 40 into 40.00.

The trap most learners fall into is the last line: printing grandTotalCents / 100 directly. It looks fine for 38.78 and then shows $40 or $40.5 the first time the total is round. The second trap is doing the maths in dollars (34.99 + 2.80 + ...) and formatting at the end; that works for some numbers and is off by a fraction of a cent for others (remember 0.1 + 0.2). Also remember that toFixed returns a string: format once, at the end, and never do more arithmetic on the result.

Check it yourself: change subtotalCents to 3621. The total becomes exactly 4000 cents, and the second line must print $40.00, not $40. In production you would usually format with new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', { style: 'currency', currency: 'USD' }).format(cents / 100), which also adds thousands separators, but the rule stays the same: integer cents inside, formatting only at the edge.

1.1.2 Variables: let, const and the ghost of var

Concept

A variable is a named bin that holds a value. In modern JavaScript you declare variables with const or let. const means the bin's contents will not be reassigned. let means they might be. There is an older keyword, var, which you should never use in new code; we explain why so you recognize it in old code.

Why does it exist?

You need names so you can refer to a value more than once and so your code reads like a description of a problem rather than a soup of literals. const freeShippingThresholdCents = 5000 tells the next reader (often you, in six months) what 5000 means. A magic number 5000 buried in a condition tells them nothing.

Mental model

const is a bin welded shut around one value — you can look inside, but you cannot swap the value for a different one. let is a bin with a lid you can open to put something new in. var is a bin that, bizarrely, teleports itself to the top of the room the moment the room is entered, which is why it causes confusing bugs.

How it works

JavaScript
const maxRetries = 3;      // cannot be reassigned
let attempt = 0;           // will be reassigned in a loop
attempt = attempt + 1;     // fine

// maxRetries = 4;         // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

A crucial subtlety: const stops you from reassigning the variable, not from changing the contents of an object it points to. An object held by const can still have its properties changed.

JavaScript
const order = { id: 'ord_1', status: 'pending' };
order.status = 'paid';     // ALLOWED: we changed a property, not the binding
// order = { id: 'ord_2' }; // NOT ALLOWED: reassigning the variable itself

This confuses every beginner once. const protects the arrow from the bin to the object, not the object.

var has two traps. It is function-scoped, not block-scoped, so a var declared inside an if block leaks out of the block. And it is hoisted: the declaration is moved to the top of the function, so you can reference a var before the line that declares it and get undefined instead of an error. Both behaviors cause bugs that let and const simply do not have.

JavaScript
// Why var is dangerous:
function demo() {
  if (true) {
    var leaked = 'I escape the block';
  }
  console.log(leaked); // works with var; would be a ReferenceError with let
}

TypeScript angle

In TypeScript, const and let behave the same but the type checker infers tighter types for const. A const status = 'paid' has the literal type 'paid', while let status = 'paid' has the wider type string, because let might be reassigned. This matters when you build the small fixed sets of values we meet in 1.1.4.

Practical example

TypeScript
// A retry loop for calling a flaky payment provider.
const maxAttempts = 3;
let lastError: unknown = null;

for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
  try {
    // callProvider() is defined later in the book; imagine it here.
    // const result = await callProvider(order);
    // return result;
    break;
  } catch (err) {
    lastError = err;
    // wait and retry (covered in Part 2)
  }
}

maxAttempts is const because the policy does not change mid-loop. attempt and lastError are let because they change on every pass.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Default to const. Reach for let only when a value genuinely must change, which is less often than beginners expect — most loops that mutate a let accumulator can be written more clearly with array methods (1.4). A codebase full of const is a codebase where the reader knows, at a glance, which things move and which do not. That is a small, free form of documentation, and seniors value it.

Common mistakes

  • Using var in new code. It has no advantage and several traps.
  • Thinking const makes an object immutable. It does not; it only stops reassignment of the variable.
  • Declaring let for values that never change, which forces the reader to wonder whether they do.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between let, const and var?
    Show answerHide answer
    let and const are block-scoped and not hoisted in a usable way; const cannot be reassigned. var is function-scoped and hoisted, which causes leaks and confusing bugs.
  2. Can you mutate an object declared with const?
    Show answerHide answer
    Yes — const protects the binding, not the object's contents. Follow-up: how do you make the contents read-only? Object.freeze, or TypeScript's readonly and as const.

Practical exercise

Take a buggy snippet that uses var inside a for loop to register three callbacks and prints 3, 3, 3 instead of 0, 1, 2. Rewrite it with let so it prints 0, 1, 2. Acceptance criteria: explain in one sentence why let fixes it (a fresh binding per iteration).

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
// Buggy: var creates ONE binding for the whole loop, shared by every callback.
const buggy: Array<() => void> = [];
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  buggy.push(() => console.log('var:', i));
}
buggy.forEach((callback) => callback()); // var: 3, var: 3, var: 3

// Fixed: let creates a fresh binding for each iteration.
const fixed: Array<() => void> = [];
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
  fixed.push(() => console.log('let:', j));
}
fixed.forEach((callback) => callback()); // let: 0, let: 1, let: 2
Text
var: 3
var: 3
var: 3
let: 0
let: 1
let: 2

The one sentence: with let, the loop creates a new binding of the loop variable for every iteration, so each callback closes over its own copy; with var there is a single function-wide binding, and by the time the callbacks run the loop has already pushed it to 3.

Notice that the callbacks do not run inside the loop. They run afterwards, which is exactly what happens with setTimeout, event handlers or promise callbacks in a real server. for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0) prints 3, 3, 3 for the same reason.

The trap: "fixing" it with for (const i = 0; i < 3; i++). It looks consistent with "default to const", but i++ reassigns the variable, so it throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable. on the first increment. const is right in for...of (for (const id of ids)), where each iteration gets a new value and nothing is reassigned; a counting loop needs let.

Check it yourself: run the file with npx tsx, then change let j to var j in the fixed half and watch it print 3, 3, 3 again. That one-word change is the whole difference.

1.1.3 Equality, truthiness and coercion

Concept

JavaScript has two equality operators. === (strict equality) compares value and type with no conversion. == (loose equality) converts the operands to a common type first, with rules so surprising that professionals simply never use it. "Truthiness" is the set of rules for which values count as true in an if.

Why does it exist?

Early JavaScript tried to be forgiving, so "5" == 5 is true. That forgiveness causes bugs: 0 == "", null == undefined and [] == false are all true, none of which you want. === exists to give you the predictable behavior you actually need.

How it works

JavaScript
console.log(5 === 5);       // true
console.log('5' === 5);     // false: different types, no conversion
console.log('5' == 5);      // true: == converts the string to a number
console.log(null == undefined); // true (a rare useful case)
console.log(null === undefined); // false

Truthy and falsy: in an if, these eight values are falsy — false, 0, -0, 0n, "" (empty string), null, undefined, and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false", [] (empty array) and {} (empty object). That last pair trips up everyone: an empty array is truthy.

JavaScript
if ([]) console.log('empty array is truthy'); // this prints
if ('0') console.log("the string '0' is truthy"); // this prints

Practical example

A common bug: checking whether a quantity was supplied.

JavaScript
function describeQuantity(quantity) {
  // Bug: if quantity is 0, this treats it as "not supplied".
  if (!quantity) return 'no quantity';
  return `quantity is ${quantity}`;
}
console.log(describeQuantity(0)); // "no quantity" -- WRONG, 0 is a real quantity

Because 0 is falsy, !quantity is true for a legitimate zero. The fix is to test for the thing you actually mean:

JavaScript
function describeQuantity(quantity) {
  if (quantity === undefined || quantity === null) return 'no quantity';
  return `quantity is ${quantity}`;
}

TypeScript helps here: quantity ?? 'no quantity' (the nullish coalescing operator ??) falls back only for null or undefined, never for 0 or "". This is one of the most useful operators in backend code.

TypeScript
const shippingNote = order.note ?? 'no note';   // keeps '' if note is ''
const retries = config.retries ?? 3;            // keeps 0 if retries is 0

Edge cases & failure modes

  • !value to check "is it missing" treats 0, "" and false as missing. Use === undefined, === null, or ??.
  • NaN === NaN is false, so === cannot detect NaN.
  • Comparing objects with === compares identity, not contents: {a:1} === {a:1} is false because they are two different objects.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reads if (!x) as a smell and asks "what exactly is being tested — null, undefined, zero, or empty?" Vague truthiness checks are a top source of production bugs where a legitimate zero or empty string is dropped. Be explicit about the condition you mean, and prefer ?? over || whenever 0, "" or false are valid values.

Common mistakes

  • Using == and getting bitten by coercion.
  • Using || for defaults when 0 or "" are valid (count || 10 turns a real 0 into 10); use ??.
  • Comparing arrays or objects with === and expecting content comparison.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between == and ===?
    Show answerHide answer
    === compares without coercion; == coerces types first, with surprising rules. Always use ===.
  2. Which values are falsy in JavaScript?
    Show answerHide answer
    false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Follow-up: is [] truthy? Yes.
  3. When would you use ?? instead of ||?
    Show answerHide answer
    When 0, "" or false are legitimate values and only null/undefined should trigger the fallback.

Practical exercise

Write a function getPageSize(requested) that returns requested if it is a number between 1 and 100, and 20 otherwise. It must accept 0? No — 0 is invalid here, so it falls back. But it must not accidentally reject a valid 1. Acceptance criteria: getPageSize(0) returns 20, getPageSize(1) returns 1, getPageSize(500) returns 20, getPageSize(undefined) returns 20.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
const DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE = 20;
const MAX_PAGE_SIZE = 100;

function getPageSize(requested: unknown): number {
  // Say exactly what "valid" means; never rely on truthiness.
  if (
    typeof requested === 'number' &&
    Number.isInteger(requested) && // also rejects NaN, Infinity and 2.5
    requested >= 1 &&
    requested <= MAX_PAGE_SIZE
  ) {
    return requested;
  }
  return DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE;
}

console.log(getPageSize(0));         // 20
console.log(getPageSize(1));         // 1
console.log(getPageSize(100));       // 100
console.log(getPageSize(500));       // 20
console.log(getPageSize(undefined)); // 20
console.log(getPageSize(NaN));       // 20
console.log(getPageSize('50'));      // 20: a string is not a number
Text
20
1
100
20
20
20
20

Why it is right: the condition states the rule in full, "a whole number from 1 to 100", and everything else falls through to the default. Taking unknown instead of number means the function is safe even when someone passes a string or undefined from a query string. Number.isInteger quietly handles the odd cases too: NaN, Infinity and 2.5 are all rejected, because a page size of 2.5 rows makes no sense.

The trap most learners fall into is reaching for truthiness: return requested || 20. That happens to turn 0 into 20, so it seems to pass the first test, but it lets 500 straight through and would let -5 through as well. The second trap is checking only one bound (requested > 0) and forgetting the maximum, which in a real API is how a client asks for a million rows in one request.

A real request delivers ?limit=50 as the string '50', which this function rejects on purpose: converting and validating input is the job of the request boundary (in NestJS, a DTO with class-validator, shown in 6.5), and this helper only accepts a number that has already been parsed.

Check it yourself: run the file and compare with the expected output, or replace the console.log lines with assertions so a wrong answer fails loudly:

TypeScript
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
assert.equal(getPageSize(0), 20);
assert.equal(getPageSize(1), 1);
assert.equal(getPageSize(500), 20);
assert.equal(getPageSize(undefined), 20);

1.2 TypeScript types: the second half of the language

1.2.1 Why types, and basic type annotations

Concept

TypeScript lets you write down what type a variable, parameter or return value is supposed to be, and then a compiler checks that you never violate it. The types are erased before the code runs — Node never sees them — so types cost nothing at runtime. Their entire value is catching mistakes before the code ever runs.

Why does it exist?

In plain JavaScript, a typo like order.totl (missing an a) is undefined at runtime and crashes three functions later with a useless stack trace. A function that expects a number but receives a string fails deep inside some library. TypeScript catches both at the moment you write them, in your editor, with a red underline. On a backend of any size, this turns a whole category of 2 a.m. incidents into a squiggle you fix in two seconds.

Mental model

Think of TypeScript as a spell-checker for data shapes. A spell-checker does not change what you write; it underlines words that cannot be right. TypeScript underlines data flows that cannot be right — passing a string where a number is required, reading a property that does not exist, forgetting that a value might be null.

How it works

You add a type after a colon:

TypeScript
const orderTotalCents: number = 4299;
const currency: string = 'USD';
const isPaid: boolean = false;

function applyDiscount(totalCents: number, percent: number): number {
  return Math.round(totalCents * (1 - percent / 100));
}

applyDiscount(4299, 10);     // fine
// applyDiscount('4299', 10); // Error: string is not assignable to number

Most of the time you do not need to write the type, because TypeScript infers it. const currency = 'USD' is already known to be a string. The rule professionals follow: let TypeScript infer local variables, but always annotate function parameters and return types, because those are the contracts other code depends on.

The any escape hatch and why it is dangerous

any turns the type checker off for a value. It is the single most misused feature in TypeScript. The moment a value is any, every mistake involving it becomes invisible again.

TypeScript
let data: any = JSON.parse('{"total": 4299}');
data.total.toUpperCase(); // no error at compile time, crashes at runtime

Prefer unknown when you genuinely do not know the type yet. unknown forces you to check the type before using it, which is exactly what you want for data coming from the outside world (a request body, a JSON file, a third-party API).

TypeScript
let data: unknown = JSON.parse('{"total": 4299}');
// data.total;          // Error: data is unknown, you must narrow first
if (typeof data === 'object' && data !== null && 'total' in data) {
  // now TypeScript lets you proceed, after you have proven the shape
}

Practical example

A function that parses a price from a request. With unknown and narrowing, bad input is caught at the boundary instead of corrupting the database.

TypeScript
function parsePriceCents(input: unknown): number {
  if (typeof input !== 'number' || !Number.isInteger(input) || input < 0) {
    throw new Error('price must be a non-negative integer number of cents');
  }
  return input;
}

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats any as technical debt and unknown as the honest tool for untrusted data. They turn on strict mode in tsconfig.json on day one, because without it TypeScript allows null to sneak into everything and most of the value is lost. The slogan is "parse, don't trust": every piece of data entering the system from outside is unknown until a validator has proven its shape, after which it is a precise type for the rest of its life.

Common mistakes

  • Sprinkling any to make red squiggles disappear; this just defers the crash to runtime.
  • Not enabling strict mode, which leaves null and undefined holes everywhere.
  • Over-annotating obvious local variables, which adds noise without value.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between any and unknown?
    Show answerHide answer
    any disables checking; unknown requires you to narrow the type before use. Use unknown for external data.
  2. Do TypeScript types exist at runtime?
    Show answerHide answer
    No — they are erased during compilation. You cannot check x instanceof SomeInterface; interfaces do not exist at runtime.
  3. Why enable strict mode?
    Show answerHide answer
    It turns on strictNullChecks and other flags that catch the largest class of real bugs (null/undefined access).

Practical exercise

Write a function coerceStatus(input: unknown): 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled' that accepts an unknown value, checks it is one of the three allowed strings, and throws otherwise. Acceptance criteria: the return type is the exact union of three strings, and the function throws a clear error for any other input, including 'PAID' in the wrong case.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
const ORDER_STATUSES = ['pending', 'paid', 'cancelled'] as const;
type OrderStatus = (typeof ORDER_STATUSES)[number]; // 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled'

function coerceStatus(input: unknown): OrderStatus {
  if (typeof input !== 'string') {
    throw new Error(`status must be a string, got ${typeof input}`);
  }
  // Find the allowed value that equals the input exactly (case-sensitive).
  const match = ORDER_STATUSES.find((status) => status === input);
  if (match === undefined) {
    throw new Error(
      `invalid status ${JSON.stringify(input)}; expected one of: ${ORDER_STATUSES.join(', ')}`,
    );
  }
  return match; // already typed OrderStatus, no cast needed
}

for (const input of ['paid', 'PAID', 'shipped', 42, null]) {
  try {
    console.log('ok    ', coerceStatus(input));
  } catch (err) {
    console.log('error ', (err as Error).message);
  }
}
Text
ok     paid
error  invalid status "PAID"; expected one of: pending, paid, cancelled
error  invalid status "shipped"; expected one of: pending, paid, cancelled
error  status must be a string, got number
error  status must be a string, got object

Why it is right: the list of allowed statuses is written once, as a read-only array (as const), and the type is derived from it, so the runtime check and the compile-time type can never drift apart. Adding 'refunded' to the array updates both. find with === is case-sensitive, so 'PAID' is rejected, and because find returns an element of the array, its type is already OrderStatus. The error message names the bad value and the allowed ones, which is what the person reading the log at 2 a.m. needs.

The trap most learners fall into is the cast: if (typeof input === 'string') return input as OrderStatus;. It compiles, the return type looks right, and 'shipped' sails straight into your database. as tells the compiler to stop checking; it proves nothing. A second, smaller trap: ORDER_STATUSES.includes(input) does not compile, because includes on this array only accepts the three literal strings, not any string. That is why the answer uses find. Lower-casing the input "to be helpful" is a product decision, not a fix: the exercise asks you to reject 'PAID'.

Check it yourself: run it and compare the five lines. Then hover over coerceStatus in your editor; the return type must read 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled', not string.

1.3 Checkpoint: what you have so far

We covered values and the primitive types, why money lives in integer cents, variables with const and let (and why var is retired), equality and truthiness (and the ?? operator), and the opening ideas of TypeScript: annotations, inference, any versus unknown, and strict mode. The next sections build on this with functions, objects, arrays and the type tools that describe them — interfaces, generics and unions — which together let you model the nouns of a real backend.

1.4 Functions

1.4.1 Declaring and calling functions

Concept

A function is a named, reusable block of code that takes inputs (called parameters), does something, and usually gives back an output (the return value). Functions are how you break a big problem into small, nameable pieces. Almost everything you write in a backend lives inside a function.

Why does it exist?

Without functions, you would copy the same logic everywhere it is needed, and fixing a bug would mean fixing it in twenty places. A function is a single place where one idea lives. "Calculate the order total" should exist once; every part of the system that needs an order total calls that one function. When the tax rules change, you change one function.

Mental model

Imagine a vending machine. You put in coins and a code (the inputs), the machine does its internal work, and a snack drops out (the return value). You do not need to know how the machine is wired inside; you only need to know what it takes and what it gives back. A well-named function is a vending machine with a clear label.

How it works

There are two main ways to write a function. A function declaration uses the function keyword. An arrow function uses => and is stored in a variable. In modern backend code you will see both; arrow functions are more common for small helpers and callbacks.

TypeScript
// Function declaration
function orderTotalCents(subtotal: number, tax: number, shipping: number): number {
  return subtotal + tax + shipping;
}

// Arrow function stored in a const
const orderTotalCents2 = (subtotal: number, tax: number, shipping: number): number => {
  return subtotal + tax + shipping;
};

// Calling them is identical
const total = orderTotalCents(3499, 280, 599); // 4378

The parts of a function: the name (orderTotalCents), the parameters in parentheses with their types, the return type after the colon, and the body in braces. The return statement sends a value back to whoever called the function. A function with no return gives back undefined.

Parameters: default, optional and rest

TypeScript
// Default parameter: used when the caller omits the argument.
function paginate(page: number, pageSize: number = 20): { skip: number; take: number } {
  return { skip: (page - 1) * pageSize, take: pageSize };
}
paginate(3);        // pageSize defaults to 20 -> { skip: 40, take: 20 }
paginate(3, 50);    // { skip: 100, take: 50 }

// Optional parameter: may be undefined. Marked with ?.
function greet(name: string, title?: string): string {
  return title ? `${title} ${name}` : name;
}

// Rest parameter: collects any number of trailing arguments into an array.
function sumCents(...amounts: number[]): number {
  return amounts.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0);
}
sumCents(100, 200, 50); // 350

Practical example

A function that decides shipping cost. Notice it takes typed inputs and returns a typed output, and that it has one job.

TypeScript
function shippingCostCents(
  subtotalCents: number,
  isPrimeMember: boolean,
  country: string,
): number {
  if (isPrimeMember) return 0;
  if (country !== 'US') return 2500;          // flat international rate
  if (subtotalCents >= 5000) return 0;        // free over $50 domestic
  return 599;                                  // standard domestic
}

NestJS example

This is a sneak peek at Part 6. In NestJS, the methods on a service are just functions with a decorator on the class. The function below is pure business logic; the framework calls it.

TypeScript
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class ShippingService {
  // A method is a function that belongs to a class.
  cost(subtotalCents: number, isPrimeMember: boolean, country: string): number {
    if (isPrimeMember) return 0;
    if (country !== 'US') return 2500;
    return subtotalCents >= 5000 ? 0 : 599;
  }
}

The business rules did not change at all. They moved into a class so NestJS can share one instance of ShippingService across the whole application. We explain that machinery in Part 6 and, in depth, in Part 16 (dependency injection).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A function that returns undefined implicitly (no return) when the caller expected a value is a classic bug. TypeScript's return-type annotation catches it: declaring : number forces every path to return a number.
  • Passing arguments in the wrong order (shippingCostCents(country, isPrime, subtotal)) compiles only if the types happen to line up. This is why a single argument object is often safer than many positional parameters (see 1.4.3).
  • A function that both returns a value and changes something outside itself (a "side effect") is harder to test and reason about. Prefer functions that only transform their inputs where you can.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior aims for functions that are small, named for what they produce, and free of hidden side effects where possible. The test they apply: "Can I describe this function in one sentence without the word 'and'?" If the sentence needs an "and", the function is doing two jobs and should be split. They also prefer pure functions — same input always gives same output, no side effects — for business rules, because pure functions are trivial to unit-test (Part 45) without a database or network.

Common mistakes

  • Giant functions that do ten things; impossible to name, test or reuse.
  • Forgetting a return, so the function silently yields undefined.
  • Too many positional parameters, so callers pass them in the wrong order.
  • Mutating a parameter that is an object or array, surprising the caller (covered in 1.5).

Interview questions

  1. What is a pure function and why is it desirable?
    Show answerHide answer
    A function whose output depends only on its inputs and which has no side effects. It is easy to test and reason about, and safe to call repeatedly.
  2. What is the difference between a function declaration and an arrow function?
    Show answerHide answer
    Beyond syntax, arrow functions do not have their own this and are not hoisted. For most backend helpers the difference rarely matters; this matters inside classes.
  3. When would you pass an options object instead of positional parameters?
    Show answerHide answer
    When there are more than two or three parameters, or several are optional, to avoid order mistakes and make call sites self-documenting.

Practical exercise

Write a pure function orderSummary that takes subtotalCents, taxCents, shippingCents and discountCents and returns an object { subtotalCents, taxCents, shippingCents, discountCents, grandTotalCents }. Acceptance criteria: the grand total never goes below zero (clamp it), and the function has no side effects.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
interface OrderSummary {
  readonly subtotalCents: number;
  readonly taxCents: number;
  readonly shippingCents: number;
  readonly discountCents: number;
  readonly grandTotalCents: number;
}

function orderSummary(
  subtotalCents: number,
  taxCents: number,
  shippingCents: number,
  discountCents: number,
): OrderSummary {
  // Clamp: a discount bigger than the order never produces a negative total.
  const grandTotalCents = Math.max(0, subtotalCents + taxCents + shippingCents - discountCents);
  return { subtotalCents, taxCents, shippingCents, discountCents, grandTotalCents };
}

console.log(orderSummary(3499, 280, 599, 500));
console.log(orderSummary(1000, 80, 0, 5000).grandTotalCents); // 0, not -3920

// Purity check: same input gives the same output, and nothing outside changed.
const first = orderSummary(3499, 280, 599, 500);
const second = orderSummary(3499, 280, 599, 500);
console.log(JSON.stringify(first) === JSON.stringify(second)); // true
Text
{
  subtotalCents: 3499,
  taxCents: 280,
  shippingCents: 599,
  discountCents: 500,
  grandTotalCents: 3878
}
0
true

Why it is right: Math.max(0, x) returns x when it is positive and 0 when it is negative, which is exactly "clamp at zero". The function is pure: it reads only its four parameters, it does not touch any variable outside itself, it does not log, write to a database or call the network, and it builds a brand-new object every time. Same input, same output, always. The readonly fields stop a caller from quietly changing the summary afterwards. The shorthand { subtotalCents, taxCents, ... } means { subtotalCents: subtotalCents, ... }.

The trap most learners fall into is adding "just one" side effect: a console.log inside the function, or updating a running total in an outer variable, or accepting an order object and writing order.grandTotalCents = ... onto it. Each of those makes the function harder to test and surprises its callers (1.4.1). A subtler trap: clamping hides bad input. A negative subtotalCents is a bug somewhere upstream, and clamping turns it into a silent zero. A stricter version would throw when any input is negative or not an integer, and clamp only the legitimate case of a discount larger than the order.

Check it yourself: run it, then write the two cases as a unit test (Part 45 — Testing Backend Systems with Jest and NestJS, 45.3): expect(orderSummary(1000, 80, 0, 5000).grandTotalCents).toBe(0). Because the function is pure, the test needs no database, no mocks and no setup.

1.4.2 Scope, closures and the call stack

Concept

Scope is the set of variables a piece of code can see. A closure is a function that remembers the variables from where it was created, even after that place has finished running. The call stack is the list of functions currently in progress. These three ideas explain a lot of otherwise-mysterious behavior.

Why does it exist?

Scope exists so that two functions can both use a variable named i without colliding — each has its own. Closures exist so a function can carry some private state with it, which is how you build things like a counter, a rate limiter, or a configured client. Understanding the call stack is how you read a stack trace, which is the single most useful debugging skill (Part 13.15).

Mental model

Imagine nested rooms. Code in an inner room can see out through the open doors into the rooms that contain it, but code in an outer room cannot see into the inner rooms. A closure is like taking a photograph of what the outer rooms held at the moment you walked into the inner room — even after those rooms are torn down, the function still has the photo.

How it works

TypeScript
function makeCounter(): () => number {
  let count = 0;                 // this lives in makeCounter's scope
  return () => {
    count = count + 1;           // the inner function "closes over" count
    return count;
  };
}

const next = makeCounter();
console.log(next()); // 1
console.log(next()); // 2  -- count survived, private to this counter
const other = makeCounter();
console.log(other()); // 1  -- a separate count

makeCounter finished running after the first call, yet count is still alive, held by the returned function. That is a closure. Each call to makeCounter creates a fresh count, which is why next and other are independent.

The call stack: when a() calls b() which calls c(), the stack is a -> b -> c. When c returns, it is popped off. If c throws an error, the error message includes the whole stack, so you can see the exact path that led to the failure.

Text
Error: payment declined
    at chargeCard        (payment.service.ts:42)   <- where it threw
    at processOrder      (orders.service.ts:88)    <- who called that
    at OrdersController   (orders.controller.ts:23) <- who called that

Read a stack trace top to bottom: the top line is where the error happened, and each line below is the caller.

Practical example

A closure that builds a configured API client. The base URL and key are captured once and reused by every call.

TypeScript
function makePaymentClient(baseUrl: string, apiKey: string) {
  // baseUrl and apiKey are private to the returned functions.
  return {
    charge: async (amountCents: number) => {
      // uses baseUrl and apiKey without them being global
      return fetch(`${baseUrl}/charges`, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
        body: JSON.stringify({ amountCents }),
      });
    },
  };
}

Edge cases & failure modes

  • The classic loop-closure bug. With var i in a for loop, all closures share the one i and see its final value. With let i, each iteration gets a fresh i. This is the single most common closure bug and the reason let exists.
  • Stack overflow. A function that calls itself with no stopping condition fills the call stack until Node crashes with Maximum call stack size exceeded. Every recursive function needs a base case (Part 11).
  • Memory leaks via closures. A closure keeps its captured variables alive. If a long-lived closure captures a huge object, that object cannot be garbage-collected (Part 13). This is a real source of slow memory growth in long-running servers.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Closures are not an exotic trick; they are everywhere in backend code — every event handler, every middleware, every configured client is a closure. A senior is comfortable reading them and is alert to the memory implication: a closure captured by something long-lived (a cache, a global event emitter) can quietly pin large objects in memory. When they read a stack trace, they read it as a story: this called that called the thing that broke.

Common mistakes

  • The var-in-a-loop closure bug (use let).
  • Recursion with no base case, causing a stack overflow.
  • Capturing large objects in long-lived closures, leaking memory.
  • Not reading the stack trace and guessing at the cause instead.

Interview questions

  1. What is a closure?
    Show answerHide answer
    A function bundled with the variables from the scope where it was created, which it can access even after that scope has returned. Follow-up: give a use (private state, configured client, memoization).
  2. Why does the classic for loop with var print the final value in every callback?
    Show answerHide answer
    All iterations share one var binding; let creates a new binding each iteration.
  3. How do you read a stack trace?
    Show answerHide answer
    Top line is where it threw; each line below is the caller up the chain.

Practical exercise

Write makeRateLimiter(maxPerMinute) that returns a function allow() which returns true the first maxPerMinute times it is called within a rolling minute and false afterward, using a closure to hold the timestamps privately. Acceptance criteria: two separate limiters created by two calls to makeRateLimiter do not share state.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
const WINDOW_MS = 60_000;

// `now` is injectable so a test can control time; it defaults to the real clock.
function makeRateLimiter(maxPerMinute: number, now: () => number = Date.now): () => boolean {
  const timestamps: number[] = []; // private: only allow() below can reach it

  return function allow(): boolean {
    const t = now();
    // Forget calls that have slid out of the rolling one-minute window.
    while (timestamps.length > 0 && timestamps[0] <= t - WINDOW_MS) {
      timestamps.shift();
    }
    if (timestamps.length >= maxPerMinute) return false;
    timestamps.push(t);
    return true;
  };
}

// A fake clock we move by hand, so the demo runs instantly.
let fakeTime = 0;
const clock = (): number => fakeTime;

const limiterA = makeRateLimiter(3, clock);
const limiterB = makeRateLimiter(3, clock);

console.log('A:', [limiterA(), limiterA(), limiterA(), limiterA()]); // 4th call refused
console.log('B:', [limiterB()]);                                      // B has its own budget
fakeTime = 30_000;
console.log('A at 30 s:', limiterA()); // still inside the window
fakeTime = 60_001;
console.log('A at 60 s:', limiterA()); // the early calls slid out
Text
A: [ true, true, true, false ]
B: [ true ]
A at 30 s: false
A at 60 s: true

Why it is right: timestamps is declared inside makeRateLimiter, so every call to makeRateLimiter creates a new, separate array, and the returned allow function is the only code that can see it. That is the closure doing its job, and it is why limiter B still has its full budget after A ran out. "Rolling minute" means "the last 60 seconds counted from now", so on every call we first drop timestamps older than 60 seconds, then decide. The array never holds more than maxPerMinute entries, because we only record calls we allowed.

The trap most learners fall into is declaring const timestamps: number[] = [] at the top of the file, outside makeRateLimiter. Everything still works with one limiter, and the moment you create a second one, both share one array: exactly the failure the acceptance criteria test for. The second trap is building a fixed window instead ("reset the counter at the start of each minute"), which lets a client send maxPerMinute calls at 10:00:59 and another maxPerMinute at 10:01:00.

Passing now as a parameter is what makes this testable without waiting a real minute (45.11 covers testing time). Check it yourself: run the file and compare. Note that this limiter lives in one process's memory; with three API instances behind a load balancer, each has its own count, which is why production rate limits usually live in Redis (30.11; 11.17 builds the algorithms properly).

1.4.3 Typing functions well

Concept

TypeScript lets you describe a function's shape as a type: what it takes and what it returns. This lets you pass functions around safely (as callbacks) and define contracts that many functions must satisfy.

How it works

TypeScript
// A type for a function value.
type PriceRule = (subtotalCents: number) => number;

const tenPercentOff: PriceRule = (subtotal) => Math.round(subtotal * 0.9);
const fiveDollarsOff: PriceRule = (subtotal) => Math.max(0, subtotal - 500);

// A function that takes another function as an argument (a "higher-order function").
function applyRules(subtotalCents: number, rules: PriceRule[]): number {
  return rules.reduce((total, rule) => rule(total), subtotalCents);
}

applyRules(5000, [tenPercentOff, fiveDollarsOff]); // 4000, then 3500

A function that takes or returns another function is called a higher-order function. applyRules is one. The array methods you meet next (map, filter, reduce) are all higher-order functions: you hand them a function and they call it for you.

Function overloads and the options-object pattern

When a function takes many parameters, pass a single typed object instead. It is self-documenting at the call site and immune to argument-order mistakes.

TypeScript
interface CreateOrderInput {
  userId: string;
  items: { productId: string; quantity: number }[];
  couponCode?: string;
  giftWrap?: boolean;
}

function createOrder(input: CreateOrderInput): void {
  // input.userId, input.items, etc. -- order of fields does not matter
}

createOrder({
  userId: 'usr_1',
  items: [{ productId: 'p1', quantity: 2 }],
  giftWrap: true,
}); // clear and order-independent

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior types callbacks and higher-order functions precisely, because a wrong callback signature is a bug that only shows up at runtime otherwise. For any function with more than two or three parameters, or with optional ones, they switch to an options object, because six months later nobody remembers whether createOrder(a, b, c, d) puts the coupon before or after the gift-wrap flag.

Common mistakes

  • Untyped callbacks (rules: Function[]), which lets any shape of function through.
  • Long positional parameter lists that callers get wrong.

Interview questions

  1. What is a higher-order function?
    Show answerHide answer
    One that takes a function as an argument or returns a function. Examples: map, filter, reduce, and any function that accepts a callback.
  2. Why prefer an options object over many positional parameters?
    Show answerHide answer
    Self-documenting call sites, order-independence, and easy optional fields.

Practical exercise

Define a type Validator = (value: unknown) => boolean and write a higher-order function validateAll(value, validators) that returns true only if every validator passes. Acceptance criteria: it short-circuits (stops) at the first failing validator.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
type Validator = (value: unknown) => boolean;

function validateAll(value: unknown, validators: readonly Validator[]): boolean {
  // every() stops at the first validator that returns false.
  return validators.every((validator) => validator(value));
}

// Wrap a validator so we can see whether it actually ran.
const traced =
  (name: string, check: Validator): Validator =>
  (value) => {
    console.log(`  ran ${name}`);
    return check(value);
  };

const isString = traced('isString', (v) => typeof v === 'string');
const isEmailShaped = traced('isEmailShaped', (v) => typeof v === 'string' && /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+$/.test(v));
const isShortEnough = traced('isShortEnough', (v) => typeof v === 'string' && v.length <= 254);
const rules = [isString, isEmailShaped, isShortEnough];

console.log('alice@example.com ->', validateAll('alice@example.com', rules));
console.log('42 ->', validateAll(42, rules));
Text
  ran isString
  ran isEmailShaped
  ran isShortEnough
alice@example.com -> true
  ran isString
42 -> false

Why it is right: Array.prototype.every calls the callback for each element in order and stops the moment one returns false, so the short-circuit comes for free. The trace proves it: for 42, only isString ran. traced is itself a higher-order function, one that takes a validator and returns a new validator, which is the same idea as validateAll turned around.

The trap most learners fall into is validators.map((v) => v(value)).every(Boolean), or a reduce that ANDs the results. Both give the right true/false, but map runs every validator first, so there is no short-circuit. That matters for more than speed: later validators often assume earlier ones passed. A length check written as (v) => (v as string).length <= 254 would crash with Cannot read properties of null when given null, if it ran after a failed isString.

One edge case to decide on purpose: validateAll(x, []) returns true, because "every one of zero validators passed" is true. That is usually what you want; if an empty list means a configuration mistake in your system, throw instead.

Check it yourself: run the file and confirm that the 42 case prints only one ran line. Then swap every for the map version and watch all three run.

1.5 Objects and arrays

1.5.1 Objects: grouping related data

Concept

An object is a collection of named values. Each name is a property (or key), and each property holds a value. Objects are how you represent a thing with several attributes — an order has an id, a status, a total and a list of items, so an order is naturally an object.

Why does it exist?

Primitives hold one value each. Real things have many attributes that belong together. Passing around five separate variables for one order (orderId, orderStatus, orderTotal, ...) is error-prone; passing one order object keeps them together and named. Objects are the backbone of every API request and response, because JSON — the format APIs speak — is objects and arrays.

Mental model

An object is a labelled drawer unit. Each small drawer has a label on the front (the key) and holds one thing (the value). You open the drawer by its label: order.status opens the drawer labelled status.

How it works

TypeScript
const order = {
  id: 'ord_1001',
  status: 'pending',
  totalCents: 4299,
  customer: {                      // a nested object
    id: 'usr_42',
    email: 'alice@example.com',
  },
};

// Reading properties: two ways.
console.log(order.status);          // dot notation: "pending"
console.log(order['status']);       // bracket notation: same thing
console.log(order.customer.email);  // reaching into a nested object

// Writing properties
order.status = 'paid';              // change an existing one
// order.trackingNumber = 'XZ99';   // in plain JS you can add new ones freely

Bracket notation matters when the key is in a variable: order[fieldName] where fieldName is 'status'. Dot notation needs a literal key.

Destructuring pulls properties out into variables in one line. You will use this constantly.

TypeScript
const { status, totalCents } = order;      // two new variables
console.log(status, totalCents);           // "paid" 4299

// Rename while destructuring, with a default:
const { status: orderStatus, giftWrap = false } = order;

Spread copies properties from one object into another. It is the standard way to make a changed copy without mutating the original.

TypeScript
const paidOrder = { ...order, status: 'paid', paidAt: new Date() };
// order is unchanged; paidOrder is a new object with status overridden

Typing objects with interfaces and type aliases

In TypeScript you describe an object's shape with an interface or a type alias. They are nearly interchangeable for this purpose; teams usually pick one and stay consistent.

TypeScript
interface Order {
  id: string;
  status: 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled';  // a union of literals
  totalCents: number;
  customer: Customer;
  trackingNumber?: string;                    // optional
  readonly createdAt: Date;                   // cannot be reassigned
}

interface Customer {
  id: string;
  email: string;
}

// The same thing as a type alias:
type OrderStatus = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled';

Now TypeScript enforces the shape. Reading order.totl is an error. Assigning status = 'shipped' is an error, because 'shipped' is not in the union. Forgetting totalCents when building an order is an error. This is the type system doing its job: the shape of your core nouns becomes impossible to get wrong.

Practical example

Turning a database row into an API response, dropping internal fields.

TypeScript
interface OrderRow {
  id: string;
  status: OrderStatus;
  total_cents: number;    // snake_case from the database
  internal_notes: string; // must NOT go to the client
  created_at: Date;
}

interface OrderResponse {
  id: string;
  status: OrderStatus;
  totalCents: number;     // camelCase for the API
  createdAt: string;      // ISO string for JSON
}

function toResponse(row: OrderRow): OrderResponse {
  return {
    id: row.id,
    status: row.status,
    totalCents: row.total_cents,
    createdAt: row.created_at.toISOString(),
    // internal_notes is deliberately not copied
  };
}

This "mapper" pattern — convert a database row to a response shape — is one you will write hundreds of times. Doing it explicitly (rather than returning the raw row) is how you avoid leaking internal fields like internal_notes or a password hash to clients, which is a real and common security bug.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Mutation surprises. Objects are passed by reference. If function A changes a property of an object that function B still holds, B sees the change. The spread copy ({ ...order }) makes a shallow copy — one level deep. Nested objects are still shared. For a deep copy use structuredClone(order) (built into modern Node).
  • Accessing a property of null/undefined throws Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email'). Use optional chaining order.customer?.email, which yields undefined instead of throwing if customer is missing.
  • Key order is mostly preserved but should not be relied on for logic. Treat objects as unordered maps of key to value.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior defines the core domain objects (Order, Customer, Product) as interfaces first, before writing much logic, because those shapes are the contract everything else depends on. They keep separate types for the database row, the internal domain object, and the API response, and they map between them on purpose — never returning a raw database row to a client, never trusting a raw request body as a domain object. They prefer making changed copies with spread over mutating in place, because shared mutable objects cause the bugs that are hardest to trace.

Common mistakes

  • Returning raw database rows to clients, leaking internal or sensitive fields.
  • Mutating an object that other code still holds, causing spooky action at a distance.
  • Forgetting that spread is a shallow copy and mutating a nested object inside the "copy".
  • Crashing on obj.a.b when a might be missing; use obj.a?.b.

Interview questions

  1. What does spread ({ ...obj }) do, and is it a deep copy?
    Show answerHide answer
    It copies top-level properties into a new object; it is a shallow copy, so nested objects are shared.
  2. How do you safely read a deeply nested property that might be missing?
    Show answerHide answer
    Optional chaining: a?.b?.c, which yields undefined instead of throwing.
  3. Why map a database row to a response object instead of returning it directly?
    Show answerHide answer
    To control which fields leave the system (security) and to translate naming and date formats for the API contract.

Practical exercise

Write a function publicProfile(user) where the user object has id, email, passwordHash and createdAt. Return an object with only id, email and createdAt (as an ISO string), and prove with a TypeScript type that passwordHash cannot appear in the return type. Acceptance criteria: changing the function to include passwordHash must cause a compile error.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
interface User {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  passwordHash: string;
  createdAt: Date;
}

// The public shape. `passwordHash?: never` means "this key may never hold a value".
interface PublicProfile {
  id: string;
  email: string;
  createdAt: string; // ISO string, ready for JSON
  passwordHash?: never;
}

function publicProfile(user: User): PublicProfile {
  return {
    id: user.id,
    email: user.email,
    createdAt: user.createdAt.toISOString(),
  };
}

const user: User = {
  id: 'usr_42',
  email: 'alice@example.com',
  passwordHash: 'not-a-real-hash',
  createdAt: new Date('2026-11-05T09:30:00Z'),
};
console.log(publicProfile(user));
Text
{
  id: 'usr_42',
  email: 'alice@example.com',
  createdAt: '2026-11-05T09:30:00.000Z'
}

Now prove the acceptance criterion by trying to leak the hash in the two ways people actually do it:

TypeScript
// Attempt 1: the extra field written out in the literal.
function leak1(user: User): PublicProfile {
  return { id: user.id, email: user.email, createdAt: user.createdAt.toISOString(), passwordHash: user.passwordHash };
}

// Attempt 2: the sneaky one, via spread.
function leak2(user: User): PublicProfile {
  return { ...user, createdAt: user.createdAt.toISOString() };
}

Add both functions below the two interfaces and run npx tsc --noEmit --strict public-profile.ts. It rejects both (your line numbers depend on your file):

Text
public-profile.ts(19,85): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'undefined'.
public-profile.ts(24,3): error TS2322: Type '{ id: string; email: string; passwordHash: string; createdAt: string; }' is not assignable to type 'PublicProfile'.
  Types of property 'passwordHash' are incompatible.
    Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'undefined'.

Why passwordHash?: never is needed: without it, TypeScript only catches attempt 1. Its "excess property check" runs on properties you write out in an object literal, but not on properties that arrive through a spread or from another variable. So with a plain { id; email; createdAt } type, attempt 2 compiles, and the hash goes out in the JSON. Declaring the key as optional never turns "this key is not part of the type" into "this key is forbidden", and the compiler then checks it however the object was built. (The message mentions undefined because an optional never property can only ever be missing.)

The trap most learners fall into is Omit<User, 'passwordHash'>. It reads like a guarantee, but it only removes the key from the type; it does not forbid it, so the spread version still compiles. The real defence is the habit from the mapper above: build the response field by field, never by spreading the database row (1.5.1).

Check it yourself: paste the two leak functions into your file and run npx tsc --noEmit --strict on it; both must fail. Then delete passwordHash?: never from PublicProfile and run it again: attempt 2 now compiles, which shows why the line is there.

1.5.2 Arrays and the methods you will actually use

Concept

An array is an ordered list of values. An order has a list of items; a page of results is a list of orders; a user has a list of addresses. Arrays hold those lists. The array methods — functions that live on every array — are how you transform lists without writing manual loops, and they are the single most-used tool in day-to-day backend code.

Why does it exist?

Almost all backend work is "take a list, turn it into another list, or boil it down to one value". Take the order items, turn each into a line total (a transform), keep only the in-stock ones (a filter), and sum them (a reduction). You could write for loops for all of this, but the array methods say what you mean in one readable line and avoid the off-by-one errors manual loops are famous for.

Mental model

Imagine an assembly line. map is a station that does the same operation to every item and passes each along (10 items in, 10 items out). filter is a gate that lets some items through and drops others (10 in, maybe 6 out). reduce is the station at the end that combines everything into a single result (10 in, 1 out). find is a worker who grabs the first item matching a description and stops looking.

How it works — the core methods

TypeScript
interface Item { productId: string; quantity: number; priceCents: number; inStock: boolean; }

const items: Item[] = [
  { productId: 'p1', quantity: 2, priceCents: 1000, inStock: true },
  { productId: 'p2', quantity: 1, priceCents: 2500, inStock: false },
  { productId: 'p3', quantity: 3, priceCents: 500, inStock: true },
];

// map: transform each element. Here, item -> line total in cents.
const lineTotals = items.map((item) => item.quantity * item.priceCents);
// [2000, 2500, 1500]
