// filter: keep elements that pass a test.
const available = items.filter((item) => item.inStock);
// [p1, p3]

// reduce: collapse to one value. The 0 is the starting accumulator.
const subtotalCents = items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.quantity * item.priceCents, 0);
// 6000

// find: first element matching a test, or undefined.
const expensive = items.find((item) => item.priceCents >= 2000);
// the p2 item

// some / every: do any / do all match?
const hasOutOfStock = items.some((item) => !item.inStock); // true
const allHaveQuantity = items.every((item) => item.quantity > 0); // true

// sort: reorder. The comparator returns negative, zero or positive.
const byPriceAsc = [...items].sort((a, b) => a.priceCents - b.priceCents);

Two rules that save you from bugs: map, filter, some, every, find, reduce do not change the original array — they return a new array or value. But sort and reverse mutate the original, which is why we copy first with [...items] before sorting. Forgetting this and sorting an array that other code depends on is a real production bug.

Chaining

Methods return arrays (except reduce/find/some/every), so you can chain them into a readable pipeline:

TypeScript
const inStockSubtotalCents = items
  .filter((item) => item.inStock)
  .map((item) => item.quantity * item.priceCents)
  .reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);
// filter to in-stock, turn each into a line total, sum them -> 3500

Read it top to bottom as a sentence: "of the items, keep the in-stock ones, turn each into a line total, and add them up." That readability is the whole point.

Typing arrays

TypeScript
const ids: string[] = ['a', 'b', 'c'];       // array of strings
const totals: number[] = [100, 200];          // array of numbers
const orders: Order[] = [];                    // array of Order objects
const matrix: number[][] = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];   // array of arrays

Practical example — building an order summary

TypeScript
interface CartLine { productId: string; name: string; unitCents: number; qty: number; }

function summarize(lines: CartLine[]) {
  const subtotalCents = lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.unitCents * l.qty, 0);
  const itemCount = lines.reduce((s, l) => s + l.qty, 0);
  const names = lines.map((l) => l.name);
  return { subtotalCents, itemCount, names };
}

Production scenario

An endpoint returns the top 10 products by revenue for a dashboard. You fetch the raw sales rows, map each to { productId, revenue }, reduce into a per-product total using an object keyed by product id, turn that back into an array, sort by revenue descending, and slice(0, 10). The whole transformation is maybe eight lines and reads like its own description. The alternative — nested for loops with manual index bookkeeping — is longer, harder to read, and where off-by-one bugs live.

Failure scenario

At 09:00 a reporting endpoint starts returning the wrong order of results intermittently. The cause: the code called allOrders.sort(...) on an array that was also cached and shared across requests. sort mutated the shared array in place, so two concurrent requests sorting by different fields corrupted each other's data. The fix was one character of intent: [...allOrders].sort(...), sorting a copy. The lesson — know which methods mutate — is exactly the kind of thing that separates working code from correct code.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • sort without a comparator sorts as strings, so [10, 2, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 2]. Always pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
  • find returns undefined when nothing matches; using the result without checking throws.
  • reduce with no initial value throws on an empty array; always pass the initial accumulator.
  • map over a huge array builds a whole second array in memory; for millions of rows, stream instead (Part 13).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reaches for map/filter/reduce by default and writes a manual for loop only when they need early exit for performance, or index arithmetic, or when the loop body has side effects that read awkwardly in a method. They always pass a comparator to sort, always copy before sorting shared data, and always provide reduce's initial value. They are also aware of the cost: these methods create new arrays, which is fine for a cart of 20 items and wrong for a stream of 20 million, where they switch to streaming.

Common mistakes

  • sort without a comparator (string sort) on numbers.
  • Sorting a shared array in place and corrupting other code.
  • Using find's result without handling undefined.
  • reduce with no initial value on a possibly-empty array.
  • Reaching for forEach to build a result, mutating an outer variable, when map or reduce says it more clearly.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between map and forEach?
    Show answerHide answer
    map returns a new array of transformed values; forEach returns nothing and is used only for side effects. Prefer map when you want a result.
  2. Which array methods mutate the original?
    Show answerHide answer
    sort, reverse, splice, push, pop, shift, unshift, fill. The transforming methods (map, filter, slice, concat) do not.
  3. How does sort order values by default, and why is that a trap?
    Show answerHide answer
    Lexicographically (as strings), so numbers sort wrong without a comparator.
  4. What does reduce do and what is its initial value for?
    Show answerHide answer
    It collapses an array to one value by repeatedly combining; the initial value seeds the accumulator and prevents errors on empty arrays.

Practical exercise

Given an array of order objects each with status and totalCents, write one chained expression that computes the total revenue of only the 'paid' orders. Then write a second expression that returns the three highest-value paid orders. Acceptance criteria: the original array is not mutated, and both handle an empty input array without throwing.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
interface Order {
  id: string;
  status: 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled';
  totalCents: number;
}

// readonly Order[]: the compiler now refuses .sort(), .push() and friends on this array.
const orders: readonly Order[] = Object.freeze([
  { id: 'ord_1', status: 'paid', totalCents: 4299 },
  { id: 'ord_2', status: 'pending', totalCents: 1500 },
  { id: 'ord_3', status: 'paid', totalCents: 12900 },
  { id: 'ord_4', status: 'cancelled', totalCents: 99900 },
  { id: 'ord_5', status: 'paid', totalCents: 2500 },
  { id: 'ord_6', status: 'paid', totalCents: 7800 },
]);

// 1. Revenue of paid orders. The 0 makes an empty input return 0 instead of throwing.
const paidRevenueCents = orders
  .filter((o) => o.status === 'paid')
  .reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.totalCents, 0);

// 2. Three highest-value paid orders. filter() returns a NEW array, so sorting it is safe.
const topThreePaid = orders
  .filter((o) => o.status === 'paid')
  .sort((a, b) => b.totalCents - a.totalCents)
  .slice(0, 3);

console.log(paidRevenueCents);
console.log(topThreePaid.map((o) => `${o.id}=${o.totalCents}`));
console.log(orders.map((o) => o.id).join(',')); // original order untouched

// Empty input: no throw, sensible results.
const none: readonly Order[] = [];
console.log(none.filter((o) => o.status === 'paid').reduce((s, o) => s + o.totalCents, 0));
console.log(none.filter((o) => o.status === 'paid').sort((a, b) => b.totalCents - a.totalCents).slice(0, 3));
Text
27499
[ 'ord_3=12900', 'ord_6=7800', 'ord_1=4299' ]
ord_1,ord_2,ord_3,ord_4,ord_5,ord_6
0
[]

Why it is right: both expressions start with filter, which always returns a new array, so the sort that follows reorders that copy and never the original. b.totalCents - a.totalCents is negative when b is smaller, which puts larger totals first (descending). slice(0, 3) takes at most three, so a list with only two paid orders simply returns two. The 0 passed to reduce is the starting sum: on an empty list reduce returns it instead of throwing TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value. Note that the big cancelled order (99900) is correctly left out of both answers.

The trap most learners fall into is writing the steps in the other order: orders.sort(...).filter(...). The result looks the same, but sort ran on the original array and reordered it for every other piece of code that holds it, which is the shared-cache incident from the failure scenario above. Another classic is the comparator (a, b) => a.totalCents < b.totalCents, which returns a boolean instead of a number and sorts unpredictably.

Check it yourself: the readonly Order[] type and Object.freeze are the test. Write orders.sort((a, b) => b.totalCents - a.totalCents) and the compiler stops you with Property 'sort' does not exist on type 'readonly Order[]'; if you sneak past the compiler with a cast, the frozen array throws a TypeError at runtime instead of being silently reordered. On Node 20 and later you can also write .toSorted(...), which always returns a sorted copy.

1.5.3 Maps, Sets and when to use them

Concept

A Map is a collection of key-value pairs where keys can be any type (not just strings). A Set is a collection of unique values. They complement objects and arrays: use a Map for a lookup table, a Set for "have I seen this before?".

How it works

TypeScript
// Map: fast lookup by key.
const priceByProduct = new Map<string, number>();
priceByProduct.set('p1', 1000);
priceByProduct.set('p2', 2500);
priceByProduct.get('p1');        // 1000
priceByProduct.has('p3');        // false
priceByProduct.size;             // 2

// Set: uniqueness and membership tests.
const seenOrderIds = new Set<string>();
seenOrderIds.add('ord_1');
seenOrderIds.add('ord_1');       // ignored, already present
seenOrderIds.has('ord_1');       // true
seenOrderIds.size;               // 1

// De-duplicate an array in one line:
const unique = [...new Set(['a', 'b', 'a', 'c'])]; // ['a', 'b', 'c']

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Reaching the right collection is a small decision with a real performance consequence. Checking array.includes(x) scans the whole array every time (slow for large lists); a Set.has(x) is near-instant. Building a lookup by scanning an array inside a loop is accidentally quadratic; building a Map once and looking up is linear. For the data structures behind these (hash tables), see Part 10; here, the habit is: list of things to iterate is an array, lookup by key is a Map, uniqueness or membership is a Set.

Interview questions

  1. When would you use a Map instead of a plain object?
    Show answerHide answer
    When keys are not strings, when you need reliable insertion order and size, or when you add and remove keys frequently. Objects are fine for fixed, string-keyed shapes.
  2. Why is Set.has better than array.includes for repeated membership tests?
    Show answerHide answer
    Set.has is roughly constant time; array.includes scans the array each call, which is slow for large lists and can make an algorithm quadratic.

Practical exercise

You have 100,000 order IDs already processed (in an array) and a new batch of 10,000. Write code that returns only the new batch IDs not already processed, using a Set so it runs in linear time. Acceptance criteria: do not use array.includes inside a loop.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
// Test data: 100,000 processed ids, and a batch of 10,000 where half were already seen.
const processedIds: string[] = Array.from({ length: 100_000 }, (_, i) => `ord_${i}`);
const batch: string[] = Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, i) => `ord_${95_000 + i}`);

function newIdsOnly(processed: readonly string[], incoming: readonly string[]): string[] {
  const seen = new Set(processed);                  // one pass: O(n)
  return incoming.filter((id) => !seen.has(id));    // one pass, O(1) per lookup: O(m)
}

let start = performance.now();
const fresh = newIdsOnly(processedIds, batch);
console.log(`Set:      ${fresh.length} new ids in ${(performance.now() - start).toFixed(1)} ms`);
console.log(fresh[0], fresh[fresh.length - 1]);

// For comparison only: the slow version the exercise forbids.
start = performance.now();
const slow = batch.filter((id) => !processedIds.includes(id));
console.log(`includes: ${slow.length} new ids in ${(performance.now() - start).toFixed(1)} ms`);
Text
Set:      5000 new ids in 7.7 ms
ord_100000 ord_104999
includes: 5000 new ids in 3263.0 ms

(Timings are from one laptop run; yours will differ, but the gap will not.)

Why it is right: building the Set touches each of the 100,000 processed ids once. After that, seen.has(id) answers in roughly constant time, because a Set is a hash table: it jumps straight to where the id would be instead of scanning. The whole job is about 100,000 + 10,000 steps. The includes version scans up to 100,000 ids for each of the 10,000 batch ids, up to a billion comparisons, which is why it is about 400 times slower here and gets worse as either list grows.

The trap most learners fall into is building the Set in the wrong place: batch.filter((id) => !new Set(processedIds).has(id)). It uses a Set, so it looks right, but it rebuilds a 100,000-entry set for every one of the 10,000 ids, and is even slower than includes. Build the lookup once, outside the loop. A second point to decide: if the batch itself contains the same id twice, this keeps both copies. If you need each new id only once, add each id to seen as you keep it.

Check it yourself: the expected answer is 5,000 ids, from ord_100000 to ord_104999, because the batch runs from ord_95000 to ord_104999 and everything below ord_100000 was already processed. Then double the size of processedIds and run again: the Set time barely moves, while the includes time roughly doubles.

1.6 Control flow

1.6.1 Conditionals and branching

Concept

Control flow is how a program decides what to do next. Conditionals (if, else, switch) choose between paths. Loops (for, while) repeat. Together they turn a static list of statements into a program that reacts to its data.

Why does it exist?

Real logic is full of decisions. Is the order paid? Then ship it. Is the user an admin? Then allow the delete. Is the inventory zero? Then reject the purchase. Without branching, every program would do exactly the same thing every time regardless of its input, which is to say it would not be a program at all.

How it works

TypeScript
function describeOrder(status: OrderStatus): string {
  if (status === 'paid') {
    return 'ready to ship';
  } else if (status === 'pending') {
    return 'awaiting payment';
  } else {
    return 'closed';
  }
}

The ternary operator is a compact if/else that yields a value:

TypeScript
const label = isPaid ? 'Paid' : 'Unpaid';

switch is cleaner than a long if/else if chain when branching on one value:

TypeScript
function nextStatus(status: OrderStatus): OrderStatus {
  switch (status) {
    case 'pending':
      return 'paid';
    case 'paid':
      return 'paid';        // already paid, no change
    case 'cancelled':
      return 'cancelled';
    default:
      // With a union type, TypeScript ensures every case is handled.
      throw new Error(`unknown status: ${status}`);
  }
}

The default case with a union type gives you exhaustiveness checking: if someone later adds 'refunded' to OrderStatus and forgets to handle it, TypeScript can flag the gap (with the never trick shown in 1.7). This is a quiet superpower — the compiler reminds you to update every switch when the set of statuses grows.

Guard clauses

A guard clause handles the exceptional or invalid case first and returns early, so the main logic is not buried inside nested ifs. Senior code is full of guard clauses.

TypeScript
// Nested, hard to read:
function charge(order: Order) {
  if (order.status === 'pending') {
    if (order.totalCents > 0) {
      // ... the real work, two levels deep
    }
  }
}

// Guard clauses, flat and clear:
function chargeBetter(order: Order) {
  if (order.status !== 'pending') throw new Error('order not pending');
  if (order.totalCents <= 0) throw new Error('nothing to charge');
  // ... the real work, at the top level
}

Practical example — an order state machine

A state machine lists which transitions are allowed. This pattern prevents illegal states, like shipping a cancelled order. We draw it as a diagram because that is how backend engineers reason about states.

TypeScript
type Status = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled' | 'refunded';

const allowed: Record<Status, Status[]> = {
  pending: ['paid', 'cancelled'],
  paid: ['shipped', 'refunded'],
  shipped: ['delivered'],
  delivered: [],
  cancelled: [],
  refunded: [],
};

function canTransition(from: Status, to: Status): boolean {
  return allowed[from].includes(to);
}
canTransition('pending', 'shipped'); // false: must be paid first

This data-driven approach (a lookup table of allowed transitions) is cleaner than a tangle of ifs and is easy to extend. We return to state machines in Part 73.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior keeps the happy path at the top indentation level and pushes error and edge cases into guard clauses at the top of the function. They prefer switch with exhaustiveness checking over long if/else chains on a single value, because the compiler then forces every branch to be handled when the set of values grows. They model important state changes as explicit state machines rather than scattering if (status === ...) checks across the codebase, because scattered checks drift out of sync and allow illegal states.

Common mistakes

  • Deeply nested ifs instead of guard clauses; hard to read and easy to get the logic wrong.
  • switch with a missing break in plain JavaScript (falling through to the next case unintentionally); in the return-per-case style above this cannot happen.
  • Scattering status checks everywhere instead of one state machine, so illegal transitions slip through.

Interview questions

  1. What is a guard clause and why use it?
    Show answerHide answer
    An early return for an invalid or edge case, keeping the main logic unindented and readable.
  2. What is exhaustiveness checking in a switch?
    Show answerHide answer
    Using a union type and a never default so the compiler forces you to handle every case, catching missed branches when the union grows.

Practical exercise

Implement transition(order, to) that uses the allowed table above, throws a clear error for an illegal transition, and returns a new order object (not mutated) with the updated status. Acceptance criteria: adding a new status to the Status union without updating allowed must cause a TypeScript error.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
type Status = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'shipped' | 'delivered' | 'cancelled' | 'refunded';

interface Order {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly status: Status;
  readonly totalCents: number;
}

// Record<Status, ...> demands one key per member of the union.
const allowed: Record<Status, readonly Status[]> = {
  pending: ['paid', 'cancelled'],
  paid: ['shipped', 'refunded'],
  shipped: ['delivered'],
  delivered: [],
  cancelled: [],
  refunded: [],
};

class IllegalTransitionError extends Error {
  constructor(orderId: string, from: Status, to: Status) {
    super(`order ${orderId}: cannot go from '${from}' to '${to}' (allowed: ${allowed[from].join(', ') || 'none'})`);
    this.name = 'IllegalTransitionError';
  }
}

function transition(order: Order, to: Status): Order {
  if (!allowed[order.status].includes(to)) {
    throw new IllegalTransitionError(order.id, order.status, to);
  }
  return { ...order, status: to }; // a new object; the input is untouched
}

const placed: Order = { id: 'ord_1001', status: 'pending', totalCents: 4299 };
const paid = transition(placed, 'paid');
console.log(placed.status, '->', paid.status, '| same object?', placed === paid);

try {
  transition(placed, 'shipped');
} catch (err) {
  console.log((err as Error).message);
}
try {
  transition({ ...paid, status: 'delivered' }, 'refunded');
} catch (err) {
  console.log((err as Error).message);
}
Text
pending -> paid | same object? false
order ord_1001: cannot go from 'pending' to 'shipped' (allowed: paid, cancelled)
order ord_1001: cannot go from 'delivered' to 'refunded' (allowed: none)

Now the acceptance test. Add 'disputed' to the Status union and change nothing else; npx tsc --noEmit --strict fails:

Text
transition.ts(10,7): error TS2741: Property 'disputed' is missing in type '{ pending: ("cancelled" | "paid")[]; paid: ("refunded" | "shipped")[]; shipped: "delivered"[]; delivered: never[]; cancelled: never[]; refunded: never[]; }' but required in type 'Record<Status, readonly Status[]>'.

Why it is right: Record<Status, readonly Status[]> means "an object with exactly one key for every member of Status". The day someone adds a status, the table stops compiling until they decide which transitions the new status allows. The guard clause throws before anything changes, and the error names the order, both states and the legal options, so the log line explains itself. { ...order, status: to } builds a new object; placed === paid is false, and placed.status is still pending. The readonly fields make order.status = to a compile error, so nobody can "simplify" it into a mutation later.

The trap most learners fall into is typing the table loosely, as { [key: string]: Status[] } or Partial<Record<Status, Status[]>>. Both compile today and both quietly drop the exhaustiveness check, which is the whole point of the exercise. Then allowed['disputed'] is undefined at runtime and .includes throws a confusing TypeError in production instead of a clear compile error on your laptop.

Check it yourself: run the file and compare the three lines, then add 'disputed' to the union and confirm the compile error appears.

1.6.2 Loops

Concept

Loops repeat a block of code. The main forms are for (counted), for...of (over the values of an array or other iterable), for...in (over the keys of an object — use sparingly), and while (until a condition is false).

How it works

TypeScript
const ids = ['a', 'b', 'c'];

// for...of: the modern default for iterating values.
for (const id of ids) {
  console.log(id);
}

// Classic for: when you need the index.
for (let i = 0; i < ids.length; i++) {
  console.log(i, ids[i]);
}

// while: when you do not know the count in advance.
let remaining = 3;
while (remaining > 0) {
  remaining--;
}

// for...in iterates object KEYS (as strings). Rarely what you want for arrays.
const prices = { p1: 1000, p2: 2500 };
for (const key in prices) {
  console.log(key, prices[key as keyof typeof prices]);
}

break exits a loop early; continue skips to the next iteration. Use break when you have found what you are looking for and need not continue — this is the main reason to write a manual loop instead of an array method.

When to use a loop vs an array method

Text
Transform every element into a new value        -> map
Keep some elements                               -> filter
Combine into one value                           -> reduce
Find the first match, then stop                  -> find (or for...of + break)
Do a side effect for each (log, call an API)     -> for...of
Need the index, or step by 2, or go backwards    -> classic for
Repeat until a condition with no fixed count     -> while

Practical example — retry with a loop

TypeScript
async function withRetry<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>, maxAttempts = 3): Promise<T> {
  let lastError: unknown;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn();           // success: return immediately
    } catch (err) {
      lastError = err;
      // backoff would go here (Part 2)
    }
  }
  throw lastError;                 // all attempts failed
}

A counted for loop is the right tool here because we need the attempt number and an early return on success.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Infinite loops. A while (true) with no break, or a for whose condition never becomes false, hangs the process. On a single-threaded Node server, an infinite loop freezes the entire server for every user, not just one request (Part 13).
  • for...in over arrays iterates indices as strings and includes inherited properties; use for...of for array values.
  • Modifying an array while iterating it with a classic for can skip or repeat elements. Build a new array instead.
  • await inside a loop runs iterations one after another (serial). If they are independent, that is needlessly slow; use Promise.all (Part 2) to run them together.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior defaults to array methods for data transformation and reserves explicit loops for early exit, index math, and side effects that read more clearly as a loop. They are acutely aware that on Node a long synchronous loop blocks the event loop and therefore every concurrent request (Part 13), so a loop over a million rows gets rewritten to stream or to yield control. They watch for the accidental-serial-await-in-a-loop pattern, one of the most common causes of a slow endpoint.

Common mistakes

  • await in a loop for independent work, making an endpoint 10x slower than needed.
  • A long synchronous loop blocking the event loop and freezing the server.
  • for...in on arrays.
  • Mutating the array being iterated.

Interview questions

  1. Why can a long synchronous loop freeze an entire Node server?
    Show answerHide answer
    Node runs your JavaScript on one thread; while the loop runs, the event loop cannot handle any other request (see Part 13).
  2. What is wrong with for (const x of items) { await save(x); } when saves are independent?
    Show answerHide answer
    It runs serially; await Promise.all(items.map(save)) runs them concurrently and is far faster.
  3. When do you write a manual for loop instead of map/filter?
    Show answerHide answer
    When you need early exit (break), the index, custom stepping, or side effects that are clearer as a loop.

Practical exercise

Rewrite a serial loop that fetches 20 product details one at a time (for...of with await) into a concurrent version using Promise.all, and explain in one sentence why the concurrent version is faster. Acceptance criteria: the concurrent version preserves the order of results.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
interface Product {
  id: number;
  name: string;
}

function wait(ms: number): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

// A pretend product API: each call takes 30-70 ms, in random order.
async function fetchProduct(id: number): Promise<Product> {
  await wait(30 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 40));
  return { id, name: `product-${id}` };
}

const ids = Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => i + 1);

// Before: serial. Each await waits for the previous fetch to finish.
async function fetchAllSerial(productIds: number[]): Promise<Product[]> {
  const results: Product[] = [];
  for (const id of productIds) {
    results.push(await fetchProduct(id));
  }
  return results;
}

// After: concurrent. Start all 20 fetches first, then wait for all of them.
async function fetchAllConcurrent(productIds: number[]): Promise<Product[]> {
  return Promise.all(productIds.map((id) => fetchProduct(id)));
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  let start = Date.now();
  const serial = await fetchAllSerial(ids);
  console.log(`serial:     ${serial.length} products in ${Date.now() - start} ms`);

  start = Date.now();
  const concurrent = await fetchAllConcurrent(ids);
  console.log(`concurrent: ${concurrent.length} products in ${Date.now() - start} ms`);

  // Order check: results come back in the order of the input ids, not finish order.
  const inOrder = concurrent.every((product, index) => product.id === ids[index]);
  console.log('order preserved:', inOrder, concurrent.slice(0, 3).map((p) => p.id));
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
Text
serial:     20 products in 1067 ms
concurrent: 20 products in 69 ms
order preserved: true [ 1, 2, 3 ]

The one sentence: the concurrent version is faster because all 20 requests are waiting at the same time, so the total is roughly the slowest single request (about 70 ms) instead of the sum of all twenty (about 1 second).

Why the order is preserved: Promise.all returns its results in the same positions as the promises you gave it, whatever order they finish in. Product 7 may arrive before product 2, but it still lands at index 6. The random delays in fetchProduct exist precisely to prove this: finish order is shuffled, result order is not. The code is wrapped in main() because top-level await only works when the file runs as an ES module (Part 2 explains async/await in depth).

The trap most learners fall into is ids.forEach(async (id) => results.push(await fetchProduct(id))). forEach does not wait for async callbacks, so the function returns an empty array immediately, and when results do arrive they are pushed in finish order, not input order. The second trap is applying this pattern without limit: 20 concurrent calls are fine, but 5,000 at once can exhaust a connection pool or trip a rate limit; the worked answer in 2.3 shows how to cap concurrency. And remember that Promise.all rejects as soon as any one call fails; use Promise.allSettled when partial results are acceptable.

Check it yourself: run it a few times with npx tsx. The timings change slightly every run, but order preserved: true must never change.

1.7 Modules, interfaces and generics

1.7.1 Modules: splitting code across files

Concept

A module is a single file of code that explicitly states what it shares (export) and what it needs from other files (import). Modules are how a backend of thousands of lines stays organized — each file does one job and declares its public surface.

Why does it exist?

One giant file is unmaintainable. Modules let you put the order logic in orders.service.ts, the shipping logic in shipping.service.ts, and have each use the other through clear imports. The export/import boundary is also where you decide what is public (part of the module's contract) and what is private (an internal helper nobody else should call).

How it works

Modern JavaScript and TypeScript use ES modules (import/export). You will also see the older CommonJS (require/module.exports) in Node code; recognize it but write ES modules in new code.

TypeScript
// money.ts  -- a module that exports helpers
export function formatCents(cents: number): string {
  return `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
}

export const USD = 'USD';

// A default export (one per file, imported without braces):
export default function sum(amounts: number[]): number {
  return amounts.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
}
TypeScript
// orders.ts  -- imports from money.ts
import sum, { formatCents, USD } from './money';   // default + named imports

const total = sum([1000, 2500]);
console.log(formatCents(total)); // "$35.00"

Named exports (in braces) are the common case; prefer them because they are explicit and tooling can rename them safely. The file path in the import is relative (./money) for your own files and a bare name ('@nestjs/common') for installed packages.

Barrel files and import organization

A "barrel" is an index.ts that re-exports from several files so callers import from one place. Useful in moderation; overused, it creates circular imports.

TypeScript
// orders/index.ts
export * from './orders.service';
export * from './orders.controller';

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats a module's exports as its public API and keeps it small: export the service, not every helper. They avoid circular imports (file A imports B which imports A), which cause subtle undefined bugs at startup, by keeping dependencies flowing in one direction — controllers depend on services, services depend on repositories, never the reverse. The module boundary is the first and cheapest form of architecture, long before you reach for layers or microservices (Part 15).

Common mistakes

  • Circular imports, causing values to be undefined during module initialization.
  • Exporting internal helpers that should stay private, widening the contract accidentally.
  • Mixing CommonJS require and ES import in ways that break under the module system configured in tsconfig.json.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a named export and a default export?
    Show answerHide answer
    Named exports are imported by name in braces and there can be many; a default export is imported without braces and there is one per file. Named exports are generally preferred for clarity and tooling.
  2. What problem do circular imports cause and how do you avoid them?
    Show answerHide answer
    A value may be undefined when first accessed because one module is still initializing. Avoid them by keeping dependency direction one-way.

Practical exercise

Split a single file containing money formatting, order totalling and a main that prints a summary into three modules (money.ts, orders.ts, main.ts) with explicit exports and imports. Acceptance criteria: main.ts imports only from orders.ts, and orders.ts imports only from money.ts — no circular imports.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
// money.ts: knows about cents and dollars, and nothing else. Imports nothing.
export function formatCents(cents: number): string {
  return `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
}

export function sumCents(amounts: readonly number[]): number {
  return amounts.reduce((total, amount) => total + amount, 0);
}
TypeScript
// orders.ts: order rules. Depends on money.ts only.
import { formatCents, sumCents } from './money';

export interface OrderLine {
  name: string;
  unitCents: number;
  qty: number;
}

export function orderTotalCents(lines: readonly OrderLine[]): number {
  return sumCents(lines.map((line) => line.unitCents * line.qty));
}

// main.ts needs a printable summary; orders.ts produces it, so main never touches money.ts.
export function orderSummaryText(orderId: string, lines: readonly OrderLine[]): string {
  const rows = lines.map((l) => `  ${l.qty} x ${l.name} @ ${formatCents(l.unitCents)}`);
  return [`Order ${orderId}`, ...rows, `  Total: ${formatCents(orderTotalCents(lines))}`].join('\n');
}
TypeScript
// main.ts: the entry point. Depends on orders.ts only.
import { orderSummaryText, type OrderLine } from './orders';

const lines: OrderLine[] = [
  { name: 'Sonic toothbrush', unitCents: 4999, qty: 1 },
  { name: 'Replacement heads (4)', unitCents: 1250, qty: 2 },
];

console.log(orderSummaryText('ord_1001', lines));

Run npx tsx main.ts, then list every import:

Text
$ npx tsx main.ts
Order ord_1001
  1 x Sonic toothbrush @ $49.99
  2 x Replacement heads (4) @ $12.50
  Total: $74.99

$ grep -n "^import" *.ts
main.ts:2:import { orderSummaryText, type OrderLine } from './orders';
orders.ts:2:import { formatCents, sumCents } from './money';

Why it is right: the dependencies form a straight line, main -> orders -> money, and nothing points back. money.ts imports nothing at all, so it can never be part of a cycle, and it could be reused by an invoices module tomorrow. The key design decision is that orders.ts exports a ready-made orderSummaryText, so main.ts gets a formatted summary without ever needing formatCents itself. Each file exports only what its callers need; type OrderLine imports just the type, which is erased at runtime.

The trap most learners fall into is letting main.ts "just quickly" import formatCents from money.ts to print one value. It works, and it breaks the acceptance criterion: main now depends on two layers. The second trap is the cycle: putting a currencyForOrder(order: OrderLine) helper into money.ts means money.ts imports from orders.ts, and you now have orders -> money -> orders, where one module can see the other's exports as undefined while the files are still loading.

Check it yourself: the grep above is the test, with exactly one import line per file and in the right direction. For a bigger project, npx madge --circular --extensions ts . scans every file and reports any import cycle it finds.

1.7.2 Interfaces, type aliases and unions

Concept

We met interfaces in 1.5. Here we complete the picture: interfaces and type aliases describe object shapes; unions describe "one of several"; intersections combine shapes. These are the tools you use to model a domain precisely.

How it works

TypeScript
// Union: a value that is one of several types.
type Id = string | number;
type Status = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled';   // union of string literals

// Intersection: a value that satisfies several shapes at once.
interface Timestamped { createdAt: Date; updatedAt: Date; }
interface Order { id: string; totalCents: number; }
type PersistedOrder = Order & Timestamped;        // has all four fields

// Discriminated union: the pro move for modelling events or results.
type PaymentResult =
  | { kind: 'success'; chargeId: string }
  | { kind: 'declined'; reason: string }
  | { kind: 'error'; message: string };

function handle(result: PaymentResult) {
  switch (result.kind) {
    case 'success':
      return result.chargeId;      // TypeScript knows chargeId exists here
    case 'declined':
      return result.reason;        // and reason here
    case 'error':
      return result.message;
    default:
      // Exhaustiveness: if a new kind is added, this line errors.
      const _never: never = result;
      return _never;
  }
}

The discriminated union (a union of objects that share a common literal field, here kind) is one of the most valuable patterns in TypeScript backend code. It models "a thing that is one of several shapes" — a payment result, a webhook event, a command — and the compiler narrows to the right shape inside each case. The never default gives you exhaustiveness checking for free.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior models the domain with unions so that illegal combinations cannot be represented. Instead of an object with success: boolean, chargeId?: string and reason?: string (where every combination is technically possible, including the nonsensical ones), they use a discriminated union where a success always has a charge id and a decline always has a reason, and nothing else is expressible. "Make illegal states unrepresentable" is the principle; discriminated unions are the main tool for it in TypeScript.

Common mistakes

  • Boolean-and-optional-field soup ({ ok: boolean; data?: T; error?: string }) instead of a discriminated union, allowing impossible combinations.
  • Using interface and type inconsistently across a codebase; pick a convention.

Interview questions

  1. What is a discriminated union and why is it useful?
    Show answerHide answer
    A union of object types sharing a literal "tag" field; the compiler narrows to the correct shape per branch, and it prevents illegal field combinations.
  2. Interface vs type alias — when does it matter?
    Show answerHide answer
    Rarely for plain object shapes; interfaces can be re-opened and are conventional for public contracts, type aliases can express unions and intersections. Consistency matters more than the choice.

Practical exercise

Model a WebhookEvent as a discriminated union with three kinds (order.created, order.paid, order.cancelled), each carrying different fields, and write a process function with exhaustiveness checking. Acceptance criteria: adding a fourth kind without handling it causes a compile error.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
// Each kind carries only the fields that make sense for it.
type WebhookEvent =
  | { type: 'order.created'; orderId: string; customerId: string; totalCents: number }
  | { type: 'order.paid'; orderId: string; chargeId: string; paidAt: string }
  | { type: 'order.cancelled'; orderId: string; reason: 'customer_request' | 'payment_failed' };

// Called only when every kind has been handled; otherwise `event` is not `never` and this fails to compile.
function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`unhandled webhook event: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

function processEvent(event: WebhookEvent): string {
  switch (event.type) {
    case 'order.created':
      return `create order ${event.orderId} for ${event.customerId}, ${event.totalCents} cents`;
    case 'order.paid':
      return `mark ${event.orderId} paid (charge ${event.chargeId})`;
    case 'order.cancelled':
      return `cancel ${event.orderId}: ${event.reason}`;
    default:
      return assertNever(event);
  }
}

const events: WebhookEvent[] = [
  { type: 'order.created', orderId: 'ord_1001', customerId: 'usr_42', totalCents: 4299 },
  { type: 'order.paid', orderId: 'ord_1001', chargeId: 'ch_9f3a', paidAt: '2026-11-05T09:31:00Z' },
  { type: 'order.cancelled', orderId: 'ord_1002', reason: 'customer_request' },
];
for (const event of events) console.log(processEvent(event));
Text
create order ord_1001 for usr_42, 4299 cents
mark ord_1001 paid (charge ch_9f3a)
cancel ord_1002: customer_request

The function is called processEvent rather than process so it does not shadow Node's global process object; the idea is identical.

Now the acceptance test. Add a fourth kind to the union, | { type: 'order.refunded'; orderId: string; amountCents: number }, without adding a case. npx tsc --noEmit --strict fails:

Text
webhooks.ts(22,26): error TS2345: Argument of type '{ type: "order.refunded"; orderId: string; amountCents: number; }' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'.

Why it is right: inside each case, TypeScript narrows event to the one member whose type matches, which is why event.chargeId is allowed under 'order.paid' and would be an error under 'order.cancelled'. After the three handled cases, nothing is left, so in default the type of event is never, and passing it to assertNever(value: never) compiles. Add a fourth kind and event in default becomes that kind, which is not never, so the build fails and names exactly the case you forgot. If a bad value ever slips in at runtime anyway, assertNever throws instead of silently doing nothing.

The trap most learners fall into is a default that returns something harmless, such as return 'ignored'. It compiles today and stays compiling after the union grows, so new events are dropped without a trace. The other trap is typing the field as type: string: then there is nothing to narrow on, and every field has to be optional.

One production note: a real webhook arrives as untrusted JSON, so it is unknown until a validator has checked its shape (1.2.1). Only after that check is it a WebhookEvent.

Check it yourself: run it, then add the order.refunded member and confirm the build fails; add the missing case and it compiles again.

1.7.3 Generics: types that take parameters

Concept

A generic is a type with a blank to fill in. Array<T> is a generic: T is the blank, so Array<string> is an array of strings and Array<Order> is an array of orders. Generics let you write one reusable function or type that works for many element types while staying fully type-safe.

Why does it exist?

Without generics, you would either write a separate firstString, firstNumber, firstOrder for each type (repetitive), or use any and lose all safety. A generic first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined works for every type and keeps the exact type: first(orders) returns Order | undefined, not any.

How it works

TypeScript
// A generic function. T is a placeholder filled in at the call site.
function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined {
  return items.length > 0 ? items[0] : undefined;
}

const o = first([{ id: 'ord_1' }]); // o is typed as { id: string } | undefined
const n = first([1, 2, 3]);          // n is number | undefined

// A generic interface: a reusable "page of results" shape.
interface Page<T> {
  items: T[];
  total: number;
  cursor: string | null;
}

const orderPage: Page<Order> = { items: [], total: 0, cursor: null };

// Constrained generic: T must have an id. "extends" sets the constraint.
function indexById<T extends { id: string }>(items: T[]): Map<string, T> {
  const map = new Map<string, T>();
  for (const item of items) map.set(item.id, item);
  return map;
}

The constraint T extends { id: string } means "T can be any type, as long as it has a string id". That lets the body safely read item.id while still working for any entity with an id.

Practical example — a typed generic repository

This previews a pattern used throughout the book: one generic base repository that every entity's repository extends.

TypeScript
interface Repository<T extends { id: string }> {
  findById(id: string): Promise<T | null>;
  save(entity: T): Promise<T>;
  delete(id: string): Promise<void>;
}

// A concrete repository just fills in T:
type OrderRepository = Repository<Order>;

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior uses generics to remove duplication without sacrificing type safety — the generic Page<T>, the generic Result<T, E>, the generic repository. They do not over-engineer: a generic with four type parameters and nested constraints is usually a sign something is too clever. The rule is "reach for a generic when you are about to copy a function only to change its element type." The tools (Page<T>, Promise<T>, Record<K, V>, Partial<T>, Pick<T, K>) become second nature and let them describe real API shapes exactly.

Common mistakes

  • Using any where a generic would keep the type (function first(items: any[]): any).
  • Over-complicated generics that are harder to read than three concrete versions would be.
  • Forgetting a constraint (T extends ...) and then being unable to touch the value's properties.

Interview questions

  1. What problem do generics solve?
    Show answerHide answer
    Reuse across element types without losing type safety or resorting to any.
  2. What does T extends { id: string } mean?
    Show answerHide answer
    A constraint: T may be any type that has a string id property, letting the function safely use id.
  3. Give a real backend use of a generic type.
    Show answerHide answer
    A Page<T> pagination wrapper, a Result<T, E> type, or a base Repository<T>.

Practical exercise

Write a generic function groupBy<T, K extends string>(items: T[], keyFn: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]> that groups array elements by a computed key. Test it by grouping orders by status. Acceptance criteria: the return type correctly reflects the key type, and the original array is not mutated.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
function groupBy<T, K extends string>(items: readonly T[], keyFn: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]> {
  const groups = {} as Record<K, T[]>; // starts empty; filled below
  for (const item of items) {
    const key = keyFn(item);
    (groups[key] ??= []).push(item);    // create the bucket on first use, then add
  }
  return groups;
}

type OrderStatus = 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled';
interface Order {
  id: string;
  status: OrderStatus;
  totalCents: number;
}

const orders: Order[] = [
  { id: 'ord_1', status: 'paid', totalCents: 4299 },
  { id: 'ord_2', status: 'pending', totalCents: 1500 },
  { id: 'ord_3', status: 'paid', totalCents: 12900 },
  { id: 'ord_4', status: 'cancelled', totalCents: 2500 },
];
const before = JSON.stringify(orders);

const byStatus = groupBy(orders, (o) => o.status); // Record<OrderStatus, Order[]>
console.log(Object.keys(byStatus));
console.log(byStatus.paid.map((o) => o.id));
console.log('original unchanged:', JSON.stringify(orders) === before);

// The key type flows through: a typo is a compile error, not undefined at runtime.
// byStatus.payed;  // Error: Property 'payed' does not exist on type 'Record<OrderStatus, Order[]>'

// The honest caveat: a status with no orders has no bucket at runtime.
const onlyPaid = groupBy(orders.filter((o) => o.status === 'paid'), (o) => o.status);
console.log(onlyPaid.pending); // undefined, although the type says Order[]
Text
[ 'paid', 'pending', 'cancelled' ]
[ 'ord_1', 'ord_3' ]
original unchanged: true
undefined

Why it is right: TypeScript infers K from what keyFn returns. o.status has the type 'pending' | 'paid' | 'cancelled', so K becomes that union and the result is Record<OrderStatus, Order[]>. That is what makes byStatus.paid autocomplete and byStatus.payed a compile error. The function only reads items (the readonly T[] parameter makes sure of it) and builds new arrays, so the input is untouched, which the JSON.stringify comparison checks. groups[key] ??= [] means "if there is no bucket for this key yet, create an empty one", and the expression returns the bucket, ready for push.

The last two lines show the one honest weakness of the signature the exercise asks for: Record<K, T[]> promises a bucket for every key, but a status with no orders simply has none, so onlyPaid.pending is undefined while its type claims Order[]. Partial<Record<K, T[]>> is the truthful return type, and it is what the built-in Object.groupBy (Node 21 and later) returns. With it, the compiler makes you handle the missing bucket (byStatus.pending ?? []).

The trap most learners fall into is writing it with reduce and spread: items.reduce((acc, item) => ({ ...acc, [keyFn(item)]: [...(acc[keyFn(item)] ?? []), item] }), {}). It looks elegant, but it copies the whole accumulator for every item, which is quadratic and very slow on 100,000 rows. The second trap is a key function that returns a plain string (for example when status is typed as string), which makes K just string and loses the precise keys.

Check it yourself: run it and compare the four lines, then uncomment the byStatus.payed line and confirm the compile error.

1.8 Classes and object-oriented code

So far we have modelled data with interfaces and plain objects, and behaviour with functions. That is enough for a surprising amount of backend code. But the moment you open a NestJS project you will see class everywhere: OrdersController, OrdersService, CreateOrderDto, Order entity. This section teaches classes from the ground up, the one JavaScript trap that comes with them (this), and the handful of design ideas (composition, SOLID) that decide whether class-based code stays pleasant or turns into a maze. It ends by showing exactly how these pieces become a NestJS service.

1.8.1 What a class is: fields, constructor, methods and new

Concept

A class is a blueprint for objects that carry both data (fields) and behaviour (methods) together. You write the blueprint once; new stamps out as many objects (called instances) as you need. A constructor is the special method that runs once when an instance is created and sets its starting state.

Why does it exist?

Imagine a shopping cart. With only plain objects and functions, the cart's data (lines) lives in one place and the rules (addItem, totalCents) live somewhere else. Nothing stops another file from pushing a line with a negative quantity straight into cart.lines. A class keeps the data and the rules that protect it in one unit, so the only way to change a cart is through its methods, and the methods can enforce the rules every time.

Mental model

Imagine a cookie cutter. The class is the cutter; each new ShoppingCart() is a cookie with the same shape but its own dough, so adding an item to Asha's cart does not touch Ravi's.

How it works

TypeScript
interface CartLine {
  sku: string;
  unitCents: number;
  qty: number;
}

class ShoppingCart {
  // Fields: the data each instance carries.
  readonly customerId: string;
  private lines: CartLine[] = [];          // every new cart starts empty

  // The constructor runs once, when `new ShoppingCart(...)` is called.
  constructor(customerId: string) {
    this.customerId = customerId;           // `this` is the instance being built
  }

  // Methods: behaviour that reads and changes this instance's data.
  addItem(line: CartLine): void {
    if (line.qty <= 0) throw new Error(`qty must be positive, got ${line.qty}`);
    const existing = this.lines.find((l) => l.sku === line.sku);
    if (existing) existing.qty += line.qty;  // same SKU: merge instead of duplicating
    else this.lines.push({ ...line });       // copy so the caller cannot mutate our line later
  }

  totalCents(): number {
    return this.lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.unitCents * l.qty, 0);
  }

  itemCount(): number {
    return this.lines.reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.qty, 0);
  }
}

const asha = new ShoppingCart('cus_asha');
const ravi = new ShoppingCart('cus_ravi');
asha.addItem({ sku: 'BRUSH-01', unitCents: 4999, qty: 1 });
asha.addItem({ sku: 'BRUSH-01', unitCents: 4999, qty: 1 });
console.log(asha.itemCount(), asha.totalCents()); // 2 9998
console.log(ravi.itemCount());                     // 0: each instance has its own lines

What new ShoppingCart('cus_asha') does, step by step:

  1. Creates a new empty object.
  2. Links that object to ShoppingCart.prototype, the shared object where the methods live. Methods are stored once, not copied into every instance.
  3. Runs the field initialisers (lines = []), then the constructor body, with this pointing at the new object.
  4. Returns the object.

A class exists at runtime (typeof ShoppingCart is 'function'), unlike an interface, which TypeScript erases (1.7.2). It is also a type: function checkout(cart: ShoppingCart) accepts anything with the class's public shape.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting new. ShoppingCart('cus_1') throws TypeError: Class constructor ShoppingCart cannot be invoked without 'new'.
  • Exposing the internal array (getLines() { return this.lines; }). The caller can now push into it and skip every rule. Return a copy ([...this.lines]) or a read-only view.
  • Writing a class with no behaviour, only public fields and getters and setters for each. That is a plain object wearing a costume; an interface is simpler.

1.8.2 this, and how it is bound

Concept

Inside a method, this means "the object this method was called on". The catch is the word called: this is decided at the moment of the call, by how the call is written, not by where the method was defined. Call cart.totalCents() and this is cart. Take the method out of the object and call it on its own, and this is undefined.

Why does it exist?

JavaScript functions are values that can be passed around (1.4). The same function can be attached to many objects, so the language decides this per call. That flexibility is why methods can be shared on the prototype, and it is also the source of the most common class bug in Node code.

Mental model

Imagine a waiter told "bring this table its bill". If the manager says it while standing at table 7, "this table" is table 7. If someone writes the instruction on a card and hands it to a new waiter with no table in sight, "this table" means nothing. Extracting a method is handing over the card without the table.

How it works — the extraction bug

TypeScript
class PriceFormatter {
  constructor(private readonly currency: string) {}

  format(cents: number): string {
    return `${this.currency} ${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}

const formatter = new PriceFormatter('USD');

console.log(formatter.format(1999));       // 'USD 19.99': called on formatter, so this = formatter

const prices = [1999, 500];
console.log(prices.map(formatter.format)); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'currency')

prices.map(formatter.format) passes only the function, not the object. map later calls it as a plain function, so this is undefined. (Class bodies always run in strict mode, which is why this is undefined and not the global object.) The same bug appears whenever a method is handed to someone else to call later: an event listener, a callback to a library, promise.then(service.handle).

The last row deserves a warning: in Node, a timer calls its callback with this set to the internal Timeout object, so instead of a crash you silently read undefined fields. Silent bugs are worse than crashes.

How it works — three fixes

TypeScript
const formatter = new PriceFormatter('USD');
const prices = [1999, 500];

// Fix 1: wrap the call in an arrow function. The call is written as formatter.format(...),
// so this = formatter. Clear, local, and the most common fix.
prices.map((cents) => formatter.format(cents));

// Fix 2: bind. Returns a new function with this permanently set to formatter.
const boundFormat = formatter.format.bind(formatter);
prices.map(boundFormat);

// Fix 3: define the method as an arrow-function field inside the class.
class SafePriceFormatter {
  constructor(private readonly currency: string) {}

  // An arrow function has no `this` of its own; it uses the `this` of the place it was
  // created, which for a field initialiser is the instance being built.
  format = (cents: number): string => `${this.currency} ${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
}

const safe = new SafePriceFormatter('INR');
console.log(prices.map(safe.format)); // [ 'INR 19.99', 'INR 5.00' ]

Each fix has a cost. The arrow wrapper must be written at every call site. An arrow-function field is created once per instance (an own property, not on the shared prototype), so it costs memory across millions of instances, and a subclass cannot reach it with super.format(). Wrapping at the call site is the simplest default.

Production scenario

A payments team passes this.webhookHandler.handle as a callback to a message-queue library: consumer.on('message', this.webhookHandler.handle). In local testing with a fake queue the handler is called directly and works. In staging, the library calls the callback as a plain function, this.repo is undefined inside handle, and every webhook fails with Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'repo'). The fix is one line, consumer.on('message', (msg) => this.webhookHandler.handle(msg)), and the lesson is to treat "I passed a method as a value" as a code-review red flag.

Common mistakes

  • Passing service.method as a callback and expecting this to follow.
  • Using a regular function () {} callback inside a method and expecting it to see the outer this. Use an arrow function, which keeps the outer this.
  • Turning every method into an arrow-function field "just in case". It hides the real rule and breaks super calls in subclasses.

Interview questions

  1. What decides the value of this in a JavaScript method?
    Show answerHide answer
    How the function is called, not where it is defined. obj.m() gives obj; a detached call gives undefined in strict mode.
  2. Why does array.map(obj.method) fail but array.map((x) => obj.method(x)) work?
    Show answerHide answer
    The first passes a bare function, so map calls it without an object; the second writes the call as obj.method(x).
  3. What is the trade-off of arrow-function class fields?
    Show answerHide answer
    this is always the instance, but the function is created per instance and cannot be reached with super.

1.8.3 Access modifiers: public, private, protected, readonly and #private

Concept

Access modifiers say who may read or change a member of a class. They let a class publish a small, safe surface and hide its internals, the same idea as exporting only what callers need from a module (1.7.1).

Modifier Who can access Enforced when
public (the default) Anyone Always allowed
private Only code inside this class Compile time only (TypeScript)
protected This class and its subclasses Compile time only (TypeScript)
readonly Anyone may read; assigned only in the declaration or constructor Compile time only (TypeScript)
#field Only code inside this class body Runtime (JavaScript itself)

Why does it exist?

Without them, any file can reach into an object and break its rules: set a wallet's balance to -500, or reassign an order's id. Modifiers turn "please do not touch this" comments into errors.

How it works — private versus #private

The crucial difference: TypeScript's private, protected and readonly are erased when TypeScript compiles to JavaScript, like every other type annotation (1.2). They protect you while you write code, not while it runs. The # prefix is a real JavaScript feature, enforced by the runtime.

TypeScript
class Wallet {
  #balanceCents = 0;                 // hard private: the runtime itself blocks outside access
  private auditNote = 'opened';      // soft private: TypeScript blocks it, JavaScript does not
  readonly id: string;

  constructor(id: string) {
    this.id = id;
  }

  deposit(cents: number): void {
    if (!Number.isInteger(cents) || cents <= 0) throw new Error('deposit must be a positive integer');
    this.#balanceCents += cents;
  }

  get balanceCents(): number {       // read-only view of the hidden field
    return this.#balanceCents;
  }
}

const w = new Wallet('wal_1');
w.deposit(2500);
// w.#balanceCents = 1;      // SyntaxError in JavaScript, compile error in TypeScript
// w.auditNote;              // compile error: 'auditNote' is private
// w.id = 'wal_2';           // compile error: cannot assign to 'id' because it is read-only
console.log(JSON.stringify(w));      // {"auditNote":"opened","id":"wal_1"}  (no balance)
console.log((w as any).auditNote);   // 'opened': the TypeScript check is gone at runtime

Notice the JSON.stringify output. A private field is an ordinary property at runtime, so it appears in JSON, in Object.keys, and in anything that serialises the object, such as a log line or an API response. A # field does not. That matters for a backend: a private passwordHash on a user object will happily appear in a JSON response if the object is returned from a controller as is, whereas #passwordHash would not.

protected is private plus subclasses: a BasePaymentProvider can keep a protected log() helper that subclasses call but outside code cannot.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The default is private readonly for collaborators, private for state, and public only for what callers need. private is a design tool, not a security boundary, so secrets are kept out of logs and responses by an explicit response DTO (6.2) and log redaction, never by a modifier. #private is for when runtime privacy genuinely matters, such as a library used from plain JavaScript. NestJS code conventionally uses TypeScript private, partly because parameter properties (1.8.4) only exist in that form.

Common mistakes

  • Believing private hides a field from JSON.stringify or console.log. It does not.
  • Thinking readonly makes an object deeply immutable. readonly items: string[] stops reassigning items, not items.push(...); use readonly string[] for that (1.5.2).
  • Making everything public "for tests". Test through the public methods; if that is hard, the class probably does too much (1.8.8).

Practical exercise

Extend Wallet with withdraw(cents) that rejects non-positive or non-integer amounts and refuses to go below zero, throwing an InsufficientFundsError that carries the shortfall. Acceptance criteria: the balance can only change through deposit and withdraw, a failed withdrawal leaves the balance unchanged, and the balance never appears in JSON.stringify.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
class InsufficientFundsError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly shortfallCents: number) {
    super(`insufficient funds: short by ${shortfallCents} cents`);
    this.name = 'InsufficientFundsError';
  }
}

class Wallet {
  #balanceCents = 0;
  constructor(readonly id: string) {}

  deposit(cents: number): void {
    this.#assertAmount(cents);
    this.#balanceCents += cents;
  }

  withdraw(cents: number): void {
    this.#assertAmount(cents);
    if (cents > this.#balanceCents) {
      throw new InsufficientFundsError(cents - this.#balanceCents); // check first, change nothing
    }
    this.#balanceCents -= cents;
  }

  get balanceCents(): number {
    return this.#balanceCents;
  }

  #assertAmount(cents: number): void {          // private methods can use # too
    if (!Number.isInteger(cents) || cents <= 0) {
      throw new Error(`amount must be a positive integer of cents, got ${cents}`);
    }
  }
}

const wallet = new Wallet('wal_7');
wallet.deposit(3000);
wallet.withdraw(1200);
try {
  wallet.withdraw(5000);
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof InsufficientFundsError) console.log(e.message, e.shortfallCents);
}
console.log(wallet.balanceCents, JSON.stringify(wallet));
Text
insufficient funds: short by 3200 cents 3200
1800 {"id":"wal_7"}

Why it is right: the only writes to #balanceCents are inside deposit and withdraw, and the runtime forbids any other code from touching it, so the balance can only change through the rules. withdraw validates and checks the balance before subtracting, so a failed withdrawal changes nothing (1,800 is 3,000 minus 1,200; the 5,000 attempt left it alone). The error carries shortfallCents as data, so a caller can show "you need 32.00 more" without parsing the message.

The trap most learners fall into is subtracting first and checking afterwards (this.#balanceCents -= cents; if (this.#balanceCents < 0) throw ...), which leaves the wallet negative after the throw. In a real system the balance lives in PostgreSQL, and this same rule becomes a CHECK (balance_cents >= 0) constraint plus a row lock (Part 24 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control); the class is the first line of defence, not the last.

1.8.4 Parameter properties: the constructor form NestJS uses

Concept

A parameter property is a TypeScript shortcut that declares a field and assigns it from a constructor parameter in one go. You get it by putting a modifier (private, public, protected or readonly) in front of a constructor parameter.

How it works

The two constructors below compile to the same JavaScript:

TypeScript
interface OrderRepository {
  findById(id: string): Promise<{ id: string; status: string } | null>;
}

// Long form: declare, accept, assign.
class OrdersServiceLong {
  private readonly repo: OrderRepository;
  constructor(repo: OrderRepository) {
    this.repo = repo;
  }
}

// Parameter property: the modifier does all three.
class OrdersService {
  constructor(private readonly repo: OrderRepository) {}

  async getStatus(id: string): Promise<string> {
    const order = await this.repo.findById(id);   // available as this.repo
    if (!order) throw new Error(`order ${id} not found`);
    return order.status;
  }
}

constructor(private readonly repo: OrderRepository) {} reads as: "this class needs an OrderRepository to exist; keep it in a field called repo; nobody outside may see it; nobody, not even this class, may replace it after construction". That sentence is exactly what you want to say about a collaborator, which is why almost every NestJS controller and service starts this way (you have already seen constructor(private readonly products: ProductsService) {} in 6.2).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A parameter without a modifier is just a parameter. constructor(repo: OrderRepository) {} stores nothing, and this.repo is a compile error.
  • Parameter properties are TypeScript-only syntax that generates code, so they need a real compiler step (tsc, tsx, SWC, or the Nest CLI). Recent Node versions can run a .ts file directly, but only by stripping erasable type syntax, so node orders.service.ts stops with a syntax error at the first parameter property. TypeScript's erasableSyntaxOnly option (TypeScript 5.8 and later) flags them for the same reason. NestJS projects compile with tsc or SWC, so this only bites if you try to run .ts files with plain node.

1.8.5 Interfaces versus abstract classes

Concept

Both describe a contract that other classes fulfil. An interface is a pure shape: names and types, no code, erased at runtime. An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated with new; it can hold shared code and fields, and marks some methods abstract, meaning "every subclass must write this one".

How it works

TypeScript
interface ChargeResult {
  providerRef: string;
  status: 'succeeded' | 'declined';
}

// Interface: the contract only. A class promises to fit it with `implements`.
interface PaymentGateway {
  charge(orderId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<ChargeResult>;
}

// Abstract class: contract plus shared behaviour.
abstract class BasePaymentGateway implements PaymentGateway {
  protected abstract readonly providerName: string;

  // Every subclass must implement this.
  protected abstract doCharge(orderId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<ChargeResult>;

  // Shared code, written once: validation and logging around the provider call.
  async charge(orderId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<ChargeResult> {
    if (!Number.isInteger(amountCents) || amountCents <= 0) throw new Error('invalid amount');
    const started = Date.now();
    const result = await this.doCharge(orderId, amountCents);
    console.log(`${this.providerName} charge ${orderId}: ${result.status} in ${Date.now() - started} ms`);
    return result;
  }
}

class CardGateway extends BasePaymentGateway {
  protected readonly providerName = 'card';
  protected async doCharge(orderId: string): Promise<ChargeResult> {
    return { providerRef: `card_${orderId}`, status: 'succeeded' };   // a real one calls the provider's API
  }
}

// new BasePaymentGateway();  // compile error: cannot create an instance of an abstract class

Decision table

Question Interface Abstract class
Exists at runtime? No, erased Yes, a real class
Can hold shared code or fields? No Yes
How many can one class use? Implement many Extend only one
Usable as a NestJS injection token? No, needs a string or symbol token Yes, the class itself is the token
Best for Describing shapes and pluggable behaviours A family that genuinely shares an algorithm

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Start with an interface; it is the lightest promise. Reach for an abstract class only when implementations really share code, as above where validation and timing are identical for every provider. The runtime row matters in NestJS: interfaces vanish, so Nest cannot find "the PaymentGateway" by its interface. Teams either register it under a token (@Inject(PAYMENT_GATEWAY)) or make the contract an abstract class and use that as the token, as 1.8.9 shows.

1.8.6 Inheritance versus composition

Concept

Inheritance (class B extends A) says "B is a kind of A": B gets all of A's members and can override some. Composition says "B has an A": B keeps a reference to another object and delegates work to it. The long-standing advice, which Part 16 — Clean Code Principles and Design Patterns covers in depth (16.8), is to prefer composition.

Why does it exist?

Inheritance looks like free reuse, and for one level it often is. The trouble starts when requirements combine. Imagine order notifications: email first, then SMS, then "email and SMS for high-value orders", then "WhatsApp but only in India". With inheritance, every combination becomes a new subclass, and a change to the base class ripples into all of them.

TypeScript
// Inheritance going wrong: one subclass per combination.
class OrderNotifier { notify(orderId: string): void { /* email */ } }
class SmsOrderNotifier extends OrderNotifier { /* overrides notify to send SMS */ }
class EmailAndSmsOrderNotifier extends OrderNotifier { /* copies code from both */ }
class HighValueEmailAndSmsOrderNotifier extends EmailAndSmsOrderNotifier { /* ... and so on */ }

Mental model

Imagine a phone. Inheritance is buying a different phone model for each new feature. Composition is one phone that takes apps: install the email app, the SMS app, remove one, add another, without buying anything new.

How it works — the composed version

TypeScript
interface NotificationChannel {
  readonly name: string;
  send(to: string, message: string): Promise<void>;
}

class EmailChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  readonly name = 'email';
  async send(to: string, message: string): Promise<void> {
    console.log(`[email to ${to}] ${message}`);    // a real one calls an email provider
  }
}

class SmsChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  readonly name = 'sms';
  async send(to: string, message: string): Promise<void> {
    console.log(`[sms to ${to}] ${message}`);
  }
}

interface Customer { id: string; email: string; mobile: string }

// The notifier HAS channels. Which channels is decided when it is built, not by its class.
class OrderNotifier {
  constructor(private readonly channels: readonly NotificationChannel[]) {}

  async orderConfirmed(customer: Customer, orderId: string): Promise<void> {
    const message = `Order ${orderId} is confirmed`;
    for (const channel of this.channels) {
      const to = channel.name === 'sms' ? customer.mobile : customer.email;
      await channel.send(to, message);
    }
  }
}

const standard = new OrderNotifier([new EmailChannel()]);
const highValue = new OrderNotifier([new EmailChannel(), new SmsChannel()]);

Adding WhatsApp is now a new WhatsAppChannel class and one change where notifiers are built. No existing class is edited.

Read the diagram like this: a hollow-diamond line means "has" (composition), and a dashed line with a hollow triangle means "implements". - marks a private member and + a public one.

When inheritance is right

Inheritance is fine for a genuine, stable "is a" relationship with shared code, usually one level deep: the CardGateway extends BasePaymentGateway template in 1.8.5, or custom errors (class InsufficientFundsError extends Error, which you have already written). Test it with one question: "Could the subclass be used everywhere the parent is used without surprising anyone?" If not, it should not inherit.

Common mistakes

  • Inheriting to reuse one helper method. Move the helper to its own class or function and compose it.
  • Hierarchies three or more levels deep, where understanding one method means reading four files.
  • Overriding a parent method to throw "not supported". The subclass is not really a kind of the parent.

Practical exercise

A payments module has class PaymentProcessor with a pay() method, and subclasses RetryingPaymentProcessor, LoggingPaymentProcessor and now a requested RetryingLoggingPaymentProcessor. Redesign it with composition so that retrying and logging can be combined in any order without new classes. Acceptance criteria: a CardProcessor that fails twice then succeeds is wrapped with retry (three attempts) and logging, the payment succeeds, and the log shows every attempt.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
TypeScript
interface PaymentProcessor {
  pay(orderId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<string>;   // returns a provider reference
}

class CardProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
  private calls = 0;
  constructor(private readonly failuresBeforeSuccess: number) {}
  async pay(orderId: string): Promise<string> {
    this.calls += 1;
    if (this.calls <= this.failuresBeforeSuccess) throw new Error(`provider timeout (call ${this.calls})`);
    return `card_${orderId}`;
  }
}

// Each wrapper HAS an inner processor and adds one behaviour around it.
class RetryingProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
  constructor(private readonly inner: PaymentProcessor, private readonly maxAttempts: number) {}
  async pay(orderId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<string> {
    let lastError: unknown;
    for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= this.maxAttempts; attempt++) {
      try {
        return await this.inner.pay(orderId, amountCents);
      } catch (e) {
        lastError = e;              // a real version waits with backoff between attempts (Part 34)
      }
    }
    throw lastError;
  }
}

class LoggingProcessor implements PaymentProcessor {
  constructor(private readonly inner: PaymentProcessor) {}
  async pay(orderId: string, amountCents: number): Promise<string> {
    try {
      const ref = await this.inner.pay(orderId, amountCents);
      console.log(`pay ${orderId} ok ${ref}`);
      return ref;
    } catch (e) {
      console.log(`pay ${orderId} failed: ${(e as Error).message}`);
      throw e;
    }
  }
}

// Logging inside retry: every attempt is logged.
const processor = new RetryingProcessor(new LoggingProcessor(new CardProcessor(2)), 3);
processor.pay('ord_42', 4999).then((ref) => console.log('result', ref));
Text
pay ord_42 failed: provider timeout (call 1)
pay ord_42 failed: provider timeout (call 2)
pay ord_42 ok card_ord_42
result card_ord_42

Why it is right: every class implements the same PaymentProcessor interface, and each wrapper holds an inner one. Because they all fit the same contract, they stack in any order with no new classes. Order matters and is now visible in one line: logging inside retry logs every attempt (what the acceptance criteria asked for); new LoggingProcessor(new RetryingProcessor(...)) would log only the final outcome. This shape has a name, the Decorator pattern (Part 16, 16.16).

The trap most learners fall into is keeping one class with flags ({ retry: true, log: true }) and if statements inside pay: every new behaviour edits the same method. The second trap: retrying a payment is only safe if the provider call is idempotent, so a real retry sends the same idempotency key every time (Part 33 — Distributed Transactions: Sagas, Outbox, Inbox and Idempotency).

1.8.7 Static members, getters and setters

Concept

A static member belongs to the class itself, not to any instance: you call OrderNumber.next(), not someOrderNumber.next(). A getter (get total()) is a method you read like a field; a setter (set qty(v)) is a method you assign like a field.

How it works

TypeScript
class OrderNumber {
  static readonly PREFIX = 'ORD';                    // one shared constant
  private static issued = 0;                          // shared counter (in memory, for illustration only)

  private constructor(readonly value: string) {}     // private: force callers through the factories

  // Static factory methods: named ways to build an instance.
  static next(): OrderNumber {
    OrderNumber.issued += 1;
    return new OrderNumber(`${OrderNumber.PREFIX}-${String(OrderNumber.issued).padStart(6, '0')}`);
  }

  static parse(raw: string): OrderNumber {
    if (!/^ORD-\d{6}$/.test(raw)) throw new Error(`not an order number: ${raw}`);
    return new OrderNumber(raw);
  }
}

class OrderLine {
  #qty = 1;
  constructor(readonly sku: string, readonly unitCents: number) {}

  get qty(): number { return this.#qty; }
  set qty(value: number) {                            // validation runs on every assignment
    if (!Number.isInteger(value) || value < 1 || value > 99) throw new Error(`qty out of range: ${value}`);
    this.#qty = value;
  }

  get totalCents(): number { return this.unitCents * this.#qty; }  // computed, never stale
}

console.log(OrderNumber.next().value, OrderNumber.parse('ORD-000042').value); // ORD-000001 ORD-000042
const line = new OrderLine('BRUSH-01', 4999);
line.qty = 3;
console.log(line.totalCents);                         // 14997

Static factories (fromRow, parse, create) are the most useful static members in backend code: they give construction a name and a place for validation. Static mutable state, like the counter above, is risky in a server: shared by every request, lost on restart, different in every process. Real order numbers come from a database sequence.

Getters are good for computed values such as totalCents, which cannot go stale because they are calculated on read. Keep them cheap and free of side effects; a getter that runs a database query surprises everyone.
