Then run it again and start the API in another terminal about ten seconds later:

Text
$ ./wait-for-api.sh
attempt 1/20: status 000
attempt 2/20: status 000
attempt 3/20: status 000
attempt 4/20: status 000
attempt 5/20: status 000
API is up after 6 attempt(s)
$ echo $?
0

Why it is right: the shebang and set -euo pipefail come first, as required. ${1:-http://localhost:3000} takes the first argument or the default. Each attempt asks only for the status code and compares it with 200 as a string; exit 0 ends the script the moment the API answers. Otherwise it sleeps and tries again, and after the twentieth failure exit 1 reports the failure. Nineteen sleeps of 2 seconds plus twenty quick refused connections is just under 40 seconds, matching the measured real 0m39.2s. The progress lines go to stderr (>&2), so a caller that captures stdout gets only the final result.

The trap most learners fall into is leaving out || true on the curl line. When nothing listens on the port, curl exits with code 7 ("could not connect"). A variable assignment from $(...) takes that exit code, and set -e ends the script on the spot: no message, exit code 7, on the very first attempt. The same applies to any x=$(curl ...) line in a set -e script, so test every script once with the server down. A second trap is forgetting --max-time: against a host that drops packets instead of refusing them, each curl can hang for minutes, and "20 attempts" no longer means "about 40 seconds". With --max-time 2, the worst case is 20 attempts of 2 seconds plus the sleeps, about 78 seconds.

Check it yourself: run both scenarios and print echo $? right after each; you must see 1 and 0. A CI job or a Docker entrypoint can then use it as ./wait-for-api.sh && npm run test:e2e.

4.12 Worked example: a night on call with only a terminal

This example strings the whole Part together. Every command in it has appeared in 4.1 to 4.11.

The page

At 01:52 you are paged: "Orders API error rate above 20 % for 5 minutes". You have a laptop, a terminal and SSH access to the API server orders-api-2.

Step 1: get in, and know where you are (4.7, 4.1)

Shell
ssh alice@orders-api-2.internal
whoami && hostname && date            # alice, orders-api-2, 01:54 UTC: the right machine, the right user

Step 2: check the gauges (4.9)

Shell
df -h /            # Use% 41%: disk fine
free -h            # available 2.9Gi of 7.7Gi: memory fine
uptime             # load average: 1.92, 1.88, 1.10 on 2 cores (nproc): busy, not overloaded

The machine is not the problem.

Step 3: is the process alive, and what is it doing? (4.3)

Shell
ps aux | grep '[n]ode dist/main.js'   # the [n] trick stops grep from matching itself
# alice 1874 38.0 9.2 ... node dist/main.js     <- running, normal CPU

Step 4: ask the API directly (4.10)

Shell
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' http://localhost:3000/health
# 200 0.004s
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' http://localhost:3000/orders?limit=5
# 500 5.012s                         <- orders fail, and they take 5 seconds to fail

The API is up, but /orders fails after exactly 5 seconds. Exactly 5 seconds smells like a timeout.

Step 5: read the logs with a pipeline (4.4, 4.8)

Shell
tail -n 2000 /var/log/orders-api/application.log | grep ERROR | cut -d']' -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
#  612  Connection terminated due to connection timeout
#    9  Request validation failed
#    2  Payment provider returned 502

612 of the recent errors are database connection timeouts.

Step 6: check the dependency (4.10, 4.5)

Shell
env | grep -i '^DB_HOST'              # DB_HOST=orders-db.internal (from the environment, 4.5)
nc -vz -w 3 orders-db.internal 5432   # nc: test a TCP connection; -z: just connect, -w 3: 3 s timeout
# nc: connect to orders-db.internal port 5432 (tcp) timed out

The API server cannot reach the database at all. That is a network or database problem, not a code problem, and now you know which team to wake and exactly what to tell them: "from orders-api-2, TCP to orders-db.internal:5432 times out since about 01:47; the API is healthy otherwise."

Step 7: write it down as you go

Shell
history | tail -n 15 > ~/incident-2026-11-05.txt    # the exact commands you ran, for the incident notes

In the morning, the database team finds that a security-group change at 01:46 removed the API servers' access to port 5432 (Part 50.9 covers VPC networking). The postmortem's action items include an alert on database connection errors and a script, ci/check-db-reachability.sh, that runs the nc check from every API server after each infrastructure change.

What made this fast

Step Time Ruled out
Who and where 10 s Wrong machine
Gauges 30 s Disk, memory, CPU
Process 10 s Crashed process
curl 20 s Whole API down; found the failing endpoint and the 5 s pattern
Log pipeline 30 s Guessing; found the error that dominates
nc 15 s Our code; found the broken dependency

About two minutes of commands, each one answering one question and ruling something out. That is what command-line fluency buys you.

Practical exercise

Rehearse this night on your own machine with the API from Part 6.

Acceptance criteria:

  • Stop PostgreSQL (docker stop on its container, Part 6), then use only the terminal to show: the API process is running, /health answers, a data endpoint fails, the log's most common error is a database connection error, and nc -vz localhost 5432 fails.
  • Start PostgreSQL again and show that the same curl now succeeds.
  • Save the commands you used with history into a notes file, and turn steps 4 to 6 into a script with set -euo pipefail that prints one line per check.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

Set up. Start the Part 6 API so its log also lands in a file you can search. In terminal 1, from your project folder:

Shell
npm run start:dev 2>&1 | tee ~/practice/api.log    # tee: show the log AND save it

Break the database and gather the evidence, in terminal 2:

Shell
docker stop shop-db
ps aux | grep '[d]ist/main'
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' http://localhost:3000/health
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' http://localhost:3000/products
grep -oE 'ECONNREFUSED|Connection terminated[a-z ]*' ~/practice/api.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3
nc -vz -w 3 localhost 5432
Text
shop-db
alice     4821  1.2  2.1 1188240 171204 pts/1  Sl+  11:40   0:03 node --enable-source-maps /home/alice/products-api/dist/main
200 0.003512s
500 0.018204s
     14 ECONNREFUSED
      1 Connection terminated unexpectedly
nc: connect to localhost (127.0.0.1) port 5432 (tcp) failed: Connection refused

That covers every acceptance point: the process runs, /health answers 200, /products fails with 500, the dominant log error is the database refusing connections (the exact wording depends on your driver version), and nc cannot open port 5432. On macOS, nc words it as nc: connectx to localhost port 5432 (tcp) failed: Connection refused.

Notice one difference from the story: here /products fails in 18 ms, not 5 seconds. A stopped container refuses the connection at once, while the security-group change in the story silently dropped packets, so the API waited for its 5-second timeout. "Fails fast" points at something refusing; "fails after exactly N seconds" points at a timeout.

Recover:

Shell
docker start shop-db
sleep 3                                              # give PostgreSQL a moment to accept connections
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' http://localhost:3000/products
Text
shop-db
200 0.011736s

Save your notes. history is a feature of your interactive shell, so run it at the prompt, not inside a script:

Shell
history | tail -n 20 > ~/practice/rehearsal-notes.txt    # zsh: history -20 > ~/practice/rehearsal-notes.txt

The script, check-path.sh:

Shell
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check-path.sh: steps 4 to 6 of the on-call night, one line per check.
# usage: ./check-path.sh [base-url] [log-file] [db-host] [db-port]
set -euo pipefail

BASE_URL="${1:-http://localhost:3000}"
LOG_FILE="${2:-$HOME/practice/api.log}"
DB_HOST="${3:-localhost}"
DB_PORT="${4:-5432}"
failed=0

# Step 4: ask the API directly. "|| true": a refused connection prints 000 instead of ending the script.
for path in /health /products; do
  result=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s' --max-time 5 "${BASE_URL}${path}" || true)
  echo "api ${path}: ${result}"
  case "$result" in 200*) ;; *) failed=1 ;; esac
done

# Step 5: the most common network error code in the last 2000 log lines.
# grep -o prints only the matching part, so stack traces and JSON around it do not matter.
if [ -f "$LOG_FILE" ]; then
  top=$(tail -n 2000 "$LOG_FILE" \
    | grep -oE 'E(CONNREFUSED|CONNRESET|TIMEDOUT|NOTFOUND|HOSTUNREACH)|Connection terminated[a-z ]*' \
    | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1 || true)
  echo "log top error: ${top:-none}"
else
  echo "log top error: no log file at ${LOG_FILE}"
fi

# Step 6: can we open a TCP connection to the database at all?
if nc -z -w 3 "$DB_HOST" "$DB_PORT" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo "db tcp ${DB_HOST}:${DB_PORT}: reachable"
else
  echo "db tcp ${DB_HOST}:${DB_PORT}: UNREACHABLE"
  failed=1
fi

exit "$failed"

With the database stopped, then started again:

Text
$ ./check-path.sh; echo "exit: $?"
api /health: 200 0.003512s
api /products: 500 0.018204s
log top error:      14 ECONNREFUSED
db tcp localhost:5432: UNREACHABLE
exit: 1
$ docker start shop-db && sleep 3 && ./check-path.sh; echo "exit: $?"
shop-db
api /health: 200 0.002981s
api /products: 200 0.011736s
log top error:      14 ECONNREFUSED
db tcp localhost:5432: reachable
exit: 0

Why it is right: each check prints exactly one line, and the script exits non-zero if any API call or the database connection fails, so it is usable from CI or another script. Every command that is allowed to fail is handled on purpose: curl with || true, nc inside an if (commands tested by if do not trigger set -e), and the log pipeline with || true, because grep exits 1 when it finds nothing and pipefail would pass that on. grep -o with a list of Node's network error codes finds the error wherever it sits in a log line, including inside a JSON object or a stack trace.

The trap most learners fall into is reading the log line in the second run as "still broken". The log shows history: the old ECONNREFUSED lines are still in the last 2,000 lines; what matters is that the count stopped growing while the live checks (curl, nc) pass. The other trap is putting history inside the script, where it prints nothing, because a non-interactive shell keeps no history.

Check it yourself: run the script once in each state and confirm exit: 1 with the database stopped and exit: 0 with it running.

Senior Checklist — Part 4

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can navigate the filesystem and read logs with tail -f and less
  • I understand file permissions and lock secrets files to 600
  • I can find, inspect and signal processes, preferring SIGTERM over SIGKILL
  • I can compose pipelines to analyze logs (grep | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn)
  • I configure apps with environment variables and keep .env out of git
  • I commit lock files and use npm ci for reproducible builds
  • I use key-based SSH and protect the private key
  • I use Tab completion, Ctrl+R and history instead of retyping long commands, and keep secrets out of history
  • I can edit a config file on a server with nano, after making a backup
  • I can check disk, memory and load in a minute with df -h, du, free -h and uptime, and read each correctly
  • I know why deleting an open log file does not free space, and how to fix a full disk safely
  • I can test an API with curl -i, read JSON with jq, and find which process owns a port
  • I can write a small shell script with a shebang, set -euo pipefail, quoted variables and a meaningful exit code

Part 4 — Key Takeaways

  • The command line is where backend engineers operate servers; fluency in it separates writing code from running systems.
  • Always know who you are, where you are and which machine you are on before acting; rm -rf has no undo.
  • Permissions control read/write/execute per owner/group/others; secrets files are 600 and apps run as a non-root user (least privilege).
  • A process has a PID; manage it with ps, top and kill, always trying SIGTERM (graceful) before SIGKILL (forceful).
  • Pipes compose small tools into powerful pipelines; grep | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head answers "most common X" for any log, and always sort before uniq -c.
  • Configure applications with environment variables so one build runs everywhere; validate required ones at startup and never commit .env.
  • Package managers install dependency trees reproducibly; commit the lock file, use npm ci in CI, and be conservative about adding dependencies (supply-chain risk).
  • SSH gives an encrypted shell on a remote server; use key-based authentication, guard the private key as your most sensitive file, and prefer automated deploys over manual SSH.
  • Let the shell type for you: Tab, Ctrl+R and Alt+. are faster and make fewer typos than you do.
  • Check the gauges before the engine: df -h, free -h and uptime rule out the most common non-code outages in a minute.
  • curl -i shows exactly what an API sent; check health, then the failing endpoint, then the log.
  • Script anything you do twice, start with set -euo pipefail, quote every variable, and exit non-zero on failure.

Volume 0: From Scratch

Part 5 — Git Basics and the Development Workflow

  • 1 h 27 min read
  • 11 sections
  • 3 diagrams
  • 100 code examples

What you will learn

  1. 5.1What Git is and why it exists
  2. 5.2Branches
  3. 5.3Remotes and pull requests
  4. 5.4Merging and resolving conflicts
  5. 5.5The development workflow, end to end
  6. 5.6Setting up Git on a new machine
  7. 5.7Undoing things safely
  8. 5.8Reading history: log, show, diff and blame
  9. 5.9Stash and tags
  10. 5.10Keeping your branch up to date and handling review feedback
  11. 5.11Worked example: one feature from ticket to merged pull request

Every real software project uses version control, and in practice that means Git. Git records the history of your code: every change, who made it, when, and why. It lets many people work on the same codebase without overwriting each other, lets you undo mistakes, and lets you see how any line of code came to be. You cannot work on a team — or even safely on your own — without it.

This Part is the beginner's on-ramp to Git. Part 52 covers Git deeply (internals, rebasing strategies, bisect, reflog recovery, advanced workflows); this Part teaches the foundation you need before that makes sense: what Git is and why, the core commands (init, clone, add, commit, status, log), branches and merging, remotes and pull requests, and how to resolve a conflict without panic. By the end you will be able to clone a repository, make a change on a branch, commit it, push it, open a pull request, and handle a merge conflict — the everyday loop of professional development.

We teach the command line Git here, because it is universal and because understanding the commands makes the graphical tools make sense. Once you know the commands, use whatever interface you like.

5.1 What Git is and why it exists

5.1.1 Version control and the commit

Concept

Git is a version control system: a tool that records snapshots of your project over time. Each snapshot is called a commit. A commit captures the exact state of all your files at a moment, along with a message explaining the change, who made it, and when. The full history of commits is your project's memory — you can look at any past state, compare any two, and undo back to any point.

Why does it exist?

Without version control, you save over your files and the previous version is gone. You keep folders named project-final, project-final-v2, project-really-final. Two people editing the same file overwrite each other. You cannot tell when a bug was introduced or by whom. Git solves all of this: every version is kept forever, changes from different people merge together, and every line's history is recoverable. It is the difference between working with a safety net and working without one.

Mental model

Imagine a photographer taking a snapshot of your entire project every time you finish a meaningful change, and filing each snapshot with a note about what changed. You can flip back through the album to any past snapshot, see exactly what the project looked like then, and compare any two snapshots to see what moved. You can even start an alternate album (a branch) to try something risky, and either merge it back or throw it away without affecting the main album. Git is that photographer and that album system, automated and precise.

How it works

Git tracks your project through three "places" a change moves through:

Text
Working directory  ->  Staging area (index)  ->  Repository (commits)
   (your files)         (changes you          (permanent history)
                         marked to save)
      |                       |                        |
   you edit               git add                  git commit
  1. Working directory: the actual files you edit. Git watches them and notices changes.
  2. Staging area: a holding area where you place the specific changes you want in your next commit. git add moves changes here. This lets you commit some changes but not others.
  3. Repository: the permanent history. git commit takes everything staged and records it as a new commit forever.

Each commit has a unique id (a long hash like a43fe077...), a parent (the commit before it), an author, a timestamp, and a message. The chain of commits, each pointing to its parent, is the history.

The core commands

Shell
git init                 # start tracking a new project in the current directory
git clone <url>          # copy an existing remote repository to your machine
git status               # what has changed, what is staged (run this constantly)
git add file.ts          # stage one file's changes for the next commit
git add .                # stage all changes in the current directory
git commit -m "message"  # record staged changes as a commit with a message
git log                  # show the history of commits
git log --oneline        # compact one-line-per-commit history
git diff                 # show unstaged changes (what you edited but didn't stage)
git diff --staged        # show staged changes (what will go in the next commit)

git status is the command you run most. It tells you where you are: what has changed, what is staged, which branch you are on. Run it before and after almost everything until the state is obvious to you.

Writing a good commit message

A commit message explains why a change was made, not just what. "Fix bug" is useless in six months; "Fix order total to include tax before applying discount" tells the next person (often you) what happened and why. The common convention is a short summary line (under ~50 characters), a blank line, then more detail if needed.

Shell
git commit -m "Add idempotency key to order creation

Clients retry failed POST /orders requests, which was creating
duplicate orders. The idempotency key lets the server detect and
reject duplicates. Fixes TSB-4422."

Practical example — your first commits

Shell
mkdir my-api && cd my-api
git init                              # start a repository
echo "node_modules/" > .gitignore     # tell git to ignore node_modules
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add gitignore"
# ... create src/index.ts ...
git add src/index.ts
git status                            # confirm it is staged
git commit -m "Add entry point"
git log --oneline                     # see your two commits

The .gitignore file

Some files should never be committed: node_modules/ (huge, rebuildable), .env (secrets), build output (dist/), editor settings. A .gitignore file lists patterns Git should ignore. Setting it up early is important — committing node_modules or .env is a classic beginner mistake (the first bloats the repo, the second leaks secrets).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Committing secrets (.env, API keys) puts them in history forever, even if deleted in a later commit; this is a security incident requiring secret rotation (Part 44 — Security, 44.32). Prevent it with .gitignore.
  • Committing node_modules bloats the repository massively; always gitignore it.
  • Huge commits mixing many unrelated changes are hard to review and hard to revert cleanly; make focused commits.
  • Useless messages ("stuff", "wip", "fix") make history worthless for understanding why code is the way it is.
  • Forgetting to git add before commit, so your change is not actually included; git status catches this.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats commit history as documentation that future engineers (including themselves) will read to understand why the code is the way it is. They make small, focused commits each doing one thing, with messages that explain the reasoning, so that history can be read, searched and selectively reverted. They set up .gitignore before the first commit to keep secrets and junk out of history permanently, because what enters git history is effectively permanent. They run git status and git diff before every commit to know exactly what they are recording, never blindly git add . without looking.

Common mistakes

  • Committing secrets or node_modules (prevent with .gitignore).
  • Giant unfocused commits mixing unrelated changes.
  • Vague commit messages that explain nothing.
  • git add . without checking what it is staging, accidentally committing unintended files.

Interview questions

  1. What are the three areas a change moves through in Git?
    Show answerHide answer
    Working directory (your files), staging area (changes marked for the next commit via git add), and the repository (committed history via git commit).
  2. Why does a committed secret require rotating the secret, not just deleting it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Git history is permanent; the secret remains in past commits even after deletion, so anyone with the repo can recover it.
  3. What makes a good commit message?
    Show answerHide answer
    A concise summary of what changed and, importantly, why; focused on a single logical change.
  4. Why make small, focused commits?
    Show answerHide answer
    They are easier to review, understand and revert cleanly, and they make the history a useful record.

Practical exercise

Create a new Git repository, add a .gitignore that excludes node_modules/ and .env, make two separate focused commits (one for a config file, one for a source file) with clear messages, and view the history with git log --oneline. Then run git status and git diff to confirm the working directory is clean. Acceptance criteria: history shows two focused commits with meaningful messages, and neither node_modules nor .env is tracked.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

The .gitignore is the config file, so it is the first commit, made before any secret exists:

Shell
mkdir practice-api && cd practice-api
git init
printf 'node_modules/\n.env\n' > .gitignore      # one pattern per line
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Ignore node_modules and .env"
Text
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/asha/work/practice-api/.git/
[main (root-commit) 451ab9a] Ignore node_modules and .env
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore

Now the source file, plus a dummy .env and a node_modules folder, so we can prove they are ignored:

Shell
mkdir src node_modules
echo "console.log('hello');" > src/index.ts
echo "DATABASE_PASSWORD=change_me" > .env       # a dummy value, never a real secret
touch node_modules/placeholder.js
git status
Text
On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    src/

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

git status lists only src/: .env and node_modules/ are already invisible to it. Commit the source file and check the result:

Shell
git add src/index.ts
git commit -m "Add entry point that logs a greeting"
git log --oneline
git status
git diff                                         # prints nothing when there are no unstaged edits
git ls-files                                     # exactly what Git tracks
git check-ignore -v .env node_modules/placeholder.js
Text
5779562 (HEAD -> main) Add entry point that logs a greeting
451ab9a Ignore node_modules and .env
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
.gitignore
src/index.ts
.gitignore:2:.env	.env
.gitignore:1:node_modules/	node_modules/placeholder.js

git ls-files is the real proof for the acceptance criteria: only .gitignore and src/index.ts are tracked. git check-ignore -v names the line of .gitignore that ignores each file.

Why this is right. Each commit does one thing and its message says what changed, so either one can be read or reverted on its own. The ignore rules were committed before .env existed, so the secret never had a chance to enter history.

The trap. Creating .env, running git add ., and only then writing .gitignore. A .gitignore stops untracked files from being added; a file that is already tracked stays tracked whatever .gitignore says. If that happened to you, git rm --cached .env untracks it (5.7 shows the full fix), and if the commit was ever pushed, the values in it must be rotated.

5.2 Branches

5.2.1 Working in parallel without stepping on each other

Concept

A branch is an independent line of development. The default branch (usually main) holds the stable, shared code. When you start work, you create a branch off main, make your commits there, and later merge them back. Branches let many people (and many features) progress in parallel without interfering, and let you keep risky or unfinished work away from the stable code.

Why does it exist?

If everyone committed directly to main, every unfinished or broken change would immediately affect everyone else, and two people editing the same area would constantly overwrite each other. Branches isolate work-in-progress. Your feature lives on your branch, broken or unfinished, until it is ready; only when it is reviewed and working does it merge into main. This is how teams of dozens work on one codebase without chaos.

Mental model

Think of main as the trunk of a tree and branches as limbs growing off it. You climb out onto your own limb to build something, in your own space, without disturbing anyone on the trunk or on other limbs. When your work is solid, you graft your limb back onto the trunk (merge), and everyone on the trunk now has your work. If the limb turns out to be a bad idea, you simply cut it off, and the trunk is untouched.

How it works

Shell
git branch                           # list branches; * marks the current one
git branch feat/add-coupons          # create a branch (does not switch to it)
git switch feat/add-coupons          # switch to that branch
git switch -c feat/add-coupons       # create AND switch in one step (common)
git switch main                      # go back to main
git branch -d feat/add-coupons       # delete a merged branch

(You will also see the older git checkout -b feat/... and git checkout main; switch is the newer, clearer command for changing branches.)

A branch is really just a movable pointer to a commit. When you commit on a branch, the pointer advances. main points to the latest stable commit; your feature branch points to your latest work. This is why branching in Git is instant and cheap — it is just creating a pointer, not copying files.

Here, two feature branches grew from the same point on main. Each developer works independently. When each is ready and reviewed, it merges back into main.

Branch naming

Teams use conventions so a branch name tells you what it is. A common one, which matches this book's example repo:

Text
feat/TSB-4422-notification-filter    a feature, with the ticket number
fix/login-timeout                    a bug fix
chore/upgrade-nestjs                 maintenance

Including the ticket number (like TSB-4422) links the branch to the task tracker (Jira, in this project), so anyone can trace code back to the reason it exists.

Practical example — the everyday loop

Shell
git switch main                       # start from the stable branch
git pull                              # get the latest from the remote (5.3)
git switch -c feat/add-coupons        # create your feature branch
# ... edit code, make commits ...
git add .
git commit -m "Add coupon validation to checkout"
# ... more work, more commits ...
git push -u origin feat/add-coupons   # push your branch to the remote (5.3)
# then open a pull request (5.3)

This is the loop you will run every working day: branch off up-to-date main, commit your work, push, open a pull request. Never work directly on main.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Working directly on main defeats the purpose of branches and makes every unfinished change affect everyone; always branch.
  • A long-lived branch that diverges from main for weeks accumulates painful conflicts when it finally merges; keep branches short-lived and merge often.
  • Uncommitted changes when switching branches: Git may refuse to switch or carry changes along confusingly; commit or git stash first.
  • Forgetting which branch you are on and committing to the wrong one; git status always shows the current branch.
  • Deleting an unmerged branch with git branch -D (capital D forces it) loses that work; the lowercase -d refuses to delete unmerged branches as a safeguard.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior keeps branches short-lived and focused — one branch per feature or fix, merged within days, not weeks — because the longer a branch lives apart from main, the more it diverges and the more painful the eventual merge. They always branch off an up-to-date main and never commit directly to the shared branch. They use clear, ticket-linked branch names so work is traceable. They treat git stash as the tool for "I need to switch branches but am mid-change", and they rely on git status to always know where they are, because committing to the wrong branch is a common and avoidable slip.

Common mistakes

  • Committing directly to main.
  • Long-lived branches that become a merge nightmare.
  • Switching branches with uncommitted changes and getting confused.
  • Losing work by force-deleting an unmerged branch.

Interview questions

  1. What is a branch, mechanically?
    Show answerHide answer
    A movable pointer to a commit; branching is cheap because it creates a pointer rather than copying files.
  2. Why work on a branch instead of directly on main?
    Show answerHide answer
    To isolate unfinished or risky work from the stable shared code and let people work in parallel without conflict.
  3. Why keep branches short-lived?
    Show answerHide answer
    The longer a branch diverges from main, the more conflicts accumulate; frequent small merges are far less painful than one big one.
  4. What does git stash do and when would you use it?
    Show answerHide answer
    It temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch branches cleanly, then reapply them later.

Practical exercise

From an up-to-date main, create a branch feat/practice, make two commits on it, switch back to main and confirm those commits are not there, then switch back to your branch. Try switching branches with an uncommitted change and observe Git's behavior, then use git stash to handle it. Acceptance criteria: you can explain why the commits appear only on your branch and demonstrate stashing to switch cleanly.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

Continuing in the repository from 5.1:

Shell
git switch main
git pull                                         # only if the repository has a remote
git switch -c feat/practice
echo "export const greeting = 'hello';" > src/greeting.ts
git add src/greeting.ts                          # a new file must be added explicitly
git commit -m "Add greeting constant"
# edit src/index.ts so it imports and logs greeting
git commit -am "Log the greeting constant from index"   # -a stages files Git already tracks
git log --oneline --graph --all
Text
* 52cf9a6 (HEAD -> feat/practice) Log the greeting constant from index
* 09284b5 Add greeting constant
* 5779562 (main) Add entry point that logs a greeting
* 451ab9a Ignore node_modules and .env

Switch back to main and look:

Text
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git log --oneline
5779562 (HEAD -> main) Add entry point that logs a greeting
451ab9a Ignore node_modules and .env
$ ls src
index.ts

The explanation the exercise asks for: a branch is a pointer to a commit. Your two commits moved the feat/practice pointer forward; main still points at 5779562. Switching branches rewrites your working directory to the snapshot the pointer names, so greeting.ts disappears from disk. It is not lost; it lives in commit 09284b5.

Now an uncommitted change:

Text
$ git switch feat/practice
Switched to branch 'feat/practice'
$ echo "// edit in progress" >> src/index.ts
$ git switch main
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
    src/index.ts
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting

Git refuses because src/index.ts differs between the two branches, and switching would overwrite your edit. If the edited file were identical on both branches, Git would switch and quietly carry the edit along, which is the confusing case 5.2 warns about. Stash it instead:

Text
$ git stash push -m "index edit in progress"
Saved working directory and index state On feat/practice: index edit in progress
$ git status
On branch feat/practice
nothing to commit, working tree clean
$ git switch main
Switched to branch 'main'
$ git switch feat/practice
Switched to branch 'feat/practice'
$ git stash pop
On branch feat/practice
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   src/index.ts

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
Dropped refs/stash@{0} (cbff4654ca02a32fb99b09f902940e23cefb4183)

The trap. Running git stash pop before switching back. A stash applies to whichever branch you are on, so popping on main puts your feature edit on main. Check git status (it names the branch) before every pop, and git stash list afterwards should be empty.

5.3 Remotes and pull requests

5.3.1 Sharing work through a remote repository

Concept

A remote is a copy of the repository hosted somewhere everyone can reach — on GitHub, GitLab or similar. Your local repository and everyone else's are copies; the remote is the shared central copy they synchronize through. You push your commits up to the remote and pull others' commits down. A pull request (PR) — called a merge request on GitLab — is a proposal to merge your branch into main, where teammates review it before it is accepted.

Why does it exist?

Git is distributed: every developer has the full history on their machine. But to collaborate, everyone needs a shared point to sync through, and teams need a checkpoint where changes are reviewed before entering the stable branch. The remote provides the shared copy; the pull request provides the review gate. Together they are how code goes from one engineer's laptop to the shared main safely, with at least one other person having looked at it.

Mental model

Imagine a shared document in the cloud that everyone has a local copy of. You make changes locally, then upload them (push) so others can download them (pull). But before your changes are accepted into the official version, you submit them for review — a colleague reads them, comments, requests tweaks, and approves. Only approved changes become part of the official document. The cloud document is the remote; the review-and-approve step is the pull request.

How it works

Shell
git clone <url>                       # get a copy of a remote repo (sets up 'origin')
git remote -v                         # show configured remotes (usually 'origin')
git push -u origin feat/add-coupons   # push your branch up the first time (-u links them)
git push                              # push subsequent commits
git pull                              # fetch others' commits and merge them into your branch
git fetch                             # download remote changes WITHOUT merging (safer to inspect first)

origin is the conventional name for the main remote (the one you cloned from). git push -u origin <branch> the first time links your local branch to a remote branch so later you can just type git push and git pull.

The pull request workflow:

  1. You push your branch to the remote.
  2. You open a pull request: "please merge feat/add-coupons into main", with a description of what and why.
  3. Automated checks run (tests, linting — Part 51 on CI/CD).
  4. Teammates review the code, leave comments, maybe request changes.
  5. You address feedback with more commits and push again (the PR updates automatically).
  6. Once approved and checks pass, the PR is merged into main and the branch is deleted.

The pull request description

A good PR description tells the reviewer what changed, why, and how to verify it. It links the ticket. It calls out anything risky. A reviewer who understands the intent reviews faster and better than one staring at a raw diff.

Text
Title: Add idempotency key to order creation (TSB-4422)

What: POST /orders now accepts an Idempotency-Key header and rejects
duplicate submissions within 24 hours.

Why: Clients retry failed requests, which was creating duplicate orders
(see incident INC-883).

How to test: POST the same order twice with the same key; the second
returns the first order, not a new one.

Risk: Low. New behavior is behind the header; requests without the
header are unchanged.

Practical example — from branch to merged

Shell
git switch main && git pull                  # start fresh and up to date
git switch -c fix/login-timeout              # branch
# ... fix the bug, commit ...
git commit -am "Increase login token timeout to 30 minutes"
git push -u origin fix/login-timeout         # push
# open the PR in the web UI, fill in the description, request a reviewer
# reviewer comments; you address them:
git commit -am "Address review: make timeout configurable via env"
git push                                      # PR updates automatically
# reviewer approves, checks pass, merge via the web UI, delete the branch
git switch main && git pull                   # bring the merged change into your local main

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Pushing to the wrong branch or force-pushing over others' work (git push --force) can destroy commits; avoid force-push on shared branches (Part 52 covers the safe --force-with-lease).
  • A stale local main: forgetting to git pull before branching means you build on old code and hit conflicts; always start from up-to-date main.
  • A huge PR (thousands of lines) is nearly impossible to review well; reviewers rubber-stamp it and bugs slip through. Keep PRs small.
  • Merging your own PR without review skips the quality gate that catches mistakes; follow the team's review requirement.
  • Secrets in a PR: pushing a commit with a secret exposes it to everyone with repo access, even if later removed; prevent with .gitignore and pre-commit checks.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior keeps pull requests small and focused, because a PR a reviewer can actually read in ten minutes gets a real review, while a 2,000-line PR gets a rubber stamp. They write PR descriptions that explain intent and how to verify, treating the reviewer's time as valuable. They always branch from up-to-date main and pull frequently to keep divergence small. They never force-push shared branches. They see code review not as a gate to get past but as the main mechanism by which a team shares knowledge and catches defects early, and they both give and receive review thoughtfully (Part 52 — Git from Intermediate to Senior, 52.13, covers the pull request workflow and review).

Common mistakes

  • Branching off a stale main, causing avoidable conflicts.
  • Giant PRs that cannot be reviewed meaningfully.
  • Force-pushing shared branches and destroying others' commits.
  • Thin or missing PR descriptions that waste the reviewer's time.
  • Merging without review when the team requires it.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
    Show answerHide answer
    fetch downloads remote changes without merging (so you can inspect first); pull fetches and immediately merges into your branch.
  2. What is a pull request and what purpose does it serve?
    Show answerHide answer
    A proposal to merge a branch into main, providing a review and automated-check gate before changes enter the stable branch.
  3. Why keep pull requests small?
    Show answerHide answer
    Small PRs get genuine review and are easier to understand and revert; large ones get rubber-stamped and hide bugs.
  4. Why is force-pushing a shared branch dangerous?
    Show answerHide answer
    It rewrites history others may have based work on, potentially destroying their commits; use it only on your own branches, and prefer --force-with-lease.

Practical exercise

Clone a repository (or use one you created), create a branch, make a commit, push it with git push -u origin <branch>, and open a pull request with a description covering what, why, how to test, and risk. Acceptance criteria: the PR has a meaningful description and links to the branch; you can explain what origin and the -u flag did.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

Using a practice repository on GitHub (GitLab prints the same Git lines with its own "merge request" link):

Shell
git clone git@github.com:shop-example/practice-api.git
cd practice-api
git switch -c feat/health-endpoint
# ... add src/health.ts ...
git add src/health.ts
git commit -m "Add GET /health endpoint for load balancer checks"
git push -u origin feat/health-endpoint
Text
Enumerating objects: 6, done.
Counting objects: 100% (6/6), done.
Delta compression using up to 8 threads
Compressing objects: 100% (3/3), done.
Writing objects: 100% (4/4), 431 bytes | 431.00 KiB/s, done.
Total 4 (delta 1), reused 0 (delta 0), pack-reused 0
remote: Resolving deltas: 100% (1/1), completed with 1 local object.
remote:
remote: Create a pull request for 'feat/health-endpoint' on GitHub by visiting:
remote:      https://github.com/shop-example/practice-api/pull/new/feat/health-endpoint
remote:
To github.com:shop-example/practice-api.git
 * [new branch]      feat/health-endpoint -> feat/health-endpoint
branch 'feat/health-endpoint' set up to track 'origin/feat/health-endpoint'.

Open the link Git printed, check that the base branch is main and that the "Files changed" tab shows only your change, then fill in the description:

Text
Title: Add GET /health endpoint for load balancer checks

What: GET /health returns {"status":"ok"} with 200.
Why: The load balancer needs a cheap endpoint to decide whether this
instance should receive traffic.
How to test: npm run start:dev, then curl http://localhost:3000/health
Risk: Low. New read-only route; no existing route changes.

The explanation the exercise asks for. origin is the short name git clone gave the remote it cloned from; git remote -v shows the URL behind it. -u (long form --set-upstream) links your local branch to origin/feat/health-endpoint, which is what the last output line confirms. From now on, plain git push and git pull know where to go, and git status reports how far ahead or behind you are:

Text
$ git branch -vv
* feat/health-endpoint 3e1a9f0 [origin/feat/health-endpoint] Add GET /health endpoint for load balancer checks
  main                 5779562 [origin/main] Add entry point that logs a greeting

The trap. Pushing the first time without -u and then typing git push, which fails with fatal: The current branch feat/health-endpoint has no upstream branch. Git prints the git push --set-upstream origin feat/health-endpoint command to fix it. The second trap is a pull request against the wrong base branch; if "Files changed" shows commits you did not write, stop and fix the base before asking for review.

5.4 Merging and resolving conflicts

5.4.1 Bringing branches together

Concept

Merging combines the commits from one branch into another — typically merging your feature branch into main. Most merges are automatic: Git figures out how to combine the changes. Sometimes two branches changed the same lines of the same file in different ways, and Git cannot decide which to keep. That is a merge conflict, and you resolve it by telling Git which change wins (or how to combine them).

Why does it exist?

When work happens in parallel on branches, those branches must eventually come back together. Merging is that reunion. Conflicts arise because Git is careful: rather than guess wrong and silently lose someone's change, it stops and asks you when two changes genuinely overlap. A conflict is not an error or a failure — it is Git correctly refusing to make a decision only a human can make.

Mental model

Imagine two editors marking up the same paragraph of a document separately. Most of the time they edit different paragraphs, and combining their work is trivial — Git does it for you. But if both rewrote the same sentence differently, no automated rule can know which rewrite is right. Git brackets both versions and hands them to you: "you decide." Resolving a conflict is reading both versions and writing the correct final one.

How it works

A typical merge:

Shell
git switch main
git pull                              # make sure main is current
git merge feat/add-coupons            # merge the feature branch into main
# If there are no conflicts, done. If there are, Git tells you which files conflict.

When a conflict happens, Git marks the conflicting sections inside the file with markers:

Text
<<<<<<< HEAD
const timeoutMs = 30000;        // the version currently on your branch (main)
=======
const timeoutMs = 60000;        // the version from the branch being merged
>>>>>>> feat/add-coupons

To resolve, you edit the file to the correct final version and remove all three markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>):

Text
const timeoutMs = 60000;        // you decided the incoming value is correct

Then:

Shell
git add src/config.ts                 # mark the conflict as resolved
git commit                            # complete the merge (Git pre-fills a message)

The commands for handling a conflict:

Shell
git status                            # lists the files with conflicts
# ... edit each conflicting file, remove markers, keep the correct content ...
git add <resolved-file>               # stage each resolved file
git commit                            # finish the merge
git merge --abort                     # OR: give up and go back to before the merge

Rebase: the other way (brief)

Besides merge, Git has rebase, which replays your branch's commits on top of the latest main, producing a straighter history. It is powerful and common, but it rewrites commits, so it has its own rules and risks. Part 52 covers rebase, when to use it versus merge, and the "golden rule of rebase" (never rebase commits others have based work on). As a beginner, understand merge first; reach for rebase once you are comfortable.

Practical example — resolving a real conflict

Two people both edited the shipping-cost function. You merge and hit a conflict:

Shell
git switch main && git pull
git merge feat/free-shipping
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/shipping.ts
git status                            # shows src/shipping.ts as "both modified"

Opening src/shipping.ts:

Text
<<<<<<< HEAD
if (subtotalCents >= 5000) return 0;         // free over $50 (from main)
=======
if (subtotalCents >= 4000) return 0;         // free over $40 (from the branch)
>>>>>>> feat/free-shipping

You check the ticket, learn the business decided on $40, edit the file to keep that line, remove the markers, then:

Shell
git add src/shipping.ts
git commit                            # completes the merge

Crucially, you also re-run the tests (Part 45 — Testing Backend Systems) after resolving, because a conflict resolution can be syntactically valid but logically wrong — you might keep both lines, or the wrong one, and only tests catch that.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Leaving a conflict marker (<<<<<<<) in the file and committing it breaks the code; search for markers before committing, and tests/linting catch them.
  • Resolving wrong — keeping the wrong side or an inconsistent mix — compiles but behaves incorrectly; always re-run tests after resolving.
  • Panicking and making it worse: git merge --abort cleanly undoes an in-progress merge so you can start over calmly.
  • A huge conflict from a long-diverged branch is painful; prevent it by keeping branches short and pulling main often.
  • Binary file conflicts (images, compiled files) cannot be merged line-by-line; you pick one version wholesale, which is a reason not to commit binaries casually.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior sees a conflict as routine, not alarming — it is Git doing its job. They resolve it by understanding both changes and the intent behind them (often checking the ticket or asking the other author), not by blindly picking a side. They always re-run the tests after resolving, because a conflict resolution is a code change like any other and can be subtly wrong. They prevent most conflicts by keeping branches short-lived and frequently pulling the latest main into their branch, so divergence stays small. When a merge goes sideways, they know git merge --abort gives them a clean slate, so they never feel trapped.

Common mistakes

  • Committing conflict markers left in the file.
  • Resolving conflicts without understanding the other change, keeping the wrong version.
  • Not re-running tests after resolving, shipping a logically broken resolution.
  • Letting branches diverge for weeks, turning a routine merge into a nightmare.

Interview questions

  1. What causes a merge conflict?
    Show answerHide answer
    Two branches changed the same lines of the same file differently, so Git cannot automatically decide which to keep and asks you.
  2. How do you resolve a conflict?
    Show answerHide answer
    Edit the file to the correct final content, remove the conflict markers, git add the file, and git commit; then re-run tests.
  3. Why re-run tests after resolving a conflict?
    Show answerHide answer
    A resolution is a code change that can be syntactically valid but logically wrong; tests catch an incorrect merge.
  4. How do you prevent painful conflicts?
    Show answerHide answer
    Keep branches short-lived and merge/pull main frequently so branches do not diverge far.
  5. What does git merge --abort do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Cancels an in-progress merge and returns to the state before it started, so you can retry calmly.

Practical exercise

Create a repository, make a branch, and on both main and the branch edit the same line of the same file differently. Merge the branch into main, resolve the resulting conflict by choosing the correct final line and removing the markers, and complete the merge. Then deliberately leave a marker in a second conflict and observe how tests or a linter catch it. Acceptance criteria: you resolve the first conflict cleanly, complete the merge, and can explain why leaving a marker is dangerous.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

Set up one file and change the same line on two branches:

Shell
mkdir conflict-practice && cd conflict-practice && git init
mkdir src
printf "export const timeoutMs = 30000;\nexport const retries = 3;\n" > src/config.ts
git add . && git commit -m "Add config with timeout and retries"

git switch -c feat/longer-timeout
# edit src/config.ts: timeoutMs = 60000
git commit -am "Raise timeout to 60 seconds for slow payment provider"

git switch main
# edit src/config.ts: timeoutMs = 45000
git commit -am "Raise timeout to 45 seconds"
git merge feat/longer-timeout
Text
Auto-merging src/config.ts
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/config.ts
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

git status lists both modified: src/config.ts under "Unmerged paths", and the file reads:

Text
<<<<<<< HEAD
export const timeoutMs = 45000;
=======
export const timeoutMs = 60000;
>>>>>>> feat/longer-timeout
export const retries = 3;

The branch's commit message gives the reason (the payment provider is slow), so 60 seconds wins. Edit the file to exactly export const timeoutMs = 60000; plus the untouched retries line, with no markers left, then:

Text
$ git add src/config.ts
$ git commit --no-edit
[main f5c91f4] Merge branch 'feat/longer-timeout'
$ git log --oneline --graph
*   f5c91f4 Merge branch 'feat/longer-timeout'
|\
| * 4cfe671 Raise timeout to 60 seconds for slow payment provider
* | c25193e Raise timeout to 45 seconds
|/
* 752cb70 Add config with timeout and retries

Now the second conflict, done badly on purpose: change retries to 5 on a branch and to 2 on main, merge, and git add the file without editing it. Git does not stop you:

Text
$ git diff --cached --check
src/config.ts:2: leftover conflict marker
src/config.ts:4: leftover conflict marker
src/config.ts:6: leftover conflict marker
$ git commit --no-edit
[main ea2409f] Merge branch 'feat/retries'
$ npx tsc --noEmit
src/config.ts(2,1): error TS1185: Merge conflict marker encountered.
src/config.ts(4,1): error TS1185: Merge conflict marker encountered.
src/config.ts(6,1): error TS1185: Merge conflict marker encountered.

Why leaving a marker is dangerous. For Git, git add means "resolved", whatever the file contains. It happily records the markers in a commit, and if that commit is pushed, everyone who pulls gets a file that does not compile. The TypeScript compiler catches it here, and so would the test run in CI (Part 51), but only if something runs. To fix it, edit the file to the correct value and make a new commit; before committing, git merge --abort would have thrown the whole merge away instead.

How to verify every time. Run git diff --check (or git diff --cached --check after git add) before you commit a merge, and run the tests after it.

5.5 The development workflow, end to end

5.5.1 Putting it together

Concept

The everyday professional Git workflow is a short, repeatable loop that ties together everything in this Part: start from up-to-date main, branch, commit focused changes with good messages, push, open a pull request, respond to review, merge, and clean up. Knowing the loop as a single rhythm is what makes Git second nature rather than a series of commands you look up.

How it works

Text
1. git switch main && git pull          start from the latest stable code
2. git switch -c feat/TSB-1234-thing    branch (named after the ticket)
3. edit, git add, git commit            make small focused commits with clear messages
4. git push -u origin feat/...          push your branch
5. open a pull request                   describe what, why, how to test, risk
6. automated checks run                   tests and lint (CI, Part 51)
7. address review feedback               more commits, git push; PR updates
8. merge into main                        once approved and green
9. git switch main && git pull           pull the merged change locally
10. git branch -d feat/...               delete the finished branch

This loop runs once per feature or fix, often several times a day. Everything else in Git (rebasing, cherry-picking, bisecting, reflog recovery) is a refinement or a rescue tool layered on top of this core loop, and Part 52 covers those.

A quick command reference

Shell
# Starting work
git clone <url>                  git switch main                  git pull
git switch -c feat/my-feature

# Saving work
git status                       git diff                         git add .
git commit -m "message"

# Sharing work
git push -u origin feat/my-feature    git push    git pull    git fetch

# Branches
git branch                       git switch <name>                git branch -d <name>

# History and inspection
git log --oneline                git show <commit>                git diff main..feat/x

# Undoing (basics; Part 52 goes deeper)
git restore <file>               # discard unstaged changes to a file
git restore --staged <file>      # unstage a file (keep the edits)
git revert <commit>              # make a new commit that undoes an old one (safe on shared history)

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior has internalized this loop so thoroughly that it costs no thought, which frees their attention for the actual work. They know the small set of "undo" commands for the common mistakes (discard a change, unstage a file, revert a commit) and know that for anything scarier, git reflog (Part 52) can recover almost anything, so they are never afraid of Git. They favor the safe tools on shared history — git revert rather than rewriting published commits — because the history others depend on is not theirs to rewrite. Above all they keep the loop small and frequent: short branches, small commits, small PRs, frequent merges, which keeps the whole team moving smoothly.

Common mistakes

  • Treating Git as scary and avoiding it, leading to lost work and bad habits; the reflog makes almost everything recoverable (Part 52).
  • Rewriting shared history; use git revert on anything others have.
  • Skipping git pull before branching, building on stale code.

Interview questions

  1. Walk me through your everyday Git workflow.
    Show answerHide answer
    Pull latest main, branch, make focused commits, push, open a PR with a clear description, address review, merge once approved and green, pull main, delete the branch.
  2. How do you safely undo a change that is already on a shared branch?
    Show answerHide answer
    git revert creates a new commit that undoes it, without rewriting history others depend on.
  3. What is the difference between git restore <file> and git restore --staged <file>?
    Show answerHide answer
    The first discards unstaged edits to the file; the second unstages a staged file while keeping the edits.

Practical exercise

Run the full loop end to end on a practice repository: from up-to-date main, branch, make two focused commits, push, open a PR with a complete description, then (simulating approval) merge it, pull main, and delete the branch. Along the way, practice git restore to discard a change and git restore --staged to unstage one. Acceptance criteria: you complete the full loop without looking up commands, and can explain each step's purpose.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

The loop, with the two restore practices folded in where they naturally happen:

Shell
git switch main && git pull                      # 1. start from the latest main
git switch -c feat/health-check                  # 2. branch
# edit src/app.service.ts
git add src/app.service.ts
git commit -m "Add health status to AppService"  # 3. first focused commit
echo "console.log('debug');" >> src/app.controller.ts

That debug line was a mistake. Discard it with restore before it goes anywhere:

Text
$ git status --short
 M src/app.controller.ts
$ git restore src/app.controller.ts
$ git status --short
$

Now make the real controller change, and stage too much by accident:

Text
$ git add .
$ git status --short
M  src/app.controller.ts
A  notes.txt
$ git restore --staged notes.txt
$ git status --short
M  src/app.controller.ts
?? notes.txt

notes.txt is unstaged but still on disk (?? means untracked). Commit the controller and share the branch:

Shell
git commit -m "Expose GET /health in AppController"   # 3. second focused commit
git push -u origin feat/health-check                  # 4. push
# 5. open the PR: what, why, how to test, risk (5.3)
# 6. CI runs; 7. answer review with more commits and git push
# 8. simulate approval: click "Merge pull request" (a merge commit)
git switch main && git pull                            # 9. bring the merged result down
git branch -d feat/health-check                        # 10. delete the finished branch
Text
Updating 5779562..8b2d4f1
Fast-forward
 src/app.controller.ts | 5 +++++
 src/app.service.ts    | 4 ++++
 2 files changed, 9 insertions(+)
Deleted branch feat/health-check (was 3e1a9f0).

Checks that prove the loop worked. git log --oneline --graph -5 on main shows your two commits joined by a "Merge pull request" commit; git branch lists only main; git status says Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'.

Why -d worked here. The merge commit brought your branch's own commits onto main, so Git can see the branch is fully merged. With squash merge, -d refuses and you need -D, as 5.10 explains.

The trap. Mixing up the two restores. git restore <file> throws away unstaged edits for good (they were never committed, so even the reflog cannot bring them back). git restore --staged <file> only takes the file out of the next commit and keeps your edits. When unsure, run git status first: it prints the right command for each state.

5.6 Setting up Git on a new machine

5.6.1 Identity, defaults and SSH access to GitHub or GitLab

Concept

Before your first commit on a new laptop, Git needs to know three things: who you are (name and email, stamped on every commit), a few sensible defaults (the default branch name, your editor), and how to authenticate to the remote server (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), usually with an SSH key (4.7). This is a ten-minute job you do once per machine, and doing it right prevents a surprising number of problems later.

Why does it exist?

Because every commit records an author, and that author is how your team, your company's audit trail and your own git log know who made a change. A commit authored as root@ip-10-0-3-17 or with a personal email on a work repository is confusing at best and a compliance problem at worst. And without working authentication, git push fails with errors that look scary to a beginner ("Permission denied (publickey)").

Mental model

Imagine joining a company. On day one you get a name badge (your identity), a desk set up the way the office does things (defaults), and a key card for the building (your SSH key). You could work without them for an hour, but every door would be a problem.

How it works

Identity and defaults, stored in ~/.gitconfig:

Shell
git config --global user.name "Asha Rao"
git config --global user.email "asha.rao@shop.example"       # use the email your Git host knows
git config --global init.defaultBranch main                   # new repositories start on main
git config --global core.editor "nano"                         # the editor Git opens for messages (4.8)
git config --global pull.rebase false                          # git pull merges; see Part 52 before changing this
git config --list --show-origin                                # see every setting and which file it comes from

--global writes to your user's config, used by every repository on this machine. Without --global, the setting applies only to the current repository, which is how you use a different email for a work repository and a personal one:

Shell
cd ~/work/shop-api
git config user.email "asha.rao@shop.example"                  # only for this repository

SSH access to the Git host. You created a key pair in 4.7. Now give the public half to your Git host:

Shell
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub              # copy this line (it starts with ssh-ed25519)
# GitHub: Settings -> SSH and GPG keys -> New SSH key -> paste
# GitLab: Preferences -> SSH Keys -> Add new key -> paste
ssh -T git@github.com                  # test: "Hi asha-rao! You've successfully authenticated..."
ssh -T git@gitlab.com                  # GitLab: "Welcome to GitLab, @asha-rao!"

Then use the SSH form of repository URLs:

Shell
git clone git@github.com:shop-example/shop-api.git            # SSH URL: uses your key
git clone https://github.com/shop-example/shop-api.git        # HTTPS URL: needs a personal access token instead
git remote -v                                                 # which URL does this repository use?
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:shop-example/shop-api.git   # switch an existing clone to SSH

With HTTPS, Git hosts no longer accept your account password for git push; they require a personal access token or a credential helper (such as Git Credential Manager) that signs you in through the browser.

Practical example — a new laptop, start to first push

Shell
git --version                                         # git version 2.4x: installed?
git config --global user.name "Asha Rao"
git config --global user.email "asha.rao@shop.example"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "asha.rao@shop.example"      # 4.7; accept the default path, set a passphrase
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub                             # add to GitHub as above
ssh -T git@github.com                                 # authenticated
git clone git@github.com:shop-example/shop-api.git
cd shop-api
git log -1 --format='%an <%ae>'                       # someone else's last commit: the repository works

Then create a small commit on a branch (5.2) and git push -u origin it (5.3) to prove the whole path works.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • "Permission denied (publickey)": the key is not added to the host, the SSH agent does not have it loaded (ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519), or the repository URL is for a different host or user.
  • Wrong email on commits: commits pushed with a personal email to a work repository; fix the config, then git commit --amend --reset-author on the last unpushed commit (5.7).
  • HTTPS password prompts that never accept your password: you need a token or credential helper, not your account password.
  • Several Git hosts or accounts: an ~/.ssh/config file with a Host entry per account picks the right key.
  • Corporate proxies that block SSH on port 22; GitHub and GitLab also offer SSH over port 443 (ssh.github.com, altssh.gitlab.com).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior sets up identity and SSH on day one and checks them with git config --list --show-origin and ssh -T before touching a real repository. They use a separate work identity per repository where needed, protect the SSH key with a passphrase (4.7), and many teams also sign commits (with an SSH or GPG key) so the host can show them as verified; Part 52 goes further.

Common mistakes

  • Committing for weeks with a default or wrong identity.
  • Mixing SSH and HTTPS remotes and fighting both kinds of authentication.
  • Pasting the private key into the Git host instead of the .pub file.

Interview questions

  1. Where does Git get the author name and email for a commit?
    Show answerHide answer
    From user.name and user.email in the repository config, else the global ~/.gitconfig.
  2. What do you paste into GitHub or GitLab to use SSH?
    Show answerHide answer
    The public key (id_ed25519.pub), never the private key.
  3. Why does git push over HTTPS reject your account password?
    Show answerHide answer
    Hosts require personal access tokens or a credential helper for Git operations.

Practical exercise

On your machine, configure Git with your name, email, default branch main and nano as editor; add your SSH public key to a GitHub or GitLab account; and clone a repository with its SSH URL. Acceptance criteria: git config --list --show-origin shows your four settings from ~/.gitconfig, ssh -T greets you by username, and git remote -v shows a git@ URL.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
Shell
git config --global user.name "Asha Rao"
git config --global user.email "asha.rao@shop.example"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "nano"
git config --list --show-origin | grep -E 'user\.|init\.|core\.editor'
Text
file:/Users/asha/.gitconfig	user.name=Asha Rao
file:/Users/asha/.gitconfig	user.email=asha.rao@shop.example
file:/Users/asha/.gitconfig	init.defaultbranch=main
file:/Users/asha/.gitconfig	core.editor=nano

All four lines come from ~/.gitconfig, which is the first acceptance check. (Git prints key names in lower case, so defaultBranch shows as defaultbranch; it is the same setting.)

Next, the key. If ls ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub finds nothing, create one as in 4.7 with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "asha.rao@shop.example". Copy the public half into GitHub (Settings, SSH and GPG keys, New SSH key) and test:

Text
$ cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAI...(one long line)... asha.rao@shop.example
$ ssh -T git@github.com
Hi asha-rao! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

The first time, SSH asks whether you trust github.com and shows a key fingerprint. Compare it with the fingerprints GitHub publishes in its documentation before you type yes. Note that ssh -T exits with status 1 even on success, because GitHub refuses the shell; the greeting is what counts.

Finally clone with the SSH URL and confirm:

Text
$ git clone git@github.com:shop-example/shop-api.git && cd shop-api
$ git remote -v
origin	git@github.com:shop-example/shop-api.git (fetch)
origin	git@github.com:shop-example/shop-api.git (push)

Why this is right. Identity is set once, globally, before the first commit, so every commit carries the right author. The SSH key authenticates every push without passwords or tokens, and the git@ URL makes Git use it.

The trap. Two common ones. First, cloning with the HTTPS URL out of habit: git remote -v shows https://... and pushes ask for credentials. Fix it with git remote set-url origin git@github.com:shop-example/shop-api.git. Second, Permission denied (publickey) from ssh -T, which almost always means the public key was not saved on the host or the agent does not have the key loaded (ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519). Never "fix" it by pasting the private key anywhere.

5.7 Undoing things safely

5.7.1 restore, amend, revert and reset, and when to use each

Concept

Everyone makes mistakes in Git: staging the wrong file, a typo in a commit message, a commit that breaks something, a change you want to throw away. Git can undo all of them, but there are several undo commands, and they differ in one important way: some rewrite history and some add to it. Rewriting is fine for commits only you have seen. For commits already pushed and shared, you add a new commit that undoes the old one.

Why does it exist?

Because "undo" means different things at different stages. Undoing an edit you have not staged is different from removing a file from the staging area, which is different from fixing your last commit, which is different from undoing a commit your teammates already pulled. Using the wrong tool either does nothing or, worse, rewrites history that other people depend on.

Mental model

Imagine writing in a notebook that you share with your team. Before you show a page to anyone, you can tear it out and rewrite it; nobody will know. Once the team has copied the page into their own notebooks, tearing it out of yours does not remove it from theirs, and now the notebooks disagree. The polite way is to write a new entry: "the entry on page 12 was wrong; here is the correction".

How it works

The commands, with what each one changes:

Shell
# 1. Throw away edits in the working directory (not staged). The edit is gone.
git restore src/orders/orders.service.ts

# 2. Unstage a file but keep your edits.
git restore --staged .env                     # oops, staged the secrets file

# 3. Fix the last commit (only if not pushed): message, or a forgotten file.
git commit --amend -m "Add coupon validation to checkout"
git add src/coupons/coupon.dto.ts && git commit --amend --no-edit   # add a file, keep the message

# 4. Undo local commits (not pushed). HEAD~1 means "one commit before the current one".
git reset --soft HEAD~1                       # undo the commit, keep its changes staged
git reset HEAD~1                              # (--mixed, the default) undo it, keep changes unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1                       # undo it AND delete its changes: dangerous

# 5. Undo a pushed commit by adding a new one that reverses it. Safe on shared branches.
git revert a43fe07                            # opens the editor with "Revert ..." as the message

And the safety net. Git records every place HEAD has pointed in the reflog, for about 90 days by default:

Shell
git reflog
# 9c1e2f0 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
# 4d2a771 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add coupon validation      <- the commit you "lost"
git reset --hard 4d2a771                              # go back to it: the commit is back

The reflog is local to your machine and only knows about commits that existed on it. Changes you never committed, discarded with git restore or reset --hard, are not in it, which is why committing often is itself a safety measure.

Which command, when:

I want to... Not pushed yet Already pushed
Discard edits I have not staged git restore <file> (not applicable)
Unstage a file git restore --staged <file> (not applicable)
Fix the last commit's message or contents git commit --amend New commit, or ask your team before rewriting
Remove the last few commits, keep the work git reset --soft HEAD~n git revert each commit
Undo a commit that broke main (not applicable) git revert <sha>

Practical example — "I committed the .env file"

You ran git add . and git commit -m "Add order endpoints", then noticed .env in the commit. It is not pushed yet:

Shell
git show --stat HEAD                       # confirm: .env is listed in the commit
git rm --cached .env                       # remove it from the repository, keep the file on disk
echo ".env" >> .gitignore                  # make sure it never comes back (5.1)
git add .gitignore
git commit --amend --no-edit               # rewrite the last commit without .env
git show --stat HEAD                       # .env is gone; .gitignore is there

If it was pushed, amending your local copy does not remove it from the remote or from anyone who pulled. Treat the values in it as leaked: rotate every secret (Part 44 — Security, 44.32), then remove the file with a normal commit. Rewriting the shared history to erase it is possible (Part 52) but needs the whole team's coordination and does not un-leak anything.

Practical example — a commit broke main

A teammate's merged commit a43fe07 makes POST /orders return 500. The fix will take an hour; users are affected now.

Shell
git switch main && git pull
git revert a43fe07                         # creates a new commit that reverses a43fe07's changes
git push                                   # (or via a pull request, if main is protected)
git log --oneline -3
# 7b1c9d2 Revert "Apply delivery fee before discount"
# a43fe07 Apply delivery fee before discount
# 5e0f311 Add coupon endpoint

History now shows what happened honestly: the change, and its reversal. When the fix is ready, the teammate can re-apply the change with the fix in a new pull request.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • git reset --hard and git restore delete uncommitted work permanently; the reflog cannot bring back what was never committed.
  • Amending or resetting pushed commits makes your branch disagree with the remote; git push is then rejected, and forcing it rewrites history for everyone (Part 52 covers --force-with-lease and when it is acceptable on your own branch).
  • Reverting a merge commit needs git revert -m 1 <sha> to say which parent to keep; Part 52.8 explains it.
  • HEAD~1 with uncommitted changes: reset --hard throws those away too; run git status first.
  • The reflog is per machine and expires; it is a rescue tool, not a backup.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior picks the undo by asking one question first: "has anyone else seen these commits?" If not, they rewrite freely (amend, reset --soft) to keep their history clean. If yes, they add to history (revert) and never rewrite it without the team. They commit early and often on their branch precisely because committed work is recoverable from the reflog, and they treat --hard as a command that deserves a git status and a second look.

Common mistakes

  • Using reset --hard to "undo" and losing uncommitted work.
  • Amending a commit that was already pushed, then force-pushing over a shared branch.
  • Deleting a leaked secret with a new commit and not rotating it.
  • Panicking and recloning the repository instead of checking the reflog.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between git revert and git reset?
    Show answerHide answer
    Revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one, safe on shared history; reset moves the branch pointer back, rewriting history, safe only for unpushed commits.
  2. You committed to the wrong branch and have not pushed. How do you fix it?
    Show answerHide answer
    Note the commit, git reset --soft HEAD~1 (or git reset HEAD~1) on the wrong branch, switch to the right branch, and commit there; or cherry-pick the commit and reset the wrong branch.
  3. How do you recover a commit after a bad reset --hard?
    Show answerHide answer
    Find it in git reflog and reset or branch to it.
  4. You pushed a commit containing an API key. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Rotate the key immediately; then remove it from the code; rewriting history is secondary and needs coordination.

Practical exercise

In a practice repository, perform each undo once: discard an unstaged edit with restore; unstage a file with restore --staged; change the last commit's message with --amend; undo two local commits with reset --soft HEAD~2 and recommit them as one; revert a commit; then do reset --hard HEAD~1 and recover the commit with reflog. Acceptance criteria: git log --oneline after each step shows what you expected, and you can say for each command whether it rewrote history or added to it.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

Do this on a local practice repository with nothing pushed; steps 3, 4 and 6 rewrite history and must never be done on commits others have pulled. Start from one commit, f751fd5 Add module a.

1 and 2. restore and restore --staged (no history involved):

Text
$ echo "junk" >> src/a.ts
$ git status --short
 M src/a.ts
$ git restore src/a.ts                  # the edit is gone; status is clean again
$ echo "export const b = 2;" > src/b.ts && git add src/b.ts
$ git status --short
A  src/b.ts
$ git restore --staged src/b.ts         # unstaged, file kept
$ git status --short
?? src/b.ts

3. Amend the last message (rewrites the last commit; it gets a new hash):

Text
$ git add src/b.ts && git commit -m "add b modul"
$ git commit --amend -m "Add module b"
$ git log --oneline
