    if (err.status === 404) { card.remove(); setStatus('That product no longer exists.'); return; }
    msg.textContent = err.issues[0]?.message ?? err.message;
    f.elements.price.setAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
    save.disabled = false;
  }
});

novalidate switches off the browser's own checks on this small form, so a negative price reaches the API and its message appears under the input, as the acceptance criteria ask; the server rules are the ones that count (7.9.2 shows the same idea with the main form). Wrapping the input in its <label> labels it without needing a unique id per card. Both listeners sit on the list, so editors opened on cards added later work too, and nothing accumulates when an editor is closed.

7.6 Meeting CORS for real

7.6.1 The error, the preflight and the NestJS fix

Concept

An origin is the triple of scheme, host and port: http://localhost:5500 and http://localhost:3000 are different origins because the ports differ. The browser's same-origin policy stops JavaScript loaded from one origin from reading responses from another. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is how a server tells the browser "scripts from these origins may read my responses", using Access-Control-Allow-* headers. Part 3 (3.6) introduced the idea with curl; now you will hit it with a real page.

Why does it exist?

Imagine you are logged in to your bank in one tab and open a malicious site in another. Without the same-origin policy, that site's JavaScript could call the bank's API, the browser would attach your bank cookies, and the script could read your balance. The policy stops the reading. CORS exists because legitimate apps do need cross-origin calls, like a frontend on admin.shop.example calling an API on api.shop.example, and the server must be able to approve exactly those.

Mental model

The browser is a careful personal assistant who fetches letters for whatever website you are looking at. Before handing a reply from api.shop.example to the website admin.shop.example, the assistant checks the reply for a line saying "admin.shop.example may read this". No line, no handover, even though the letter was delivered. For anything unusual (a DELETE, a JSON body), the assistant phones ahead first to ask whether such a letter is welcome: that phone call is the preflight.

How it works

Serve the Products screen from a static server on port 5500 (7.8) while the API runs on port 3000, with no CORS configuration. Open the page and DevTools:

Text
Console:
Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:3000/products?limit=20' from origin 'http://localhost:5500'
has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the
requested resource.

The list shows "Could not load products: Could not reach the server", because fetch rejected with a TypeError and api() mapped it to NETWORK. The Network panel shows the GET with CORS error in the Status column. Yet the request did reach the API and was answered with 200. The Part 6 API logs only failures, so its terminal stays quiet, but you can replay the browser's request by hand: curl -i -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5500' 'http://localhost:3000/products?limit=20' prints 200 and the products, and no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. The server did the work; the browser refused to hand over the result. That is why curl "works": curl is not a browser and enforces nothing.

Submit the form and the Console shows a different message:

Text
Access to fetch at 'http://localhost:3000/products' from origin 'http://localhost:5500' has been
blocked by CORS policy: Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check:
No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

This time the POST never reached your controller. A POST with Content-Type: application/json is not a "simple" request, so the browser first asked permission with an OPTIONS request and got no approval:

Which of our requests are preflighted:

Request Preflight? Why
GET /products no GET with no custom headers is a "simple" request; it is sent, and only the reading is checked
POST /products with JSON yes application/json is not one of the three simple content types (form, multipart, plain text)
PATCH and DELETE /products/:id yes only GET, HEAD and POST can be simple
anything with an X-Request-Id or Authorization header yes custom headers need approval

Notice the first row. A simple cross-origin request is sent and executed; CORS only decides whether the script may read the answer. So CORS is never protection for your data or your writes. Authentication and authorization protect your API (Part 44); CORS protects your users' browsers from other websites.

NestJS example

The fix is on the server. NestJS's app.enableCors() registers the widely used cors middleware. We read the allowed origins from configuration, validated at start-up like every other setting (6.5), and refuse wildcards.

TypeScript
// src/config/env.validation.ts (addition to the Env class from 6.5)
@IsOptional() @IsString() CORS_ORIGINS: string = '';   // comma-separated exact origins; empty = no browser origins
TypeScript
// src/config/cors.ts
export function parseOrigins(raw: string): string[] {
  const origins = raw.split(',').map((s) => s.trim()).filter(Boolean);
  for (const o of origins) {
    let exact = false;
    try {
      exact = new URL(o).origin === o;     // rejects "*", paths and trailing slashes
    } catch {
      exact = false;
    }
    if (!exact) throw new Error(`CORS_ORIGINS: "${o}" must be an exact origin such as https://admin.shop.example`);
  }
  return origins;
}
TypeScript
// src/configure-app.ts (6.6, now with CORS)
import type { INestApplication } from '@nestjs/common';
import { ConfigService } from '@nestjs/config';
import { validationPipe } from './common/validation';
import { ApiExceptionFilter } from './common/api-exception.filter';
import { parseOrigins } from './config/cors';

export function configureApp(app: INestApplication): INestApplication {
  const config = app.get(ConfigService);
  app.enableCors({
    origin: parseOrigins(config.get<string>('CORS_ORIGINS', '')),  // exact list, never '*' or true
    methods: ['GET', 'POST', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
    allowedHeaders: ['Content-Type', 'X-Request-Id'],
    exposedHeaders: ['X-Request-Id'],     // lets browser code read our request ID header (6.6)
    credentials: false,                   // this API uses no cookies; see Part 81 before turning this on
    maxAge: 600,                          // browsers may cache a preflight answer for 10 minutes
  });
  app.useGlobalPipes(validationPipe);
  app.useGlobalFilters(new ApiExceptionFilter());
  app.enableShutdownHooks();
  return app;
}
Text
# .env
CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5500

With an array, the middleware compares the request's Origin header with each entry. On a match it echoes that origin back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and adds Vary: Origin, so caches do not serve one origin's answer to another. On no match it simply leaves the header out, and the browser blocks the page. Because the middleware runs before routing, error responses from the exception filter carry the header too, so the page can read a 400's issues. And because configureApp is shared with the tests (6.7), the e2e suite exercises the same CORS setup as production:

TypeScript
// test/setup-env.ts (addition)
process.env.CORS_ORIGINS = 'http://localhost:5500';
TypeScript
// test/products.e2e-spec.ts (addition)
it('approves the preflight for an allowed origin only', async () => {
  const ok = await request(app.getHttpServer())
    .options('/products')
    .set('Origin', 'http://localhost:5500')
    .set('Access-Control-Request-Method', 'POST')
    .set('Access-Control-Request-Headers', 'content-type')
    .expect(204);
  expect(ok.headers['access-control-allow-origin']).toBe('http://localhost:5500');

  const evil = await request(app.getHttpServer())
    .options('/products')
    .set('Origin', 'https://evil.example')
    .set('Access-Control-Request-Method', 'POST');
  expect(evil.headers['access-control-allow-origin']).toBeUndefined();
});

Reload the page: the list appears, and the form works. The curl -X OPTIONS command from Part 3 (3.6), pointed at port 3000 with Origin: http://localhost:5500, shows the same headers by hand, including Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5500 and Vary: Origin.

Failure scenario

At 09:05 on the morning after the admin site moved from https://shop-admin.example to https://admin.shop.example, every staff member saw "Could not load products". The API's dashboards were green: GET /products was answering 200 at the usual rate, and curl returned products. The on-call engineer opened DevTools on the admin page, read "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present", and found the cause in two minutes: the API's CORS_ORIGINS still listed the old domain. A teammate proposed origin: true "to make it go away"; that setting reflects any origin, which would let every website's scripts read the API's responses with the user's browser. Instead, the team added the new origin to the configuration, redeployed, and added a step to the release checklist: a post-deploy smoke test that sends a preflight with the production frontend's origin and fails the pipeline if the allow header is missing.

Edge cases & failure modes

  • localhost and 127.0.0.1 are different origins. A page opened at http://127.0.0.1:5500 is blocked when only http://localhost:5500 is allowed.
  • A trailing slash never matches. The Origin header has no path, so http://localhost:5500/ in the allow list matches nothing; parseOrigins rejects it at start-up for this reason.
  • * cannot be combined with credentials. Browsers reject Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * on requests that send cookies; teams then reach for origin: true, which is worse.
  • A CORS error can hide a 502 or 504. If a load balancer or proxy answers with its own error page, that page has no CORS headers, and the browser reports CORS instead of the real failure. Check the API's and the proxy's logs before editing CORS settings.
  • Pages opened from disk send Origin: null. Never add null to the allow list; sandboxed iframes and other odd contexts also send it. Serve the page over HTTP instead (7.8).
  • Custom response headers are hidden by default. Without exposedHeaders, res.headers.get('x-request-id') returns null in the browser even though DevTools shows the header.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior treats CORS as configuration with an owner, not as an error to silence. The allow list is explicit, per environment, validated at start-up and covered by a test. They never ship * for an API that uses cookies, never ship origin: true, and never confuse CORS with access control: an attacker with curl ignores CORS entirely, so every endpoint still needs authentication and authorization. And they prefer architectures where the question disappears: serving the frontend and API from one origin (7.8) or behind one domain with a reverse proxy removes preflights and CORS configuration altogether. Part 14 (14.13) covers CORS in depth and Part 81 covers cookies, credentials and CSRF.

Common mistakes

  • "Fixing" CORS in the frontend (adding mode: 'no-cors', which makes the response unreadable, or adding Access-Control-Allow-Origin as a request header, which does nothing).
  • Using app.enableCors() with no options in production, which allows every origin.
  • Forgetting that the preflight is a separate request that must succeed before the real one.
  • Assuming CORS stops other servers or curl from calling the API.

Interview questions

  1. Why does a request work in curl but fail in the browser with a CORS error?
    Show answerHide answer
    CORS is enforced by browsers for scripts; the server did not send an Access-Control-Allow-Origin that matches the page's origin. Fix the server's allow list.
  2. What is a preflight request and what triggers it?
    Show answerHide answer
    An OPTIONS request the browser sends first to ask whether a method and headers are allowed; triggered by methods other than GET, HEAD and POST, non-simple content types like JSON, or custom headers.
  3. Does CORS protect your API from unwanted callers?
    Show answerHide answer
    No. It only controls whether browser scripts can read responses; simple requests still reach and execute on the server. Authentication and authorization protect the API.
  4. The browser shows a CORS error, but the API logs show no request at all. What might be happening?
    Show answerHide answer
    A failed preflight (the real request was never sent), a proxy error page without CORS headers, or a request to the wrong host; check the Network panel for the OPTIONS row and the proxy logs.

Practical exercise

Configure CORS for three environments: development allows http://localhost:5500 and http://127.0.0.1:5500; staging allows https://admin.staging.shop.example; production allows https://admin.shop.example. Make a misconfigured value stop the app at start-up. Acceptance criteria: CORS_ORIGINS=* and CORS_ORIGINS=https://admin.shop.example/ both fail at boot with a clear message; the e2e test above passes; a preflight from an unlisted origin gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin; and the browser page can read X-Request-Id from a response.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

The code above already does most of it; the work is in configuration and checks.

Text
# development .env
CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5500,http://127.0.0.1:5500
# staging (set by the deployment, not committed)
CORS_ORIGINS=https://admin.staging.shop.example
# production (set by the deployment, not committed)
CORS_ORIGINS=https://admin.shop.example
Shell
CORS_ORIGINS='*' npm run start:dev
# Error: CORS_ORIGINS: "*" must be an exact origin such as https://admin.shop.example
CORS_ORIGINS='https://admin.shop.example/' npm run start:dev
# Error: CORS_ORIGINS: "https://admin.shop.example/" must be an exact origin such as https://admin.shop.example

new URL('*') throws, and new URL('https://admin.shop.example/').origin drops the trailing slash and no longer equals the configured string, so both fail at boot. Remove exposedHeaders and res.headers.get('x-request-id') returns null in the page while DevTools still shows the header: a quick way to prove the option does something.

7.7 Browser DevTools for beginners

7.7.1 Elements, Console, Network and Application, and one debugging walkthrough

Concept

DevTools are the debugging tools built into every major browser. Open them with F12 (Cmd+Option+I on a Mac) or right-click on the page and choose Inspect. Four panels cover almost everything a backend engineer needs: Elements (the live DOM and its styles), Console (errors, logs, and a place to run JavaScript in the page), Network (every request the page made, with headers, bodies and timing) and Application (cookies and browser storage). The examples use Chrome's names; Firefox and Safari have the same panels with slightly different labels.

Why does it exist?

Because the browser hides most of what it does. A failed fetch, a script that threw on line 12, a CSS rule that lost the cascade, a request that never left: none of these appear on the page. DevTools is to the browser what curl -v (Part 3) and your server logs are to the backend. Without it, frontend debugging is guessing.

How it works

Panel What you use it for Details worth knowing
Elements See the current DOM, not the HTML file; check styles The Styles pane shows every matching rule, with losing declarations crossed out (7.3); the box diagram shows margin, border and padding; the selected element is available in the Console as $0
Console Read errors and logs; try code Each error links to the file and line; red messages about CORS, failed module loads and uncaught exceptions appear here first
Network See every request and response Filter by Fetch/XHR for API calls; tick Preserve log to keep requests across reloads and Disable cache while debugging; click a row for Headers, Payload (the request body), Preview (parsed JSON), Response (raw) and Timing
Application Inspect cookies, Local Storage, Session Storage, IndexedDB Anything stored here is readable by any script on the page, which is why tokens in localStorage are an XSS risk (Part 81, 81.1)

Three Network features you will use weekly. Timing splits a request into phases: queueing, connection setup, "Waiting for server response" (time to first byte, mostly your API) and content download; a 900 ms wait with a 2 ms download is a backend problem, not a frontend one. Copy as cURL (right-click a request, then Copy) gives you the exact request, headers and body included, to replay in a terminal or attach to a bug ticket. Throttling (a drop-down in the Network toolbar) simulates a slow phone network or going offline, which is how you see your "Saving..." state and your timeout (7.5) actually work. The device toolbar (the phone icon, or Cmd+Shift+M) resizes the page to phone widths for checking the media query from 7.3.

Practical example — "the list is empty but the API works in curl"

A teammate reports: the Products page says "No products yet", but curl http://localhost:3000/products returns products. Walk it the same way every time: Console, then Network, then the code.

In this case the Console is clean. The Network panel, filtered to Fetch/XHR, shows products?limit=20 with status 200. Preview shows { items: [ {...}, {...} ], nextCursor: null }. The teammate's code, written against the 6.2 version of the API, is:

JavaScript
const products = await api('/products?limit=20');
if (!products.length) setStatus('No products yet.');   // an object has no length: undefined, so !undefined is true

The API changed shape in 6.5, from an array to a page object. An object has no length, so the "empty" branch runs without any error. The fix is page.items, and the lasting fix is a contract that would have caught the change: Part 80 (80.2 and 80.10) generates typed clients and runs contract tests so a shape change fails CI instead of a user's screen.

The same walkthrough catches the other usual suspects:

What DevTools shows Likely cause Fix
Console: "blocked by CORS policy"; Network: CORS error page origin missing from CORS_ORIGINS add the exact origin (7.6)
Network shows app.js from "(disk cache)", old code runs browser cached an old script Disable cache while debugging; versioned file names in production (Part 84, 84.3)
No request at all, Console says module failed to load page opened from disk or served with the wrong MIME type serve over HTTP (7.8)

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Opening DevTools after the page loaded misses the first requests; reload with the Network panel open.
  • Red "Failed to load resource: ... status of 409" lines appear in Chrome's Console for every 4xx and 5xx response, even ones your code handles correctly, and for a missing favicon.ico; they are network logs, not script errors.
  • A CORS-blocked response hides its body from the page and largely from DevTools; check the server log for what actually happened.
  • Production code is minified: line 1, column 48,213 tells you nothing without source maps (Part 76, 76.7, and Part 84, 84.6).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior uses DevTools to decide in one minute which side of the wire is wrong. Status and Preview right, page wrong: frontend. Status or body wrong: API, and Copy as cURL turns it into a backend reproduction. They connect the two worlds with the request ID: the requestId in a problem body (or the X-Request-Id header, once exposed) is the key to the exact server log line from 6.6, and Part 84 (84.7) extends that to full traces from a click to a database write.

Interview questions

  1. A page shows stale data after a deploy. What do you check in DevTools?
    Show answerHide answer
    Whether scripts and API responses came from cache (Size column, Disable cache), and the response headers (Cache-Control) of the API and the static files.
  2. How do you tell whether slowness is in the frontend or the API?
    Show answerHide answer
    Network Timing: a long "Waiting for server response" is server time; a fast response followed by a slow page is frontend work, which Part 75 (75.10) and Part 82 dig into.
  3. How do you turn a browser bug into a backend reproduction?
    Show answerHide answer
    Copy the failing request as cURL, strip secrets, replay it, and use the request ID to find the server log line.

Practical exercise

With the Products screen running, use only DevTools to answer: what is the request ID of a duplicate-SKU error, how many milliseconds did the server spend on GET /products, which CSS rule makes an invalid input's border red, and what happens in the UI when you set throttling to Offline and press Refresh. Acceptance criteria: a value or observation for each, and the panel you found it in.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

Create SKU DM-001 twice. Network: the failing products row has status 409; Preview shows code: "PRODUCT_SKU_TAKEN" and the requestId, also in the X-Request-Id header. Timing on a GET /products row: "Waiting for server response", a few milliseconds locally. Elements: select the SKU input after the error; Styles shows input[aria-invalid="true"] winning over the base input rule. Offline throttling plus Refresh: fetch rejects, the status line reads "Could not load products: Could not reach the server", and the Network row shows a failure with no status code, the "no response at all" case from 3.1.

7.8 Serving the frontend

7.8.1 A file on disk, a static server, or NestJS, and ES modules

Concept

A frontend is a handful of static files: index.html, styles.css, app.js, api.js. "Static" means the server sends them exactly as they are on disk, with no code running per request. Something still has to send them, and where they are served from decides their origin, which decides whether CORS is involved at all. There are three choices for local work: open the file straight from disk, run a tiny static server, or let NestJS serve the files next to the API.

Why does it exist?

Because browsers treat pages differently depending on where they came from. A page opened from disk has the strange origin null and is denied things a page served over HTTP is allowed. A page served from the API's own origin needs no CORS at all. Choosing on purpose saves an afternoon of confusing errors.

How it works

Option 1: open the file from disk (file:///Users/you/products-web/index.html). Our page fails at once:

Text
Access to script at 'file:///Users/you/products-web/app.js' from origin 'null' has been blocked
by CORS policy: Cross origin requests are only supported for protocol schemes: http, ...

Module scripts (<script type="module">) are fetched with CORS rules, and file:// pages have the opaque origin null, so the browser refuses. Even a classic script that did load would send Origin: null to the API, which you must never allow (7.6). Opening from disk is fine for a plain HTML mock-up and nothing else.

Option 2: a tiny static server on its own port. Either of these serves the current folder over HTTP:

Shell
cd products-web
python3 -m http.server 5500 --bind 127.0.0.1    # ships with Python 3; serves on http://127.0.0.1:5500
# or
npx http-server . -p 5500 -c-1                   # the http-server npm package; -c-1 turns off caching

The page's origin is now http://localhost:5500 (or http://127.0.0.1:5500, a different origin; use the one in your CORS_ORIGINS), and the API on port 3000 is cross-origin, so you need the NestJS CORS setup from 7.6. This is how most frontend development works: a frontend dev server on one port, the API on another. Avoid npx serve here without a port flag: it defaults to port 3000, which the API already uses.

Option 3: serve the files from NestJS. The official @nestjs/serve-static package serves a folder from the same Nest application, so the page and the API share one origin:

Shell
npm install @nestjs/serve-static
TypeScript
// src/app.module.ts (addition to imports)
import { join } from 'node:path';
import { ServeStaticModule } from '@nestjs/serve-static';

ServeStaticModule.forRoot({
  rootPath: join(__dirname, '..', 'public'),   // products-api/public holds index.html, styles.css, app.js, api.js
  serveRoot: '/app',                            // the page is at /app/; API routes such as /products are untouched
}),

Open http://localhost:3000/app/. In index.html, set <meta name="api-base" content="">, so api() calls relative URLs like /products. Same scheme, host and port: no preflight, no CORS headers needed, and CORS_ORIGINS can stay empty. Serving under /app keeps the static handler away from the API's routes, so a typo in a URL never returns index.html where JSON was expected. In the Docker image (6.8), add COPY --from=build /app/public ./public to the final stage.

ES modules in the browser. <script type="module" src="app.js"> loads app.js as an ES module, the same import/export system you know from TypeScript and Node (Part 1). Four browser-specific facts:

  1. Modules are deferred. They run after the HTML is parsed, so document.querySelector('#product-list') finds the element even though the script tag is in <head>.
  2. Each module has its own scope. A top-level const list in app.js is not a global, so you cannot call loadProducts() from the Console; that is a feature, not a bug.
  3. Import paths are URLs. Write import { api } from './api.js' with the ./ and the .js extension. Bare names like import x from 'lodash' fail without a bundler or an import map, because the browser has no node_modules lookup.
  4. The server must send JavaScript's MIME type (text/javascript). A server that returns an HTML 404 page for a mistyped path produces "Failed to load module script: Expected a JavaScript module script but the server responded with a MIME type of text/html".

Each module is one HTTP request. Two or three files are nothing; three hundred are why bundlers exist (Part 76, 76.1 and 76.3).

Edge cases & failure modes

  • Stale files after an edit: the browser cached the old app.js; tick Disable cache in DevTools while developing, and use versioned file names in production (Part 84, 84.3).
  • ServeStatic without serveRoot puts a catch-all next to the API, and an unknown API path can return index.html with status 200.
  • Releasing the frontend with the API couples their deploys: a CSS fix needs an API release. Fine for an internal tool, a real cost for a busy product.
  • Security headers such as Content Security Policy now apply to the page too; Part 44 (44.33) and Part 84 (84.9) cover what to send.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior picks the topology first and lets CORS follow from it. For a small internal tool, serving from NestJS (or putting the frontend and API behind one domain with a reverse proxy) removes a whole class of problems. For a public product with its own frontend team and release cadence, a separate static host or CDN plus an API on its own subdomain is normal, and CORS is configured as a deliberate, tested allow list. Either way, they write the decision down, because the next person will ask why.

Option Page origin CORS needed? Good for Watch out for
File from disk null breaks module scripts a static mock-up nothing that calls an API works properly
Static server on its own port http://localhost:5500 yes frontend development, this Part's CORS lesson allow list per environment
NestJS ServeStaticModule same as the API no internal tools, one deployable coupled releases, static caching headers
CDN or static host, API on a subdomain https://admin.shop.example yes public products, independent deploys CORS and cookie settings (Part 81, Part 84, 84.1)
One domain, reverse proxy routes /api and / same no a common production default proxy configuration and path prefixes

Interview questions

  1. Why does a page that uses <script type="module"> fail when opened from disk?
    Show answerHide answer
    Module scripts are fetched under CORS rules and a file:// page has the opaque origin null, so the browser blocks them.
  2. How does serving the frontend from the API's origin remove CORS?
    Show answerHide answer
    CORS only applies to cross-origin requests; same scheme, host and port means no preflight and no allow headers are needed.
  3. What are the costs of serving the frontend from NestJS?
    Show answerHide answer
    Coupled releases, the API process serving static files, and caching and security headers to manage in one place.

Practical exercise

Serve the Products screen from NestJS under /app, with CORS_ORIGINS empty, and prove it works without CORS. Acceptance criteria: http://localhost:3000/app/ loads and creates products; the POST in the Network panel has no preceding OPTIONS row; the page served from port 5500 at the same time is blocked by CORS.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer

Copy the four files into products-api/public/, set <meta name="api-base" content="">, add the ServeStaticModule block and restart. At http://localhost:3000/app/ the Network panel shows POST /products with 201 and no OPTIONS row before it. The copy on port 5500, pointing at port 3000, now fails with the preflight error from 7.6, because the empty CORS_ORIGINS allows no cross-origin pages. CORS is a property of the relationship between two origins, not of the API alone.

7.9 Worked example: the Products screen

7.9.1 The four files

Concept

Here is the whole screen in one place: a single page that lists products with "Load more", creates a product from a form, shows validation errors next to the right fields, and deletes a product after confirmation, talking to the unmodified Part 6 API plus the CORS setup from 7.6. It is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step.

Why plain JavaScript and not TypeScript? Browsers run JavaScript, not TypeScript. TypeScript would need tsc (or a bundler) to compile app.ts to app.js before every reload, which is one more moving part between your edit and what the browser runs, and for 150 lines the safety it buys is small. If you want type checking without a build, put // @ts-check at the top of a .js file: editors that use the TypeScript language service (VS Code, for example) then check it as you type. Part 76 sets up TypeScript for the browser properly, with Vite.

Practical example

index.html:

HTML
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <meta name="api-base" content="http://localhost:3000">   <!-- "" when served by NestJS (7.8) -->
  <title>Products - Shop Admin</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
  <script type="module" src="app.js"></script>
</head>
<body>
  <header class="toolbar">
    <h1>Products</h1>
    <button type="button" id="refresh">Refresh</button>
  </header>
  <main class="layout">
    <section class="panel" aria-labelledby="new-heading">
      <h2 id="new-heading">New product</h2>
      <form id="create-form">
        <!-- the four .field blocks from 7.2.2 (name, sku, price, currency), unchanged -->
        <p class="error" id="form-error" role="alert"></p>
        <button type="submit">Add product</button>
      </form>
    </section>
    <section class="panel" aria-labelledby="list-heading">
      <h2 id="list-heading">All products</h2>
      <p id="status" role="status"></p>
      <ul id="product-list" class="cards"></ul>
      <button type="button" id="load-more" hidden>Load more</button>
    </section>
  </main>
</body>
</html>

styles.css is the rules from 7.3.1 and 7.3.2 (variables, box-sizing, the toolbar, the cards, the grid and its media query, error and focus styles), plus:

CSS
[hidden] { display: none !important; }            /* hidden always wins, even over display rules (7.3.2) */
.field { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 0.25rem; margin-bottom: 0.75rem; }
.hint { margin: 0; color: var(--muted); font-size: 0.875rem; }
#status { margin: 0 0 0.75rem; color: var(--muted); }
#status.is-error { color: var(--danger); }
#status:empty { display: none; }

api.js is exactly the module from 7.5.1. app.js assembles the functions from 7.4 and 7.5 and adds delete:

JavaScript
// app.js -- the Products screen
import { api } from './api.js';

const form = document.querySelector('#create-form');
const formError = document.querySelector('#form-error');
const list = document.querySelector('#product-list');
const statusEl = document.querySelector('#status');
const loadMoreBtn = document.querySelector('#load-more');
const FIELD_FOR_PATH = { name: 'name', sku: 'sku', priceCents: 'price', currency: 'currency' };
const EMPTY_TEXT = 'No products yet. Add the first one with the form.';
let nextCursor = null;
let submitting = false;

function formatPrice(cents, currency) {
  try {
    return new Intl.NumberFormat(undefined, { style: 'currency', currency }).format(cents / 100);
  } catch {
    return `${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)} ${currency}`;   // an unknown currency code must not break the list
  }
}

// Paste these functions here unchanged (the functions only, not the const lines above them):
//   productCard(p)                                           from 7.4.1
//   setStatus() and loadProducts(), using EMPTY_TEXT          from 7.5.1
//   the form's submit listener, clearErrors(), showErrors()  from 7.5.2

list.addEventListener('click', async (event) => {        // one delegated listener for every Delete button
  const button = event.target.closest('button[data-action="delete"]');
  if (!button) return;
  const card = button.closest('li');
  const name = card.querySelector('h3').textContent;
  if (!window.confirm(`Delete "${name}"? This cannot be undone.`)) return;
  button.disabled = true;
  try {
    await api(`/products/${encodeURIComponent(card.dataset.id)}`, { method: 'DELETE' });   // 204, no body
    card.remove();
    if (list.children.length === 0) setStatus(EMPTY_TEXT);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.status === 404) {                             // someone else deleted it first: the screen was stale
      card.remove();
      setStatus('That product had already been deleted.');
    } else {
      button.disabled = false;
      setStatus(`Could not delete "${name}": ${err.message}`, true);
    }
  }
});

document.querySelector('#refresh').addEventListener('click', () => loadProducts());
loadMoreBtn.addEventListener('click', () => loadProducts({ append: true }));
loadProducts();                                           // module scripts run after parsing, so the elements exist

The confirm() dialog is the simplest honest confirmation: blocking, accessible and built in. The exercise below replaces it with a styled <dialog>. The delete is also safe against a stale screen: a 404 means the product is already gone, which is the outcome the user wanted, so the card disappears with a note instead of an error.

7.9.2 Running it end to end, and where to go next

How it works

Shell
# terminal 1: the Part 6 API with the CORS setup from 7.6.
# With npm run start:dev, put CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5500 in .env. With Compose, add
# CORS_ORIGINS: "http://localhost:5500" under the api service's environment (the image has no .env).
cd products-api && docker compose up --build      # or: npm run start:dev with the database running
# terminal 2: the frontend
cd products-web && python3 -m http.server 5500 --bind 127.0.0.1
# open http://localhost:5500 (the origin in CORS_ORIGINS; 127.0.0.1 would be a different origin)

Try it yourself

Predict what the screen shows, then try it.

  1. Create "Dental Mirror", SKU DM-001, price 12.99. Then create another product with SKU DM-001.
  2. Remove required and min="0" from the price input in the Elements panel, type -5 and submit.
  3. Stop the API (docker compose stop api) and press Refresh.
  4. Set Network throttling to a slow preset and add a product, pressing Enter twice quickly.

Answers.

  1. The first appears at the top of the list as "DM-001 - $12.99" (formatting follows your browser's locale). The second gets 409 PRODUCT_SKU_TAKEN, and "A product with this SKU already exists" appears under the SKU field, because the Part 6 filter sends issues: [{ path: "sku" }].
  2. The browser's own checks are gone, so the request is sent; the API answers 400 VALIDATION_FAILED and "priceCents must not be less than 0" appears under Price. The server, not the HTML, is the authority.
  3. "Could not load products: Could not reach the server". fetch rejected, there is no status code, and the list does not pretend to be empty.
  4. The button shows "Saving..." and is disabled; one POST appears in the Network panel, not two.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

The decision that matters is not "which framework" but "what does this screen need". For one admin screen maintained by backend engineers, plain HTML, CSS and a 150-line module is the simplest thing that works, has no dependencies to update, and runs for years. When the tool grows to a dozen screens with shared components, routing and cached server data, a framework starts paying for itself.

Question Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript A framework (React with Vite, or Next.js)
How many screens? one or a few many, sharing components and layout
How much UI state? a list, a form, a status line many pieces of state that depend on each other
Build step none: the browser runs your files required (Part 76)
Escaping user data your job, every time (textContent) done by default in JSX (Part 77, Part 81, 81.7)
Data fetching and caching a hand-written api() libraries such as TanStack Query (Part 78)
Who maintains it backend engineers, occasionally a team that works on it every week
Verdict for this Products screen the right size worth it once the tool grows

Where to go next. Volume 7 picks up exactly where this Part stops:

  • Part 75 — How the Browser Builds a Page: from bytes to pixels, with deeper forms (75.2), CSS (75.4), script loading (75.6), the main thread (75.7), storage (75.8), accessibility (75.9) and DevTools (75.10).
  • Part 76 — Frontend Tooling and TypeScript in the Browser: the build step, Vite and TypeScript, sharing contracts with NestJS.
  • Part 77 — React Fundamentals for Backend Engineers and Part 78 — Client State, Data Fetching and Caching: this screen as components, forms (77.7), double-submit protection (77.8), cancellation (78.10) and loading, empty and error states (78.11).
  • Part 79 — Next.js and Rendering Strategies, Part 80 — Frontend–Backend Contracts (generated clients and error contracts, 80.6) and Part 81 — Auth and Security in the Browser.
  • Parts 82–85: performance, testing (Playwright, 83.7; axe, 83.10), shipping frontends, and a full-stack worked project; then Part 87 — Frontend and Full-Stack Interview Preparation.

Interview questions

  1. When would you choose plain JavaScript over a framework for a frontend?
    Show answerHide answer
    For small, stable screens with little state and no dedicated frontend team: fewer dependencies, no build, easy to maintain. Choose a framework when screens, shared components and state grow.
  2. Walk through what happens, end to end, when a user adds a product on this screen.
    Show answerHide answer
    Submit event, preventDefault, values read and converted, JSON POST (preflight first if cross-origin), ValidationPipe, service, unique constraint, 201 or problem+json, card added or errors placed under fields.
  3. How does this screen stay correct when two people use it at once?
    Show answerHide answer
    It re-renders from server responses, treats 404 on delete as "already gone", relies on the unique SKU to reject duplicates, and offers Refresh; it never assumes its list is the truth.

Practical exercise

Two improvements. First, replace window.confirm() with a styled <dialog> that has Cancel and Delete buttons and can be dismissed with Escape. Second, remember the last chosen currency in localStorage so the form starts with it next time. Acceptance criteria: Escape cancels the delete; keyboard focus moves into the dialog and returns afterwards; the saved currency survives a reload and a successful submit (form.reset() must not wipe it); and the page still works if localStorage throws (some browsers block it in private modes).

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
HTML
<dialog id="confirm-delete" aria-labelledby="confirm-text">
  <form method="dialog">                          <!-- a button press closes the dialog and sets returnValue -->
    <p id="confirm-text"></p>
    <button value="cancel">Cancel</button>
    <button value="delete">Delete</button>
  </form>
</dialog>
JavaScript
const dialog = document.querySelector('#confirm-delete');

function confirmDelete(name) {
  document.querySelector('#confirm-text').textContent = `Delete "${name}"? This cannot be undone.`;
  dialog.returnValue = '';                         // Escape does not change returnValue, so clear the last answer
  dialog.showModal();                              // modal: focus moves inside, the page behind is inert
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    dialog.addEventListener('close', () => resolve(dialog.returnValue === 'delete'), { once: true });
  });
}
// in the delete listener, replace window.confirm(...) with:
//   if (!(await confirmDelete(name))) return;

const CURRENCY_KEY = 'products.currency';
function restoreCurrency() {
  try {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem(CURRENCY_KEY);
    if (saved) form.elements.namedItem('currency').value = saved;
  } catch { /* storage blocked: keep the default */ }
}
form.elements.namedItem('currency').addEventListener('change', (e) => {
  try { localStorage.setItem(CURRENCY_KEY, e.target.value); } catch { /* not fatal */ }
});
restoreCurrency();
// in the submit handler, call restoreCurrency() right after form.reset()

showModal() moves focus into the dialog, makes the rest of the page inert and closes on Escape; when the dialog closes, the browser returns focus to the element that opened it, the Delete button. Resetting returnValue matters: without it, cancelling with Escape after an earlier "delete" answer would still read "delete" and delete the wrong product. In the Application panel (7.7) you can watch products.currency change under Local Storage. A currency preference is harmless to store there; a token is not (Part 81, 81.1).

Senior Checklist — Part 7

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can explain how a page loads: HTML first, then the CSS and JavaScript it names, then API calls from scripts
  • I write semantic HTML with one h1, real buttons and links, and a <label> for every input
  • I know what a browser does with a native form submit and why a JSON API frontend intercepts it
  • I can predict which CSS rule wins using specificity and source order, and I set box-sizing: border-box
  • I can build a mobile-first layout with flexbox, a simple grid and one min-width media query
  • I render user data with createElement and textContent, never innerHTML, and can explain stored XSS
  • I use event delegation and know that blocking the browser's main thread freezes the page
  • I check res.ok after fetch and give every request loading, empty and error states
  • I map API issues[].path values to form fields and set aria-invalid
  • I add a timeout with AbortController, guard against double submits, and know a timed-out POST may have succeeded
  • I can read a CORS error, explain the preflight, and configure app.enableCors with an exact origin list from validated config
  • I can debug "empty list, API works in curl" with the Console, Network and Elements panels
  • I can choose where to serve a frontend and explain why same-origin removes CORS

Part 7 — Key Takeaways

  • A frontend is files the browser downloads and runs: HTML for structure, CSS for looks, JavaScript for behaviour and API calls; it never enforces rules, the backend does.
  • Semantic HTML with labels is the cheapest accessibility you will ever get; a delete action is a <button>, never a link.
  • A native form submit sends URL-encoded strings and navigates away; a JSON API frontend calls preventDefault, converts values and sends JSON with fetch.
  • In CSS, keep selectors short and class-based, start with box-sizing: border-box, use flexbox for rows and columns, grid for page structure, and write mobile-first.
  • textContent for every piece of user data; innerHTML with data is stored XSS waiting for a victim.
  • fetch resolves on 404 and 500; check the status, and design for loading, empty, failed and loaded states.
  • Good API error design (one shape, field paths, stable codes, request IDs) is what makes a good form possible.
  • Every request needs a timeout, every write needs double-submit protection, and a timed-out POST may already have happened.
  • CORS is enforced by browsers for scripts; fix it on the server with an exact, validated, tested origin list, and remember it never protects the API from curl.
  • DevTools is the browser's curl -v: Console for errors, Network for status, shape and timing, Elements for the real DOM and styles.
  • Where you serve the frontend decides its origin; same-origin serving removes CORS entirely.
  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript are the right size for one small screen; frameworks pay off as screens and state grow, and Volume 7 takes you there.

Volume 0: From Scratch

Part 8 — Your First Developer Job

  • 1 h 5 min read
  • 13 sections
