What you will learn

  1. 8.1The first week
  2. 8.2How work is organised
  3. 8.3Reading and clarifying a ticket
  4. 8.4Breaking work down and estimating honestly
  5. 8.5Asking for help well
  6. 8.6The pull request as a conversation
  7. 8.7Standups and written updates
  8. 8.8Working with QA, product and design
  9. 8.9Your first production bug and your first on-call shift
  10. 8.10Learning on the job
  11. 8.11Using AI tools responsibly at work
  12. 8.12Growing towards mid-level
  13. 8.13Common junior mistakes

Parts 1 to 7 taught you to build things: a typed program, an async request, a NestJS API on PostgreSQL, a Git branch, a screen that calls it. This Part is about the thing nobody teaches in a tutorial: doing that work inside a team, for a business, with other people's code, other people's deadlines and real customers on the other end.

What decides how your first year goes is not how many algorithms you know. It is a set of working habits: how you read a ticket, how honestly you estimate, when you ask for help, how your pull requests read, how you write a status update, and how you behave the first time something you shipped breaks in production. None of those habits needs talent. All of them can be learned on purpose, and this Part teaches them the way the rest of the book teaches a database index: concept, mechanism, example, failure, and a worked exercise.

Part 62 — The Senior Engineering Mindset and Part 63 — Junior to Principal: What Is Expected at Each Level describe the top of the ladder. This Part is the bottom rung. In Part 63's table, a junior's scope is "a task", their time horizon is "days to a sprint", and their influence is "learns from others". That is not an insult; it is a job description. Your aim this year is to do task-sized work reliably, learn fast, and become someone the team trusts with a whole feature, which is what "mid-level" means.

The examples follow one fictional junior, Aisha, in her first months at a mid-sized online shop. The backend is NestJS on PostgreSQL with Redis and a message queue, the tracker is Jira-like, code lives on GitHub, and CI runs on GitHub Actions. Her tech lead is Priya, the product manager is Lena, the QA engineer is Marco and the designer is Sam. Your company's tools will have different names; the habits transfer.

8.1 The first week

8.1.1 Access, setup and the shape of the codebase

Concept

Your first week has three jobs: get access to everything you need, get the system running on your machine, and build a rough map of the codebase and the team. You are not expected to ship much. You are expected to make steady, visible progress and to write down what confused you, because that list is valuable to the team.

Why does it exist?

Every team's setup has rotted a little since the last person joined. The README says Node 18 and the project needs Node 22. The seed script needs an environment variable nobody documented. A new person is the only one who can see those gaps, because everyone else has a working machine and has forgotten how they got it. A first week spent carefully, with notes, both onboards you and repairs the path for the next person.

Mental model

Imagine moving to a new city. In the first week you do not try to know every street. You get your keys and your transit card, find the supermarket and the pharmacy, walk one route to work until it feels familiar, and keep a list of questions for your neighbour. A codebase is the same: access first, one route through it, a list of questions.

How it works

A realistic first week, day by day:

Access checklist. Ask your manager or buddy for the team's onboarding list; if there is none, this is the usual set, and writing it down is your first contribution:

  • Email, chat (Slack, Teams) and the team's channels, including the incident channel
  • Code host (GitHub or GitLab) with the right organisation and team membership
  • SSH key or token configured (5.6)
  • Ticket tracker (Jira, Linear, GitHub Issues) and the team's board
  • Documentation space (Confluence, Notion, a docs/ folder) and the architecture overview, if one exists
  • CI dashboard and the logs and metrics tools (Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch), read-only to start
  • A local or shared development database; never production write access in week one
  • Password manager or secrets tool, and the rule for where secrets live (never in Git, never in chat)
  • The on-call schedule and paging tool, even though you are not on it yet

Local setup. Follow the README exactly, and keep a running log as you go: every command you ran, every error, every fix. When something fails, spend a bounded amount of time on it (8.5 gives the rule), then ask. When you finally get the app running, turn the log into a pull request that fixes the README. Teams remember the new joiner who did that.

Shell
# Aisha's setup log, day 2 (kept in a scratch file, later turned into a README fix)
git clone git@github.com:shop/orders-service.git && cd orders-service
nvm use                      # .nvmrc says 22; README said 18 -> README fix #1
npm ci                       # installs exactly what package-lock.json lists
cp .env.example .env         # DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, PAYMENTS_API_KEY=test-key
docker compose up -d postgres redis
npm run migration:run        # failed: "relation customers does not exist"
                             # -> needed `npm run seed:base` first; not documented -> README fix #2
npm run start:dev            # Nest application successfully started
curl -s localhost:3000/health   # {"status":"ok"}
npm test                     # 412 passed, 3 skipped

The map. Part 0 — How to Understand Any Technology (0.4.3) gives the reading order for an unfamiliar codebase: dependency file and CI config, entry points, one real request traced end to end, the tests, then git log and git blame for the odd parts. In a job, add three questions that only people can answer:

  1. What does this service do for the business, and who calls it? ("Orders. The web shop and the mobile app call it; the warehouse system consumes its events.")
  2. What breaks most often, and what is scary to touch? Every team has a module everyone tiptoes around. Know where it is.
  3. How does code reach production? Who approves, what CI checks, how deploys happen, how a rollback happens.

Practical example — tracing one request

On day 3 Aisha traces POST /orders and writes the path down in her notes. She does not understand every line; she understands the route.

Text
POST /orders
  OrdersController.create (src/orders/orders.controller.ts)
    -> CreateOrderDto validated by the global ValidationPipe
  OrdersService.create (src/orders/orders.service.ts)
    -> InventoryService.reserve        (Redis lock, then UPDATE inventory)
    -> PaymentsClient.authorize         (HTTP to the payment provider, 5 s timeout)
    -> OrdersRepository.save            (INSERT orders + order_items in one transaction)
    -> outbox row "order.created"       (picked up by a worker, published to the queue)
Questions for Priya:
  - why is the inventory reserved before payment and not after?
  - what happens if the outbox worker is down?

Those two questions show she read the code and thought about failure, which is precisely the habit the rest of this book builds. Priya's answers ("we reserve first so we never charge for something out of stock; the outbox catches up when the worker returns, see Part 33") teach her more than an hour of reading would.

Common mistakes

  • Struggling silently with setup for two days to avoid "bothering" anyone. Your setup problem is usually a documentation bug the team wants to know about.
  • Trying to read the whole codebase before touching anything. Trace one route, then learn by changing things.
  • Criticising the code in week one ("why don't you use X?"). There is usually a history you have not heard. Ask why first; suggest later.
  • Not writing anything down. You will ask the same question twice, and your fresh-eyes observations disappear by week three.

8.1.2 Your first small ticket

Concept

Most teams give a new joiner a starter ticket: a small, well-understood change, often labelled good-first-issue or onboarding. Its real purpose is not the change. It is to walk you through the whole path once: pick up a ticket, branch, change code, write a test, open a pull request, get a review, merge, deploy, and verify. After that path has worked once, every later ticket is "the same, but harder".

How it works

Practical example — Aisha's starter ticket

Text
SHOP-1423  Order history returns orders in random order
Type: Bug   Priority: Low   Labels: good-first-issue
Customers see their order history in a different order on each refresh.
Expected: newest first.
Endpoint: GET /customers/:id/orders

She reproduces it first, which takes five minutes and proves she is looking at the right thing:

Shell
curl -s localhost:3000/customers/cus_demo/orders | jq '.items[].createdAt'
# "2026-10-02T09:14:00Z"
# "2026-11-01T18:40:00Z"
# "2026-10-15T12:03:00Z"    <- not sorted

Then she finds the cause. PostgreSQL makes no promise about row order without ORDER BY (Part 21 — SQL Mastery for Backend Engineers), and the repository query has none. The fix is two lines, and the test is the important part:

TypeScript
// src/orders/orders.repository.ts
async findByCustomer(customerId: string, limit: number): Promise<Order[]> {
  return this.repo.find({
    where: { customerId },
    order: { createdAt: 'DESC', id: 'DESC' },  // id breaks ties when two orders share a timestamp
    take: limit,
  });
}
TypeScript
// test/orders-history.e2e-spec.ts (the shape the team's other e2e tests already use)
it('returns a customer order history newest first', async () => {
  await seedOrders('cus_demo', ['2026-10-02', '2026-11-01', '2026-10-15']); // the suite's own seeding helper
  const res = await request(app.getHttpServer()).get('/customers/cus_demo/orders').expect(200);
  const dates = res.body.items.map((o: { createdAt: string }) => o.createdAt.slice(0, 10));
  expect(dates).toEqual(['2026-11-01', '2026-10-15', '2026-10-02']);
});

Before opening the pull request she asks one more question in the team channel: "Is there an index on orders (customer_id, created_at)? Sorting without one could be slow for customers with many orders." There is (Part 23 — Database Indexing). Asking showed she knows sorting has a cost, and it took ten seconds.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

A senior watching a new joiner's first ticket is not grading the two-line fix. They are watching whether the person reproduced the bug before changing code, wrote a test that would have caught it, kept the pull request small, linked the ticket, and checked that the fix worked after deploy. Those habits predict everything else. A perfect fix with no test and no verification is a worse first ticket than a clumsy fix with both.

Common mistakes

  • Fixing the bug without first reproducing it, and so "fixing" something adjacent.
  • Bundling "while I was there" refactors into the starter pull request. Keep it to the ticket.
  • Considering the ticket done at merge. It is done when it works where customers are.

8.2 How work is organised

8.2.1 Tickets, the backlog, sprints and kanban

Concept

Teams track work as tickets (also called issues, stories or tasks): one unit of work with a title, a description, an owner and a status. All the tickets not yet started form the backlog, kept roughly in priority order by the product manager or tech lead. Teams then pull work from the backlog in one of two broad styles: sprints (fixed time boxes) or kanban (continuous flow).

Why does it exist?

Without a shared list, work lives in people's heads and chat threads. Two people fix the same bug, nobody fixes the important one, and nobody can answer "when will it be ready?". A tracker makes the work visible: what is planned, who is doing what, what is blocked, and what has shipped.

Mental model

Imagine a restaurant kitchen. Orders arrive on tickets. Tickets wait on a rail (the backlog), get picked up by a cook (In Progress), checked by the head chef (review), and go out to the table (Done). The rail makes it obvious when the kitchen is overloaded and which table has waited longest.

How it works

The common ticket types:

Type What it is Example
Story or feature New behaviour a user can notice "Customers can download an invoice PDF"
Bug Existing behaviour that is wrong "Order history is unsorted"
Task or chore Work with no user-visible change "Upgrade NestJS to the next major version"
Spike Time-boxed research that ends in an answer, not code "Find out whether the provider supports partial refunds (half a day)"
Epic A large goal made of many tickets "Self-service returns"

A typical lifecycle. Your team's column names will differ, but the shape is nearly universal:

Sprints (Scrum). The team works in fixed time boxes, commonly two weeks. At sprint planning it picks the tickets it believes it can finish. A short daily standup (8.7) keeps everyone in sync. At the end, a sprint review shows what was built and a retrospective asks what to improve in how the team works. Tickets are often estimated in story points, a relative size ("this is about twice the size of that"), not hours.

Kanban. There are no time boxes. Work flows continuously across the board, and the key rule is a work-in-progress (WIP) limit: at most, say, three tickets in "In Review" at once. When a column is full, people stop starting new work and help finish what is stuck. Kanban teams track cycle time, how long a ticket takes from start to done.

Sprints Kanban
Rhythm Fixed time boxes with planning and review Continuous flow
Commitment "We plan to finish these this sprint" "We finish what we start before starting more"
Change mid-cycle Discouraged; new work waits for next sprint Normal; reprioritise the top of the backlog any time
Common in Product teams with a roadmap Platform, support and operations teams with unpredictable work

Most real teams are a mix ("we do two-week sprints but keep a kanban lane for bugs"). Ask how yours works; do not assume from the book.

8.2.2 The definition of done

Concept

The definition of done (DoD) is the team's shared checklist for when a ticket may be called finished. It removes the most common argument in software: "I'm done" meaning "the code is written" to one person and "customers can use it" to another.

How it works

A realistic backend definition of done:

  • Acceptance criteria in the ticket are met
  • Code reviewed and approved by at least one teammate
  • Automated tests added or updated; CI is green
  • Database migration is backward-compatible with the running version (Part 27 — Database Migrations and Zero-Downtime Schema Changes)
  • Logs, metrics or alerts added for new failure paths
  • API documentation updated if the contract changed
  • Deployed and verified in production, or behind a feature flag with a plan to enable it
  • Ticket updated with what shipped and anything left over

Failure scenario

A junior marks a ticket "Done" when the pull request merges. The feature, a new discount field on orders, needs a configuration value in production that was only set locally. The deploy goes out on Thursday evening; no one checks. On Friday morning the support team reports that discounts silently stopped applying for 14 hours, because the code read a missing setting as "0 percent". Nobody did anything outrageous. The team simply had no shared rule that "done" includes verifying in production. They added it to the definition of done the following week, along with failing fast on missing configuration at startup (6.5.1).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors treat "done" as an outcome. They ask "how will we know it worked?" before starting, and leave a short note on the ticket when it ships: "Released in v2.41 at 14:10; error rate unchanged; first 30 invoices generated correctly." That one line saves a dozen follow-up questions.

Common mistakes

  • Moving a ticket to Done when it is merged, not when it works.
  • Silently splitting the work ("I did the API, the email part can be later") without telling anyone or creating a follow-up ticket.
  • Leaving tickets in the wrong column, so the board lies about the state of the work.

Interview questions

  1. What does "done" mean to you on a ticket?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: acceptance criteria met, reviewed, tested in CI, deployed and verified where customers use it, ticket updated. Follow-up: what do you do if you cannot verify in production?
  2. Have you worked in sprints or kanban? What did you like and dislike?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: an honest description of the rhythm and one real trade-off, for example that sprints made planning visible but encouraged rushing at the end.

Practical exercise

You join a team and find your first ticket in the "Ready" column:

Text
SHOP-1502  Add "estimated delivery date" to the order confirmation API

Using the lifecycle and definition of done above, write the list of things that must be true before you move this ticket to Done. Acceptance criteria: at least six items, each one checkable by someone other than you, and at least one item about production.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
Text
Before SHOP-1502 is Done:
1. GET /orders/:id/confirmation returns estimatedDeliveryDate (ISO date) for every
   shippable order, and null for digital-only orders. (Agreed with Lena in the ticket.)
2. The rule for computing the date is written in the ticket and covered by unit tests:
   weekends skipped, warehouse cut-off 14:00 local time.
3. An e2e test checks the field appears in the response and its format.
4. The OpenAPI description and the mobile team's contract notes are updated.
5. PR reviewed and approved; CI green.
6. Deployed to production; I called the endpoint for one real test order and the
   date was correct; the response-time dashboard shows no change.
7. Ticket comment says what shipped, in which release, and links the PR.

Why it is right: every item can be checked by another person without asking you, which is the point of a shared definition. Item 1 settles the unclear cases (digital orders) before coding, item 2 turns a business rule into tests, item 4 remembers the API's other users, and item 6 is the one juniors skip: proof that it works in production, not just on your laptop.

The trap most learners fall into is writing items that only describe activity ("write the code", "test it"). "Test it" cannot be checked; "an e2e test checks the field and its format" can. The second trap is forgetting the clients: a new response field is harmless, but if the mobile app is generated from the API description and nobody updated it, the feature does not reach users.

8.3 Reading and clarifying a ticket

8.3.1 What the ticket says, what it means, and what it forgot

Concept

A ticket is a compressed message from someone who understands a problem to someone who will solve it. It always loses information on the way. Reading a ticket well means recovering three things: what problem it solves for whom, what done looks like (the acceptance criteria), and what it does not say (edge cases, constraints, unknowns). Clarifying means asking about the third group before you write code.

Why does it exist?

The most expensive bug is building the wrong thing correctly. A developer who spends three days on a feature, then hears "that's not what I meant", has lost three days and some trust. Ten minutes of questions on day one usually prevents it. Product managers are not careless; they simply cannot imagine every question an engineer will have, and the engineer is the one who discovers the gaps.

Mental model

Imagine a builder handed a note: "Put a window in the kitchen." A good builder asks: which wall, how big, opening or fixed, and is that wall load-bearing? None of these questions is difficult. Not asking them means knocking a hole in the wrong wall.

How it works

Read every ticket in four passes:

  1. The why. Who is the user, what are they trying to do, and why now? If the ticket does not say, ask. Knowing the goal lets you suggest a cheaper way to reach it.
  2. The acceptance criteria. Concrete, testable statements of done. If they are missing, write a draft yourself and ask the author to confirm it. People find it much easier to correct a draft than to write from nothing.
  3. The gaps. Run the senior mantra from this book over it: Can it time out? Can it fail? Can it duplicate? Can it partially succeed? Who is allowed to do this? What happens to existing data?
  4. The size. Does this fit in a few days? If not, it probably needs splitting (8.4).

Notice the last step: while you wait for answers, start on the parts that are not in doubt. Clarifying does not mean stopping.

Practical example — a vague ticket, clarified

Text
SHOP-1561  Let customers cancel orders
Reporter: Lena (Product)
Customers keep emailing support to cancel orders. Add a cancel button in the app
and an API endpoint for it.

Aisha reads it in four passes and posts one comment on the ticket:

Text
Hi Lena, a few questions before I start on SHOP-1561 so I build the right thing:

1. Until when can a customer cancel? My assumption: only while status is
   'pending' or 'paid', not once it is 'packed' or 'shipped'. Is that right?
2. Refunds: if the order is paid, should cancelling also refund automatically,
   or does support refund manually? (Automatic means we call the payment provider.)
3. Partial cancellation (one item of three): in scope or a later ticket?
4. Should the customer get an email confirmation?
5. Should the warehouse be told? They read our order events, so cancelling must
   publish an "order.cancelled" event or they may pack it anyway.

Draft acceptance criteria (please correct):
- POST /orders/:id/cancel by the order's owner succeeds for pending/paid orders.
- Returns 409 with a clear message for packed/shipped/cancelled orders.
- Paid orders are refunded in full; the refund is idempotent (a retry never refunds twice).
- An "order.cancelled" event is published.
- Another customer's order returns 404 (we do not reveal that it exists).

I will start on the status rules and the endpoint now; they do not depend on 2-4.

This message is short, numbered, states assumptions so they can be confirmed with "yes", and keeps work moving. Questions 2 and 5 found real work that was not in the ticket at all: a payment provider call and an event the warehouse depends on. The last acceptance criterion is a security decision (Part 44 — Security covers why returning 404 rather than 403 avoids leaking that an order exists), and raising it now is much cheaper than in review.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors read a ticket looking for hidden system boundaries: "cancel" touches payments, the warehouse, notifications and authorisation, even though the ticket says "add a button". They ask in writing, on the ticket, so the answers outlive the chat thread. They also notice when a ticket treats a symptom ("customers email support") and ask whether the cause deserves its own ticket.

Common mistakes

  • Starting to code immediately and asking questions only when stuck.
  • Asking questions one at a time across a day of chat messages instead of one numbered list.
  • Asking open questions ("how should cancellation work?") instead of stating an assumption to confirm.
  • Treating the ticket as a contract and building exactly what it says, even when you can see it misses something important.

8.4 Breaking work down and estimating honestly

8.4.1 Splitting a ticket into steps you can finish

Concept

Breaking down means turning one ticket into a sequence of small steps, each of which can be finished, tested and ideally merged on its own. Estimating means predicting how long the work will take, honestly, including what you do not know yet.

Why does it exist?

Big, vague work hides its problems until late: a ticket that is "about a week" is often 80 percent done for two weeks. Small steps expose problems early and let you say with evidence "three of five steps are merged". Honest estimates let the team plan; optimistic ones make it plan around a fiction.

Mental model

Imagine planning a road trip. "Delhi to Jaipur, about five hours" is fine if you have driven it. If you have never driven it, the honest answer is "four to seven hours, depending on traffic at the toll plazas and whether we stop for lunch". The range is not weakness; it is information.

How it works — breaking down

Slice vertically where you can: each step delivers a thin piece that works end to end, rather than "all the database work, then all the API work". A good breakdown for SHOP-1561:

Text
SHOP-1561 Cancel orders, broken into mergeable steps
1. decideCancellation() policy + unit tests                         (no I/O, safe to merge)
2. POST /orders/:id/cancel for 'pending' orders only: owner check,
   status update in a transaction, 404/409 responses, e2e tests       (feature-flagged off)
3. Refund for 'paid' orders: payment client call with an idempotency
   key, refund recorded in the same transaction as the status change  (still flagged off)
4. Publish "order.cancelled" via the existing outbox                  (warehouse team reviews)
5. Confirmation email via the existing notifications queue
6. Enable the flag in staging, QA pass with Marco, enable in production, verify

Each line is a pull request a reviewer can read in fifteen minutes. The risky step (3, money) is isolated so it gets a careful review, and a feature flag lets half-finished work merge safely.

The diagram also shows that steps 3, 4 and 5 do not depend on each other, so in a hurry two people could share the work.

How it works — estimating

Three habits make an estimate honest:

  1. Estimate the steps, not the ticket. Small things are easier to guess. Add them up.
  2. Give a range and name what makes it wide. "Three to five days; the width is the refund step, because I have not used the payment provider's refund API yet."
  3. Say when you will know more, and come back. "After I read the provider docs this afternoon I can narrow it."

Part 62 — The Senior Engineering Mindset (62.11.4) has the senior version of this advice. The junior version adds one sentence you must be comfortable saying: "I don't know yet. I will find out by this afternoon and give you a number." Every experienced engineer respects that sentence. Nobody respects a confident "two days" that becomes eight.

Step Known? Estimate
1 Policy and tests Yes, similar code exists 0.5 day
2 Endpoint, pending only Mostly; first e2e test in this module 1 day
3 Refunds No; new API for me 1 to 2.5 days
4 Event via outbox Yes; copy an existing event 0.5 day
5 Email Yes 0.5 day
6 QA and release Depends on Marco's queue 0.5 to 1 day
Total 4 to 6 days

Failure scenario

A junior is asked in sprint planning, in front of eight people, how long a CSV export will take. Wanting to seem capable, they say "a day". It is not a day: the export must handle 2 million rows without loading them into memory (Part 13 covers streams), it needs to run as a background job because it takes minutes, and finance wants it emailed. On day four they are still working on it, embarrassed, and have not told anyone because they hope to finish "tomorrow". On day six the tech lead finds out at standup that a dependent feature cannot start. The damage was not the wrong estimate. It was the silence. Had they said on day two "this is bigger than I thought, here is why, my new range is five to seven days", the team would simply have re-planned.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors know the error bars are the useful part of an estimate. When a junior's estimate is wrong, a good senior asks "what did we not know?" rather than "why were you slow?". What they will not accept is a surprise on the due date; updating early is a skill they actively look for.

Common mistakes

  • Estimating only the coding, not testing, review, QA, deploy and verification. For small tickets those can be half the time.
  • Giving a single number under social pressure.
  • Not re-estimating when you learn the work is bigger.
  • Breaking down "horizontally" (all migrations, then all services), so nothing works until everything is done.

Practical exercise

Break down and estimate this ticket. You have used the codebase for a month but never the PDF library.

Text
SHOP-1610  Customers can download an invoice PDF for a delivered order
GET /orders/:id/invoice.pdf returns a PDF with the shop's address, the customer's
billing address, line items, tax and total. Only the order's owner may download it.

Acceptance criteria: at least four steps, each independently mergeable; a range for each step; the total as a range; and one sentence naming the biggest unknown and how you will reduce it.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
Text
SHOP-1610 breakdown
1. InvoiceData builder: pure function from order + customer to the numbers and
   lines on the invoice (tax, totals in integer cents), with unit tests.        0.5-1 day
2. Spike, time-boxed to 2 hours: render a hard-coded InvoiceData to PDF with
   the chosen library; check fonts, the rupee and euro symbols, page breaks
   for 50+ lines.                                                                0.25 day
3. PDF renderer from InvoiceData, with a snapshot test of the text content.     1-2 days
4. Endpoint: owner check (404 for others), delivered-only (409 otherwise),
   Content-Type application/pdf, Content-Disposition with a safe filename,
   e2e tests.                                                                    0.5-1 day
5. QA with Marco on real-looking orders; deploy; verify one real download.      0.5 day
Total: 2.75 to 4.75 days, so "three to five days".
Biggest unknown: the PDF library (non-Latin symbols and long orders).
I reduce it with the 2-hour spike in step 2 before committing to the rest.

Why it is right: step 1 separates the money arithmetic (easy to test, easy to get wrong) from rendering (hard to test), so the important numbers are tested without a PDF. The spike is placed early and time-boxed, so the widest uncertainty is reduced first and the estimate can be narrowed by the end of day one. The endpoint has its own step because authorisation and content headers are where security bugs hide. The total is a range with a stated reason.

The trap most learners fall into is one step called "build invoice PDF, 2 days", which hides the unknown library inside a confident number. The second trap is forgetting step 5: verification and QA are part of the work, not something that happens to it afterwards.

8.5 Asking for help well

8.5.1 When to ask, and how

Concept

Asking for help is a core engineering skill, not an admission of failure. Doing it well has two parts: timing (not so early that you learn nothing, not so late that you waste a day) and form (a question that someone can answer in two minutes without a meeting).

Why does it exist?

A junior stuck for a day on something a teammate could answer in five minutes has cost the team a day. A junior who asks about every error before reading it never learns to debug. Teams want the middle: people who try first, then ask early with a well-formed question.

How it works — the 30/60-minute rule

A widely used rule of thumb: work on a problem alone for about 30 minutes; if you have made no progress by about 60, ask. "Progress" means you learned something new about the cause, not that you tried another random change. Adjust it for the situation:

Situation When to ask
Production is down or customers are affected Immediately; say what you see in the incident channel
You might have leaked a secret or exposed data Immediately; tell your lead or security, do not try to hide or quietly fix it
You are blocked by access, permissions or missing information only a person has Immediately; there is nothing to debug
A setup or tooling problem others have certainly solved After 15 to 30 minutes
A bug in code you are learning After 30 to 60 minutes without progress
A design choice ("should this be a queue or a cron job?") After you have written down two options and their trade-offs
You are making steady progress, just slowly Keep going; mention it at standup

How it works — the shape of a good help request

Part 0 (0.4.5) teaches the minimal reproduction and the five parts of a good question. At work, a help request in chat has the same parts, compressed:

  1. Goal: what you are trying to do and why.
  2. Problem: what you expected and what happened, with the exact error as text.
  3. What you tried, and what each attempt told you.
  4. A minimal reproduction or the exact command, plus the branch or commit.
  5. Your current guess, even if it is wrong. It shows your reasoning and is often nearly right.

Practical example — a help request, before and after

Before:

Text
hey, the tests are failing on my branch, can anyone help?

Nobody can answer this without starting a conversation, so it waits until someone has time for a conversation.

After:

Text
Help please (not urgent, I'm blocked on SHOP-1561 step 2):

Goal: e2e test for POST /orders/:id/cancel.
Problem: the test fails with
  QueryFailedError: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "orders_pkey"
only when I run the whole suite (npm run test:e2e). Alone it passes.

Tried:
- Running my test alone: passes. So the code is probably fine.
- Running it after orders-history.e2e-spec.ts: fails. So it's about test order.
- Looked at the seed helper: both tests seed an order with id 'ord_test_1'.

Guess: the e2e suite does not reset the database between files, and I'm reusing
an id. Should I generate unique ids in my test, or is there a reset helper I missed?

Branch: feat/SHOP-1561-cancel, commit 8c41e2a.

Priya answers in a minute: "There's resetDb() in test/utils.ts; call it in beforeEach. Your guess was right." The question was nearly self-answering, which is normal: writing a good help request is a debugging technique in itself.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors judge a junior by the quality of their questions, not their number. A junior who asks five well-formed questions a day is learning fast and is easy to help. A junior who asks none is either a prodigy or stuck, and it is usually the second. Seniors also ask for help themselves, often and publicly, which is the best signal that asking is normal on the team.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting a whole day out of pride or fear of looking slow.
  • Asking without trying anything, so the helper does the debugging for you and you learn nothing.
  • Pasting a screenshot of an error instead of the text. Text can be searched and copied.
  • Sending sensitive data (customer emails, tokens, production rows) in a public channel while asking.

Interview questions

  1. Tell me about a time you were stuck. What did you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: a concrete story showing time-boxed independent effort, then a well-formed request for help, and what you learned. Why it matters: interviewers for junior roles are testing exactly this habit.
  2. How do you decide when to ask for help?
    Show answerHide answer
    A time box adjusted by impact: immediately for production, security or access; otherwise after a bounded effort with no new information.

Practical exercise

Rewrite this message so a busy teammate can answer it in two minutes. Invent reasonable details where needed.

Text
the payment webhook isnt working locally, i think something with the signature?

Acceptance criteria: goal, exact error, at least two things tried with what each showed, a guess, and the branch or command.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
Text
Help please (not urgent, blocking SHOP-1561 step 3):

Goal: test the refund webhook locally with the provider's CLI forwarder.
Problem: every forwarded event gets 400 from POST /webhooks/payments:
  {"code":"invalid_signature","message":"Webhook signature verification failed"}

Tried:
- Sent the same event with curl: also 400, so it's not the forwarder.
- Logged the secret our app loads: it's the value from .env.example,
  but the forwarder printed a different signing secret when it started.
- Updated PAYMENTS_WEBHOOK_SECRET to the forwarder's secret and restarted: still 400.

Guess: signature verification needs the raw request body, and our global JSON
body parser gives the controller the parsed object, so the bytes differ. Is
there a raw-body setting for this route I should use?

Branch: feat/SHOP-1561-refunds, run with: npm run start:dev, then the forwarder.

Why it is right: the goal and the exact error are at the top, each attempt says what it ruled out (the forwarder, then the secret), and the guess is specific enough for a colleague to answer "yes, see rawBody: true in main.ts" in one line. NestJS does support this: creating the app with NestFactory.create(AppModule, { rawBody: true }) makes the raw body available on the request for signature checks.

The trap most learners fall into is listing attempts without what each one taught you ("I tried restarting, I tried changing the secret"). The lesson of each attempt is what lets the helper skip straight to the remaining possibilities. The second trap is pasting the real webhook secret into the message; describe it, never paste it.

8.6 The pull request as a conversation

8.6.1 Small, described, self-reviewed

Concept

Part 5 — Git Basics and the Development Workflow taught the mechanics of a pull request (5.3) and of answering review feedback (5.10). This section is about the human side. A pull request is a conversation with your teammates about a proposed change. Your job as the author is to make that conversation short and useful: a small change, a description that explains it, and a self-review that catches the obvious problems before anyone else has to.

Why does it exist?

Reviewers are busy engineers with their own tickets. A pull request that is easy to understand gets reviewed quickly and carefully. One that is large, undescribed and full of leftover debug lines gets reviewed late, superficially, or with a long list of small comments that make everyone tired. Part 52 — Git from Intermediate to Senior (52.13) explains why review quality drops sharply as a diff grows; for a junior the practical rule is simple: aim for pull requests a reviewer can read in 15 minutes, usually under about 300 changed lines excluding generated files.

How it works — the review loop

Self-review first. Before requesting review, open your own pull request in the browser and read the diff as if a stranger wrote it. You will find things you never see in your editor. A short self-review checklist:

  • Every changed file belongs to this ticket; no stray formatting or "while I was here" edits
  • No debug output (console.log('here')), commented-out code or leftover TODOs without a ticket
  • No secrets, tokens or real customer data in code, tests or fixtures
  • Tests cover the acceptance criteria and at least one failure path
  • Names say what things are; a reader understands each function without the ticket open
  • New failure paths are logged with enough context to debug them (Part 47 — Observability: Logs, Metrics and Traces)
  • The migration, if any, is safe to run while the old code is still serving (Part 27)
  • CI is green before you ask anyone to look

Describe it. A good description answers what changed, why, how you tested it, and what is risky. Many teams have a template; fill every section honestly.

Practical example — a pull request description

Markdown
## SHOP-1561 step 2: cancel endpoint for pending orders (behind flag)

### What and why
Adds POST /orders/:id/cancel so customers can cancel orders that are still
'pending'. Paid-order refunds come in the next PR (step 3). The route is behind
the `order-cancellation` flag, off everywhere, so this is safe to merge.

### How it works
- `decideCancellation()` (merged in step 1) decides whether the status allows it.
- The status update runs in a transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the
  order row, so a cancel and a concurrent "mark as packed" cannot both win.
- Not the owner -> 404 (we do not reveal that the order exists).
  Status not cancellable -> 409 with `code: "order_not_cancellable"`.

### How I tested it
- Unit tests for the controller's error mapping.
- e2e: owner cancels pending order (200), other customer (404), packed order (409),
  cancelling twice (409 the second time).
- Manually with curl against local Docker, flag on.

### Risk
Low: flag off. The row lock is held only for one UPDATE (a few ms).

### Out of scope
Refunds (step 3), event (step 4), email (step 5).

The reviewer knows what to look at (the lock and the error mapping), what not to worry about (refunds), and why it is safe to merge. That description took ten minutes and will probably save the reviewer twenty.

8.6.2 Responding to review without defensiveness

Concept

Review comments are about the code, not about you. Responding well means: understand each comment, fix what is right, discuss what you disagree with using reasons, answer every comment, and never take it personally. That last part is the hardest at first and becomes easy with practice.

Why does it exist?

Review is the main way a team shares knowledge and catches defects before customers do. A junior who argues with every comment, or silently ignores some, makes review expensive, and people start reviewing their work less carefully. A junior who responds well becomes someone everyone is happy to review, and learns at twice the speed.

How it works

Sort each comment into one of four kinds and respond accordingly:

Comment kind Example Good response
Correct and blocking "This reads the order before taking the lock; two cancels can race." Fix it, push, reply "Good catch, fixed in a41c9e2, added a test for two concurrent cancels."
A question "Why 404 rather than 403 here?" Answer it, and if the answer is not obvious from the code, add a comment in the code too.
A preference or nit "nit: I'd call this cancellable rather than canCancel." Apply it if it is cheap; otherwise "Happy either way, I'll leave it unless you feel strongly."
You disagree "Put this logic in the controller." Explain once, with a reason: "I kept it in the service so the queue consumer can reuse it. Happy to move it if you see a problem with that."

If a discussion goes back and forth more than twice in comments, stop typing and suggest a five-minute call. Then write the outcome in the pull request so the reasoning is recorded.

Failure scenario

A new developer receives twelve comments on their first real feature. Feeling criticised, they reply to the three they agree with, push fixes for those, and re-request review without mentioning the other nine. The reviewer has to re-read everything to find what changed and what was ignored, finds that a blocking comment about a missing transaction was skipped, and writes a terse "please address all comments". Now both sides are irritated, and the pull request takes four more days. The same twelve comments, answered one by one ("done", "done", "question: do you mean X?", "I disagree because Y"), would have merged the next morning.

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors get many review comments too; they simply do not experience them as judgement. They thank reviewers for catches, change their mind easily when shown a good reason, and hold their ground politely when they have one. When they review a junior's code they label severity (blocking:, nit:, question:), explain the why, and praise what is good, because they remember their own first reviews. If your reviewers do not label severity, ask: "Which of these are blocking for you?" That is a perfectly normal question.

Common mistakes

  • Opening a 1,500-line pull request "because it's all one feature". Split it (8.4).
  • Replying "fixed" without pushing the fix, or pushing without replying.
  • Force-pushing a rewritten branch during review, so the reviewer loses track of what changed (5.10).
  • Merging over an unresolved blocking comment because "it's approved".

Interview questions

  1. A reviewer leaves a comment you think is wrong. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Make sure you understood it, then reply once with your reasoning and an offer to change it; if it continues, talk in person and record the outcome. Follow-up: and if the reviewer is senior to you? The same, respectfully; seniority does not make a comment correct, but it should make you check your reasoning twice.
  2. How big should a pull request be?
    Show answerHide answer
    Small enough to review carefully in about 15 minutes; split large changes into a sequence, using feature flags so incomplete work can merge safely.

Practical exercise

You receive these three comments on your invoice PDF pull request (SHOP-1610). Write your reply to each.

Text
1. Priya (blocking): The filename comes from the customer's name. A name with
   quotes or newlines will break the Content-Disposition header.
2. Omar: Why not generate PDFs in a background job and email them?
3. Priya (nit): `buildInvoiceData` could be `toInvoiceData`.

Acceptance criteria: each reply matches the comment's kind, the blocking one is fixed with evidence, and the design question gets a reasoned answer rather than a "no".

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
Text
1. Good catch, thank you. The filename is now built only from the order number
   (`invoice-ORD-000123.pdf`), which matches ^[A-Za-z0-9-]+$, so no customer input
   reaches the header. Added a test with a name containing quotes and a newline.
   Fixed in 7d2e0b1.

2. Good question. I considered it. Rendering takes about 80 ms for a typical
   order and the largest test order (60 lines) took about 300 ms, so doing it in
   the request is fine for now and gives customers the file immediately. If
   invoices get much bigger, or we add bulk download for finance, a job plus
   email would be the right move; I've noted it on the ticket. Does that
   reasoning work for you?

3. Agreed, renamed in 7d2e0b1.

Why it is right: the blocking comment is fixed at the root (no customer input in the header at all, rather than trying to escape it) and backed by a test and a commit reference, so Priya can verify in seconds. The design question is answered with numbers, an acknowledgement of when the other option becomes better, and an open question back, which turns a possible argument into a shared decision. The nit costs nothing, so it is simply applied.

The trap most learners fall into is answering the design question defensively ("the ticket didn't ask for a background job"), which is true and unhelpful. The second trap is fixing the header bug by escaping quotes only: newlines and other control characters remain, and a hand-written escaper is easy to get wrong. Removing user input from the header is the stronger fix.

8.7 Standups and written updates

8.7.1 Saying where you are, briefly and honestly

Concept

A standup is a short daily meeting, often 15 minutes, where each person says what they did, what they will do, and what is blocking them. Many teams also do it in writing, in a chat channel. A written update is the same idea for longer work: a few lines on a ticket or in a channel that let people know the state of things without asking you.

Why does it exist?

Its purpose is coordination, not reporting to a manager. It lets the team notice blockers early, avoid two people doing the same thing, and see who needs help. The most valuable part is the blocker: a blocker said at 10:00 can be cleared by 10:15; the same blocker kept quiet costs a day.

How it works

Three lines, each concrete, each tied to a ticket:

  1. Yesterday: what moved, as outcomes ("step 2 PR is in review"), not activity ("worked on cancellation").
  2. Today: what you expect to finish.
  3. Blockers or risks: anything that is slowing you down, including "this is bigger than I estimated".

Keep it under a minute when spoken. Long technical discussions belong after the standup with the two or three people who need them ("Priya, can we take five minutes after this about the refund API?").

Practical example — a weak update and a strong one

Weak:

Text
Yesterday I worked on the cancel stuff. Today more cancel stuff. No blockers.

Strong:

Text
SHOP-1561 cancel orders
- Done: step 2 (cancel endpoint, pending orders) is in review, CI green.
- Today: step 3, refunds. Reading the provider's refund API docs this morning.
- Risk: my estimate for step 3 was 1 to 2.5 days; I'll know which end by noon
  and update the ticket. Priya, could you review step 2 today so it doesn't
  conflict with step 3?

The strong version takes 25 seconds to say, gives the tech lead everything she needs for planning, raises the estimate risk early, and makes a specific request of a specific person.

Written updates for longer work

For anything that runs longer than a couple of days, leave a short written update on the ticket every day or two. It means nobody has to interrupt you to ask, and if you are ill tomorrow, someone can pick it up.

Text
Update on SHOP-1561 (Thu)
Status: steps 1-2 merged, step 3 (refunds) in progress, on track for Tuesday.
Learned: the provider's refund call is asynchronous; the final result arrives by
webhook. Step 3 now includes handling the refund webhook. Estimate unchanged
because step 4 turned out smaller than planned.
Next: refund webhook handler with idempotency, then step 4.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting activity ("I was in meetings, looked at some code") instead of outcomes.
  • Saying "no blockers" every day while quietly stuck.
  • Turning standup into a debugging session that keeps eight people waiting.
  • Only giving updates when asked.

8.8 Working with QA, product and design

8.8.1 The people around the code

Concept

A backend developer rarely works only with other backend developers. Product managers decide what to build and why. Designers decide how it looks and behaves for the user. QA engineers (quality assurance, sometimes called testers or SDETs) check that it works, especially in the cases nobody thought of. Frontend and mobile developers consume your API. Learning to work well with each of them is as important as learning PostgreSQL.

Why does it exist?

Each role holds information you do not have. Product knows the customer and the business; design knows how users actually behave on a screen; QA knows how the system breaks; frontend knows what the API is like to use. A backend built without their input is technically correct and practically wrong.

How it works

With product. Ask about the problem and the user, not just the feature. Offer options with costs: "Automatic refunds are about three extra days; a 'request cancellation' button that support handles is half a day. Which do you want first?" Product managers love an engineer who gives choices instead of a flat "yes" or "no". Part 62 (62.11.2) shows how seniors explain trade-offs to a product manager; start practising now.

With design. Look at designs early and ask about states the screen will need from you: loading, empty, error, partial results, very long names. If the design shows "Cancelled on 3 Nov by Aisha", the API must return who cancelled and when. Finding that in the design review costs a sentence; finding it after the endpoint ships costs a migration.

With QA. Tell QA what changed, how to turn it on, and what you are worried about. Share test data and the exact flag. When QA reports a bug, treat it as a gift: thank them, reproduce it, and fix it, or explain clearly if it is expected behaviour, then update the ticket so the expectation is written down. Never argue "works on my machine"; their environment is closer to production than your laptop.

With frontend and mobile. Agree on the API contract before building it: the request and response shapes, the error format and codes (6.6), pagination. Part 80 — Frontend–Backend Contracts covers this in depth. A mobile app cannot be updated instantly on every phone, so a response field you rename can break users for months (Part 28 — Backward Compatibility: APIs, Schemas, Events and Clients).

Practical example — handing a feature to QA

Text
@Marco SHOP-1561 is ready for QA on staging (flag `order-cancellation` is ON there).

What changed: customers can cancel pending and paid orders; paid orders are
refunded automatically (provider sandbox).
How to test: test customers cus_qa_1 to cus_qa_5 each have one pending and one
paid order. Cancel from the app's order screen or POST /orders/:id/cancel.
Expected: cancelled orders show status "cancelled"; paid ones show a refund
within about a minute (refund webhook).
What I'm most unsure about:
  1. Double-tapping Cancel quickly (should refund once).
  2. Cancelling at the moment the warehouse marks the order packed.
Known limitation: partial cancellation is out of scope (SHOP-1588).

Pointing QA at the risky areas is not asking them to do your job. It is using their skill where it matters most. Marco will test those two cases and many you did not think of.

Failure scenario

A backend developer changes an error response from { "error": "Out of stock" } to the team's new standard { "code": "out_of_stock", "message": "..." }. It is cleaner, it passes the backend tests, and it ships. The mobile app, which showed error to the user, now shows an empty red box on every out-of-stock checkout. Older app versions on customers' phones cannot be fixed by a deploy; the backend has to add the old field back alongside the new one for months. A two-minute message to the mobile team ("I'm changing the error shape on /checkout, does anything read error?") would have prevented it.

Common mistakes

  • Treating QA as an opponent and bugs as accusations.
  • Changing an API response without telling its consumers.
  • Saying "that's not in the ticket" instead of "that's a good point; should it be in this ticket or a new one?"
  • Accepting a deadline you know is unrealistic, instead of offering a smaller scope that fits.

Interview questions

  1. QA reports a bug you cannot reproduce. What do you do?
    Show answerHide answer
    Ask for exact steps, data, environment and time; check logs for that request (a request id helps, 6.6); compare their environment to yours; never close it as "works for me" without finding the difference.
  2. A product manager asks for a feature by Friday that you think needs two weeks. How do you respond?
    Show answerHide answer
    Explain what drives the estimate, then offer options: a smaller version by Friday, the full version in two weeks, or what could be dropped. Let them choose with the trade-off visible.

8.9 Your first production bug and your first on-call shift

8.9.1 When something you shipped breaks

Concept

Sooner or later something you shipped will break in production. This is not a sign you are bad at the job; it happens to everyone who ships. What matters is the response: say so quickly, help stop the damage, fix it properly, and help the team learn so the same class of bug cannot happen again. On-call is the rota of engineers who respond to production alerts outside normal hours. Most teams add juniors to it gradually, first as a shadow alongside an experienced engineer.

Why does it exist?

Production problems get worse with time: more failed orders, more angry customers, more data to repair. The engineer who says "I think my deploy at 14:10 caused this" within minutes saves the team an hour of searching. The one who stays quiet hoping to fix it alone turns a 10-minute incident into a 2-hour one.

Mental model

Imagine a kitchen fire. You do not first work out who left the pan on. You shout "fire", turn off the gas and use the extinguisher. Only when it is out do you ask why the pan was left on, and the useful answer is usually "the timer was broken", not "Aisha is careless".

How it works — the first response

  1. Acknowledge the alert so others know someone is on it, and post in the incident channel.
  2. Assess impact from the dashboards: error rate, latency, which endpoints, since when.
  3. Mitigate first, diagnose later. If a recent deploy or flag change lines up with the start of the problem, rolling it back is usually the fastest fix. Understanding can wait until customers are safe. Part 62 (62.10.1) calls this "mitigate first".
  4. Follow the runbook. A runbook is a written guide for a specific alert: what it means, what to check, what to do. Part 53 — Site Reliability Engineering (53.9) shows a complete one.
  5. Escalate early. Escalation means paging the next person on the list. A junior should escalate after about 15 minutes without clear progress, or immediately if money, data or security is involved. Escalating is not failing; it is the system working as designed.
  6. Keep a timeline as you go: times, what you saw, what you did. It becomes the backbone of the postmortem.

Practical example — Aisha's first production bug

At 14:10 Aisha's refund step (SHOP-1561 step 3) is enabled in production. At 14:32 Marco notices in the support channel that two customers say their cancelled orders were refunded twice. Aisha's message, at 14:34:

Text
I think this is my change. Order cancellation with refunds went live at 14:10
(flag order-cancellation). Two reports of double refunds. I'm turning the flag
OFF now, then checking how many orders are affected. @Priya can you join?

By 14:36 the flag is off and new cancellations stop. Priya and Aisha find the cause in the logs: the mobile app retries a cancel request after 3 seconds if it has no response, and the refund call to the provider sometimes takes 4. Each retry started a new refund because the idempotency key was generated per request instead of per order cancellation. Eleven orders were refunded twice; finance recovers them with the provider's help. The fix (an idempotency key derived from the order id, plus a unique constraint on refunds (order_id) so the database itself refuses a second refund) ships the next day, with a test that sends two concurrent cancels. Part 33 explains idempotency keys in depth.

How it works — the blameless postmortem

A postmortem is a short document written after an incident: what happened, the impact, the timeline, the causes, and the actions that will prevent it from happening again. Blameless means it asks why the system allowed the mistake and why the action seemed reasonable at the time, not who to blame. Part 53 (53.10) gives the full template and a worked example; for your first one, know the shape:

Text
Postmortem: double refunds on order cancellation (2026-11-20)
Impact: 11 orders refunded twice, all recovered with the provider; 26 minutes.
Timeline: 14:10 flag on; 14:32 first report; 14:34 owner identified it; 14:36 flag off.
What happened: client retries after 3 s; refund call can take 4 s; each request
  generated its own idempotency key, so the provider treated retries as new refunds.
Why it was possible: no database constraint on one refund per order; no test for
  concurrent cancels; no alert on refunds per order > 1.
Actions: idempotency key per order (done); unique constraint (done); concurrent
  test (done); alert on duplicate refunds (SHOP-1640, owner Aisha).

Notice what is not in it: "Aisha should have been more careful". Being careful is not a fix. A unique constraint is.

Common mistakes

  • Hiding or delaying "I think it was my change".
  • Debugging the root cause while customers are still failing, instead of rolling back first.
  • Running ad-hoc write queries in production to "fix data" without a second person checking them.
  • Treating the postmortem as punishment and making it vague.

Interview questions

  1. Tell me about a production issue you caused or helped fix.
    Show answerHide answer
    Expected answer: a specific story told in order: what you noticed, how you communicated, how it was mitigated, the root cause, and the systemic fix. Why it matters: it shows ownership without defensiveness.
  2. What is a blameless postmortem, and why do teams use them?
    Show answerHide answer
    A written analysis that focuses on what in the system allowed the failure; blame makes people hide information, which leads to more incidents.
  3. During an incident, why roll back before understanding the cause?
    Show answerHide answer
    Customers are harmed while you investigate; rollback is usually fast and reversible, and you can debug safely afterwards.

Practical exercise

You are shadowing on-call. At 10:05 an alert fires: "orders-service 5xx rate 8 percent (normal under 0.5 percent) for 5 minutes". The deploy log shows a release of orders-service at 09:58 that included your teammate's change to the order search query. Write your first message in the incident channel and list your next three actions in order.

Acceptance criteria: the message states what you see, the possible link to a change, what you are doing, and who you are pulling in; the actions put mitigation before diagnosis.

Worked answer to the exercise

Show worked answerHide worked answer
Text
Looking at the orders-service 5xx alert (8%, started ~10:00).
Possible link: release at 09:58 included the order search query change (PR #2214).
I'm checking which endpoints are failing now. @primary-oncall @Omar (PR author)
can you join? Proposal: if the errors are on /orders/search, roll back to the
previous release.
Text
Next actions:
1. Dashboard: confirm which endpoints return 5xx and that the start time matches
   the 09:58 release. (2 minutes)
2. If it matches: with the primary's OK, roll back to the previous release,
   then watch the error rate return to normal. (mitigation)
3. Collect evidence for diagnosis without touching production: the error message
   and stack trace from the logs for one failing request id, and the query plan
   if it is a timeout. Add everything to the incident timeline.

Why it is right: the message is short, factual and hedged ("possible link"), so nobody chases a guess as a certainty, and it pulls in exactly the two people who can help: the primary on-call, who has authority to roll back, and the author, who knows the change. The actions confirm the correlation first, then mitigate, then gather evidence. Diagnosis waits until customers are no longer failing.

The trap most learners fall into is starting with "let me read PR #2214 to understand the bug" while 8 percent of requests fail. The second trap is rolling back alone as a shadow without telling anyone; in most teams the primary on-call or incident lead makes that call, and two people acting independently during an incident make it worse.

8.10 Learning on the job

8.10.1 Notes, a brag document and deliberate learning

Concept

You will learn more in your first year at work than in any course, but only if you capture it. Two simple tools do most of the work: working notes (what you learned, how things work here, commands you needed) and a brag document (a running list of what you shipped and what impact it had). The brag document idea was popularised by Julia Evans' essay on the subject.

Why does it exist?

Memory is unreliable and busy weeks blur together. Notes stop you asking the same question twice and become a personal manual for the codebase. The brag document solves a different problem: at review time, nobody, including you, remembers what you did in March. A list written as you go makes your progress visible to your manager and to you, which matters most on the weeks you feel slow.

How it works

Working notes, in any tool you like, organised by topic, not by date:

Text
orders-service / how things work
- Refunds are asynchronous: result arrives by webhook (/webhooks/payments).
- Never call PaymentsClient directly from a controller; go through RefundsService
  (it adds the idempotency key).
- e2e tests: call resetDb() in beforeEach; ids are reused across files.
- Feature flags: config/flags.ts; staging toggles in the admin UI; prod needs Priya.
commands
- psql against the staging read replica: see the 1Password entry "staging-replica"
- npm run test:e2e -- orders-history   # one file only

Brag document, a short entry per month or per meaningful piece of work:

Text
November
- Shipped order cancellation (SHOP-1561, 6 PRs). Support tickets about
  cancellations dropped from about 40/week to about 5/week in the first fortnight.
- Caused and helped fix the double-refund incident; wrote the postmortem;
  added the unique constraint and the duplicate-refund alert.
- Fixed two setup steps in the README; Jonas (joined 12 Nov) set up in half a day.
Learned: transactions with SELECT FOR UPDATE, idempotency keys, the outbox pattern.

Note that the incident is in the brag document. Owning and fixing a failure well is an achievement worth recording.

Deliberate learning. Pick one area per month that your work touches, and go one level deeper than the ticket needed. The refund work touched transactions, so read Part 24 — Database Transactions and Concurrency Control. The PDF ticket touched streams, so read the streams chapter of Part 13. Learning what your work already touches sticks, because you use it the next day.

8.11 Using AI tools responsibly at work

8.11.1 Helpful, plausible, and your responsibility

Concept

AI coding assistants are now normal at work: completion in the editor, chat for explanations, and agents that edit files and run commands. They can make a junior much faster. They can also produce confident, plausible, wrong code. Part 57 — AI-Assisted Engineering covers them in depth; this section gives the rules that matter in your first job.

How it works — five rules

  1. Follow your company's AI policy. Use only approved tools. Ask if you are not sure; many companies restrict which tools may see their code.
  2. Never paste secrets, customer data or production logs with personal data into a prompt (57.2.2). A pasted .env file means rotating every secret in it.
  3. You own every line you commit, whoever or whatever wrote it. "The AI wrote it" is not an answer in review or in a postmortem.
  4. Understand before you commit. If you cannot explain a line to your reviewer, you cannot ship it. Ask the assistant to explain it, then check the explanation against the documentation.
  5. Verify by running. Run the code, run the tests, and check that every package and API it uses actually exists (57.7 tells the story of a hallucinated package).

How a Senior Backend Engineer thinks about this

Seniors use AI tools heavily for work they understand well, and carefully for work they do not. Their worry about juniors is skipped learning: if an assistant writes all your transaction code, you never learn transactions, and at 2 a.m. in an incident you cannot fix them. Use it as a tutor and a pair (57.2.1): ask it to explain, to review your attempt, to suggest test cases. Write the core logic yourself while you are learning it.

8.12 Growing towards mid-level

8.12.1 From "a task" to "a feature"

Concept

Part 63 — Junior to Principal: What Is Expected at Each Level defines the jump from junior to mid-level mostly as a change in scope and ambiguity: a junior completes well-defined tasks, often told how; a mid-level engineer owns a feature, is told what to build, and decides how. The growth happens through behaviours you can practise from your first month.

How it works

You are growing when you... Instead of...
Clarify the ticket and suggest a better approach Building exactly what was written
Break your own work into steps and estimate it in ranges Waiting to be given sub-tasks
Ask fewer but better questions, and answer newer joiners' Asking the same type of question repeatedly
Find and fix the class of bug (constraint, test, alert) Fixing only the instance
Review teammates' pull requests with real comments Only receiving reviews
Notice operational concerns: logs, metrics, migrations, rollbacks Stopping at "the tests pass"
Deliver a multi-step feature end to end, with updates Delivering single tickets

Ask your manager directly: "What would I need to show to be considered mid-level here?" Write the answer down and review it with them every few months. Part 63 (63.3) describes the next jump, mid to senior; read it now to see where the road leads.

8.13 Common junior mistakes

Every item below has appeared earlier in this Part; here they are in one list to re-read after your first month, and again after your third.

  • Staying silent when stuck for hours or days, instead of asking with a well-formed question after a time box (8.5).
  • Coding before clarifying, then building the wrong thing (8.3).
  • Single-number estimates given under pressure, and no update when the work grows (8.4).
  • Huge pull requests that cannot be reviewed well (8.6).
  • Taking review personally, or leaving comments unanswered (8.6.2).
  • "Done" at merge instead of verified in production (8.2.2).
  • Hiding a mistake, especially in production; saying "I think it was my change" early is always right (8.9).
  • Changing API responses without telling their consumers (8.8).
  • Committing code you cannot explain, from an AI tool or from a copied answer (8.11).
  • Pasting secrets or customer data into chat, tickets or prompts.
  • Rewriting code you do not yet understand because it looks wrong; ask why first (8.1).
  • Not writing anything down, so learning leaks away (8.10).

Senior Checklist — Part 8

  • I understand the concept
  • I can explain it simply
  • I can implement it
  • I understand its failure modes
  • I understand its scaling limitations
  • I understand its security implications
  • I understand its operational implications
  • I can choose between alternatives
  • I can explain the tradeoffs
  • I can answer senior-level interview questions
  • I can set up an unfamiliar service locally, trace one request through it, and fix the README on the way
  • I read a ticket for the goal, acceptance criteria and gaps, and ask my questions in one numbered message
  • I break work into mergeable steps and estimate in ranges, naming the biggest unknown
  • I know when to ask for help, and my help requests include the goal, the exact error, what I tried and a guess
  • I self-review, describe my pull requests, and answer every review comment without defensiveness
  • My standup updates are outcomes, plans and blockers, tied to tickets
  • I tell QA, product, design and API consumers what changes and what I am unsure about
  • In an incident I communicate early, mitigate before diagnosing, escalate on time and write blameless postmortems
  • I keep working notes and a brag document, and I use AI tools within policy and only for code I can explain

Part 8 — Key Takeaways

  • Your first week's job is access, a running local setup and a rough map; your setup notes are a gift to the next joiner.
  • "Done" means verified where customers are, not merged.
  • Ten minutes of written questions before coding beats three days building the wrong thing.
  • Estimates are ranges with a named reason; "I don't know yet, I'll find out by this afternoon" is a professional answer.
  • Try for about 30 minutes, ask by about 60, and ask immediately for production, security or access problems.
  • A good help request (goal, exact error, what you tried, a guess) often answers itself.
  • Small, described, self-reviewed pull requests get fast, careful reviews; every comment deserves a reply.
  • Standups are for blockers and coordination; say the risk early, not on the due date.
  • QA, product, design and API consumers hold information you lack; involve them early.
  • In production, say "I think it was my change" fast, roll back first, and fix the class of bug, not just the instance.
  • You own every line you commit, including the ones an AI tool wrote.
  • Mid-level is a change of scope, from a task to a feature, and you can practise its behaviours from month one.
